item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] Nvidia added $453 billion in a day
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The stock was up 8.5 percent, Raymond James went to $515 from $352, and Marvell plus energy buying filled out the rest of the tape.
item.content:encoded:
The stock was up 8.5 percent, Raymond James went to $515 from $352, and Marvell plus energy buying filled out the rest of the tape.

Thursday was the print. Friday is the reaction. $NVDA added roughly $453 billion in market cap in a single day, the largest one-day market-cap gain ever recorded in the U.S., and the stock was up 8.5 percent.

Market context. Per the Stocks recap, Nvidia was the most-active options name at 7.4 million contracts, ahead of $TSLA at 1.6 million and $AAPL at 875,000. Software tore. The rest of the session had to digest a hawkish Warsh speech on the same stamp.

The named tape is Nvidia's day, Marvell's guide, IREN's AI-cloud print, and hedge funds overweight energy by the most since June 2024.

The scoreboard.

  • House Nvidia $192 200-day queue, due tomorrow. Today's sources do not reprint $192. They do print a $453 billion one-day add. The bearish queue is still on the book until Saturday.
  • Walmart comps thesis, due Monday. No new consumer print today.

1. The Street had to reprice Nvidia in one session. Same recap: Raymond James raised its price target to $515 from $352 and reiterated Strong Buy, citing fiscal 2028 revenue growth of approximately 70 percent and saying $1 trillion in annual sales by fiscal 2029 now looks possible. RealSimpleAriel had King $NVDA up 8.5 percent on an extraordinary report.

DeskPrice target
Raymond James$352 to $515
JPMorgan$280 to $320
Mizuho$300 to $315
Melius$400 to $425
Goldman Sachs$285 to $300
Bernstein$315 to $400
Citi$300 to $315
Stifel$282 to $315

I am not reopening Wednesday night's revenue print. The new fact is the one-day add and this wall of targets. $515 is the map. The $352 start tells you how far behind the desk was.

2. Marvell printed, and the guide did the work. $MRVL Q2 fiscal 2027 revenue $2.7 billion against $2.71 billion expected, up 37 percent year over year. Adjusted EPS $0.94 versus $0.92, up 40 percent. Data center $2.2 billion, up 46 percent.

Q3 guide $3.15 billion plus or minus 5 percent against $3.03 billion expected. Adjusted EPS $1.10 plus or minus $0.05 against $1.07. Full-year fiscal 2027 revenue roughly 45 percent year over year to about $12 billion. Fiscal 2028 roughly $18 billion, about 50 percent year over year.

BofA initiated coverage on $AMKR at Buy, price target $70. Advanced Products were 82 percent of Q2 fiscal 2026 revenue, with an expected $1.5 billion Nvidia prepayment in 2027. EPS $1.51 in 2025 to $3.41 in 2028, a 31 percent CAGR, and the $70 target sits on 21 times 2028 earnings. Packaging riding the same buildout.

3. Hedge funds are the most overweight energy since June 2024. Same recap: they bought the most global energy stocks in nearly 4 years last week, the 12th weekly purchase over the last 13 weeks. They are now the most overweight energy relative to global stocks since June 2024. That reverses February 2026, when they were the most underweight energy since 2021.

The only stretch with materially higher energy exposure was the 2022 energy bull market. This is the non-AI bid on a day Nvidia ate the headline. $TE is the named energy equity in that recap, on a Giga Arctic Norway story with no hard print.

4. Corporate profits hit a record $4.8 trillion. U.S. corporate profits surged 22.8 percent year over year in Q2 2026 to a record $4.8 trillion, the largest annual increase since Q4 2021. Excluding the pandemic recovery and the post-2008 rebound, that is the strongest year-over-year profit growth in 21 years. Since Q2 2020, profits have climbed $2.7 trillion, or 131 percent. As a share of GDP they jumped 1.0 percentage point in Q2 to 14.9 percent, an all-time high.

Earnings breadth lived here. Nvidia was the headline.

5. IREN's print is the AI-cloud conversion, with a miss on the old P&L. $IREN Q4 fiscal 2026 revenue $137.2 million, adjusted EBITDA $19.2 million versus $41.1 million expected. AI cloud Q4 $70.5 million from $33.6 million. Fiscal 2026 AI cloud $128.8 million, roughly 8 times year over year. Full-year revenue $707.0 million versus $740 million. Net loss $702.6 million, including $638.8 million of impairments.

The pipeline is the story they want you to take:

  • Operating ARR (annualized recurring revenue) $1 billion
  • Contracted ARR for 2026 capacity $4 billion
  • $2.8 billion of new GPU financing
  • $14 billion of cash and committed financing
  • Recent 3-year contract pricing up 125 percent
  • Talks around $25 million of revenue per IT megawatt

Thursday was Microsoft accepting Horizon 1. Friday is the quarter. EBITDA missed. The AI-cloud line is the one that grew.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $NVDA. $453 billion in a day, up 8.5 percent, Raymond James $515 from $352. Largest U.S. one-day market-cap gain on record. 7.4 million options contracts.
  • $MRVL. $2.7 billion, data center $2.2 billion up 46 percent, Q3 $3.15 billion plus or minus 5 percent, fiscal 2028 about $18 billion.
  • $IREN. AI cloud $70.5 million in the quarter, $128.8 million for the year, contracted ARR $4 billion. EBITDA miss against a conversion story.
  • $TE. Named energy equity next to the hedge-fund overweight. Giga Arctic in Norway. No hard print. The sector bid is the fact.
  • $RKLB. Grouped with $NBIS, $CIFR, $ONDS, and $ASTS as long-duration names that live and die on the front end. Warsh just made the front end more expensive.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] Bitcoin held $80,000 through Warsh
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Spot Bitcoin ETFs took more than $3 billion over eight days, ether ETFs more than $1.2 billion over twelve, and Glassnode still sees a wall at $81,000 to $86,000.
item.content:encoded:
Spot Bitcoin ETFs took more than $3 billion over eight days, ether ETFs more than $1.2 billion over twelve, and Glassnode still sees a wall at $81,000 to $86,000.

$BTC went into Warsh toward $80,000 and came out still there. Yesterday this desk had Cowen testing the 50-week and Gillen waiting on an $83,000 weekly close. The speech did not knock the bid out.

Market context. Per aixbt, hike odds rose from 35 percent to 46 percent, the two-year yield gained 6.6 basis points, and the dollar added 0.4 percent. Both coins erased the first dip. The BTC index sat 0.34 percent above $80,000 into Deribit expiry.

Macro owns the hike. This desk owns the fact that $80,000 held it. Per 0xResearch, Bitcoin is up 10.0 percent on the week against gold 1.8 percent and the Nasdaq 100 0.9 percent.

The scoreboard.

  • Ether squeeze thesis from August 20, due Monday: Tom Lee's show has ether running from around $1,900 to nearly $2,600 on the liquidation bounce. The alt side of that squeeze did lead. Hits.
  • Gillen's weekly close above $83,000 on Bitcoin and $2,500 on ether is still open. $80,000 through the speech is not that close.

1. $80,000 held a hawkish speech. Per Cowen, the pre-speech tape was Bitcoin rallies to $80,000. aixbt had the index a fraction above it into expiry. That is the position.

Hike odds went up and the first dip died. I am not re-arguing Warsh. I am telling you the coin that was supposed to flinch did not.

2. ETFs kept buying, and the wall is still $81,000 to $86,000. 0xResearch: Bitcoin ETF flows last week totaled over $3 billion, the first time Bitcoin has had eight consecutive days of net inflows since April 2026. Ether ETFs took over $1.2 billion, the 12th day of consecutive inflows, the first time in nearly one year, not since July 2025. Also last week: $SOL $115 million, $XRP $92 million, $HYPE $50 million.

Per Glassnode, via Scott Melker, $BTC faces a supply wall at $81,000 to $86,000 where long-term-holder breakevens, self-custody cost basis, options hedging, and short-liquidation levels stack up. Thursday Bacon tagged $81,000 and wanted the weekly close on top of it. Gillen still wants a weekly close above $83,000.

The wall is the next tape. The weekly close is not in.

3. Agents are paying onchain again, and $COIN is sitting on the float. Per Milk Road, x402 (Coinbase's machine-to-machine payments standard) saw 8.7 million weekly payments, up from 4.1 million the week before. That roughly doubled. November 2025 peaked at 20.1 million, then the count had fallen more than 95 percent to under 1 million a week by March.

AWS Bedrock AgentCore went live for every AWS customer on August 18. Ramp turned it on for 70,000-plus business customers on August 20.

ChainShare of last week's x402 payments
Base48%, from 93%
Solana38%, from 6%
Other14%

Coinbase last quarter brought in $292 million from that business, with a record $20 billion of USDC sitting inside Coinbase products, over 30 percent of every USDC in existence. That is the proxy. SOL was about $105 in the letter. Vincent's entry was $82.56.

4. The SEC put dollar caps on a new ICO path. September 15 is still a rumor. Same 0xResearch letter. Three pathways that did not exist before:

  • Subpart B: up to $5 million over four years on a Form NOR, no financial statements
  • Subpart C: Regulation A for crypto, up to $20 million per 12 months, or $75 million with audited financials and a 10 percent income or net-worth cap on non-accredited buyers
  • Subpart D: Form TR off-ramp

That is a framework, and it is the first forward-looking token-issuance map in this window. A Senate Clarity date of September 15 is circulating. Treat it as rumor. Do not harden it.

Tom Lee, on the Milk Road show, called the next five years about Ethereum after the largest short liquidation in crypto history and $500 billion of market cap added, ether from around $1,900 to nearly $2,600. Bitmine is over $14 billion of ether, 65 consecutive weeks of buying, targeting 5 percent of supply. That is color from a Thursday show. It is not a Friday print.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. Held $80,000 through Warsh. ETF inflows over $3 billion, eight straight days. Glassnode wall $81,000 to $86,000. Gillen still wants the weekly close above $83,000.
  • $ETH. ETF inflows over $1.2 billion, 12 days. Gillen wants a weekly close above $2,500. Tom Lee has the bounce to nearly $2,600 and a 5 percent Bitmine target.
  • $COIN. $20 billion of USDC in-product, $292 million last quarter, over 30 percent of USDC outstanding. The x402 rail is why that float matters this week.
  • $SOL. 38 percent of last week's x402 payments, up from 6 percent. About $105 in the letter. ETF flows $115 million last week.
  • $HYPE. $50 million of ETF inflows last week, in the same 0xResearch tape as $SOL and $XRP.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] Warsh flipped September toward a hike
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Cowen now sees a two-thirds chance of a September hike, gold futures traded under $4,600, and the BLS benchmark cut 79,000 jobs.
item.content:encoded:
Cowen now sees a two-thirds chance of a September hike, gold futures traded under $4,600, and the BLS benchmark cut 79,000 jobs.

The speech is in. Yesterday this desk was waiting on Friday 10 a.m. ET. Kevin Warsh gave his first Jackson Hole keynote as Fed chair, and the tape priced a hawkish lean.

Market context. Per aixbt, hike odds rose from 35 percent to 46 percent, the two-year yield gained 6.6 basis points, and the dollar added 0.4 percent. Per zerohedge, gold sold the hawkish read, bonds and bitcoin went flat on a neutral read, and stocks jumped to the high of day on a dovish one. Same speech. Three tapes.

Per 0xResearch, Bitcoin is up 10.0 percent on the week against gold 1.8 percent, the Nasdaq 100 0.9 percent, and the S&P 500 0.8 percent. Over the past month Bitcoin is up 25.7 percent and gold 15.6 percent. Bitcoin ETF flows last week totaled over $3 billion, eight consecutive days of net inflows, the first streak like that since April 2026. Ether ETFs took over $1.2 billion, twelve days, the first time since July 2025.

The scoreboard.

  • Warsh at Jackson Hole, due today: he spoke, and he sent a rate signal. House catalyst hits. Inflation not clearly slowing, policy not restrictive, September hike odds flipped.
  • Gold's GLD 410 / 421 map is still open, due Monday. Futures under $4,600 is the live level.

1. The hold just became the hike. Per Cowen, before the speech there was about a two-thirds chance the Fed would keep rates steady in September and about a one-third chance they would raise. After: almost a two-thirds chance of a hike and only a one-third chance they keep rates constant. The market is leaning toward two hikes this year. Cowen is not convinced they raise all the way to 4.25 percent. Raising to 4 percent might be enough.

DeskSeptember hike
Cowen (post-speech)~2/3, was ~1/3
Minervini~55%
aixbt46%, was 35%

Cowen's read on the speech: inflation readings are not under control, and he would be hard-pressed to say monetary policy is restrictive right now. Warsh, per the Stocks recap: while this summer's PCE and CPI readings were better than expected, they do not tell him that underlying trends have meaningfully improved. Scott Melker: inflation is not slowing.

BlackPantherCap: he never said the word hike. He just removed every reason not to. Strong economy. Full employment. Conditions not restrictive. An early "no rate hike decision" line floated on the ground. That is process. Do not read it as dovish guidance.

I am with Cowen on the direction. I am not all the way to two-thirds. Call it 60/40 they hike in September, and the 40 is next week's payroll and the mid-September CPI.

2. Gold sold the hawkish read, under $4,600. Thursday this desk had gold just shy of $4,700. Friday Mel Mattison was buying gold futures under $4,600 on the Warsh tape, then said the opportunity to buy under $4,600 may now be gone forever. That is a level move, not a new high. Bitcoin beat gold on the week and on the month. Gold lost the speech.

3. QT is not September, and jobs were revised 79,000. Cowen does not think quantitative tightening (the Fed shrinking its balance sheet) gets announced in September. Earliest he can see is December 2026, one year after they suspended it. More realistic is early 2027. He also does not treat QT as a substitute for a rate hike.

Zerohedge: US job growth revised lower by 79,000 in the BLS annual benchmark estimate. Headline only. Pair it with the speech. Do not turn it into a payroll print.

4. What to watch. Next week's labor report, then the mid-September inflation print. Those are the two things Cowen named that can un-flip this. He still has the midterm-year analogue: a 10 to 20 percent equity drop, often obvious only in October, the way September 2014 and September 2018 worked.

A late-cycle hike is the narrative he would use to justify it. That call is already on the book for late September. QT is a 2027 problem unless they surprise in December. Gold $4,600 is the line Mel just traded. September is a hike until the next print says it is not.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] Nvidia printed $96.2 billion and guided $108 billion
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Revenue was $96.2 billion versus $92.2 billion expected, up 106 percent, the Q3 guide is $108.0 billion plus or minus 2 percent, and the stock went minus 2 percent after hours then plus 6 percent at the open.
item.content:encoded:
Revenue was $96.2 billion versus $92.2 billion expected, up 106 percent, the Q3 guide is $108.0 billion plus or minus 2 percent, and the stock went minus 2 percent after hours then plus 6 percent at the open.

This is the print. Wednesday was the estimate. Per the call, fiscal second-quarter revenue came in at $96.2 billion versus $92.2 billion expected, up 106 percent year over year against $46 billion a year ago. Adjusted EPS $2.22 versus $2.10, up 120 percent.

I do not have an 8-K. These figures are Najarro's call plus the recap.

Market context. First print after hours, the stock dropped roughly 2 percent on the gross-margin guide. Najarro later has it up roughly 4.7 percent. 0xResearch has the chip leader gapping 6 percent into Thursday's open, Nasdaq 100 up 1 percent.

1. Data center did the work. Memory takes the guide. Per the Stocks AM recap, data center $89.0 billion versus $85.8 billion expected, up 117 percent year over year and 18 percent on the quarter. Najarro splits that as hyperscalers about $49 billion and ACE (neocloud, industrial, and enterprise, the non-hyperscaler bucket) $40 billion, with ACE up 25 percent on the quarter and 138 percent year over year.

Adjusted gross margin 75.0 percent, in line, up 250 basis points year over year. Q3 gross margin guide 74.0 percent plus or minus 50 basis points. Najarro's memory tape is prices up 80 percent and 60 percent, Micron up 60 percent and 70 percent on the quarter, and a margin hit of only 2 percentage points. Q3 revenue guide $108.0 billion plus or minus 2 percent versus $104.2 billion on the street. Buy-side was around $109 billion.

Adjusted operating income $64.0 billion, adjusted net income $54.0 billion, free cash flow $21.3 billion versus $13 billion a year ago. Returned about $26.0 billion in the quarter, about $99.0 billion left on the authorization. Outlook: no Data Center compute revenue from China.

2. Fiscal 2028 is the number the street did not have. Najarro: revenue grows approximately 70 percent next year, supply constrained. If this year is about $400 billion, 70 percent is about $680 billion versus consensus around $570 to $580 billion, a beat of over $100 billion on what the market was expecting. Vera CPU in full production, CPU revenue more than doubling in fiscal 2028 against roughly $20 billion of total server CPU demand.

Production shipments of Vera Rubin began earlier this month. Neocloud partners exit the year with 8 gigawatts, up from roughly 3 gigawatts at the end of 2025. Cloud industry backlog now exceeds $2 trillion. Top-five hyperscaler capex nearly $800 billion in 2026 and $1.3 trillion in 2027.

They invested nearly $50 billion in frontier AI labs, and AI-lab demand supported by the balance sheet is about 25 percent of the business next year. That $50 billion is money into labs. Commitments went from $119 billion last quarter to $279 billion, primarily memory, $366 billion total at Nvidia plus $56 billion in other AI cloud agreements, and OpenAI land and power about $108 billion. The Information, via the recap, also has Nvidia agreeing to acquire Hugging Face for $12.9 billion. Treat that as a rumor.

3. The banker stack is leases. Per the WSJ writeup, Nvidia backstops some $230 billion in lease obligations and residual-value deals, including a $105 billion backstop for the OpenAI Ohio lease and potentially up to $125 billion of residual-value support. CoreWeave has a $6.3 billion deal to buy unsold capacity. The byline snapshot of Nvidia minus 2.91 percent is the pre-print tape.

4. CrowdStrike and Okta reported after the bell. Per Hogue, CrowdStrike aftermarket plus 11 percent, already up 14 percent on the day. The recap is cleaner: CrowdStrike fiscal Q2 revenue $1.47 billion versus $1.44 billion, up 26 percent. Adjusted EPS $0.31 versus $0.29, up 35 percent. Free cash flow $377.4 million versus $353 million, up 33 percent.

Net new ARR (the new annualized subscription dollars) a record $333 million, up 51 percent. Total ARR $5.84 billion, up 25 percent. Full-year guide $5.99 to $6.01 billion of revenue, $1.25 to $1.26 adjusted EPS, ARR $6.60 to $6.61 billion. CrowdStrike up 10 percent after hours. Okta shares surged 20 percent in extended trading. Recap has the beat at 105 versus 96 cents on EPS.

5. Nebius printed real contracts. IREN got Microsoft to accept Horizon 1. Per Rick Orford, Nebius has four major AI cloud contracts, average total contract value more than $1 billion each, priced at $20 to $25 million per megawatt. AI cloud revenue up 514 percent to $575 million, 454 percent year over year, annualized run rate $3 billion. AI cloud adjusted EBITDA margin 50 percent in Q2. Inference more than tripled. Use $575 million and $3 billion. Ignore the ASR "half a trillion" slip in the same paragraph.

Orford on IREN: Microsoft accepted Horizon 1 inside a $9.7 billion, 5-year contract. Horizon 1 is the first of four 50-megawatt sites in 2026, 200 megawatts total. Four facilities around $1.9 billion in average annual revenue once fully on. Nvidia gave them exemplary cloud status. 52-week range from $17.76, the stock is up 103 percent, 25 percent over the past month.

Prior $2.8 billion of new AI cloud contracts, guidance $3.7 billion to more than $4 billion. Market cap around $16 billion, more than $17 for every dollar of sales. ARR target a top $4 billion by end of 2026, 85 percent already under contract. The title's 180 percent upside is not in the spoken numbers. The body has an analyst range of 10 and 150 percent.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $NVDA. $96.2 billion versus $92.2 billion, data center $89.0 billion, Q3 $108.0 billion plus or minus 2 percent, fiscal 2028 about 70 percent / $680 billion. After hours minus 2 percent, Thursday open plus 6 percent. No 8-K.
  • $CRWD. $1.47 billion, $0.31, record $333 million net new ARR. Up 10 to 14 percent after the bell.
  • $OKTA. 20 percent extended. EPS 105 versus 96 cents.
  • $NBIS. Four contracts above $1 billion TCV, $20 to $25 million per megawatt, AI cloud $575 million / $3 billion run rate.
  • $IREN. Microsoft $9.7 billion, Horizon 1 accepted, 85 percent of a $4 billion 2026 ARR target already contracted.
  • $META. $18 billion youth settlement, about $10 billion accrued in Q3. That lives on the macro desk too.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] Cowen is testing the 50-week, and Gillen wants $83,000
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Bitcoin is up 22 percent this week, Bacon tagged $81,000 on August 26, US spot ETF assets are almost $100 billion, and Warsh still speaks Friday.
item.content:encoded:
Bitcoin is up 22 percent this week, Bacon tagged $81,000 on August 26, US spot ETF assets are almost $100 billion, and Warsh still speaks Friday.

The newest tape is Cowen at 4:56 p.m. ET, and he is testing the 50-week moving average (the long weekly trend line that ended prior bulls after two weekly closes below it). This is the first time this bear has even tagged it. Per Cowen, last week it rallied about 24 percent, and this week it has already rallied up to that average. He does not print a dollar on the line. Next week is follow-through versus a rejection.

Market context. Per 0xResearch, every crypto index they track printed strong positive returns except miners. Lending is leading. AAVE, KMNO, and SPK are all up over 30 percent in this rally. Treasury-company Bitcoin flows were negative $100 million in both July and August. Per the Crypto list, Warsh speaks Friday at 10 a.m. ET, aixbt wants bigger Bitcoin and ether swings on that stamp, and after past FOMC meetings Bitcoin's mean absolute hourly return went from 0.66 percent to 1.25 percent. Ripster has COIN, HOOD, and RIOT pushing ahead of Jackson Hole.

1. Gillen is still in cash after a 22 percent week. Per Milk Road, Bitcoin is up 22 percent and John is still holding cash. Biggest week since late 2024. He will not call the bottom. The levels he wants are a weekly close above $83,000 on Bitcoin and a weekly close above $2,500 on ether. Before the squeeze, Bitcoin had been trading with more volatility in 94 percent of its history. I am with Gillen on the weekly close. I am not treating leftover $64,000 copy in that letter as the live print.

2. Bacon tagged $81,000 on August 26. The wick is not the confirm. Per VirtualBacon, Bitcoin tagged 81,000 as of last night, August 26. Confirmation is a weekly close on top of 81,000. Chasing 5 percent into 82,000 to 83,000 is the trap. He is not short. 85 percent of his portfolio is in Bitcoin. US spot Bitcoin ETFs are almost at $100 billion of assets, $99 billion, just over 6 percent of the total bitcoin supply. Saylor raised almost $2 billion over the past month, and the latest cash pile two days ago was $1.59 billion. That is a raise. It is not a buy of coins.

3. Pomp's color into Warsh is the drawdown and gold. Per Pomp, Bitcoin dropped more than 50 percent from the all-time high of $125,000. Will Clemente's chart is Bitcoin-gold correlation at an all-time high. That is debasement-trade color going into Friday. No new dollar target in the letter.

4. The compute side of the same 0xResearch letter is a weekend of Macs. Eigen Labs' Darkbloom side project, Apple Silicon inference: 1,000 machines on Monday, up from 250 on Friday. Throughput from 100 million tokens a day in mid-June to about 10 billion today. OpenRouter went free to paid August 20. Cute. Not the Bitcoin clock.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. Cowen testing the 50-week, next week follow-through or reject. Milk plus 22 percent this week, Gillen wants a weekly close above $83,000. Bacon tagged $81,000 August 26, wants that weekly close. ETF assets $99 billion, about 6 percent of supply.
  • $ETH. Gillen wants a weekly close above $2,500. aixbt has ether swinging with Bitcoin on Friday's 10 a.m. stamp.
  • $AAVE. Up over 30 percent with KMNO and SPK. Lending led. Miners did not.
  • $COIN. Ripster has Coin, Robinhood, and Riot pushing ahead of Jackson Hole.
  • $HOOD. Same tape.
  • $RIOT. Same tape.
  • $MSTR. Treasury-company flows minus $100 million in July and in August. mNAVs back toward 1.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] Warsh speaks Friday on stablecoins, and housing rolled over
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Jackson Hole is 10 a.m. ET Friday on financial innovation, July new home sales fell 10.5 percent to 607,000, and Bank of Korea hiked 25 basis points to 3.00 percent.
item.content:encoded:
Jackson Hole is 10 a.m. ET Friday on financial innovation, July new home sales fell 10.5 percent to 607,000, and Bank of Korea hiked 25 basis points to 3.00 percent.

Jackson Hole is tomorrow. The speech is not in yet. Per the Stocks list, Kevin Warsh's first keynote as Fed chair is Friday at 10 a.m. ET, and the Kansas City Fed theme is Financial Innovation: Implications for Payments and Policy. Mel Mattison has him speaking on stablecoins tomorrow, and he wants Bessent's buybacks and Warsh's QT plus stablecoins treated as one system.

Market context. Per 0xResearch, the chip leader gaps up 6 percent into Thursday's open and the Nasdaq 100 opens up 1 percent. Treasury-company Bitcoin flows were actually negative $100 million in both July and August, aggregate mNAVs (the premium, or discount, of those vehicles to the coins they hold) are trending back up toward 1, and ATM facilities stay off the table until that premium is back. Per the Financial Markets list, gold is attempting another run toward 15-week highs, still just shy of $4,700. That is continuation, not a new high.

1. New home sales fell off a cliff in July. Per the Stocks AM recap, U.S. new home sales dropped 10.5 percent on the month to 607,000, the lowest in 6 months, against minus 1.4 percent expected. Down 6.3 percent year over year, and down in 3 of the last 4 months. Midwest sales collapsed 42.7 percent on the month to 43,000, the lowest since 2012. South down 13.0 percent to 383,000. The 30-year mortgage is 6.81 percent, the highest since August 2025. That is today's domestic print.

2. Bank of Korea hiked again. Same recap: 25 basis points to 3.00 percent, the second straight hike and the first back-to-back since the COVID era. They lifted the 2026 GDP forecast to 3.3 percent from 2.6 percent. Tightening abroad while Warsh talks payments at home.

3. Meta is booking an $18 billion youth settlement. Same recap: $18 billion commitment, $17 billion in broader terms, $2.2 billion payable to California, spent over 10 years, with an independent auditor for 5 years. Accrue about $10 billion of legal expenses in Q3 2026. $5.3 billion of the settlement is tied to YouTube and TikTok putting in similar limits. That is a legal bill, not a demand print.

4. What to watch. Friday 10 a.m. ET, Warsh, plus the BLS payroll benchmark on the same stamp. aixbt says August 28 should bring bigger Bitcoin and ether swings, and after past FOMC meetings Bitcoin's mean absolute hourly return rose from 0.66 percent to 1.25 percent. List tape has S&P at 7700 and Nasdaq-100 at 715 heading in. I want the speech, not the preview.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] Nvidia reports after the bell on a $92 billion quarter
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Hogue has $92 billion of sales up 96 percent, about 20 times sales and 24 times forward earnings, an average target of $300, and there is no 8-K yet.
item.content:encoded:
Hogue has $92 billion of sales up 96 percent, about 20 times sales and 24 times forward earnings, an average target of $300, and there is no 8-K yet.

This is pre-print. Earnings are after the bell. Per Joseph Hogue, Nvidia reports Wednesday, year to date only up 16 percent, sales up 96 percent for the quarter, $92 billion just for the three months. About 20 times price to sales and 24 times forward earnings, about a 25 percent discount to last year's valuation. It has fallen after every earnings report over the last year, usually by less than about 3 percent. Average price target among 25 analysts is $300, almost 40 percent upside. High target $425. Treat that as his estimate of growth still expected, not a filing.

Market context. Per Stocks with Josh, Nvidia is on a 7-day losing streak, the longest in 4 years, and popped from 207 to almost 215 today. Broadcom CDS roughly 126 basis points. Nvidia about 87. Both record highs. That puts dollars on yesterday's plus-5-basis-point tweet. I am not re-briefing that tweet as the move.

1. Hot Chips is the new token math. Do not mix it with CoreWeave's 10 times. Per Milk Road Stocks, Blackwell token-sale net margins roughly 58 percent, climb to 78 percent with Rubin, 90 percent with later chips. Vera Rubin NVL72: up to 30 times more agentic AI throughput per megawatt, and up to 35 times lower cost per million tokens than GB300 NVL72. OpenAI Jalapeño with Broadcom: 1.5 to 1.9 times using the same electricity as Blackwell, responding up to 3.6 times faster. Google TPU shipments 2.76 million units in 2024 to 8.84 million by 2027.

Per Rick Orford, CoreWeave's first Rubin benchmark produced about 10 times more tokens per second per megawatt than Grace Blackwell NVL72. That is tokens per second per megawatt, not Milk's 30 times agentic / 35 times cost. Different metric. Nvidia introduced 800 VDC on August 11, first racks second half of 2026, up to two megawatts per row in 2027. Japan facility: 27,500 Rubin GPUs and 13,750 Vera CPUs.

2. The financing layer is credit and gigawatts, still pre-print. Per the Stocks list, building 1 gigawatt of data center costs about $50 billion, $35 billion of that into GPUs. Morgan Stanley estimates Nvidia's total credit exposure could eventually reach around $200 billion by 2028. The Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman, KKR stack is more than $500 billion of outside capital. Orford is explicit: Nvidia has not said it needs to raise $500 billion, and it has not committed to that amount itself. Josh adds a 125 billion potential backstop as phantom leverage.

3. Moderna ripped, Lilly is a trillion, Pelosi bought Intel. Milk Road Stocks has Moderna up like almost 200 percent in one day or one and a half days, 49 percent lower risk of recurrence or death at a $5,000 price tag per patient. Eli Lilly valued at a trillion dollars today. Josh has Pelosi on Intel, 10,000 shares and half a million dollars on leaps, holding into 2027.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] July PCE printed hot and gold faded off $4,700
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Headline PCE was plus 0.2 percent on the month against plus 0.1 percent expected, plus 3.7 percent year over year, gold faded to $4,613.10 midday, and the 5 to 7 year buyback took $1.19 billion against a $4 billion cap.
item.content:encoded:
Headline PCE was plus 0.2 percent on the month against plus 0.1 percent expected, plus 3.7 percent year over year, gold faded to $4,613.10 midday, and the 5 to 7 year buyback took $1.19 billion against a $4 billion cap.

The new print is PCE, not yesterday's 30-year feud. Per the Market list, July headline PCE rose 0.2 percent on the month against 0.1 percent expected, after a 0.1 percent decline prior. Year over year it was 3.7 percent against 3.6 percent expected. Core was in line, 0.2 percent month over month and 3.3 percent year over year, the second-highest reading since October 2024 and nearly twice the Fed's 2 percent target. That is today's inflation tape.

Market context. Gold opened just shy of $4,700, a continuation of Tuesday's 15-week high, then faded. The same list has spot gold down nearly 1 percent at $4,613.10 an ounce at Wednesday midday. Per 0xResearch, the dollar index hit its lowest since May, gold is up 14.9 percent on the month, and Tuesday the S&P was up 0.2 percent while Bitcoin was down 0.1 percent. Q2 GDP held at 1.5 percent annualized. GDP price index 6.4 percent against 6.2 percent expected. Real personal spending 0.0 percent.

1. The 5 to 7 year buyback undershot the cap. Per the Financial Markets list, Treasury accepted $1.19 billion in 5 to 7 year debt against a $4 billion maximum, with $8.4 billion offered. That is a different tenor from yesterday's 10s-to-30s doubling from September 10. Operations, not a new yield print. No 30-year number in today's article bodies.

2. Warsh speaks Friday. September hike odds are not one number. 0xResearch has Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole keynote as Fed chair on Friday, and September hike odds still near 40 percent. That is a Wednesday newsletter print. Charles Edwards, recorded Monday August 24 and landed in today's Milk Road show, said a 70 percent chance of at least one hike before year end. Monday ClearValue had no-hike odds at 60 percent. I am not flattening those into one figure.

3. Hayes's path is print early, then $250,000. Per Arthur Hayes on Pomp, look up and see Bitcoin at 250,000 after they print early and print often. He calls the buyback upsize like $20 billion over the scheduled amount. Irrelevant, in his words. That is a path after they print. It is not a spot call, and it is not a reopening of yesterday's Bessent-Druck op-ed.

4. What to watch. Friday Warsh at Jackson Hole. September hike still near 40 percent on 0xResearch, against a Monday recording at 70 percent for at least one hike this year. Gold $4,613.10 midday after a $4,700 open. The 5 to 7 year operation that took $1.19 billion against $4 billion.

Broadcom may need to adapt. He owns Nvidia. There are no dollars in the summary. This is not yesterday's Poolside $6 billion or the 15 to 17 percent server print.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] Bessent doubled the buyback and Druckenmiller called it a mistake
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The 30-year spiked to 5.33 percent, the Treasury lifted the cap from $2 billion to at least $4 billion per operation starting September 10, and within 24 hours the 30-year was back above 5.24 percent.
item.content:encoded:
The 30-year spiked to 5.33 percent, the Treasury lifted the cap from $2 billion to at least $4 billion per operation starting September 10, and within 24 hours the 30-year was back above 5.24 percent.

The new story is the feud, not the debt stock. Per Milk Road, mid-August 30-year yields spiked to 5.33 percent, the highest in nearly two decades, and Treasury doubled the 10-to-30-year buyback cap from $2 billion to at least $4 billion per operation. After the announcement the 30-year dropped about 10 basis points, then within 24 hours was back above 5.24 percent. Druckenmiller, via Milk, called it a mistake far larger than $4 billion suggests. Administrative buybacks cannot fix a $2 trillion annual deficit.

Market context. Per 0xResearch, yesterday Monday, Bitcoin was up 1.35 percent, gold up 1.09 percent, the S&P down 0.38 percent, and the Nasdaq 100 down 1.18 percent. Per the Financial Markets list, gold refreshed 15-week highs just shy of $4,700 then pulled back, and Bitcoin printed $81,000 in that list. Those dollar prints are tweets, not article bodies. The $40 trillion debt and 6 percent-of-GDP deficit are yesterday's Hogue stack. Context only.

1. Bessent bought the long end. Druckenmiller said let it speak. Milk Road has the 5.33 percent spike, the $2 billion to at least $4 billion cap, the 10 basis point dip, and the rebound above 5.24 percent. Net interest past $1.1 trillion, exceeding the US defense budget. The TGA is a near-$1 trillion cash pile hinted as funding for yield support.

Per 0xResearch, the doubling is from $2 billion to at least $4 billion per operation beginning September 10, regular auction schedule maintained. That start date is in 0xResearch, not in Milk.

Per Anthony Pompliano, it is Bessent and Druckenmiller, not versus. The WSJ op-ed is "Let the Bond Market Speak." TGA $1 trillion available if needed. Druck's $4 billion line is the same quote. Yields rebounded to the same level after the initial drop, with no second yield print in that body. Pomp says AI-detector tools call the op-ed 100 percent AI-written, and that the split may be coordinated. That is his inference. It is not a fact.

2. Capital Flows says long rates are a growth print. Per Capital Flows, long rates are rising from growth and term premia, not inflation swaps. Nominal GDP is 6.5 percent. The rest of the 2026 AI liquidity thesis is behind the paywall.

3. Iran is a new package, and gold is a tweet. Per Swan, Operation Economic Outcast opened five new sanctions fronts, digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, shipping, and hit nearly 60 targets. The title is Bitcoin Hit $80K. That $80,000 is in the title and summary only.

The Financial Markets list has Saylor's Strategy from a $9.5 billion plus loss to a $4.7 billion plus profit. I am not reopening yesterday's "Saylor bought zero" as if it were new.

4. What to watch. September 10 for the first bigger buyback, per 0xResearch. The 30-year back above 5.24 percent after a 10 basis point dip. Nominal GDP at 6.5 percent as the growth case for the long end. Operation Economic Outcast as the Iran clock. Gold just shy of $4,700 is a tweet until an article body prints it.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] Citadel dumped Leopold's book into the rebound
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Milk Road has Situational Awareness at $20.2 billion of US equities on June 30, down from a peak near $45 billion to around $10 billion, then sold to Citadel at 40 to 50 cents on the dollar.
item.content:encoded:
Milk Road has Situational Awareness at $20.2 billion of US equities on June 30, down from a peak near $45 billion to around $10 billion, then sold to Citadel at 40 to 50 cents on the dollar.

The new plumbing story is not another Nvidia campus. Per Milk Road Stocks, Nebius posted 841 percent revenue growth, Micron guided margins toward 80 percent, and Bloom Energy was raising full-year guidance, and the stocks kept bleeding because Leopold Aschenbrenner's portfolio blew up. That is a newsletter reconstruction of a 13F plus reported block tape. It is not an 8-K.

Market context. No Monday PM lists yet. Earnings are still Wednesday for Nvidia. The new work is who was forced to sell the AI book, what Bloomberg and The Information say about server prices, and three plumbing deals that moved $24 billion in the layer between models and enterprises.

1. The book was concentrated, leveraged, and then dumped. Milk Road has the June 30 13F at $20.2 billion in US equities. SanDisk 28 percent. Micron 27.5 percent. Bloom Energy 9.6 percent. TSMC 6.4 percent plus $24 million in calls. Nebius 6.1 percent. CoreWeave 3.7 percent.

Leverage as high as 4x. Under that leverage the portfolio reportedly lost roughly 67 percent in a single month, from a peak near $45 billion to around $10 billion. Liquidated to Ken Griffin's Citadel in late July at a reported 40 to 50 cents on the dollar. On August 11, Citadel disclosed it had already unloaded more than 80 percent of the distressed position through over 100 block trades.

The house line in that same letter is that their analysts are buying the dip and staying long. Treat the weights as a reconstruction.

2. Najarro's new chip print is 15 to 17 percent on servers, and Poolside at $6 billion. Per Jose Najarro, we are less than 72 hours from earnings. Bloomberg reported Nvidia will raise prices for some of its largest customers by at least 15 percent. He thinks The Information also reported about 17 percent to server makers. Those increases start early next year. He frames it as a memory bill of materials pass-through, not pricing power. There is no real confirmation from Nvidia in his own words. Second print: Nvidia is investing up to $6 billion with a startup called Poolside. Visibility between 2025 and 2027 of over a trillion dollars just on Blackwell and Vera Rubin. This is not yesterday's $105 billion Ohio guarantee.

3. Credo is the named optical print, with no target. Per Edelbridge, DustPhotonics is approximately $850 million to $1.2 billion in cash and stock, with $750 million cash upfront. FY2026 revenue $1.33 billion, up more than 200 percent from $436 million in FY2025. Cash $1.4 billion, zero long-term debt. Q4 non-GAAP gross margins 68.3 percent. ATM $736 million. Free cash flow $407 million against stock-based compensation of $182.6 million. Optical revenue expected to exceed $600 million in FY2027. Shares outstanding about 186.5 million. The price target is behind the fold. I am not inventing one.

4. Broadcom is a $56 billion AI-semi year on the way to above $100 billion. Per Rick Orford, Broadcom expects fiscal 2026 AI semiconductor revenue of about $56 billion, next year around double that, above a hundred billion. Fiscal second quarter about $22.2 billion of revenue, AI semis about $11 billion, up 143 percent year over year. AI networking around 40 percent of AI semi revenue that quarter. Apple multi-year agreement expected to exceed $30 billion, custom ASIC through 2031. Free cash flow around $10 billion in the quarter, roughly 46 percent of quarterly revenue. Top five customers 45 percent of first-half 2026 revenue. Stock range $281 to just under $500, up about 40 percent over the past year.

5. The plumbing layer: Stripe, Marvell, Databricks. Per Jordamøn, last week moved $24 billion into the layer between AI models and the enterprises that deploy them. Stripe acquired OpenRouter for approximately $7.5 billion. Marvell granted Google a warrant to purchase up to 59 million shares at $206.58, worth approximately $12.2 billion if fully exercised, vesting per $500 million of chips through fiscal 2033. Broadcom fell roughly 5 percent on that news. Marvell climbed more than 10 percent. Databricks closed a $5 billion round on August 13 at a $190 billion valuation, up from $134 billion six months earlier and $62 billion in January 2025, with $7 billion of annualized revenue growing 80 percent year over year.

6. Perplexity is a tweet, not a filing. Per the Market list, Nvidia discusses a Perplexity deal at over $30 billion value, per The Information. Treat it as a tweet.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $NVDA. Less than 72 hours. New work is Bloomberg at least 15 percent and The Information about 17 percent on servers, Poolside up to $6 billion, and a Perplexity $30 billion Information tweet.
  • $MU. 27.5 percent of the Leopold book. One of the names that kept bleeding while the fundamentals printed.
  • $SNDK. 28 percent of that same book.
  • $AVGO. $56 billion of AI semis this year, above $100 billion next, $11 billion in FQ2, Apple north of $30 billion.
  • $MRVL. Google warrant, 59 million shares at $206.58, about $12.2 billion if exercised. Stock up more than 10 percent on the news.
  • $CRDO. $1.33 billion FY26 revenue, $1.4 billion cash, zero long-term debt. No target on this page.
  • $BE. 9.6 percent of Leopold, raising full-year guidance, still in the unwind.
  • $NBIS. 6.1 percent of the book, 841 percent revenue growth, still bleeding with the rest.

Strategy sat it out. Saylor bought 12,000 and 79,000 Bitcoin into the two prior plus-20 percent weeks and added nothing this time.

Market context. No CoinGecko 2:00 p.m. ET table in text today, so I am not inventing a Monday spot. VirtualBacon has live price at 77,400 while he talks. The weekly close still decides Mayne's new bar. Roughly $1.4 billion of short liquidations is 0xResearch's print. I am not merging it with last week's other liquidation totals.

1. The $82,000 cluster is the live confirmation, not 67,200. Per Milk Road, the number John is watching closely is $82,000, the bull-market support band. Two retrace levels if things cool off: $74,000 first, then $71,500. Bhutan and Wintermute have both been moving Bitcoin onto exchanges. ETF dollars are not in that letter. The "best week ever" title has no percent in the text.

Per Trader Mayne, above 82K there is zero reason to be bearish on this chart. He will wait to see how the weekly candle closes, and if we pull back he will probably start buying more spot. That replaces yesterday's 67,200 bar. They are not the same level.

Per VirtualBacon, the bull market can only be confirmed above the higher band at 81k, 81.7k, 81,700. Live 77,400. He wants a wait until price is 5 percent higher to clear above 82K. Fallback buy 66k. His 40 percent versus 80 percent coloring is his, not a market print.

Per Lark Davis, overhead around $82,500, 200-day EMA around $72,000, bottom call 57K, priced from 64 to 77K. Bitcoin ETFs took around $2 billion last week, best week since October 2025, eating back half of June's $4.5 billion outflow month. That $2 billion is his round number. 0xResearch's $2.4 billion is the other dated print. I am not averaging them.

2. Ether tagged 1,500 and is sitting on Cowen's fair value. Per Benjamin Cowen, Ethereum had a sizable drop all the way back down to around 1,500, then rallied to the quote unquote fair value, around 23 to 2400 on his regression. The main area it is pushing up against is the 200-week moving average. If there is no drop in stocks, the odds of the low being in for Ethereum are probably like 70 percent. That 70 percent is coloring. Lark has Ethereum at 2,500, with $2,800 the big number to beat, and Solana currently $96, wanting a solid close over about a hundred.

3. Jordi's new line is the $58,000 low. Per Jordi, the sentiment symmetry of its $58,000 low. The 22 percent week is yesterday. I am not leading with it. Both prior episodes led to substantial further gains. The pattern is evidence, never a mechanical price target.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. 0xResearch around $77,800 for the week. Bacon live 77,400. Confirmation cluster 81,700 to 82,500. Milk Road retrace $74,000 then $71,500. Mayne buys more spot on a pullback after the weekly close.
  • $ETH. Up 28 percent to about $2,440 on 0xResearch. Cowen fair value 23 to 2400 after a tag around 1,500. Lark 2,500 / 2,800.
  • $SOL. Lark at $96, close over about $100. Not the lead.
  • $MSTR. Saylor added nothing this week against 12,000 and 79,000 on the two prior plus-20 percent weeks.
  • $IBIT. $1.65 billion of the $2.4 billion US spot week, after $140 million of outflows the week before.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] The 10-year is at 4.7 percent and debt just printed $40 trillion
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Hogue has the 10-year up three-quarters of a percent since March to 4.7 percent, later says it hit 4.8 percent, and US debt passed $40 trillion this week with a 6 percent-of-GDP deficit.
item.content:encoded:
Hogue has the 10-year up three-quarters of a percent since March to 4.7 percent, later says it hit 4.8 percent, and US debt passed $40 trillion this week with a 6 percent-of-GDP deficit.

The new rates print is the 10-year, not last week's 30-year. Per Joseph Hogue, the rate on the 10-year Treasury is up three-quarters of a percent since March to 4.7 percent, as high as it has been since 2007. Later in the same transcript he says the 10-year Treasury hit 4.8 percent. Those are two prints in one video. I am not flattening them. US national debt passed $40 trillion this week. That is the fiscal side of the same tape.

Market context. Per the Financial Markets list, gold kicked off Monday at three-month highs above $4,650, with the dollar taking the brunt of a Treasury buyback headline, US-Canada tariff woes, and looming US sanctions on Iran. The buyback is still a headline, not a Treasury primary. No Monday PM lists were in yet. The 30-year 5.337 print is yesterday's memo. I am not reopening it.

1. Hogue dated the 10-year, and the fiscal stack is $40 trillion with a 6 percent deficit. Hogue is the first dated 10-year print since the weekend 30-year tape. 4.7 percent since March. 4.8 percent later in the same body, in a Google Gemini aside.

Twenty trillion of the $40 trillion came in the last 10 years. Outlays forecast at $7 trillion this year. A historic deficit of 6 percent of the entire economy, a number that could be underestimated by as much as $3 trillion.

Mortgage rates topping 6.6 percent. New home construction plunged 12 percent in July, worst year since 2011. GDP grew just 1.5 percent last quarter. Kraft Heinz is still saddled under $19 billion in debt, profits expected to fall by 21 percent this year, paying nearly a billion dollars in interest, net debt $16.3 billion.

2. ClearValue has September 16 as a 60 percent no-hike, up from 45 percent. Per ClearValue Tax, the next Federal Reserve meeting is September 16. When he made the wager the no-hike odds were 45 percent. As of August 24, the odds of the Fed not raising rates have increased to 60 percent. He does not name the odds source. CPI came in at 3.4 percent for July, better than 3.5 percent in June. Japan holds 1.1 trillion Treasuries. Three voting members wanted to hike in July. After September he flags October and December, with December after the midterms as the ideal hike window in his telling.

3. Private credit is about $2 trillion, and PIK is how the loss hides. Per Cory Klippsten, there is somewhere around $2 trillion of it now. The names are Ares, Blackstone, Blue Owl, and Apollo. The PIK example is $100 million at 10 percent, with $10 million added to what you owe instead of cash. The borrower can stop sending cash. The fund can still report income. The manager can collect a cash fee on income the fund only received as a bigger claim. He does not think 2008 is the right analogy. No default rate in the short.

4. What to watch. September 16, with ClearValue at 60 percent no-hike as of today. The 10-year at 4.7 percent, with a 4.8 percent print in the same Hogue transcript. Gold above $4,650. Private credit at $2 trillion with no default print. If you need the buyback or the 30-year, it is already written. Nothing new from Treasury today.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] Nvidia's $500 billion MOUs meet a $3 trillion off-balance-sheet bill
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Street is looking for about $92 billion of Nvidia revenue on Wednesday, nine top tech names carry some $3 trillion of off-balance-sheet commitments, and Wednesday's SOX drop of 5.0 percent was the midweek warning.
item.content:encoded:
Street is looking for about $92 billion of Nvidia revenue on Wednesday, nine top tech names carry some $3 trillion of off-balance-sheet commitments, and Wednesday's SOX drop of 5.0 percent was the midweek warning.

This channel's week was one question asked three ways. Who pays for the AI build. What $NVDA is allowed to print on Wednesday. And whether memory is still the crowded long after the SOX lost 5.0 percent in a day. The financing stack is the story. The earnings print is the referee. This memo is both sides of that stack, and what I would actually hold into August 26.

The week in one arc

DayWhat changed
Sunday–TuesdayNvidia's more-than-$500 billion third-party capital MOUs land, and Applied Materials guides its first $10 billion quarter while the stock fades
Wednesday 19SOX −5.0 percent, Micron −7.0 percent, SK Hynix ADR −9.2 percent, on yields and the "how is AI financed" question
Thursday 20The Treasury buyback hits the risk-off, and the tape starts looking through Wednesday toward Nvidia
Friday 21Micron versus CXMT, fuel cells and local power politics, Nvidia sitting near $212 to $214 into the report
Saturday 22The Street preview firms around $92 billion of revenue and a $5.2 trillion market cap

The through-line is that Wednesday priced the funding risk, and Thursday's macro bid papered over it. The funding risk did not leave.

1. The $500 billion is still a memorandum, and the $3 trillion is already a bill

Nate B Jones has Nvidia signing MOUs with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman, and KKR to mobilize more than $500 billion of third-party capital. He flags they are MOUs, subject to execution of the final agreements. Rick Orford ran the same stack the same week. I am not treating a memorandum as cash in the door.

The harder number is the one that showed up as a reprint, not as the paywalled original. The August 16 WSJ piece, via /u/Wild_Space, says nine top tech names had some $3 trillion of off-balance-sheet commitments. Traditional capex was about $600 billion over the past year. Uncommenced leases $1.2 trillion. Purchase obligations $1.9 trillion. Alphabet purchase commitments $811 billion as of June 30. Meta's Hyperion: Blue Owl majority, $27 billion in debt off Meta's balance sheet, Meta's initial lease about $12.3 billion, Meta uncommenced leases $347 billion as of June.

That is the financing story this channel has been circling all month. The house already has an open call that the AI rally is funded by hundreds of billions of purchase commitments against a thin sliver of direct equity. This week put a $3 trillion label on the same structure. Macro owns the "who funds the build" driver. The names that have to live with it sit here.

2. Nvidia is the referee, and the Street is clustered at $91 to $92 billion

There is no official 8-K in what I have. Earnings is still ahead. Stocks with Josh, on August 21, says earnings is Wednesday of next week, maps a swing from 212 to 227, and wants a Monday dip to 212.

Jose Najarro has Nvidia sitting at $214, up roughly 13.7 percent year to date, market cap roughly $5.2 trillion. Street revenue this quarter is roughly $92 billion. He would not be surprised by 94 or 95 billion. Watch Vera Rubin, the Q3 and Q4 ramp, margins, CPU TAM, and LPX.

Rick Orford is working off the last print. Data-center around $75.2 billion, up 92 percent. Networking almost 200 percent. EPS $1.87 against $1.77. Gross margin around 75 percent. Inventory around $26 billion. Supply commitments roughly $119 billion. China data-center compute zero, against $4.6 billion a year ago. Guide $91 billion, give or take 2 percent. Street $91.92 billion. Sequential growth implied about 11.5 percent against about 20 percent the prior two quarters. His read: sold-out, China, and a product transition, not a demand crack.

The open house call is the one I am carrying into Wednesday. Nvidia has guided to $91 billion. A next guide above $105 to $108 billion means no deceleration. Near $100 billion means a real slowdown. I am not rewriting that on a Saturday preview.

3. Memory is still the crowded long, and Wednesday showed you the crowding

Blockworks on August 19 is the midweek tape: SOX −5.0 percent, $MU −7.0 percent, SK Hynix ADR −9.2 percent. That is what a crowded memory long looks like on a 5.3 percent 30-year.

The fundamental tape underneath it did not break. Orford on Micron versus CXMT has Micron's 52-week range $113 to $1,255, data-center $11.5 billion of revenue in the third quarter of fiscal 2026 at an 87 percent gross margin. CXMT raised about $8.6 billion through July 2026 in its IPO, with Q1 profits about $3.7 billion. Milk Road on August 17 has JPMorgan raising the Micron target from $550 to $1,540, and BofA taking free cash flow from $55.7 billion this year to $188.6 billion by 2030. That last pair is a newsletter claim. I am leaving it labeled.

The house memory call is still 60/40 that multiples expand before they compress. Monday's ledger already scored the $991 confirmation as a hit when Micron reclaimed $1,000. The 1022, then 1037 to 1051, map is still the one I am using. Wednesday's −7.0 percent is what the crowding tax looks like, not a thesis change.

Applied Materials is the other side of the same week. Guided toward its first-ever quarter over $10 billion, year-over-year growth at the midpoint over 50 percent, annualized $40 billion-plus, Q3 FY26 revenue just over $9.1 billion. The stock sold off anyway. A $10 billion guide that the tape fades is the same funding-and-duration problem, not a demand miss.

4. Power is the bottleneck that showed up as politics

Daniel Koss has Nebius ($NBIS) forced off 32 natural-gas engines at 350 megawatts in Vineland, New Jersey, and onto fuel cells. The rumor is Bloom sold out into 2029 and 2030. The leftover name is $FCEL. That is local permitting doing what a 30-year cannot: rationing the build by the megawatt.

The same week's color around it, ranked lower: Applied Digital at $36 billion of contracted lease revenue and $86 billion of option upside, Q4 FY26 revenue just over $250 million, up over 400 percent, 1.4 gigawatts contracted. Nebius with Nvidia at $2 billion and 9.3 percent beneficial ownership, Goldman at 7.2 percent, the stock pulled back 13 percent after a 188 percent year, more than $40 billion of contracted revenue plus $15 billion potential, 24 percent short. Those are position facts. They are not the week's argument.

5. The bull case, the bear case, and the arbitration

The bull case is that the build is pre-sold and the referee is eight sessions from a print the Street already expects. $91 to $92 billion is not a surprise. A beat toward 94 or 95 billion, with Vera Rubin and the Q4 ramp intact, lets the $500 billion MOU stack get treated as real capacity rather than a press release. Memory already has 87 percent data-center gross margins at Micron and a JPMorgan target at $1,540. Power rationing is a volume constraint, not a demand one.

The bear case is that $3 trillion off the balance sheet is the bill coming due, and Wednesday already priced a piece of it. MOUs are not capital. China data-center compute at zero against $4.6 billion a year ago is a hole in the last print. Sequential growth slowing from about 20 percent to about 11.5 percent is the deceleration the house call is watching. A crowded $MU that loses 7.0 percent in a day is what happens when the 30-year and the funding question show up on the same tape.

I am 55/45 that Wednesday's Nvidia print holds the AI-infra bid, and I am saying that is a low-conviction number on purpose. The Street is already at $91.92 billion. The information is in the next guide, not in a beat of a number everyone already has.

What would change my mind: a guide that clusters near $100 billion, or a memory print that breaks the 87 percent margin. What keeps me at 55/45: the $3 trillion is real, the MOUs are not cash, and the buyback that bounced the SOX on Thursday has not spent a dollar yet.

What to do with it

Hold the structural memory and power names through Wednesday. Do not add $NVDA into $214 on a Saturday preview. Josh's 212 dip is the only entry on this tape I would take, and only as a swing into the print, not as a new core.

Own the funding risk as a size problem, not as a short. The $3 trillion is why I will not let this channel become a one-name Nvidia memo. $MU, $AMAT, $NBIS, $FCEL, and $APLD are how the same bill shows up in names you can actually trade.

Watchlist for the week ahead. $NVDA into August 26, $91 billion last guide, Street around $92 billion, house line on the next guide at $105 to $108 billion versus near $100 billion. $MU into 1022, then 1037 to 1051, with CXMT as the China comp. $AMAT on a $10 billion quarter the tape already faded. $NBIS and $FCEL on the Vineland-to-Bloom power ration. $APLD on $36 billion of contracted lease revenue the market has not paid up for.

The scoreboard, Stocks & ETFs

Three calls resolved on this channel's book this week, one hit and two expiries.

ResolvedOutcome
Micron needs a close above $991 to confirm the next leg toward $1,022, houseHit. Micron reclaimed $1,000 on Monday and put 1022 in play
CPUC vote August 13 on the Cox merger, houseExpired. The date passed with no update in the material. Left unresolved rather than invented
CoreWeave August 21 $75 put as the short-put entry, Invest with HenryExpired. No $80 print. CoreWeave stayed the battered AI-infra name into its own report

House record: 2 hits, 1 miss, and 1 expiry on four settled calls. The new hit is the Micron $991 confirmation. The miss is still the SpaceX squeeze, wrong on timing. The CPUC line died as an expiry, not as a miss.

One hundred sixty-six open calls carried into next week. The ones that matter: memory multiples expand before they compress, still 60/40. Nvidia's next guide, $105 to $108 billion versus near $100 billion, due August 26. Micron's ladder into that same print. Applied Materials on the $10 billion quarter. Applied Digital on the $36 billion contracted stack. And Walmart's 2.6 percent US comps as the consumer half of the rotation, still open into month-end.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] Bitcoin ripped off the buyback and the weekly dollar record is live
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Bitcoin ran from roughly $64,400 to almost $72,000 in under 24 hours, then printed over $77,000, and a Sunday close above $74,200 would be the biggest weekly dollar gain in its history.
item.content:encoded:
Bitcoin ran from roughly $64,400 to almost $72,000 in under 24 hours, then printed over $77,000, and a Sunday close above $74,200 would be the biggest weekly dollar gain in its history.

Last Sunday this channel was dating an autumn low. This Sunday it is scoring a squeeze that became a flow. Bitcoin spent Sunday through Tuesday stuck around $62,000 to $64,000. Wednesday night through Friday it ran. The driver sits on the Macro desk. The position sits here. This memo is the tape, the flow, and the call I have to eat.

The week in one arc

DayWhat changed
Sunday–TuesdayVol crushed, "boring Bitcoin" as the bull case, spot stuck about $62,000 to $64,000, ETFs still flippy
Wednesday 19SOX and memory risk-off hit the miners (HUT −12.5 percent, CIFR −11.9 percent that day)
Wednesday night–ThursdayBuyback headline plus the White House meeting. Bitcoin roughly $64,400 to almost $72,000 in under 24 hours
Friday 21Over $77,000, plus 18 percent in 48 hours, plus 22 percent on a 5-to-7-day window, ETF week-to-date +$1.6 billion
Saturday 22Victory laps, not a new catalyst. A title of $79,000 is out there. I am not treating that print as confirmed

The single most important line in the week is Milk Road's Sunday condition. If Bitcoin closes Sunday night above $74,200, it marks the single biggest weekly gain in dollar terms in Bitcoin's history. That close has not printed yet as I write this.

1. The rip, with the numbers the bodies actually printed

Milk Road on August 20 has Bitcoin from roughly $64,400 to almost $72,000 in under 24 hours, forcibly closing about $1.1 billion of shorts, the biggest single day of short liquidations in Bitcoin's recorded history, over $1 billion inside about an hour. Prices as of 2:00 p.m. ET, CoinGecko. The trigger they name is the Treasury buyback.

Arbitrage Andy has $2.5 billion of crypto shorts liquidated in the last 24 hours, at one point over $1.2 billion in 60 minutes. Same White House guest list as the policy desk. Polymarket odds creeping toward the 77,000 to 80,000 range. The odds percentage is not in the extract I have.

Klippsten has the rip from 64K to 70,000, then up to almost 72,000, more than a billion dollars of Bitcoin shorts in about an hour, and the next level right around 74K. The ETF inflow dollar figure in that clip cuts off.

Blockworks on August 21 has Bitcoin up 18 percent in 48 hours, more than $1 billion of positions wiped, perps up over 28 percent on the week, and more than $1 billion of Bitcoin shorts from August 19 through the first 6 hours of August 21, roughly $630 million on August 19 alone. BTC ETF inflows recorded the highest daily print since May 2026. The daily and weekly ETF dollar total is not in that graf.

Milk Road on August 21 then has Bitcoin from roughly $64,000 to $77,000 in less than 48 hours, and the $74,200 Sunday-close condition. Ether "doing even better." No ETH print in that extracted head.

Anthony Pompliano has a surge to over $77,000, a 22 percent increase in the last 5 days, and Galaxy's Alex Thorn: Bitcoin ETFs see the biggest weekly net flow since the October 2025 all-time-high week, net flow this week +$1.6 billion, week not over yet.

Those definitions do not match, and I am not going to mash them. $1.1 billion is Bitcoin-only on Milk Road. $2.5 billion is all-crypto on Andy. $1 billion-plus is the 48-hour Bitcoin window on Blockworks. The range is the honest version of the squeeze.

A Saturday stream titled "Bitcoin Just Hit $79,000" is in the pile. That number is a title and a summary, not a transcript print. I am not using it as a level.

2. The flow is why this is not only a squeeze

Thorn's +$1.6 billion, week-to-date, is the demand number I will keep. Blockworks' "highest daily print since May" is the same story without a dollar figure. Klippsten's ETF sentence dies in the cut. I am not inventing the missing daily print.

Swan's Friday summary has Bitcoin up 22 percent this week and reclaiming its 200-day moving average for the first time since November 2025. That 200-day reclaim is also how Friday's house call resolved: a daily close above $67,000 was the bear invalidation, and the close above $72,000 killed it.

Jordi Visser, on August 22, called it a seven-sigma week, 60-day vol of 23, with prior analogs in April 2019 and January 2023, tapes that broke above the 200-day. Pomp on that same show: Bitcoin now up 22 percent over the last 7 days.

The early-week contrast is the reason the flow matters. Blockworks on August 17 still had Bitcoin down 3.1 percent the prior week, stuck between $62,000 and $64,000, ETFs at $159 million of net outflows that week. You do not get a +$1.6 billion week from that base without a real bid showing up after the shorts were already gone.

3. Policy is the second bid, and it is dated

The White House meeting is a Macro event that set a crypto position. Andy named Armstrong, Nazarov, Tenev, and the Winklevoss on tokenization and CLARITY. Blockworks has Trump saying the CFTC was working to bring Hyperliquid to the US. Trader Mayne has the same naming, and "$12,000 off the bottom."

CLARITY stays a Macro bill. The position here is $COIN, $HYPE, and whether alts need the bill. Lark's September 15, 2:00 p.m. Senate vote is the date. House call on this channel is still that CLARITY's failure stays priced for Bitcoin and is not priced for alts, at 65/35. A rip that started on a Treasury headline does not retire that.

Ether and Solana are the breadth I actually have. The Milk Road Show has Bitcoin broken out above 72K, Ethereum up over 20 percent and pushing 2400, Solana mid-80s. David Duong, the former Coinbase institutional-research voice on that show, sees a bottom at 55 to 60 and notes the Bessent double has not started yet, early September. That is the pullback case with a name on it.

4. The call I have to eat

Last Sunday I held 60/40 that Bitcoin sees $58,000 before $75,000. That call is still open in the book. The sourced bodies this week printed over $77,000. The $58,000-first branch is dead even if the ledger has not closed the row.

I am not going to dress that up. I dated an autumn low into a week that produced the squeeze, the 200-day reclaim, and a $1.6 billion ETF week. The clocks can still be right about October. They were wrong about this week.

I am moving the live house lean to 65/35 that the Q4 lower-low call is wrong, matching Friday's book, with a retest of the 200-day near $72,000 as the healthy pullback. That is a lean, not a victory lap. RSI-style vertical weeks fade. Duong's 55 to 60 is still a named other side. The buyback that started this rip still has not spent a dollar.

The honest weakness in the new lean is the Sunday close. Above $74,200, Milk Road gets its dollar-record week. Below it, this is still a historic squeeze that failed the weekly condition the desks spent Friday advertising. I will not pre-score a close that has not printed.

What to do with it

Do not chase the first $72,000 to $77,000. Use a 200-day retest near $72,000 if you want spot. The squeeze already happened. The flow is the reason to stay involved. The entry is not the spike.

Keep $COIN and $HYPE as the policy pair, not as a second Bitcoin. Hyperliquid is the named onshore trade. Coinbase is the listed one. CLARITY on September 15 is their date, not Bitcoin's.

Watchlist for the week ahead. $BTC into the Sunday $74,200 condition and, after that, the $72,000 200-day retest. $ETH at 2400, up over 20 percent, the breadth check. $COIN as the listed CLARITY proxy. $HYPE on the CFTC and onshore mention. $MSTR as the leverage proxy now that the coin is back through the treasury companies' cost basis in the sourced prints.

The scoreboard, Bitcoin & Crypto

Three calls resolved on this channel's book this week, all hits, and two of them are the house's.

ResolvedOutcome
A daily close above $67,000 invalidates the bear side of the $69,500 reclaim, houseHit. Bitcoin closed above $72,000, first daily close above the 200-day since November
That 200-day close sets up a run at $75,000, houseHit. Sourced bodies printed over $77,000 inside two days. I am not adding the $79,000 title as a confirming print
The August 19 White House crypto meeting happens with the named guest list, houseHit. The summit ran Wednesday

House record: 3 hits and 0 misses on three settled calls. Last Sunday this book had no settled house calls. This week it got three, and it still owes the reader the $58,000-before-$75,000 call, which the tape has already beaten and the ledger has not yet closed.

Eighty-five open calls carried into next week. The ones that matter: the 65/35 lean against a Q4 lower low, with the $72,000 retest as the pullback. CLARITY's failure priced for Bitcoin and not for alts, at 65/35, into September 15. Ether's 20 percent move to $2,306 as confirmation the alt side led. Hyperliquid's fee switch. And the old $58,000-before-$75,000 row, which I am treating as dead in prose until the book marks it.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] Treasury doubled the long-end buyback and the 30-year cracked
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The 30-year hit 5.337 percent, the highest since 2007, then fell to 5.196 percent after desks said the Treasury is lifting long-end buybacks from $2 billion to at least $4 billion a run from September 9 through November 4.
item.content:encoded:
The 30-year hit 5.337 percent, the highest since 2007, then fell to 5.196 percent after desks said the Treasury is lifting long-end buybacks from $2 billion to at least $4 billion a run from September 9 through November 4.

This channel spent the week arguing about the long end, and Wednesday answered it. The 30-year printed 5.337 percent, the highest since 2007, then the desks said Treasury is at least doubling the long-end buyback. That is the week's driver. Everything else is the dissent, the fiscal math underneath it, and the two dates that settle whether this is a managed pullback or a one-day headline.

The week in one arc

DayWhat happened
Sunday–TuesdayCowen says the cutting cycle is over and the dollar goes higher into year end, while the long bond is already the worry
Wednesday 19Equity positioning looks too aggressive, credit sits at cycle lows against a high 30-year, and the SOX gets hit
Thursday 20Desks say Treasury is lifting long-end buybacks from $2 billion to at least $4 billion a run, 9 Sep through 4 Nov, after 5.337 percent
Friday 21The debasement tape runs in gold and Bitcoin. The 30-year is back at 5.196 percent on the Milk Road print
Saturday 22The same buyback is still the story. The first bigger operation has not started

The single line I am keeping is this. The buyback is not in a Treasury press release I can cite. It is a secondary claim from Milk Road, Arbitrage Andy, and Cory Klippsten. Three desks, same size, same start date. I am treating the print as real and the primary text as still missing.

1. The buyback is small against the stock and large against the tape

Milk Road has Treasury at least doubling long-end buybacks from $2 billion to at least $4 billion per operation, starting September 9 through November 4, after the 30-year hit 5.337 percent and then fell back to 5.196 percent. Andy has the same $2 billion to $4 billion, begin September 9. Klippsten has the 30-year "reaching 5.34 percent, highest since 2007" and the lift to "at least 4 billion per operation," then long-term yields fell, the dollar weakened, and stocks and gold rallied.

Desks are calling that stealth yield-curve control. Four billion against a $32 trillion Treasury market is still a warning shot. Swan later put the same $4 billion at 0.01 percent of the federal debt stock. The market still sold the 30-year from a 2007 high back through 5.20 percent on the headline. Size and reaction are two different facts.

Capital Flows frames the yen tape plus the buyback as a coordinated Bessent, Warsh, and Trump warning shot. No new yield print in that body. I am taking the coordination as a thesis, not as a table of levels.

2. Cowen is the named dissent, and he did not blink

The consensus this week is debasement. Cowen is not in it.

On August 17 he said the rate-cutting cycle is over. Last NFP, in his telling, lost 23,000 jobs. His base case is a midterm correction that does not start until September, and an energy-forced hike is the bigger risk against a dovish pivot. The companion report is "The Balance of Risks (August 2026)."

On August 18 he said the market is wrong about the dollar. His stated view is DXY higher into year end, and that it is likely to come alongside a rate hike. He did not give a DXY level in the transcript I have.

I am not making his hike the house base case. I am keeping it on the page because the buyback only works if the long end is the problem the Treasury is willing to manage. A hike into $4 gasoline and a still-high 30-year is the other regime, and Cowen is the one still arguing it.

3. The fiscal stack the buyback is managing

Adam Livingston put the arithmetic in one sitting. America is now $40 trillion in debt. Another $7.8 trillion is in intragovernmental holdings. Debt held by the public is around 101 percent of GDP. CBO has a $3.1 trillion federal deficit within 10 years, deficit-to-GDP from 5.8 percent to 6.7 percent, and net interest from 3.3 percent to 4.6 percent by 2036. The one-million-Bitcoin strategic reserve in that same piece is his case, not a confirmed purchase. I am leaving the coin out of this channel.

That stack is why a $4 billion operation can move a 30-year that just printed a 19-year high. The Treasury is the largest issuer in a market that just showed it can reprice the long end in a week. Buying your own duration is what you do when you will not let the term premium float.

Capital Flows on August 19 said short-term equity positioning is too aggressive, and that credit spreads are at cycle lows while thirty-year yields sit at highs. Tripwires named: crude, core CPI, inflation data. No numeric spread and no fresh 30-year print in that extract. The Wednesday SOX drop of 5.0 percent is the tape version of that warning, and the Thursday buyback is the policy version of the answer.

The AI-financing overlap lives here as a driver. The tickers stay on Stocks. Nine top tech names carry some $3 trillion of off-balance-sheet commitments against about $600 billion of traditional capex, and Nvidia's more-than-$500 billion MOUs are still memoranda. Who finances the build is this channel. What $NVDA prints on Wednesday is Stocks.

4. CLARITY is the other dated policy clock

Lark Davis dates the CLARITY Act to September 15 at 2:00 p.m., a US Senate vote. Republicans hold roughly 53 Senate seats. The bill needs 60 votes for cloture. Only two Democrats have supported it in committee. The blocker is the ethics provision. There are two to three weeks of Senate session before the October election recess. His $40 trillion institutional-unlock line is his framing, not a figure in the bill text.

The White House meeting on Wednesday sat next to that clock. Andy named Armstrong, Nazarov, Tenev, and the Winklevoss in the room on tokenization and CLARITY. Trump naming the CFTC and Hyperliquid is a crypto position. The bill itself stays here.

The house call on this channel is still that CLARITY does not become law this year, at 80/20. September 15 is the first roll-call test of that call.

5. The arbitration, and the prints that settle it

The bull case on the buyback is that Treasury will not let the 30-year live at a 2007 high while it funds a $40 trillion stock of debt, and that hard assets are the release valve. The bear case is that $4 billion is 0.01 percent of the debt, the first operation is still three weeks out, and Cowen's hike-plus-dollar path can reassert once the headline fades.

I am 60/40 that the long end stays managed from here, meaning the 30-year does not hold a new cycle high through the first September operation. That is a view on the Treasury's reaction function, not a claim I have seen the press release.

What settles it, in order:

The eventWhat it decides
The first bigger buyback, September 9If $4 billion actually prints and the 30-year stays under the 5.337 percent spike, the secondary claim is confirmed in the market
Warsh at Jackson Hole, August 28His debut. A rate signal versus no-forward-guidance is the Fed side of the same funding problem
CLARITY cloture, September 15 at 2:00 p.m.The ethics provision either finds 60 votes or it does not
The next inflation or crude printCapital Flows named those as the tripwires against cycle-low credit and a high 30-year

I said last Sunday that if the long end keeps selling into prints that should have helped it, that is the regime change. This week the Treasury answered before the next print could. The 30-year at 5.3 percent as a structural bond bear is still an open house call. The buyback is the first evidence against it, and it has not started yet.

The scoreboard, Macro & Policy

Four calls resolved on this channel's book this week, three hits and one expiry, and two of the hits are the house's.

ResolvedOutcome
The Fed minutes decide whether the 30-year at 5.3 percent is regime change or a pullback, houseHit. The minutes landed, and Treasury answered first by doubling long-end buybacks to $4 billion an operation, taking the 30-year below 5.20 percent
Oil is the swing variable, Iran-Oman plan versus a further ADNOC attack, houseHit. Iran declared economic war and Brent pushed back above $92
The July 27 Abqaiq strike was inflated by recycled 2019 material, Anas AlhajjiHit. The strikes were real and far short of 2019. The oil story moved to Hormuz
Abqaiq as a live 5-to-7 percent supply shock, The Hormuz Letter and zerohedgeExpired. The strike was limited. The due date passed. The driver is the blockade. The plant is no longer the story
