House record: 4 hits and 3 misses on seven settled calls. Last Sunday this book was 2 and 3. The two new wins are the minutes-and-buyback call and the Hormuz swing. The three losses are still the oil-higher-two-weeks call, the Iran-Oman announcement, and the CPI. A winning week on a still-small sample.

Seventy-six open calls carried into next week. The ones that matter: CLARITY does not become law in 2026, at 80/20, with September 15 the first test. The 30-year at 5.3 percent as a structural bond bear, now sitting against a buyback that starts September 9. Gold as the debasement trade after the GLD fund ran $370 to $422 in two weeks. Warsh at Jackson Hole on August 28. And Iran holding Brent above $92 into that same September 15 window.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] Nvidia's $105 billion OpenAI guarantee is a newsletter print
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Edelbridge has Nvidia backing up to $105 billion of guarantees on an 8 GW Ohio campus, first 800 MW in 2028, and server prices up more than 15 percent in early 2027 on memory.
item.content:encoded:
Edelbridge has Nvidia backing up to $105 billion of guarantees on an 8 GW Ohio campus, first 800 MW in 2028, and server prices up more than 15 percent in early 2027 on memory.

The new number is not the $91 to $92 billion Street guide I already wrote this morning. Per Edelbridge, Nvidia committed to provide up to $105 billion in guarantees supporting OpenAI's planned Ohio data center campus, designed to reach 8 GW of IT capacity, with the first 800 MW expected online in 2028. That is a newsletter claim. There is no 8-K in what I have. Name the source and size it that way.

Market context. Sunday, so no index recap. The week is earnings: CrowdStrike, Nvidia, and Salesforce, with Intuit on Andy's list too. The new work is the guarantee stack, the SpaceX gigawatt math, and what neoclouds are getting paid per megawatt.

1. Edelbridge put $105 billion of guarantees on Ohio, and called the 2027 price hike. The August 23 portfolio note is the source. Up to $105 billion in guarantees on OpenAI's Ohio campus. Eight gigawatts of IT capacity eventually. First 800 MW in 2028. Prices for servers containing Nvidia AI chips could rise by more than 15 percent in many cases for systems shipping in early 2027, primarily due to higher memory costs. The SOX line in that same note is last week's tape. I already used it. I am not reopening it.

2. Najarro's new angle is the commitment jump, and SpaceX as a $200 billion customer. Per Jose Najarro, the Street $92 billion and the $214 spot are already on this morning's page. The new question is what happens if commitments jump from like $130 billion to $200 billion, against about $130 billion in cash flow from operations. Elon and SpaceX announced they were going exclusively with Nvidia GPUs and would build about 5 gigawatts in 2027, $200 billion potentially from SpaceX. That is the add. Vera Rubin versus Blackwell is the margin question he is watching into Wednesday.

3. The neoclouds are getting paid a lot more per megawatt, and CoreWeave's book is named. Per the Stocks list, the annual run-rate print is $CRWV $9.8 million, $NBIS $9.4 million, $IREN $10.4 million. Nebius just revealed on their earnings call they are now signing deals at $40 to $50 million per megawatt, 4 times their baseline from the start of the year. CoreWeave: over $63 billion in disclosed customer commitments this year alone. OpenAI over $21 billion through 2031. Meta $35 billion plus. Nvidia a $6.3 billion deal as a paying customer. Jane Street $6 billion in April.

The same lists carry a dated financing stack that is not the $3 trillion reprint. Hyperscalers sold $108 billion of those bonds in 2025, about 26 percent of their capex, and $194 billion in the first half of this year alone. Goldman is expecting $400 billion against 2027 capex. Alphabet posted its first negative free cash flow quarter since 2004 in July. Meta handed BlackRock an 80 percent stake in its El Paso site, with $12.5 billion of debt behind it. Same five firms have already disclosed about $1.2 trillion of lease commitments. $1.14 trillion has to get borrowed.

4. CrowdStrike is Wednesday's non-Nvidia print, and NuScale is the nuclear leftover. Per Joseph Hogue, it is a big earnings week with CrowdStrike, Nvidia, and Salesforce. $CRWD reports Wednesday, stock up 62 percent year to date, revenue expected up 23 percent this year, earnings leveraged up 32 percent. His Nvidia line is $92 billion of sales for the three months and earnings nearly double to $29 a share, the same Street cluster I already have. Super Micro: an internal investigation found no evidence that senior management beyond those already indicted were part of the chip-smuggling operation, only director Wally Louu and a few other employees.

Per Rick Orford, the UAMPS Carbon Free Power Project, six NuScale modules at Idaho National Laboratory for 462 MW, was terminated in November 2023. NuScale stock has fallen 74 percent over the past year, 52-week range from $7.58, up 9 percent over the past month. Microsoft's PPA is the restart of an 835 megawatt nuclear facility in Pennsylvania. First SMR targeted for 2030 through 2035.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $NVDA. The new work is Edelbridge's $105 billion OpenAI guarantee and Najarro's $130 billion to $200 billion commitment scare, plus SpaceX at 5 GW and $200 billion potential in 2027. Wednesday after the close.
  • $CRWD. Wednesday. Up 62 percent year to date. Revenue up 23 percent, earnings up 32 percent on Hogue's numbers.
  • $CRM. On the same earnings week. No new print in today's pile beyond the calendar.
  • $CRWV. $9.8 million per megawatt baseline, $63 billion of disclosed commitments this year, OpenAI $21 billion, Meta $35 billion plus, Nvidia $6.3 billion, Jane Street $6 billion.
  • $NBIS. $9.4 million baseline, now signing at $40 to $50 million per megawatt.
  • $IREN. $10.4 million per megawatt on the same list.
  • $SMCI. Internal investigation cleared senior management beyond those already indicted. Wally Louu is the named director.
  • $AAPL. Josh has a giant seller wick after a prior $198 to $350 buyer wick, and a live call that 344 was the end of it.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] Miner fee revenue is the worst yearly average since 2011
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Milk Road has no dollar figure on the fees, Riot is already pivoting to AI infrastructure, and Mayne wants a weekly close above 67,200 before he calls the low in.
item.content:encoded:
Milk Road has no dollar figure on the fees, Riot is already pivoting to AI infrastructure, and Mayne wants a weekly close above 67,200 before he calls the low in.

The squeeze tape is this morning's memo. Today's new bear is the fee line. Per Milk Road, Bitcoin's fee revenue just hit its lowest yearly average since 2011, and miners like Riot are already pivoting to AI data infrastructure instead. There is no dollar fee figure in that graf. As block subsidy trends toward zero, fees alone will not be enough to keep miners securing the network.

Market context. Crypto trades Sunday. Andy has volatility since last week's run-up, a slight pullback the bears celebrated prematurely, then a reverse. No $74,200 close is in any body I have. The weekly close is still ahead. Mayne's bar is a different number than this morning's dollar-record condition.

1. Fee revenue is the 2011 low, and Riot is leaving the pure-miner seat. Milk Road is the source. Lowest yearly average since 2011. Riot already pivoting to AI data infrastructure. No dollar print, so I am not inventing one. This is the miner-economics story the squeeze does not answer. $RIOT as an AI-revenue name is the position, not a restatement of last week's liquidations.

2. Mayne's low-is-in bar is 67,200 on the weekly close. Per Trader Mayne, if we get a weekly close above 67,200, the weekly internal swing high, he is going to assume the low is in. That is a different bar from the $74,200 Sunday-night dollar-record condition I already wrote. One is a structure call. The other is a weekly-gain record. Neither has printed as of this edition.

3. Andy is still sidelined, and the $40,000 crowd is early. Per Andy, the slight pullback reversed. People who previously thought we were going to $40,000 are calling for lower. This evening will provide some solid clues. His core three are Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Chainlink. The rest of the watchlist is behind the paywall. I am not inventing names.

4. Jordi restated the 22 percent week and the 200-day bail rule. I already have that. Per Jordi, Bitcoin starts to show up in its third wave, in its adoption phase, in the same way that AI did a year ago. The 22 percent week, the seven-sigma line, 23 vol, and the bail if Bitcoin goes back under the 200-day are this morning's tape. The add is the third-wave framing, not a new spot print.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. Mayne: weekly close above 67,200 and he assumes the low is in. The $74,200 dollar-record close is still unprinted. Andy wants this evening's clues and is not chasing the $40,000 calls.
  • $ETH. On Andy's core three with Bitcoin and Chainlink. No new ether print in today's pile.
  • $RIOT. The named miner already pivoting to AI infrastructure on the 2011-low fee year.
  • $SOL. Josh will buy some alts about a month after he feels Bitcoin has bottomed. He already holds some Solana and Tao. No Bitcoin level in the short.
  • $LINK. Andy's third core name, above the fold.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] CLARITY is stalled, and the earliest pass is September 15
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Andy has the bill alive but stuck in the Senate, a procedural vote is expected September 15, and Wednesday is PCE plus Q2 GDP with Warsh at Jackson Hole on Friday.
item.content:encoded:
Andy has the bill alive but stuck in the Senate, a procedural vote is expected September 15, and Wednesday is PCE plus Q2 GDP with Warsh at Jackson Hole on Friday.

The new policy print is the stall, not the buyback. Per Andy, as of August 23, 2026, CLARITY is alive, but it stalled in the Senate, and the earliest the bill can now pass is September 15, when a procedural Senate vote is currently expected. That is the dated clock. The week ahead is PCE and Q2 GDP on Wednesday and Kevin Warsh of the Fed at Jackson Hole on Friday.

Market context. Sunday, so no session recap. The week that matters is Wednesday's PCE plus Q2 GDP, Friday's Warsh debut at Jackson Hole, and the September 15 procedural vote. Salesforce, CrowdStrike, and Intuit also report this week. Nvidia reports Wednesday after the close, already on the Stocks desk.

1. CLARITY is alive and it is stalled. Andy is the dated source. Alive is not the same as a floor vote. September 15 is a procedural Senate vote, not a signed law. The house call on this channel is still that the CLARITY Act does not become law this year. This print is the calendar, not a change in that lean.

2. Wednesday is the data, Friday is Warsh. Andy's week-ahead list is PCE inflation plus Q2 GDP on Wednesday, and Kevin Warsh of the Fed at Jackson Hole on Friday. Those are the two prints that can move the long end without a new Treasury release. I already wrote the buyback this morning. There is still no primary Treasury text today.

3. The data-center power bill is small, and it plateaus. Per Cremieux, there is an effect of new data centers on electricity prices. The effect is small, and it appears to plateau. Average price effects from a hyperscale 250 MW data center being built locally look small for a typical household as of August 21, 2026. The site is wattsmybill.org. The dollar-per-kWh figure is in a chart, not in the text, so I am not inventing it. This is the policy-side answer to the power-politics story Stocks is running. It is a household bill, not a permitting ration.

4. What to watch. Wednesday's PCE and Q2 GDP. Friday's Warsh speech at Jackson Hole. September 15 for the CLARITY Act procedural vote. If you need the Bessent-and-buyback tape, it is this morning's memo. Nothing new printed on it today.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] The memory trade is running straight into Nvidia's report
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Micron and Marvell are back at the highs on a DRAM spike, Nvidia limps into earnings down six straight days, and fuel cells and healthcare carry the non-AI bid.
item.content:encoded:
Micron and Marvell are back at the highs on a DRAM spike, Nvidia limps into earnings down six straight days, and fuel cells and healthcare carry the non-AI bid.

Yesterday the theme was the consumer cracking and the semis going quiet. Today the semis answered: memory is the loudest trade in the market, DRAM pricing is at records, and the whole complex is leaning into Nvidia's report next week. The broad tape slipped on the lingering Walmart drag, but the AI rotation into the enablers is on, and two non-AI pockets, fuel cells and healthcare, are carrying real bids of their own.

Market context. Per the Kalshi list, the S&P fell about 0.9 percent with the Dow about 1.3 percent as the Walmart read kept dragging consumer names. Per the Polymarket list, Nvidia fell a sixth straight day, its worst losing streak in four years, into its August 26 report. The memory names went the other way: Micron reclaimed its 50-day and Marvell kept its bid, Per the People list while Merck touched an all-time high and Moderna stayed near its squeeze. Gold and Bitcoin running is the macro wind at the AI trade's back.

The scoreboard. The CoreWeave put-selling thesis hit its August 21 expiry with no confirmation from today's sources: no $80 print, and CoreWeave stayed the most-battered name in the AI-infra complex into its report. I am marking the short-put entry expired rather than claimed, because nothing in today's tape settled the level. The call's substance, that the AI-infra names got oversold into the financing unwind, is the same thesis the Citadel clearance supports, so the idea lives on even though the dated put is dead.

1. Memory is the momentum story and it is now a pricing story. Per the Stocks list, DRAM contract pricing is up 700 percent year over year and spot NAND is running roughly 7x its prior high, with the memory makers passing through record take-or-pay contracts that lock in revenue through 2030. Per the Stocks list, Micron reclaimed its 50-day at 963 and cleared the 972 resistance, and Per the Stocks list the next levels are 1022 then 1037 to 1051. Per the Micron video, HBM supply is secured for all of 2026, and Per the People list JPMorgan sees DRAM and NAND revenue near $1.8 trillion in 2028. The buybacks are the tell: SK Hynix authorized a roughly $28.7 billion repurchase that cancels shares, Samsung a package near $72 billion, and SanDisk added $14 billion. When the memory makers themselves are buying back hard into a pricing supercycle, the trade has a floor under it.

2. Marvell is the custom-silicon survivor and it just guided up. Per the Marvell video, Marvell guided second-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue to about $2.7 billion, up 35 percent year over year, and raised its outlook on AI bookings, trading at roughly 75 times earnings against a Broadcom at 71 times, with the analysts still carrying upside in their price targets. Its edge is the memory-pooling and custom-silicon portfolio it handed to Google and others, the same CXL and photonic-fabric demand that is lifting the memory complex. At this valuation it is a momentum hold, not a value buy, but the guide is the proof the AI custom-chip demand is real.

3. Power and fuel cells are the next bottleneck and Bloom is sold out. Per the Daniel Koss piece, data-center moratoriums are spreading, 269 since January 2023, and Bloom Energy is reportedly sold out into 2029 to 2030, leaving FuelCell Energy as the next name. FCEL trades near $18 with a market cap just over $1.6 billion and a bull case to roughly $80 on 500 megawatts of capacity by mid-2028. Per the power video, the bigger theme is Nvidia moving to an 800-volt architecture where Infineon is the top pick, down about 40 percent from its June high, and Onsemi's per-rack content rising from $15,000 to $115,000. Power is the trade that shows up once the AI capex numbers are real, and this run's sources keep pointing at the same few names.

4. The Citadel-Situational Awareness unwind cleared the AI overhang. Per the People list, Ken Griffin sold about 80 percent of the risk his firm absorbed from the collapse of Leopold Aschenbrenner's fund, roughly $4 billion in block trades, and the holdings were the same high-beta AI names the drawdown punished: SanDisk at 28 percent of the book, Micron at 27.5 percent, then Bloom, TSMC and Nebius. The overhang that suppressed these names is clearing, a structural reason the AI-infra complex is finding a bid beyond the memory story.

5. Healthcare is the non-AI bid and it is real. Per the People list, Morgan Stanley upgraded Merck to Overweight with a $179 price target, about 54 percent above its prior level, after the mRNA cancer-vaccine read, and Merck touched an all-time high, up 15.8 percent on the week. Moderna held most of its historic squeeze, Per the People list and Cramer called Celsius the winner over Coke while the healthcare complex kept its bid. This is the clearest rotation pocket outside the AI trade, and the breadth the edition needs to carry.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $MU. Back above its 50-day at 963, next resistance 1022 then 1037 to 1051. Memory pricing at records with the buybacks as a floor.
  • $MRVL. Guided revenue up 35 percent and raised the outlook. Expensive, but the custom-silicon demand is proven.
  • $NVDA. Down six straight, its worst streak in four years, into the August 26 report. The whole semis tape trades off the guide.
  • $FCEL. The next fuel-cell name after Bloom sold out. Bull case to roughly $80 on 500 megawatts by mid-2028.
  • $BE. Sold out into 2029 to 2030 on the data-center power shortage. The leader of the fuel-cell shortage trade.
  • $MRK. Upgraded to $179, an all-time high after the vaccine read. The healthcare bid that balances the AI-heavy tape.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] Bitcoin's record week is now a demand story, not a squeeze
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: BTC ripped to $79,000 on pace for the biggest weekly dollar gain in its history, ETH is leading at $2,400, and Clarity odds jumped back to 50 percent.
item.content:encoded:
BTC ripped to $79,000 on pace for the biggest weekly dollar gain in its history, ETH is leading at $2,400, and Clarity odds jumped back to 50 percent.

Yesterday was the invalidation. Today is the confirmation. Bitcoin cleared $79,000, on pace for the biggest weekly dollar gain in its history, after the largest short-liquidation event this market has ever printed. The important shift is that the forced buying is over and the spot and ETF demand has taken over, and that is the difference between a bear-market bounce and a real reclaim. The one fight left is whether a Q4 lower low still comes, and this edition takes both sides.

Market context. Per the Financial Markets list, Bitcoin pushed to $79,000 with spot ETFs on a four-day inflow streak totaling $1.6 billion in five days and the RSI overbought near 80. Per the Stocks list, the move marked the market's seventh-largest liquidation event on record, with $3.5 billion of leveraged positions wiped in a day while the total crypto market cap still added about $280 billion. Per the Financial Markets list, Ether hit about $2,400, its first time there in three months, and the proxy equities ran with it, Coinbase up roughly 30 percent on the week.

The scoreboard. The house call from yesterday, that the 200-day reclaim sets up a run at $75,000, resolved today and resolved in our favor: Per the Financial Markets list, BTC cleared $79,000, straight through the $75,000 target, and Per the Kalshi list the market now prices a 32 percent chance of $100,000 by year end, up from 28 percent. The call that defined this week is a hit.

1. BTC went from $64K to $79K and the squeeze turned into demand. Per the Crypto list, Bitcoin ran from roughly $64,400 to $72,000 in under 24 hours, forcibly closing about $1.1 billion of shorts in the biggest single day of short liquidations in its recorded history, over a billion of it inside an hour. Per the Milk Road piece, the move is on pace to be the biggest weekly dollar gain in Bitcoin's history if it closes above $74,200 on Sunday. The read across the tape is that the initial squeeze gave way to real spot and ETF buying, Per the Blockworks piece with the strongest Bitcoin ETF inflows since May and a record level of shorts cleared out of the majors. That is the demand confirmation the whole reclaim was waiting on.

2. ETH is leading and the laggard just caught up. Per the Financial Markets list, Ether rose to about $2,400, its first time there in three months, up 20 to 30 percent in three days, with its spot ETF inflow day the best in ten months. Per the Stocks list, the read from the desks is that ETH is the most underowned major, and Coinbase has outperformed both the coin and Bitcoin in this week's squeeze, up 30 percent against Bitcoin's 22. The ETH to BTC ratio breaking out is the signal that this is a broad repricing, not a one-coin event.

3. The dissent that matters: a Q4 lower low is still on the table. Per the 365-day video, the bear case points at a pattern where each of the last three cycles took exactly 365 days from top to bottom, and this cycle is on day 318, which leaves about 47 days and would land a final low near early October. The house holds the reclaim but flags the risk honestly: RSI near 80 and a vertical move argue for a pullback, and a retest of the 200-day around $72,000 is the healthy setup rather than a sign the bottom failed. Per the Milk Road show, the former Coinbase head of institutional research David Duong puts the bottom in at 55,000 to 60,000 and says the flows will turn positive over the next six to eight weeks, and that is the other side of the argument. The house is roughly 65/35 that the lower-low call is wrong, but this is the exact debate to hold open into October.

4. Clarity odds jumped back and the regulatory bid is on. Per the Kalshi list, the Clarity Act pass odds jumped back to 50 percent on Coinbase's call, and Per the People list the SEC chair set the vote for September 15 and called the bill his most important priority. Per the Crypto list, XRP rallied with the regulatory optimism and Ripple launched a $RLUSD credit fund with ClearPool and Cicada for institutional lending on the XRP Ledger. This is the divergence that defined last week, a market repricing the bill as dead while the price ran anyway, and a jump back to coin-flip odds turns a dead story into a live catalyst.

5. HYPE is the catalyst trade on the book. Per the Crypto list, Hyperliquid's Aqav2 upgrade goes live in about six days, adding roughly 500,000 to 600,000 a day in extra fees that get burned, and the token sits near its highs with a clean breakout above $77 pointing at $100. Per the Milk Road show, the push to bring Hyperliquid onshore, named by Trump, turned it from a yield story into a regulatory one. The fee switch is the named catalyst, and the onshore nod is the floor under the token.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. Cleared $79,000 on the biggest weekly dollar gain in history. The demand confirmation is in, watch the $72,000 retest for the pullback setup.
  • $ETH. First time at $2,400 in three months, leading the majors. The laggard that caught up.
  • $HYPE. Aqav2 goes live in about six days, breakout above $77 points at $100. The catalyst trade on the book.
  • $COIN. Up roughly 30 percent on the week, a named voice on the September 15 vote. The clearest regulatory tailwind it has had.
  • $MSTR. Back in profit, roughly $1.4 billion unrealized on its Bitcoin stack as the coin crossed $79,000. The leverage proxy that moves with the reclaim.
  • $XRP. Rallied with the Clarity odds jump and a new institutional lending fund on the ledger. The alt tied to the regulatory bid.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] Bessent doubled the buyback and the debasement trade is running
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The Treasury pushed its long-end bond buyback past $4 billion, gold broke out to $422, Bitcoin ripped to $79,000, and Jackson Hole is the next test.
item.content:encoded:
The Treasury pushed its long-end bond buyback past $4 billion, gold broke out to $422, Bitcoin ripped to $79,000, and Jackson Hole is the next test.

Yesterday the long end rejected the first rescue in under a day. Today Bessent answered by making the rescue bigger, and the market stopped arguing with him in yields and started voting in gold and Bitcoin. Equities sagged on the Walmart drag and a still-elevated long end, but the debasement trade is the day's real story, and the calendar now runs at Jackson Hole next Friday. The question has moved from whether the Treasury intervenes to how far it is willing to go.

Market context. The market slipped with the consumer drag and long-end pressure while the debasement assets ran. Per the Kalshi list, the S&P fell about 0.9 percent and the Dow about 1.3 percent on the Walmart read, with the Russell 2000 down a similar amount. Per the Financial Markets list, gold extended its breakout as the GLD fund ran from $370 to $422, a 14 percent move in two weeks, and Per the Financial Markets list Bitcoin pushed to $79,000. Per the Kalshi list, Brent moved toward $93 a barrel. A trading weekday, so the recap is live.

1. Bessent doubled the buyback and dared the market to test him. Per the Financial Markets list, the Treasury said it is doubling its bond buyback program to $4 billion per operation, and Per the People list Bessent signaled the operations could run bigger than that. Per the Stocks list, the 30-year had hit 5.337 percent on Tuesday, its highest since 2007, and fell back to 5.196 percent on the announcement before drifting higher as the market tests whether the program is big enough. The read across the book is a Treasury running an activist bid on the long end to hold down the cost of its own debt, not a regime change in the deficit.

2. Gold is the market's verdict on the program. Per the Financial Markets list, the GLD fund ran from $370 to $422, a 14 percent move in two weeks, and gold rose about 4 percent on the buyback day. The tape reads it as financial repression: more deficits, more debt, the Treasury flattening the long end, and hard assets as the pressure release. Per the Gold video, the swing trader's "final boss" level for gold sits around 410 with the next resistance at 421 and a stop set at 406. Gold breaking out is the cleanest single tell that the market now trusts the debasement read more than the bond market's protest.

3. Iran keeps the oil bid and the risk premium. Per the Kalshi list, Brent moved toward $93 a barrel on Trump's comments that the US has complete control of the Strait of Hormuz, and Per the Financial Markets list a Houthi strike hit a Saudi Aramco facility in Najran. Per the Market list, Brent is up 53 percent and US crude 51 percent year to date. The Saudis are rerouting crude north through SUMED to dodge the Bab el-Mandeb, and the Panama Canal cut its daily transit slots on drought. Oil at these levels is the transmission that makes a Fed rate path concrete, so the strait and the long end are the two clocks that matter together.

4. The fiscal backdrop the buyback is managing. Per the Financial Markets list, US national debt crossed $40 trillion, up $658 billion since July 1, and Per the Crypto list Japan has dumped $123 billion of US Treasuries since February to its lowest holdings since January 2025. This is the arithmetic behind Bessent saying the deficit may have peaked while the Street keeps watching the long end. A Treasury that must keep its own borrowing costs down while foreign buyers step back is exactly the setup that bids up scarce assets.

5. What to watch: Jackson Hole next Friday. Per the People list, Fed chair Kevin Warsh speaks at 10am ET on August 28, his debut at the symposium, and the market is split on whether he sends a rate signal or holds his no-forward-guidance line. The first bigger buyback lands September 9 and runs through November 4. Those two dates, plus the Iran oil clock, decide whether the debasement trade holds or fades into the fall.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] Walmart cracked and the AI trade went quiet into Nvidia
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The consumer bellwether fell 9 percent on its worst sales growth in six years while Moderna held its squeeze and the semis waited on earnings.
item.content:encoded:
The consumer bellwether fell 9 percent on its worst sales growth in six years while Moderna held its squeeze and the semis waited on earnings.

Yesterday the theme was rotation and Moderna. Today the rotation's cleanest expression failed: Walmart posted its worst US sales growth in six years and fell the most since 2022, and the market is now asking whether the consumer side of the trade can hold. Moderna kept most of its historic gain, and the AI complex went quiet into Nvidia earnings next week. The lead is the crack in the rotation.

Market context. The S&P held near 7,720 after a soft open, with the Nasdaq up modestly while Per the Stocks list the Q's sat on five straight red days at the 50-day and the VIX rose about 7 percent intraday against a barely-down SPY, a divergence that sets up a heavy earnings week. Per the People list, Walmart fell 9.2 percent to about $103.70, its worst single day since May 2022. The AI tape was mixed: Moderna and Marvell up big, Applied Digital and Nebius down, and the semis holding a floor off Monday's lows. Walmart, Target and Lowe's retail reads land this week as the consumer test.

The scoreboard. The CoreWeave put-selling thesis is due tomorrow at $80. CoreWeave has been the most-battered name in the AI-infra complex through the drawdown, so the next two days decide it. Nothing else on the book resolves this window.

1. Walmart posted its worst sales growth in six years and the consumer call has a data point. Per the People list, US same-store sales rose 2.6 percent against 3.8 percent expected, the slowest growth in six years, and the stock fell 9.2 percent to about $103.70, its worst single day since May 2022. The full print was mixed: revenue beat at $187.94 billion against $187 billion, adjusted EPS beat at $0.81 against $0.74, and the company raised full-year guidance to $2.80 to $2.87. But the comp miss and a light Q3 guide were the tell the market traded. The read across the tape is that the higher-income customer is holding while the base softens, and that is the same split the rotation has been betting on.

2. Moderna kept most of its historic move and the healthcare complex repriced. Per the People list, Moderna is now the second-best S&P 500 performer this year, up 491 percent, behind SanDisk, after the first positive Phase 3 result for a personalized cancer vaccine. It doubled again at the open and settled well above where it started, and the 3x Moderna ETP surged 532 percent in a day. Merck fell slightly after a downgrade but the oncology complex held its bid. This is the second session of a catalyst that repriced an entire sector, and the pullback risk is now the squeeze ending, with analysts still pegging the stock far below its spike.

3. The semis went quiet into Nvidia and the setup is a divergence. Per the NVIDIA video, Nvidia has guided to 91 billion in revenue for the August 26 report, give or take 2 percent, and the next guide is the whole tape's question. The Q's are down five straight days at the 50-day while the VIX is up about 7 percent, a tape that has made the memory and AI names the most oversold they have been since the spring. Per the Stocks list, Marvell handed Google a warrant for nearly 7 percent of the company against custom-silicon revenue, and JPMorgan flagged Broadcom as an aggressive buy at current levels. The semis are holding a floor, but the direction is now a bet on the Nvidia number.

4. Applied Digital is the neocloud story the market has not fully priced. Per the Applied Digital video, the company now holds $36 billion of contracted lease revenue, up to $86 billion with renewal options, after winning three new leases worth about $20 billion from one hyperscaler that has now picked it three times in a row. Quarterly revenue topped $250 million, up more than 400 percent year over year. The stock has pulled back about 7 percent in the past month even as the backlog grew, and that gap is the setup to watch in the AI-infra complex.

5. SpaceX's second lockup is live and the float math is the story. Per the People list, up to 319 million shares, about 7 percent of the company, became eligible to trade today, the second insider lockup expiration, and the stock fell about 6 percent to near $140. History says the first unlock marked the bottom rather than the top, so the read is that this second one is more of a float-absorption event than a thesis-breaker, with the AI-factory and Starlink compounder thesis intact.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $WMT. Down 9.2 percent on the weakest US comps in six years, worst day since 2022. The consumer tape's first hard data point.
  • $MRNA. Second-best S&P performer this year after the cancer-vaccine win. Squeeze-led, so watch the pullback risk.
  • $NVDA. Has guided to 91 billion for the August 26 report. The next guide is the whole semis tape's catalyst.
  • $APLD. $36 billion contracted, up to $86 billion with renewals, down 7 percent in a month. The neocloud the market has not priced.
  • $MRVL. Handed Google a warrant for nearly 7 percent of the company against custom-silicon revenue through 2033. The survivor of the custom-chip trade.
  • $SPCX. Down 6 percent on the second lockup, but the first unlock marked a bottom. Float absorption, not a broken thesis.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] Bitcoin printed its first daily close above the 200-day since November
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: A record $3 billion short squeeze pushed BTC to $72,000 while ETH rose 20 percent, ETF flows turned sharply positive, and Clarity odds stayed collapsed.
item.content:encoded:
A record $3 billion short squeeze pushed BTC to $72,000 while ETH rose 20 percent, ETF flows turned sharply positive, and Clarity odds stayed collapsed.

Yesterday the Treasury handed crypto a bid. Today the bid turned into a breakout. Bitcoin reclaimed $72,000 with the first daily close above the 200-day moving average since November, on a record short squeeze and the largest ETF inflow in months, while Ether rose about 20 percent to reclaim $2,000 decisively. The bear side that ruled the tape for weeks just got its invalidation, and the flows are the confirmation.

Market context. Per the Crypto list, Bitcoin ripped to about $72,000, its highest since June, on the first daily close above the 200-day (a widely watched long-term trend line) since November. Per the Crypto list, more than $3 billion of shorts were liquidated in 24 hours, the biggest squeeze of the cycle, and spot Bitcoin ETFs took in a net $517 million on August 19, the largest single-day total since May 4. Per the People list, Ether rose about 20 percent to $2,306, back above $2,000 with its sharpest day in months, and the proxy equities ripped with it, Strategy up about 13 percent and Coinbase through $172.

The scoreboard. The house call from the weekend, that Bitcoin needs a daily close above $67,000 to invalidate the bear side, is now confirmed: BTC closed above $72,000 and took the 200-day with it. The white-space between the old resistance and the new close is the strongest bullish signal this book has had since the 200-week break, and the market has already repriced the path forward, with Per the Kalshi list a 60 percent chance Bitcoin sees $75,000 within the next month.

1. The squeeze cleared the level that had defined the bear case. Per the Crypto list, Bitcoin reclaimed $72,000 on the first daily close above the 200-day since November, with more than $3 billion of shorts liquidated in 24 hours, the biggest single-day squeeze of the cycle. The largest on-chain shorts got taken out in the move, and the close above the 200-day is the first durable bullish signal since the 200-week break. The house reads this as the invalidation: the level that had kept the bears in control is now the floor.

2. The flows turned and that is the confirmation. Per the Crypto list, spot Bitcoin ETFs took in a net $517 million on August 19, the largest single-day total since May 4, and the combined BTC and ETH flows have been positive three straight days. Per the Crypto list, Ether ETFs added about $178 million in a day and Bitcoin ETFs about $472 million. This is the institutional money following the price, and it is the difference between a squeeze that fades and a reclaim that sticks.

3. Ether is the alt side of the same breakout. Per the People list, Ether rose about 20 percent to $2,306, back above $2,000 with the sharpest day in months, after breaking back above the level on its highest close in months. Per the Crypto list, the ETH-BTC ratio is breaking out, with ETH outperforming BTC nearly two to one on the day, the first time the lagging major has led in a while. The read is that this is a broad repricing, not a one-coin event, and the majors all reclaimed their key moving averages.

4. The regulatory story is doing two opposite things at once. Per the Crypto list, the Clarity Act looks dead right up until a deal gets made, and the odds have collapsed. Per the People list, they cratered from 40 to 14 percent even as Per the Crypto list Coinbase's Armstrong called the September 15 Senate vote the most important next step.

Into it, Per the Blockworks piece the SEC proposed a Regulation Crypto Assets framework with a safe harbor and exemptions up to $75 million per year, and Trump confirmed the CFTC is working to bring Hyperliquid into the US compliantly. The market is repricing the pass odds as a failure while the price action says the crypto bid no longer needs the bill, and that divergence is exactly the setup where a surprise pass reprices the whole book violently.

5. Hyperliquid is the leverage proxy everyone just found. Per the Blockworks piece, Hyperliquid's perps led the day, up 20.9 percent, on the confirmation that the CFTC is working to bring it into the United States in a fully compliant way. Per the Crypto list, the token's daily revenue is back above $4 million for the first time since June, its USDC fee switch is about five days out, and Per the CRYPTO video Stanley Druckenmiller disclosed about a $23 million position in Hyperliquid Strategies. The fee switch is the named catalyst on the book, and the Trump nod turned it from a yield story into a regulatory story.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. First daily close above the 200-day since November at $72,000. The bear invalidation is in.
  • $ETH. Up about 20 percent to $2,306, leading the majors. The laggard that just caught up.
  • $COIN. Through $172 with the squeeze, and a named voice on the September 15 vote. The clearest regulatory tailwind it has had.
  • $MSTR. Up about 13 percent with the reclaim. The leverage proxy that moves first when the coin turns.
  • $HYPE. Perps up 20.9 percent on the CFTC onshore nod, daily revenue back above $4 million, fee switch about five days out. The catalyst trade on the book.
  • $GLXY. Up 15 percent in two days on the BTC rip, with the CoreWeave lease and the Etched stake now paying.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] The buyback bounce faded in a day and Iran turned the screw
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The 30-year gave back most of its relief move, US debt crossed $40 trillion, and an economic war declaration sent Brent back above $92.
item.content:encoded:
The 30-year gave back most of its relief move, US debt crossed $40 trillion, and an economic war declaration sent Brent back above $92.

Yesterday the Treasury stepped in and the long end caught a bid. Today the market decided the bid was not the answer, it was the bounce. The 30-year gave back most of the buyback relief, the 10-year erased its entire post-announcement rally in under a day, and on the same session Iran escalated to an economic war declaration that pushed Brent back above $92. The regime-change question is back where it started, plus a $40 trillion debt milestone and a hot data print.

Market context. The buyback relief was real for exactly one session. Per the People list, the 30-year fell 9 basis points Wednesday to 5.19 percent, then climbed back as much as 7 basis points today to 5.27 percent, taking back most of the move. Per the Financial Markets list, the 10-year erased its entire post-buyback rally in under a day. Oil was the real mover: Per the Financial Markets list, Brent pushed back above $92 a barrel on the Iran escalation. Jobless claims came in at 206,000 against 210,000 expected, and Per the Market list the Philly Fed printed 47.4 against 25 expected, a Goldilocks read the market read as slightly dovish. A trading weekday, so the recap is live.

The scoreboard. The oil call that went live into the week resolved today, and it resolved on the escalation side: Per the Polymarket list, Iran's economic-war declaration sent Brent back above $92, against the Hormuz shipping-traffic plan. The call is a hit, and the Iran thread stays the swing variable into the September 15 vote.

1. The long end rejected the Treasury's rescue and that is the signal. Per the People list, the 30-year climbed back to 5.27 percent and took back most of the buyback move, and Per the Financial Markets list the 10-year erased its entire relief rally in under a day. A liquidity operation that the market prices back within 24 hours is not a regime change, it is a sticking plaster. Bessent Per the Financial Markets list framed the buybacks as routine, able to exceed the $4 billion and available as unlimited liquidity, while JPMorgan called the program lacking in credibility and the reaction function broken. When the operator and the Street disagree this hard, the long end is still the argument in progress, not a settled one.

2. US debt crossed $40 trillion and the buyback is the answer to it. Per the Financial Markets list, the national debt broke $40 trillion for the first time, roughly $119,699 a person, up more than $17 trillion since 2020. The list notes net interest already runs past $1.1 trillion. This is the fiscal backdrop the buyback is trying to manage: a Treasury that floods the long end to hold down the cost of its own debt while the books keep growing. The 30-year at 5.27 percent, having rejected the first rescue, is the market voting on whether that arithmetic holds.

3. Iran declared economic war and oil is the transmission. Per the Polymarket list, Trump announced the most crushing economic operation ever taken against a country, an economic D-Day of sanctions against any lifeline, with Bessent saying the goal is to collapse the regime. Oil reacted: Per the Financial Markets list, Brent pushed back above $92 a barrel. This is the escalation side of the Hormuz question the book has carried all week, and it lands exactly when the long end is rejecting its rescue. An oil shock is the one input that makes the Fed's hike path concrete, so the two threads, rates and the strait, are now braided together.

4. The data turned Goldilocks and the Fed reads it as room to hold. Per the Market list, jobless claims came in at 206,000 against 210,000 expected and the Philly Fed beat hard at 47.4 against 25. The read across the book is roughly a 70 percent chance the Fed holds in September, with the FOMC minutes flagged as willing to hike again if inflation reaccelerates. A strong economy plus a broken long end is exactly the setup where Warsh has room to hold rather than chase, and where an oil spike changes the math in a hurry.

5. What to watch: whether oil holds and the long end holds the line. The buyback bounced and failed within a day, so the market still needs to see whether the 30-year at 5.27 percent stabilizes or rolls back toward the 5.3 handle that started this. Oil is the second clock: a Brent print above $92 that sticks turns the Iran escalation into a persistent input, and the reopening odds are the market's honest number on how much of this is posturing. Tomorrow's oil call, the Sept 9 buyback launch and the September 15 Clarity vote are the three dates that decide the regime.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] Moderna just delivered the best trading day in its history
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The first positive Phase 3 result ever for a personalized cancer vaccine doubled the stock and flipped the tape toward biotech while the Treasury broke the long end.
item.content:encoded:
The first positive Phase 3 result ever for a personalized cancer vaccine doubled the stock and flipped the tape toward biotech while the Treasury broke the long end.

The AI selloff is not what broke today. Moderna did, on a cancer vaccine, and the Treasury did, by buying the long end. The stock doubled on the first positive Phase 3 result ever for a personalized cancer vaccine, and the rate regime that had been crushing everything reversed hard. This is the read on a session where the AI trade stopped being the only story in the room.

Market context. After the Treasury doubled long-end buybacks, the S&P turned positive to near 7,724 and the semis caught a bid off their lows, with the Philadelphia index reversing from down 5 percent to roughly flat. Per the MARKET OPEN stream, Moderna doubled, lifting the biotech complex, Eli Lilly touched a $1.2 trillion market cap, and the rotation into non-AI was the day's theme. The 30-year fell below 5.20 percent, the fuel for the risk-on turn. Retail earnings are midweek with Walmart Wednesday and Target and Lowe's.

The scoreboard. The Treasury buyback answered this week's macro call before the Fed minutes printed, and it is why the AI names stopped falling. On the book's own names, the $CRWV put-selling thesis is due Friday at $80, and CoreWeave has been the most-battered of the AI infra names through the selloff, so the next two days decide it.

1. Moderna had the best day of its corporate life and it rewrote biotech. Per the People list, Moderna's personalized mRNA cancer vaccine, built from each patient's tumor mutations and paired with Merck's Keytruda, hit the first positive Phase 3 result ever for such a therapy, in resected stage IIB to IV melanoma. The stock more than doubled, up as much as 127 percent to $143 intraday, on its best single day ever. Merck rose 10 to 12 percent on the read-through, and Barclays sees a $3 billion therapy by 2035.

The ripple was the point. Per the People list, the biotech ETF is up 32.5 percent since late March and 54 percent year over year, more than double the Nasdaq. Eli Lilly hit a $1.2 trillion market cap. Personalis, the maker of the MRD test used in the trial, rose 20 percent. This is the kind of catalyst the healthcare section exists to catch, and it arrived on a day the whole complex had been waiting for.

2. Anthropic is now the biggest AI lab by revenue and OpenAI just lost the lead. Per the NVIDIA $200B video, Anthropic more than doubled its quarterly revenue to $11.6 billion, overtaking OpenAI, whose revenue rose 18 percent quarter over quarter to $6.7 billion while its operating loss widened to $12.3 billion. Anthropic swung to a small operating profit and is heading to a September IPO that Polymarket prices at 87 percent by the end of the year, up from 60 percent in July. The AI leadership race just flipped, and it is happening into the listing.

The mechanism is worth naming because it changes the Nvidia read. Per the Stock list, AWS Bedrock drives 45 percent of Anthropic's API revenue, so the compute demand behind the AI buildout is now concentrated in the winner of the revenue race, not the biggest spender. If OpenAI stumbles, the fungible capacity just goes to Anthropic. That is the strongest version of the Nvidia compute thesis there is.

3. Marvell gave Google a warrant and the semis found a floor. Per the People list, Marvell issued Google a warrant for up to 58,970,907 shares at $206.58, roughly 7 percent of the company, tied to custom chip revenue through 2033 that could run to $120 billion. The stock rose 13 percent on the day while Broadcom fell 5 percent, the clearest signal yet that the custom-silicon winners are the AI trade that survives a repricing. Google gets the silicon and Marvell gets the locked-in buyer, and the market paid for that today.

The semis had been the epicenter of the selloff, down 8 to 11 percent across the memory and AI names on the long-end spike, but the Treasury buyback took the 10-year back down and the complex caught a bid into the close. This is the rates rotation doing its work: the same long-end driver that crushed semis on Monday reversed today, and the group that fell furthest bounced hardest.

4. The rotation is the real theme and the buyback just accelerated it. Per the People list, the money has been leaving AI for healthcare, staples, and dividend payers, and today's biotech blowout is the cleanest expression of it. The flow shows the SPY call wall stacked at 775 with $2.2 billion of open interest, and the rotation names, Uber, SoFi, and the fintechs, are the ones drawing the bid.

The earnings calendar is the non-AI catalyst on it. Walmart reports Wednesday, Target and Lowe's Thursday, and a Walmart print that holds would confirm the household-spending read the rotation has been betting on. The house view is unchanged: this is a rates rotation first and a sector story second, and a long end that policy is now actively capping is fuel for the money leaving AI.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $MRNA. More than doubled on the first positive Phase 3 cancer vaccine, with Merck's Keytruda and a $3 billion therapy by 2035. The best single day in its history.
  • $MRK. Up 10 to 12 percent on the same trial. The read-through that the whole oncology complex is repricing on.
  • $MRVL. Up 13 percent after handing Google a warrant for 7 percent of the company against up to $120 billion of custom chips. The survivor of the custom-silicon trade.
  • $SPCX. Back above its $135 IPO, up 39 percent off the lows, with the first lockup tranche done and more hitting into December. The AI-factory and Starlink compounder.
  • $PLTR. Sovereign AI is the trusted-layer thesis, up 2 percent into the buyback bid with the government and commercial lines both accelerating.
  • $WMT. Reports Wednesday as the broadest read on household spending, into a tape that is rotating toward exactly the consumer names.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] Bitcoin caught the Treasury's bid and forced the biggest short squeeze in its history
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: BTC ripped to $69,500 on $1.1 billion of short liquidations as the buyback news turned the tape, and ETH reclaimed $2,000 into the White House summit.
item.content:encoded:
BTC ripped to $69,500 on $1.1 billion of short liquidations as the buyback news turned the tape, and ETH reclaimed $2,000 into the White House summit.

Bitcoin had been waiting for a reason and the Treasury handed it one. The announcement that long-end buybacks would double flipped the debasement trade back on, and Bitcoin ripped to $69,500, its best day since February, on more than a billion dollars of short liquidations. ETH reclaimed $2,000. This is the read on a tape that finally caught the bid Macro has been arguing for all week.

Market context. Per the Polymarket list, Bitcoin surged above $68,000 and closed toward $69,500, its best day since February 2026, as the Treasury buyback news broke the dollar to a three-month low. Per the Financial Markets list, more than $1.1 billion of crypto shorts were liquidated in a single hour, the largest one-day squeeze of the cycle. ETH reclaimed $2,000 with Per the People list, its highest close since May. The proxy equities ripped with it, Coinbase up 12 percent and Strategy up 13 percent. The White House crypto summit is today at 2:30pm.

The scoreboard. The house call from the weekend, that Bitcoin needs a daily close above $67,000 to invalidate the bear side, is now very much in play: the reclaim of $69,500 intraday clears it, and a close here would be the first bullish signal since the 200-week break. The White House meeting call, the catalyst that could move the Clarity pricing Coinbase is a guest at, resolves today, and the market has already repriced the pass odds hard against it.

1. The Treasury buyback is the bid Bitcoin was waiting for. The mechanism is the same one Macro has been driving all week: the dollar broke to a three-month low on the buyback news, and the debasement trade, gold up 3.5 percent, silver stronger, Bitcoin up 6 to 7 percent, all fired together. Per the Financial Markets list, more than $1.1 billion of shorts were liquidated in an hour, with the largest on-chain short at $117 million among those hit. That is the first time since the 200-week break that the bears are the ones feeling it.

The flows agree. Spot ETF inflows resumed on the move, and the day's signal is that the reclaim happened with volume behind it rather than on a thin bid. The house reads it as the strongest leg up since the range broke, and the $63,500 to $65,000 zone that was resistance is now support.

2. ETH reclaimed $2,000 and the flows turned with it. Per the People list, Ether crossed $2,000 with its highest close since May, and the move carried the whole majors tape. The spot ETH ETFs turned positive on the day, and the reclaim is the alt-side confirmation that the squeeze was broad rather than a one-coin event.

The infrastructure story underneath keeps compounding. Per the People list, BlackRock's IBIT holders redeemed only 0.2 percent of their holdings through the drawdown, a revealed preference that the institutional bid never left, and the fund keeps mirroring the gold-ETF adoption path that took 2004 through a decade of flows. That is the strongest version of the structural thesis, that the institutional buyer is patient even when the price is not.

3. The White House summit today and the SEC rule are the catalyst double. Per the Crypto list, the crypto and prediction-market executives meet the president today at 2:30pm, with Ripple, Coinbase, Kraken and Chainlink among the names in the room. Into it, the SEC proposed Per the People list, a new Regulation Crypto Assets framework, tailored exemptions up to $5 million one-time over four years and $75 million annually, a conditional safe harbor, and preemption of state securities laws, with chair Atkins calling it the most historic step yet to modernize crypto securities regulation.

The Clarity pricing is the mispricing the house has been flagging. Per the Kalshi list, the odds the Clarity Act passes this year collapsed to 23 percent from 90 percent, with the Senate vote September 15, and Per the Polymarket list, Polymarket prices it at 20 percent, down from about 50 percent in July. The market prices it to fail. That is exactly the setup where a surprise pass, or even a compromise out of today's meeting, reprices the entire alt book violently.

4. The miners are the money the rotation left behind and the proxy equities confirm it. Per the People list, Strategy is up 13 percent and Coinbase 12 percent to $164 on the day, the clearest confirmation that the squeeze hit the leverage proxies first. The 13F shift into the miners, Druckenmiller opening Bitdeer, Riot, Hut 8 and IREN, remains the institutional read that the mining complex is repricing from Bitcoin leverage to AI-revenue infrastructure, even as the miners themselves keep selling the coin to fund it.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. Ripped to $69,500 on the biggest short squeeze of the cycle. The bear side invalidates on a daily close above $67,000, and this is the strongest attempt yet.
  • $ETH. Back over $2,000 with the highest close since May. The alt side of a broad squeeze.
  • $COIN. Up 12 percent to $164 and a named guest at today's White House summit. The clearest regulatory tailwind it has had in months.
  • $MSTR. Up 13 percent with the squeeze, the leverage proxy that moves fastest when the coin finally turns.
  • $HYPE. The $200 million-a-year fee switch turns on in about ten days. The one alt printing real revenue into a rotation.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] The Treasury stepped in and the long end broke the other way
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Buybacks double to $4 billion an operation and the 30-year falls below 5.2 percent, gold jumps 3.5 percent, and the dollar hits a three-month low.
item.content:encoded:
Buybacks double to $4 billion an operation and the 30-year falls below 5.2 percent, gold jumps 3.5 percent, and the dollar hits a three-month low.

Yesterday the question was whether the long end could keep selling into data that should have helped it. Today the Treasury answered, and it answered by stepping in: buybacks on 10- to 30-year debt double to $4 billion a run starting September 9, the 30-year broke below 5.20 percent, and the debasement hedges that broke yesterday came roaring back. The minutes land this afternoon as the second act.

Market context. The buyback announcement was the whole tape. Per the People list, the 30-year fell 8 basis points, gold rose 3.5 percent, and the dollar dropped 0.7 percent, with Bitcoin ripping higher on a record short squeeze. Per the Polymarket list, the 30-year fell below 5.20 percent, and the dollar hit its lowest level in over three months. Copper sits at a record near $6.77 a pound. Per the Financial Markets list, crude stockpiles rose 4.4 million barrels to 428.8 million, a third straight build and the highest since May, even as Iran tensions stay hot. The Fed minutes land at 2pm. This is a trading weekday, so the recap is live.

The scoreboard. The call that anchored this week, that the 30-year at 5.3 percent would decide between regime change and a pullback, got its first real answer today and it was the pullback side: the Treasury doubled the buybacks and the long end caught a bid before the minutes even printed. The oil call is still live into Friday, with the crude build and the Hormuz blockade both unresolved.

1. The Treasury decided the long end would not run and the whole trade flipped. The mechanism is direct. Per the People list, the Treasury is at least doubling the size of its liquidity-support buybacks on longer-dated debt, to $4 billion per operation from $2 billion, effective September 9. That is the government buying the bond it had been flooding, and the market read it exactly as the hedge reversal: the 30-year fell 8 basis points and gold, which broke with the long end yesterday, jumped 3.5 percent.

The read is split on what it means. Per the Polymarket list, one camp calls it liquidity support, not QE, the argument being it eases the back of the curve rather than expanding the balance sheet. The other calls it the first move of fiscal dominance, with Per the Kalshi list, gold adding $3.5 trillion to its market cap in 21 days, up 12.5 percent. Either way, the line the house has watched all week, the long end as the driver that breaks the hedges, has now been answered by policy.

2. The Fed minutes land at 2pm and they are the second act. The buyback took the long end down before the minutes could, but the minutes are still the test of whether this is regime change or a managed pullback. The market had already priced the world they have to confirm or deny: the 30-year is back under 5.20 percent, and the question hanging over the book is whether Warsh can hike into a Treasury that is now buying its own long end.

Per Into the Cryptoverse, Benjamin Cowen still reads the rate-cutting cycle as over, with a hike before year-end and the Fed holding at 4 percent through 2027, and he makes the contrarian call that the dollar rallies near term toward 105 to 106 before the next leg down. That is the direct counter to the dollar trade today, and the minutes are the arbiter.

3. The dollar broke to a three-month low and the yen carry is the next shoe. The DXY drop is the tell on how far the buyback news reached: Per the People list, the dollar fell 0.7 percent to its lowest in more than three months on the same day the Treasury moved. The bearish dollar call now has a policy catalyst behind it, but the setup underneath is unchanged.

Per the overnight trading video, Japan's 30-year surged above 4 percent and the BOJ's intervention level sits at 163, the next test if 160 breaks. The carry trade borrows from Japan near 1 percent to buy US long end near 5 percent, and that spread is what keeps the unwind risk live. A Treasury that bids its own long end makes the carry more attractive, not less, and that is the next shoe on this desk.

4. Oil holds Hormuz and the swing is still two-way. The crude build is a real easing signal on supply. Per the Financial Markets list, crude stockpiles rose 4.4 million barrels to 428.8 million, a third straight increase and the highest since May, and that is the de-escalation input that helps the long end. It is not breaking the war risk. Trump has halted the Iran talks and moved to the strangle posture, the UAE has suspended trade with Iran, and the blockade stands with Hormuz open and its mines removed. Per the Polymarket list, Hormuz traffic returning to normal by the end of the year sits at 37 percent, so the market still prices a meaningful chance of a deal.

That is the same two-way open the house flagged Friday, and it is still open: the build helps the long end while a fresh strike would push oil toward the $100 forecasts and confirm the regime.

5. What to watch: the minutes, then whether gold holds. The buyback is the strongest signal yet that the long end is a policy fight, not a free fall, and gold holding its 3.5 percent gain through the minutes would confirm the hedge trade is back. Cowen's dollar-higher read is the contrarian test on the other side. The minutes answer the rates half, the next oil print answers the commodity half, and the two together decide whether today was the regime reversal or just the first buyback bounce.

Fed minutes at 2pm. The long end against gold is the trade this book has been watching all week.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] Memory held the line while the rest of AI sold off
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Micron ran another 5 percent back above $1,000 with UBS at $1,625, Nvidia caught a buy-the-dip, and the rotation into retail and dividends kept running.
item.content:encoded:
Micron ran another 5 percent back above $1,000 with UBS at $1,625, Nvidia caught a buy-the-dip, and the rotation into retail and dividends kept running.

Monday was the memory tape with everything green behind it. Tuesday is the divergence: Micron held and led while the rest of the AI complex sold off hard, and the money that left AI did not leave the market, it rotated. This is the read on a session that separated the memory trade from the AI trade.

Market context. The S&P is down about half a percent with the Nasdaq off more, and Per the Market list, the weakness is concentrated in the AI names: QQQ down near 2 percent, SOXL down almost 20 percent, SNDK down 8 percent after a 90 percent run, Nvidia flat to down near $219. Micron went the other way, up 5 percent and back above $1,000. Energy was the only green sector Monday, and the rotation this morning is out of AI into dividend payers and retail. Retail earnings kick off Tuesday with Home Depot.

1. Memory is the one AI pocket that held, and the Street is still raising targets. Per the Stocks list, Micron ran another 5 percent to sit back above $1,000, with BofA modeling $188.6 billion of free cash flow by 2030 against $55.7 billion this year, JPMorgan at $1,540 on $154 of 2028 EPS, and options targeting $1,050 to $1,075. Per the People to follow list, UBS goes further, at $1,625, arguing the market is treating Micron like a normal memory cycle while AI makes memory far more critical. The stock trades about six times forward earnings.

The supply story underneath is unchanged and getting tighter: Micron can serve only 50 to 66 percent of data-center demand, UBS models HBM prices up 79 percent year over year, and the CEO says 2027 constraints are worse than 2026. SanDisk is the mirror image, down 8 percent after a 90 percent move off the $970s, and the divergence is the cleanest read on who is chasing versus who is already in. The memory trade is now the AI pocket with a supply floor under it.

2. Nvidia caught a buy-the-dip and BofA made the case. BofA rates Nvidia a Buy with a $350 target against a price near $219 and calls the stock up to 50 percent undervalued. The nuance matters: the "despec" is not Nvidia wanting less memory, it is not being able to source it, and the roadmap still scales toward 500 gigabytes to a terabyte of HBM. That is a swing factor for Micron and SK Hynix rather than a demand problem.

The capex engine is not slowing: Per the Polymarket list, the big-five hyperscalers have $3.2 trillion locked into AI commitments, and BofA raised its AI infrastructure estimate 17 percent in one month to $3.6 trillion through 2028. Nvidia reports August 26, and the buy-the-dip consensus is now the positioning into it. The counter is the leveraged-ETF flows: Per Capital Flows Research, flows into the Micron and SanDisk products show the dip got bought, not capitulated, with one-week volatility below one-month saying the hedging is complacent at the highs.

3. The rotation is real and it is out of AI into everything else. The tape is a clean rotation, profit taking out of the AI names into less loved areas, with Meta down 3.8 percent to $547.50 and now trading below 10 times this year's operating cash flow. Meta has been one of the cheapest megacap AI names, and it is getting sold on a legal overhang, the Oakland trial and 29 state attorneys general, while the macro tape punishes the group. Google is down 12 of the last 15 weeks and Amazon 9 of the last 11 days.

The house read is that this is a rates rotation, not an earnings story: the selloff driver is the 10-year over 4.7 percent and the 30-year at 5.3 percent, the same backdrop that last took the S&P down 30 percent. Rate-sensitive, cheaper, cash-returning names are the beneficiaries, and that is where the marginal money is going.

4. The 13F books are confirming the same rotation. The filings added detail Tuesday: Per Money Stacking High with Luke, Berkshire holds $28 billion of Google after adding 24 million shares, up 45 percent, and Per the People to follow list, Druckenmiller closed his Intel and Micron positions and opened four Bitcoin miners, Bitdeer, Riot, Hut 8 and IREN. Ackman keeps Uber at 12 percent of his fund, Dalio's firm holds a billion of the SPY while selling the big semis, and the airlines and credit-card names stay the most bought. This is the consumer-and-fintech rotation the house has been calling the quarter's real theme, and it is now showing up in the books and in the tape at the same time.

5. Earnings week is the non-AI catalyst on the calendar. Per Josh, Home Depot reports Tuesday morning, Target and Lowe's Wednesday, Walmart and Deere and Alibaba Thursday, and Walmart is the broadest read on household spending, the first real consumer check in weeks. KKR agreed to buy UGI for $42.50 a share in a $9 billion deal, a cash buyout confirming that dividend infrastructure names still draw premium offers. The retail prints land into a rates tape where they could matter more than usual, because the market is rotating toward them.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $MU. Up 5 percent back above $1,000 with UBS at $1,625 and BofA modeling $188.6 billion of 2030 free cash flow. The one AI pocket with a supply floor.
  • $NVDA. BofA at $350 against $219, reading the memory despec as temporary. The buy-the-dip consensus into the August 26 print.
  • $SNDK. Down 8 percent after a 90 percent move off the $970s. The chase unwinding, and the divergence from Micron is the tell.
  • $CNDL. Per r/wallstreetbets, More than $8 million of insider buying on a $1.86 billion market cap in the last week after the stock fell from $96 to $34.50 and bounced to $41. A small-cap insider cluster.
  • $HD. The first big consumer print of the week Tuesday, into a tape that is rotating toward retail and dividend names.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] Bitcoin broke back over $65,000 and forced a big short to cover
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The squeeze came with ETF flows turning positive and a named short at $117 million partially liquidated, into the White House meeting tomorrow.
item.content:encoded:
The squeeze came with ETF flows turning positive and a named short at $117 million partially liquidated, into the White House meeting tomorrow.

Bitcoin reclaimed $65,000 Tuesday, and for the first time in weeks the move had a crowd on the wrong side of it: a short at $117 million got partially liquidated and the ETF flows turned positive on the same day. The White House meeting lands tomorrow and the Clarity vote math is still on the table. This is the read on a tape that finally caught a bid.

Market context. Bitcoin broke above $65,000 with Per the Crypto list, spot ETFs taking in $284 million on the day, net positive $777.6 million across August 3 to 17, and the largest on-chain BTC short at $117 million partially liquidated as price crossed the level. The move reverses the down tape: Bitcoin is now less volatile than the Nasdaq. Ether is up near $1,900 and Hyperliquid near $593. This is a trading weekday, so the recap is live.

The scoreboard. The week's due catalyst on this book is the White House crypto meeting Wednesday, the call that could move the Clarity pricing Coinbase is a guest at. The house call from the weekend, that Bitcoin needs a daily close above $67,000 to invalidate the bear side, is still open, but the reclaim of $65,000 is the first bullish step and it happened with volume behind it.

1. Bitcoin broke $65,000 and the short got squeezed. The day's signal is that the move finally hurt someone: Gambler 0x8c96's 1,800 Bitcoin short at $117 million was partially liquidated, 360 coins for $23.36 million, with the new liquidation price reset to $65,041. That is the squeeze the range had been setting up, and it is the first time since the 200-week break that the bears are the ones feeling it.

The flows agree. Spot ETFs took in 4,436 Bitcoin on the day, about $284 million, and stayed net positive $777.6 million across August 3 to 17. The house reads the reclaim as the first leg, not the all-clear: the bear side is invalidated on a daily close above $67,000, and the $63,500 to $65,000 zone is now support rather than resistance.

2. The White House meeting tomorrow is the catalyst, and Clarity is the mispricing. Per the Crypto list, The crypto and prediction-market executives meet the president Wednesday, August 19, with Coinbase, Polymarket, Ripple and Gemini alongside the exchanges and the DTCC. John Gillen calls it the market's biggest mispricing: Per Milk Road Show, the entire market assigns less than a 10 percent chance the Clarity Act passes, Galaxy revised its estimate from 75 percent to 10 percent for 2026, and a compromise out of Wednesday's meeting would be a violent repricing.

The setup into it is unchanged: the Senate votes September 15 at 2:00pm, and the market prices it mostly to fail. The house read has not moved: a pass is priced for failure, the upside of a surprise is not, and the meeting is the thing that moves the number this week.

3. The big money rotated into the miners. The 13F filings confirmed a real shift: Per the People to follow list, Druckenmiller closed his Intel and Micron positions and opened four Bitcoin miners, Bitdeer, Riot, Hut 8 and IREN. That is the institutional side of the same rotation Macro laid out, money leaving the crowded semis for the AI-infrastructure miners.

The counterpart is that the miners themselves are still selling the coin. Per the Crypto list, Riot sold 9,665 Bitcoin for $732.46 million in the first half of 2026 at an average price of $75,785, funding the pivot to AI hosting that Druckenmiller is now buying. The narrative is consistent, that the miners are repriced from Bitcoin leverage to AI revenue, and the smart money is following the repricing.

4. The infrastructure keeps compounding while the majors turn. The plumbing story is the live structural trade and it kept building Tuesday. Per the Stocks list, Robinhood Chain launched in July and has already crossed $1 billion in daily volume, with BlackRock's BUIDL and JPMorgan's Onyx building on Ethereum. The house keeps flagging the same shape, that this is the part of the market compounding while the majors trade flat, and it is the closest thing crypto has to a structural bid.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. Back over $65,000 with a named short squeezed and ETF flows positive. The bear side invalidates on a daily close above $67,000.
  • $MSTR. Still selling into the range and buying no coin, the premium compressing toward the treasury it holds.
  • $COIN. A named guest at tomorrow's White House meeting, the clearest regulatory tailwind it has had in months.
  • $RIOT. The miner that sold $732 million of Bitcoin and is now the AI-revenue name Druckenmiller opened.
  • $HYPE. The $200 million-a-year fee switch turns on in about ten days. The one alt printing real revenue.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] The long end is now the story and it is taking everything with it
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Ten-year yields crossed 4.7 percent, gold and silver fell on the move, and the Fed minutes land Wednesday as the test of the regime.
item.content:encoded:
Ten-year yields crossed 4.7 percent, gold and silver fell on the move, and the Fed minutes land Wednesday as the test of the regime.

Yesterday the question was whether the long end could keep selling into data that should have helped it. Today it answered: Per the Market list, ten-year yields crossed 4.7 percent, the 30-year sat at 5.3 percent, and for the first time this cycle the debasement hedges broke with it, gold down 1 percent and silver down 3 percent. The minutes are tomorrow and they are now the fulcrum of the whole tape.

Market context. The 30-year is at 5.3 percent, the highest since 2007, and the 10-year near 4.73 percent with Yardeni calling 5 percent the key line. Gold sits at $4,362.79, down 1 percent, silver at $63.72, down 3 percent, copper at a record above $6.77 a pound. Oil is above $91 with Per the Financial Markets list, Trump saying there are no Iran talks and the Hormuz blockade stands. Pending home sales fell 2.3 percent in July against a 0.6 percent expectation. The Fed minutes land Wednesday.

The scoreboard. On the 28th I carried Anas Alhajji's call that the July 27 Abqaiq strike was inflated by recycled 2019 reporting, and it proved out: the strikes were real but far short of 2019, and the oil story has moved on to the Hormuz blockade with crude above $91. The week's due catalysts on this book are the Fed minutes Wednesday, the call that decides whether the 30-year at 5.3 percent is regime change or a pullback, and the oil call due Friday, with crude above $91 and Trump confirming he is not extending the Iran deal.

1. The long end is the driver and today it broke the hedges. The 30-year at 5.3 percent was the story, and the day's signal is what it did to the assets that were supposed to hedge it. Gold fell 1 percent to $4,362.79 and silver fell 3 percent to $63.72 as yields rose, the exact trade the house flagged when the 30-year kept selling into soft data. Yardeni has the line at 5 percent on the 10-year, with the range at 4 to 5 percent and anything above 5 percent the concern.

The mechanism underneath has not changed: Per the Financial Markets list, US interest payments are now 3.3 percent of GDP, the highest level in history, and $1.4 trillion over the past year, nearly triple what they were in 2020. That is the funding cost the long end keeps pricing, and it is why the hedge trade is now the long end's victim rather than its escape.

2. The Fed minutes Wednesday decide whether this is regime change. The call the house has been building toward all week lands tomorrow. The minutes cover the decision that cut September hike odds toward 30 percent, and they are the test of whether Warsh is the one moving the 30-year. The market is already pricing the world the minutes have to confirm or deny: Per the People to follow list, Polymarket sits at 76 percent no Fed change in September against 24 percent for a hike, down from 43 percent a week ago.

Per Benjamin Cowen, Benjamin Cowen reads the rate-cutting cycle as over, expects a 25-basis-point hike in September or December, and models a 10 to 20 percent stock correction as the base case that lets Bitcoin find its cycle bottom. The house does not fully sign onto the correction size, but the direction of his argument is the same one the long end is making: the last cut was 2025, and the data is now pushing the other way.

3. Japan is the next shoe and it got louder. Per the Stocks list, Japan's 10-year sits near 2.95 percent, a 30-year high and a level unseen since 1996, and the 30-year has surged above 4 percent for the first time in history. The carry trade is the mechanism: Per the Japan video, borrow from Japan at 1 percent, put it in US Treasuries at 3.75 percent up to a little above 5 percent, and keep the spread, with Japan holding more than $1.1 trillion of US Treasuries. The carry unwind is the largest tail risk on the desk, and Per Capital Flows Research, Capital Flows flags it alongside rate volatility as the two risks nobody is hedged for.

The yen rescue has already moved up the ladder: Japan holds more than $1.1 trillion of US Treasuries and the Fed's FIMA repo can lend up to $60 billion. The house read holds, that the next yen defence needs the BOJ itself, and a September hike into an already-blowing global long end is the cross-rate pressure that finds the dollar.

4. Oil holds Hormuz and the war risk is two-way. Trump says there are no Iran talks, the naval blockade stands, and Hormuz is open with all mines removed. Oil sits above $91 with the diesel crack at a record $102, and Per the Kalshi list, Monday's only green S&P sector was energy, rising more than $2 a barrel on the renewed tensions. The Per the Polymarket list, strategic reserve is at 293.4 million barrels, the lowest since 1982.

This is the swing variable into the Fed minutes. A de-escalation drops the inflation input and gives the long end a reason to catch a bid. A further strike pushes oil toward the $100 forecasts and confirms the regime. The two-way open the house flagged Friday is still open.

5. What to watch: the minutes, then the long end against gold. The minutes land Wednesday, and the higher-signal tell is whether gold holds with them. Gold down on the same day yields rise is the debasement trade getting tested, and that is the real question: does the long end keep breaking the non-yield assets, or does gold reassert as the reserve bid. Copper at a record says the inflation bid is alive even as the metal hedges sag. The minutes answer the rates half, the next oil print answers the commodity half, and the two together decide if this is regime change or a pullback.

Fed minutes Wednesday. The long end against gold is the trade the whole book is watching.
