item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] Micron is back over $1,000 and JPMorgan just made the bull case bigger
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The memory trade led Monday on a $1,540 target, AMAT guided its first ten-billion quarter, and the 13F books are agreeing with the buildout.
item.content:encoded:
The memory trade led Monday on a $1,540 target, AMAT guided its first ten-billion quarter, and the 13F books are agreeing with the buildout.

Monday the memory trade was the tape again, only this time it carried a number that was not there Friday: Micron reclaimed $1,000 and the Street raised the top of the case. The financing story under it is unchanged, and the 13F money is still stacking the same names. This is the read on a session that re-risked the complex.

Market context. The S&P opened near a record just under 7,900 with the Dow down and the Nasdaq up, and the day's action was all in the AI complex. Micron broke back above $1,000, SanDisk ran 11 percent, Cerebras was the biggest gainer at plus 7.8 percent, Marvell traded to $235, and the SK Hynix ADR rose 4 percent. Nvidia sat flat near $225 into its August 26 earnings. Reddit joins the S&P 500 on August 18, and equity options get their first full pre-market session Monday.

The scoreboard. On the 14th I said Micron needed a close above $991 to confirm the next leg toward $1,022. It reclaimed $1,000 on Monday, clearing the level. The 1022 ladder is now the live map, and the next test is the August 26 Nvidia print.

1. Micron is back over $1,000 and JPMorgan gave the bull a fresh target. The day's headline was JPMorgan raising its Micron price target from $550 to $1,540 as the stock reclaimed $1,000, now about 17 percent off its high.

The Micron chief business officer says Per the Market list, 2027 is even tighter than 2026, with NAND prices having roughly doubled in the back half of the year, and BofA's model puts Per the Stocks list, Micron at $236 of fiscal-2030 EPS on 80 percent margins against a consensus of $136. The numbers underneath are doing the work: Micron printed quarterly revenue of $41.5 billion, up 346 percent, $25.11 of adjusted EPS and an 84.9 percent gross margin, and the 16 long-term agreements cover roughly $100 billion of contracted revenue through 2030. The stock trades about six times forward earnings. The resistance ladder is 1022, 1064, 1082, 1121 and 1155, and Micron ran to 991 overnight Friday.

2. AMAT guided its first ten-billion quarter and China is back in the mix. The name under the memory tape that barely got credit is Per Chip Stock Investor, Applied Materials, which guided to its first-ever quarter above $10 billion, more than 50 percent growth at the midpoint, with China back in growth mode at 26 percent of systems and services. It reported Q3 revenue of $9.1 billion, up 25 percent, with gross margin at 50 percent, and says it is doubling system capacity by 2028. That is the equipment side of the same shortage, and it is cheaper than the memory names. The China piece matters twice: it is both a growth engine and the vector a decoupling policy could cut.

3. The financing architecture is the same and the counter-thesis is still live. The $500 billion Nvidia financing story did not move much Monday, but the roadmap did: Per the People to follow list, Nvidia cut its OpenAI data-center backing from $250 billion to under $120 billion and eyes up to $3 billion in SB Energy's Ohio campus. Michael Burry's residual-value counter-thesis is now the named bear: with Nvidia backstopping at most Per the Stocks list, 25 percent of residual value on the platforms, he puts the overstatement of industry profits at about $176 billion over 2026 to 2028. Nvidia reports August 26 with roughly $90 billion of revenue projected, and that filing is the next window for the counter-case.

4. The 13F rotation is the non-AI story of the quarter. The filings landed and the theme is not the AI names, it is who the big money is quietly leaving them for. Per the Polymarket list, Bill Ackman exited Google, trimmed Amazon, and added Meta, Uber and Netflix. Per MARKET OPEN stream, Dalio's firm bought a billion of the SPY while selling Nvidia, Broadcom, Amazon and Google, and Renaissance bought roughly a billion of Nvidia while loading Meta, Intel and Palantir.

The clearest single theme across the books is airlines and credit cards: Delta and United both being bought, Visa and Mastercard new positions, Ackman's Uber at 12 percent of his fund. That is the consumer-and-fintech rotation the house has been waiting for, and it is the part of this quarter that does not depend on the buildout.

5. Tesla is the earnings-grade contrarian that still sits low. Tesla printed record revenue of $28.24 billion, up 26 percent, on 480,126 deliveries, but the quality is poor: Per Rick Orford, operating income fell 57 percent to $398 million on a 1.4 percent margin, GAAP EPS came in at $0.33 against a $0.54 consensus, and free cash flow was negative. A $1 billion unrealized SpaceX gain is 22 cents of the EPS. The robo-taxi proof is the weak leg: only about 21 driverless vehicles running against Waymo's 3,800. The stock still trades near 270 times forward earnings. The bull case is the delivery beat plus a 2030s story. The bear case is a broken consumer and a stretched multiple. The asymmetry is wide and it is the cleanest non-AI setup on the board.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $MU. Back over $1,000 with JPMorgan at $1,540 and BofA's model at $236 of 2030 EPS. The 1022/1064/1082/1121/1155 ladder is the map into August 26.
  • $AMAT. First-ever $10 billion quarter guided, 26 percent China mix, doubling capacity. The cheaper way to play the same shortage.
  • $NVDA. Flat into August 26 earnings with the financing platform behind it and the Burry counter-thesis to track. The catalyst for the whole complex.
  • $TSLA. Record revenue hiding a 1.4 percent operating margin and a negative cash flow quarter. A stretched valuation with a live bear case and a live bull story.
  • $UBER. Ackman keeps adding, the free-cash-flow math gets to roughly $11 billion, and it is the consumer name the 13F money keeps returning to.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] Bitcoin closed under its 200-week line and the bottom debate got louder
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The break Cowen kept flagging is here, the Clarity vote is fifteen days out, and the White House crypto meeting lands midweek.
item.content:encoded:
The break Cowen kept flagging is here, the Clarity vote is fifteen days out, and the White House crypto meeting lands midweek.

Bitcoin closed below its 200-week moving average over the weekend and that is the level this whole range has been circling. The bulls have a named bottom, the bears have a flush target, and the week hands over the White House crypto meeting and the Clarity vote math. This is the read on a market that finally made a directional decision.

Market context. Bitcoin sits near $63,500, inside the $60,000 to $67,000 range it has held for months, with 60-day volatility down to 1.47 percent and spot volume thin. Ether held $1,750 and trades near $1,900. Dominance sits at 58.4 percent. The proxy names diverged again: the memory-and-AI trade ran Monday while crypto sat still. This is a trading weekday, so the recap is live: BTC flat near $63,500, ETH up about 1.5 percent, Hyperliquid at $593 up 4 percent.

The scoreboard. The week's due catalyst on this book is the White House crypto meeting Wednesday, the call that could move the CLARITY pricing Coinbase is a guest at. The setup into it: the vote is fifteen days out, Polymarket sits near 20 percent, and the market prices the bill to fail. A pass, or a surprise from the meeting, is the un-priced side.

1. Bitcoin closed below the 200-week and the levels are now in play. The technical event the range has been working toward arrived: Bitcoin closed below its 200-week moving average, and Per the Crypto list, Benjamin Cowen reads it as the mirror of mid-August 2022, a capitulation that bounced and then gave it up.

The bull side has a number: Per Zach Pandl, Grayscale's Zach Pandl says Bitcoin probably bottomed at $58,000, held through the Coldcard attack and falling Clarity odds. The bear side is Sykodelic short from $65,000 targeting $60,000, with a daily close above $67,000 invalidating it. The house reads this as a genuine fight: the 200-week is the bull-bear line, Pandl's $58,000 is the floor the bulls defend, and $60,000 is the flush level the bears need. Both sides have a falsifiable trigger and the range is finally wide enough to mean something.

2. Clarity is fifteen days out and the White House moves midweek. The Senate votes on the Clarity Act on September 15 at 2:00pm, and the market still prices it mostly to fail: Per the CLARITY video, Polymarket sits near 20 percent, down from an 80 percent peak in February, with Galaxy near 30 percent and TD Cowen near 25 percent.

The week's catalyst is Per the Crypto list, the White House hosting crypto and prediction-market executives Wednesday, with Coinbase, Polymarket, Ripple and Gemini alongside the exchanges and the DTCC, the clearest sign the administration is not waiting on the bill. The house read has not changed: a pass on the fifteenth is priced for failure, and the upside of a surprise is not. Matt Hougan still calls the bill a zombie that may never pass, and the trade is that the meeting, not the vote, moves the number this week.

3. Strategy keeps selling the same story and the market stopped caring. Per the Market list, Strategy sold 3.46 million shares raising $333.7 million and bought no Bitcoin, leaving its 840,447 coins untouched, while repurchasing $132.2 million of STRC. The treasury company is funding its preferred dividends and its STRC buybacks by selling the very asset the stock is a leveraged claim on, and the market is barely reacting. The one-year return through last Friday is minus 75 percent. This is the position-trade version of the CLARITY bet: the premium was the position, and it keeps compressing toward the coins it holds. The interesting data point is the quiet, that the sellers are no longer the story.

4. The infrastructure keeps compounding while the majors bleed. The plumbing story is the live structural trade. Tokenized ETF market cap is up 826 percent year over year to $611.5 million, tokenized real-world assets sit at $44.7 billion on-chain, and tokenized stocks now have 1.4 million holders. On the stablecoin side, crypto-card spend hit $759 million in July, up from $306 million a year earlier, and the stablecoins on Robinhood Chain passed $650 million in weeks. The house keeps flagging the same shape: this is the part of the market compounding while the majors trade flat, and it is the closest thing crypto has to a structural bid.

5. Hyperliquid is the alt that is actually putting up revenue. The one alt with real numbers keeps showing them. Hyperliquid's fee switch turns on in about ten days, a roughly $200 million a year revenue stream going back to token holders, and fomo flipped it in 24-hour revenue. The alt coin that is buyback-and-burn rather than borrow-and-pray is the bull case, and it trades at $593 up 4 percent. It is the one name in the tier that does not need the next narrative, it is printing.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. Closed under the 200-week into $60,000 to $67,000, with Pandl's $58,000 bottom and Sykodelic's $60,000 flush on opposite sides. The Clarity vote on the fifteenth is the binary.
  • $MSTR. Selling $333.7 million of stock, buying no Bitcoin, repurchasing STRC. The premium is the position and it keeps compressing.
  • $COIN. A named guest at Wednesday's White House meeting, the clearest regulatory tailwind it has had in months.
  • $HYPE. The $200 million-a-year fee switch turns on in about ten days. The one alt printing real revenue.
  • $ETH. Holding $1,750 against the 9-month downtrend with whale accumulation underneath and a $2,400 range-high target.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] The long end is still blowing out and retail just made it worse
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The 30-year auctioned at the highest yield since 2001 into a 0.6 percent retail drop, gold keeps taking the hedge trade, and Japan is the next shoe.
item.content:encoded:
The 30-year auctioned at the highest yield since 2001 into a 0.6 percent retail drop, gold keeps taking the hedge trade, and Japan is the next shoe.

The long end was the story Friday and it is the story again Monday, only now it is colliding with the weakest retail print in over a year. That collision is the day's driver, and the dollar and gold are already voting on the side of it. This is the session that turned the regime tension into a direction.

Market context. The 30-year auctioned Monday at 5.216 percent, the highest yield on a sale since 2001, against a spot that sits near 5.3 percent. The 10-year is at 4.69 percent. Retail sales fell 0.6 percent in July, the worst month since May 2025, yet the long end did not bid. That is the whole message. Gold is at $4,410 and re-accelerating, the dollar is rolling over from 101, and Japan's 10-year hit 2.93 percent, the highest since 1996, with an 80 percent chance of a September hike priced. The Fed minutes land Wednesday.

The scoreboard. The week's due catalyst on this book is the Fed minutes Wednesday, the call that decides whether the 30-year at 5.3 percent is regime change or a pullback. The session moved the setup: July retail at minus 0.6 percent cut September hike odds toward 30 percent, so the long end, not September, is the event the minutes are really testing.

1. The long end is the regime and retail could not save it. The 30-year auctioned at 5.216 percent, the highest since 2001, and the longer-duration bond ETF is down 63 percent from its March 2020 peak as the 30-year went from an all-time low of 0.8 percent then to 5.3 percent now.

The signal in Monday's tape is what did not happen: retail sales fell 0.6 percent in July, the sharpest drop since May 2025, and the long end still would not rally on it. A bond market that cannot catch a bid on soft data is a market telling you nominal growth is running hotter than the prints, and that is the funding cost story underneath everything. The US debt sits closing in on $40 trillion and corporate equity is more than 400 percent of GDP, nearly double the dot-com peak. Capital Flows has the framing the week needed: September is a distraction, the long end is the event.

2. Gold is the hedge that moved, and BofA is leaning on it. The split the house flagged all week is now two-sided. BofA's Michael Hartnett calls the trade "long gold," as the best hedge against dollar weakness, bond losses and asset inflation, and gold funds took in $6.3 billion last week, the largest inflow since January.

Gold is Per the Financial Markets list, at $4,410 and has overtaken Treasuries as the top reserve asset, and the 30-year's blowout is the reason: a buyer who needs a store of value and a yield with no default risk is getting neither from the long end. The dollar is breaking down from 101 after crowded longs, and that breakdown is the leverage behind the metal. The McGlone counter is still live, that precious metals may have peaked against the 30-year, but the flows this week are on Hartnett's side and the house stays with the monetary bid.

3. Japan is the next rate shoe and the yen is the fault line. Japan's 10-year surged to 2.93 percent, the highest since 1996, with swaps pricing roughly an 80 percent chance of a September Bank of Japan hike. That is the carry trade unwinding again, and the yen rescue puts Asia currencies on notice. The standing house read holds: with the Exchange Stabilization Fund spent, the next yen defence needs the BOJ itself. If Tokyo hikes into an already-blowing global long end, the cross-rates pressure finds the dollar next. This is the leverage crack the Fed minutes will not cover but the market is already pricing.

4. Oil holds Hormuz and the deal clock ran out. The 60-day Iran deal deadline has passed with traffic through the strait still disrupted, and Trump is threatening to bomb Oman over the blockade while insisting he is "not in a hurry." Kalshi's odds that Hormuz traffic returns to normal keep falling, to 13 percent by March 2027. The energy complex already shows it: Per the Market list, European natural gas is up 117 percent this year, heating oil 100 percent, gasoline 86 percent, Brent 45 percent, US crude 43 percent. Oil above $170 in Asia is the swing variable into the week, and the gap between the Oman plan and the next attack is still a two-way open.

5. What to watch: the minutes, and whether the long end breaks the dollar. The Fed minutes land Wednesday, and they are the week's test of whether Warsh is the one moving the 30-year. But the higher-signal watch is the dollar: DXY is rolling over from 101 on crowded longs at the same time the long end blows out. That combination, a weaker dollar against a selling bond market, is the debasement trade confirming itself, and it is why gold, not bonds, is the asset catching the bid. The next catalyst after the minutes is Japan, and a BOJ hike into this long end would be the first real test the tape has not priced.

Fed minutes Wednesday, then Japan. If the long end keeps selling into data that should have helped it, that is the regime change, and the dollar is the casualty the books have not yet hedged.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] Memory stopped being a hope and became a number, with a new leg
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: SanDisk guided to 80 percent gross margins on $94 billion of contracts, Goldman modelled DRAM up 300 percent, and Washington handed Micron a tailwind.
item.content:encoded:
SanDisk guided to 80 percent gross margins on $94 billion of contracts, Goldman modelled DRAM up 300 percent, and Washington handed Micron a tailwind.

This channel wrote about the memory trade in every edition it published this week, and for six days the argument was whether a five-year contract structure capped the pricing lever. By Friday that argument had an answer, and it came from Washington, SanDisk and the sell side at once. This memo is the whole case, both sides, and what I would actually do with the names.

The week in one arc

DayWhat changed
SundayChip Stock Investor, holding SanDisk through a 40 percent drawdown, says the wild average selling prices are over, locked away by five-year hyperscaler contracts
MondayRick Orford's Micron bull case arrives and never mentions pricing, retreating to automotive and robotics end markets
TuesdayGoldman models DRAM prices up 250 to 300 percent next year, and I reverse my own call back toward expansion
WednesdaySanDisk unveils HBF, NAND repurposed as AI memory, at one-eighth the capex of HBM
ThursdaySanDisk guides to roughly 80 percent gross margins through 2030 on $94 billion of contracts, and Micron clears $965 on its way at $1,000
FridayThe White House advises Apple to stop buying memory from China, and BofA models Micron at four figures

The through-line is that the bear case was real and specific, and the bull case answered it with a different market than the bear was arguing about.

1. The concession was about NAND, and the shortage is in DRAM

Sunday's bear case was the strongest single thing this week said against the trade, and it came from a holder. Chip Stock Investor, down about 40 percent on SanDisk, said the really wild average selling prices on SSDs are over now that SanDisk and the other memory companies have signed five-year agreements with the hyperscalers. Take-or-pay at a fixed band protects the downside and removes the upside, and multiple expansion needs the upside.

That concession was real and it was about NAND. The whole reason I spent two days moving my own call to compression was that I generalised one company's NAND contract structure onto DRAM, a different market with different contracts. Goldman then published DRAM price forecasts up 250 to 300 percent in 2026 and 300 to 350 percent in 2027, and Bernstein models average selling prices at $2.23 a gigabyte by the end of 2027, roughly five times the 2025 level.

The mechanism is capacity. A gigabyte of high-bandwidth memory takes three times the wafer capacity of standard DRAM, so every line converted to HBM removes conventional supply at the same time, and you get a shortage in both at once. Operating margins across all three makers run 70 to 80 percent, and the confirming detail is small and hard to argue with: Google raised the Pixel 11 by $100 to $899 and cited a severe memory crunch.

2. SanDisk put a number on it, and the number is 80 percent through 2030

Thursday's investor day was not a story, it was a guide. SanDisk is targeting roughly 80 percent non-GAAP gross margins through fiscal 2030 on about $94 billion of locked long-term contracts, with multi-year agreements already covering half of fiscal 2027 bit supply and two-thirds by 2028. JPMorgan resumed coverage at overweight with a $2,250 target and the view that the contracts hold margins even at floor pricing. The stock is up about 50 percent since the fund that blew up on it liquidated.

Wednesday's architecture is the part that matters for the debate. HBF, SanDisk's NAND repurposed as AI memory, matches high-bandwidth memory at 12.8 terabytes per second of bandwidth while using one-eighth the GPU resources at one-quarter the footprint, at one-eighth the capex. Sell-side targets are running back to $3,000 from the current $1,404.

The skeptical read did not go away, and it came from the desks. Some call the HBF marketing and divide the addressable market by two to four. That debate is live, not settled, and it is the whole reason this is a 60/40 rather than a conviction.

3. Micron is the trade's front foot, and it finally has a catalyst

Micron closed Friday back above its 50-day line for the first time in about three weeks, with the resistance ladder at 1022, 1064, 1082, 1121 and 1155 and 991 the overnight gap target. It hit $987 premarket and cleared the $965 target the house had been tracking. The structural numbers underneath are the ones that matter: about 70 percent of hyperscaler capex is going to memory, projected 2027 spend is $761 billion, and demand is growing roughly 200 percent a year against 20 percent supply, with UBS modelling DRAM undersupplied until the second quarter of 2028.

Friday added the tailwind nobody had priced. The White House is advising Apple to stop buying memory chips from China, a direct reroute of demand to the US and Korean makers. And BofA put a number on the bull case: 80 percent gross margins through 2030 and $236 of EPS in fiscal 2030, a 34 percent CAGR against a consensus that has earnings peaking next year and shrinking after. At 15 to 20 times, that lands between $3,500 and $4,700 against a stock under $1,000.

4. The bull case

The shortage is structural and dated. HBM conversion shorting conventional supply, DRAM undersupplied to Q2 2028, and prices up 40 to 50 percent with a 200 percent demand growth rate against 20 percent supply. This is a supply problem that takes years to fix, not a quarter.

The contracts are a floor, not just a cap. SanDisk has $94 billion locked through 2030 at roughly 80 percent margins. The take-or-pay structure that caps the wild upside is the same structure that guarantees the downside. Nobody pays more for earnings pre-sold at a floor, and the floor is 80 percent gross margins. That is a good place to be wrong from.

The tailwinds are stacking. Apple off Chinese memory, Nvidia earnings on August 26 as the next catalyst, and the December 6 buyback-and-dividend lift that has been this name's first hard dated catalyst in months. The setup into Nvidia is about as clean as the AI trade gets.

5. The bear case

The marketing-versus-real debate is genuine. If HBF is real, SanDisk trades at a fraction of its worth. If it is largely a story, the $3,000 targets are a rerating nobody asked for. The desks that called the divide by two to four were not dismissed this week, they were the ones holding the argument.

The concession was honest and it still stands for NAND. Rick Orford's Micron bull case on Monday retreated from pricing to automotive and robotics, and he conceded analysts expect margins to normalize once supply catches up with demand. A bull case that changes the subject is a concession. Micron trades at 9.2 times earnings against SK Hynix at 19, and cheap is not the same as early.

The froth is the counterweight to every bull case. Margin debt at a record near $1.5 trillion, the Shiller CAPE near 41, and a memory complex that has already run. A stock that has run has farther to fall if the cycle breaks, and the leverage is where the fragility lives.

The arbitration

Both cases are correct about different markets. The bear is right about NAND and about the multiple. The bull is right that the DRAM shortage is structural and that the contracts underwrite it. I moved this call three times in seven days, the honest sign that it is a view rather than a position, and it sits at 60/40 that multiples expand before they compress.

What would change my mind: a SanDisk quarter that misses the 80 percent margin guide, or a DRAM price print that breaks the Goldman trajectory. What keeps me at 60/40: the tape has not turned, spot is still ripping, and the next hard catalyst is eight sessions out.

What to do with it

Own the structural DRAM names through the cycle and let the levels run. Micron into the 991 confirmation toward 1022, with the buyback lift in December as the dated catalyst. SanDisk on the $94 billion contract base, sized for the marketing debate.

Respect the levels and the calendar. The resistance ladder is published and Nvidia earnings is the next referee. A stock at $1,000 on a $965-cleared target is a stock that needs the next leg to confirm, not one to chase.

Watchlist for the week ahead. $MU into Nvidia earnings and the December lift. $SNDK on the contract base and the HBF debate. $NBIS, where the neocloud earnings this week validated the same demand picture from the compute side. $CRWV on the margin question now answered and the funding question not. And the optics complex, $AAOI and $LITE and $COHR, which are the physical layer that has not yet had the squeeze the memory names already have.

The scoreboard, Stocks & ETFs

Five calls resolved on this channel's book this week, three hits and two misses, and all five were earnings prints that landed on schedule.

ResolvedOutcome
CoreWeave's first quarter is the true margin bottom, Jose NajarroHit. $2.6 billion of revenue, a 59 percent adjusted EBITDA margin, and a first green earnings reaction in six tries
Figure reports with margins and guidance as the open question, VanEck and Milk RoadHit. $0.35 EPS against $0.25, volume up 132 percent, and a Q3 guide raised on every line
The July low holds into mid-August, house, 60/40Hit. The S&P closed at a record 7,798.99 with hedge funds buying $6.8 billion of US equities, the most in 18 years
Nebius into Burry's short, Rick OrfordMiss. Nebius beat anyway, revenue up 454 percent, and squeezed the short from $211.77
Supermicro's backlog guide beats a balance sheet, Rick OrfordMiss. Revenue missed at $11.1 billion against $11.55 billion, and the stock rose 8 to 10 percent on the guide

House record: 1 hit and 1 miss on two settled calls. The hit is the July low. The miss is the SpaceX squeeze, wrong on timing rather than mechanism. That is a sample too small to quote a percentage, and the honest line is that the book is young and the memory call is the one carrying real weight.

One hundred fifty-four open calls carried into next week. The ones that matter: memory at 60/40 for expansion, recorded under pressure after the three moves. Burry's short on Micron and Nebius, both now underwater into the squeeze. The hyperscaler capex case at $761 billion for 2027. The optics complex repricing. And Nvidia earnings on August 26, the single catalyst the whole AI trade is now waiting on.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] Every clock points at an autumn bottom, and the biggest buyer just became a seller
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Three frameworks converge on October, Eckel puts the low at $56,000, and the treasury companies that used to catch every dip are now liquidating into it.
item.content:encoded:
Three frameworks converge on October, Eckel puts the low at $56,000, and the treasury companies that used to catch every dip are now liquidating into it.

This channel's defining argument of the week was not whether Bitcoin goes down. It was where the bottom is and when it lands, and by Friday four independent frameworks had put it in the autumn. This memo is the timing debate, the one new force the bear case gained, and what I would actually hold into a fourth-quarter low.

The week in one arc

DayWhat changed
SundayThe $66,000 weekly close fails, Sykodelic fills his short, and two whales distribute 14,000 coins into the best ETF week since April
MondayThree frameworks converge on $67,000 as the flip, and Saylor sells 1,638 coins on his own published book-value line
TuesdayJesse Eckel dates the capitulation to October and puts the low at $56,000, ruling out $40,000 outright
WednesdayArthur Hayes names the FIMA cap as the next liquidity trigger, and the rate-hike trade breaks Bitcoin's way
ThursdayBitcoin loses $63,000, and Strategy sells 6,948 coins below cost to fund buybacks
FridayBitcoin holds about $63,000 and stops sliding, while the 13F money quietly keeps buying the ETFs

The single most important line in the week is from Sunday, carried across two editions. A weekly close above $66,000 sends Bitcoin higher, and a rejection puts $60,000 first. The close failed and the short filled at $65,300 into a target of $60,500. That is the frame the whole week traded inside.

1. Three clocks, and they agree on the season

The timing debate is not one desk's guess, it is a convergence. Benjamin Cowen leans toward breakdown near the end of midterm years, dates the cycle low as most likely October, possibly late September, and notes the MVRV Z-score has not gone below zero, which has marked every prior bottom. Jesse Eckel puts price and the 200-day meeting around October, one year after this cycle's high, with a drop from 63,000 to about 56,000 in an October capitulation. His decay arithmetic rules out $40,000 and $30,000 for this cycle, because the drawdown is already far shallower than 2017 or 2021.

Against those two, a third set landed on a different line but the same direction. On-Chain Mind's adaptive trend model turns back at $67,000, after being bearish for 87 days since it flipped in mid-May. VirtualBacon wants a daily close above $67,000 before going long, and Sykodelic's short carries its invalidation at a strong daily close above $67,000. Four frameworks, two different lines, and a shared conclusion: the low is lower and it is in the autumn, not this week.

That convergence is why I am holding 60/40 that $58,000 comes before $75,000. When a trend model, a risk-reward frame, a short's stop and a cycle-dating model all agree on direction and disagree only on the line, the direction is the information.

2. The bear case gained a force it did not have a month ago: the biggest buyer is selling

This is the genuinely new thing this week. The treasury companies that spent the cycle accumulating are now liquidating at a loss. Strategy sold 6,948 Bitcoin across four disclosures, all of it below the $75,385 average cost, to fund preferred-share buybacks. Saylor still holds about 847,000 coins, but he has also said the structure stays over-collateralized even if Bitcoin fell to $5,000, and the actions speak louder than the stress-test. The bid that used to catch every dip is a seller at the margin.

The mechanism underneath is the STRC gate. Strategy owes about $1.7 billion a year in perpetuity to its preferred holders against a roughly $4.65 billion reserve, and the 12 percent rate supports par, so issuance stays shut below $100 and reopens at $99 to $100. The largest holder returns as a buyer only if that preferred clears, and Bitcoin only gets the bid if the proceeds actually buy Bitcoin. That is a four to five percent move in one security deciding whether the sector's biggest accumulator comes back.

3. The bull case: the flow is building while the price bleeds, and the squeeze is loaded

The counterweight is that the institutional bid never left. The 13F filings are the clearest sign. iShares Bitcoin's list is 1,500 holders deep even after a 50 percent pullback, with Point72 and Tudor holding 688,529 shares worth about $22.9 million at June 30, up from the prior quarter. JPMorgan raised its BlackRock Bitcoin ETF stake by 25 percent and more than quadrupled its ether position. That is institutional accumulation into weakness, the opposite of the retail flight the tape implies.

And the squeeze setup is loading. Bitcoin sits just above the on-chain cost floor near $49,692, with a cluster of long liquidation risk at $63,500 where a roughly 2,000-coin short sits against a thin book. Prediction markets still price a 45 percent chance Bitcoin falls below $50,000, and that wide bear dispersion is exactly what a squeeze feeds on. The rate tailwind also just turned: the September hike odds collapsed from 42.1 to 29 percent this week, and a four-hike year was the single biggest headwind this asset had been fighting.

4. The arbitration

The bull and the bear are not arguing about the same variable. The bear is arguing about the price path into October. The bull is arguing about what has already built underneath it. Both are true, and the resolution is a timing question rather than a direction one.

The honest weakness in the bull case is the resolution condition. A fundamentals case with no catalyst is a reason to own something, not a reason to expect it to move. The honest weakness in the bear case is that the perfect catalysts keep arriving and producing nothing. The Coldcard exploit, the Korean market down 45 percent, AI stocks halved, and Bitcoin has still not broken $60,000. A bear case whose best shots fail to break the floor is a bear case on a clock.

I am holding 60/40 that Bitcoin sees $58,000 before $75,000, and I am saying plainly that it is a low-conviction number. The clocks put the low in October. Eckel says $56,000, my call says $58,000, Sykodelic's short targets $60,500, and the realised cap sits near $53,000. I am not going to pretend a $2,000 difference between credible desks is insight.

What to do with it

Own the downside through options, not spot, because the timing is the part nobody has. Clemente's structure this week is the honest expression of the view: build spot again, still open to one final leg down this year, and hedge with cheap options. That is how you hold a 60/40 into a dated October low without getting run over by the timing.

Do not read a stabilization as a bottom. Bitcoin found a bid and made a higher low, but it has not confirmed it. The first confirmation condition is a strong daily close above $67,000, and nothing this week produced one.

Watchlist for the week ahead. $BTC into the autumn low, with $62,662 the last support before the June low near $57,000 and the $63,500 short-liquidations cluster the squeeze trigger. $MSTR on whether the STRC preferred holds $99 to $100, which decides if the biggest buyer comes back. $ETH on the flow divergence, with JPMorgan quadrupling its ether stake while Bitcoin funds bleed. $IBIT as the 13F accumulation floor. And the White House crypto meeting on Wednesday, the policy event that could move the CLARITY number the whole complex is waiting on.

The scoreboard, Bitcoin & Crypto

Two calls resolved on this channel's book this week, one hit and one miss, and the miss is the one that matters.

ResolvedOutcome
A weekly close above $66,000 sends Bitcoin higher, a rejection puts $60,000 first, SykodelicHit. The close failed at $66,000, the rejection branch fired, and the short filled at $65,300 toward $60,500
Hold $64,000 and Bitcoin runs to $70,000 to $71,000, John GillenMiss. Bitcoin closed the week at $62,829, below every major moving average, and the sweep toward the $57,000 to $58,000 channel bottom is live

House record: zero settled calls. No house call has resolved on this channel yet, so there is no hit rate to report and quoting one off two relayed calls would be advertising. The honest line remains that this book has not been tested.

Seventy-eight open calls carried into next week. The ones that matter: Bitcoin at $58,000 before $75,000 at 60/40, dated to the autumn. Ether one more leg down at 60/40, with the staking ratio holding above 34 percent through a red month as the tell. CLARITY at 85/15 against becoming law in 2026, with the September 15 cloture vote the date. And the adoption-versus-price divergence, which keeps building the plumbing while the majors bleed.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] Iran kept the strait all week and the oil market is paying for it
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The Oman deal never reopened Hormuz, Iran set six maximal preconditions, oil crossed $170 in Asia, and the odds of a normal strait this year are now 40 percent.
item.content:encoded:
The Oman deal never reopened Hormuz, Iran set six maximal preconditions, oil crossed $170 in Asia, and the odds of a normal strait this year are now 40 percent.

Every edition this channel published this week carried the same driver, and it resolved against the people who wanted a deal. Monday the strait and the route got separated out loud. Friday the blockade was indefinite and crude had gone through $170. This memo is the full arc, both cases, and the one set of prints that settles it.

The week in one arc

DayWhat happened
SundayIran says it is very close to an agreement with Oman on a transit route, and warns that it still does not reopen the strait
MondayRezaei says the route and the strait are separate matters, with war ended and Iranian funds unfrozen named as the price
TuesdayThe announcement window expires with no deal, and Iran rejects talks outright
WednesdayIran says no vessel transits without its permission, and the US sends a fresh carrier group
ThursdayThe US says the blockade is indefinite, and a Kharg VLCC loads its first 2 million barrels in two weeks
FridayOil trades above $170 a barrel in Asia, US pump prices are the highest ever for this point in August

The single line that explains all of it is from Monday. Mohsen Rezaei, Iran's national security secretary, said if an Iran-Oman transit agreement is reached, it will be a separate matter from the closure of the strait. Per the Market list, he set the reopening price three minutes earlier: the war ended, Iranian funds unfrozen, and other conditions passed through mediators.

That is the thing I got wrong twice, and naming it is the point of this memo. I kept treating the route as a proxy for the strait. Iran spent the entire week explaining that it is not.

1. The route is real and the strait is a different negotiation

The Oman track genuinely is alive. Qatar says the Iran-Oman negotiations are at an advanced stage with positive feedback, and Pakistan's defence minister told Bloomberg the US and Iran are close to some sort of arrangement. The sticking point is a toll. Iran wants its right to collect tolls on transit recognised, Washington disagrees, and that rejection triggered the worst fighting since the April ceasefire.

The toll dispute is small enough to sound trivial and structural enough to be the whole story. A chokepoint state asserting a toll on the world's crude is a sovereignty claim. Oman has reportedly secured Gulf Arab backing for a voluntary toll system, and the two capitals remain far apart on it. Iran absorbed the strikes without conceding, so the price of a deal went up rather than down.

Trump's framing that Iran agrees privately and refuses publicly is consistent with both a genuine negotiation and a stall. There is no way to tell them apart from outside, and this week the market stopped trying.

2. The maximal ask is what makes this a war economy, not a trade dispute

Iran's stated preconditions to reopen Hormuz are explicit and total. Per the Polymarket list: US forces withdrawn from the region, the naval blockade lifted, sanctions removed and frozen assets released, an end to proxy warfare, war reparations, and an end to hostile rhetoric. Rezaei then said Iran has no talks to extend the ceasefire, that it never officially took effect, and that Washington breached it inside 48 hours.

Read that list against the physical market and the shape of it is a war economy. Oil traded above $170 a barrel in Asia, diesel cracks broke through $98 after the Houthis hit a Saudi Aramco refinery, US gas is $4.07 a gallon, and the strategic petroleum reserve sits at its lowest since 1983 after a 52 percent drawdown in five years. The Reaper drone fleet is down about a quarter, with 45 MQ-9s lost at a replacement cost above $1.3 billion, and the Pentagon is seeking $67 billion to replenish them. Washington ordered embassies to draw up reduced-staff plans.

The pricing is the honest part. Kalshi puts only a 40 percent chance Hormuz traffic returns to normal this year, down from the near-certainty that opened the window. A separate contract on the blockade ending by year end decayed from above 95 cents to about 81. The market spent the week pricing the deal further away.

3. The bull case: this is the setup for a hard spike, and the sellers have nothing left

The escalation side is real and named. Bessent says Washington is readying an economic isolation of Iran the world has never seen, and the UAE accuses Iran of a third attack on its ADNOC facilities. Trump keeps threatening to declare Hormuz US territory. Only two vessels crossed the strait on Friday and neither carried crude. A market oversupplied on paper at 106.3 million barrels a day against 104.8 million of demand is closed at a chokepoint it cannot control, and the last time a supply shock of this shape hit, Brent blew through every $120 call.

The physical buffer is the bear's problem. The strategic reserve at 1983 lows, diesel cracks at all-time highs, and a strait carrying a fifth of global LNG closed to that traffic means there is no cushion left to absorb the next incident. One drone on a refinery moved cracks $4 to $5. The base is not a stable $170. It is a market one headline from materially higher.

4. The bear case: the reroute is real, demand is soft, and every spike has been faded

The other half is that the physical market keeps finding supply around the blockage. Iran confirmed an agreement with Oman on a new Hormuz shipping-traffic plan, the classic way a chokepoint trade unwinds. US crude stockpiles posted an unexpected build, Russian output ran nearly a million barrels a day below its OPEC quota, and US imports of Venezuelan crude hit a nine-year high. The IEA revised 2025 demand up to 104.8 million barrels a day, but that is demand growth while the shortage has not shown up.

And oil fell on the day Iran asserted control. That reaction is the case for the fade trade. The market has now twice priced a reroute and sold the escalation, and that is why crude sits at $170 instead of higher. A war premium only persists while the market believes the supply is actually trapped, and the tankers keep finding a way around.

5. The arbitration, and the prints that settle it

Both cases are live because they are describing different intervals. The bear case is a within-week fade on every headline. The bull case is a structural argument that the buffer is gone and the next incident compounds. I opened this week's Hormuz call at 70/30 and it finished at zero, resolved as a miss on Tuesday. The lesson was pricing the route as the strait. I am not repeating it.

I am 55/45 that oil is higher this time next month than it is today, and that is a low-conviction number for a reason. The difference between the Oman toll deal and the next ADNOC attack is a gap in either direction, and both are genuinely on the table.

What settles it, in order of what I am watching:

The eventWhat it decides
The toll agreementIf Oman, Qatar and the Gulf Arabs push a voluntary toll through, the reroute becomes real and the premium bleeds out
The October 31 blockade-ending contractSitting at 73 cents, it prices the indefinite read and is the cleanest market referendum on Washington's commitment
The next strait incidentA tanker hit or a refinery strike retests the $170 plus level and tests whether buyers still fade
The Fed minutes and the yenThe yen at 160 reopens the intervention question, and the 30-year at 5.3 percent is the funding side of the same deficit that keeps the dollar in play

The yen is the part this channel has been flagging all week and it is the quiet link. Japan's two-year yield hit 1.64 percent, the highest since 1995, and the yen pushed back toward 160, the level that triggered the first coordinated US-Japan intervention since 1998 and the Bessent proposal to expand the FIMA repo facility. Oil above $170 and a yen at 160 is how a war premium and a funding squeeze arrive in the same tape. If the long end keeps selling into prints that should have helped it, that is the regime change this channel called last week, not a pullback.

The scoreboard, Macro & Policy

Two calls resolved on this channel's book this week, and both went against the house.

ResolvedOutcome
A joint Iran-Oman announcement inside a week, house, 70/30Miss. No announcement landed. Iran separated the route from the strait, rejected talks, and the window closed
August 12 CPI settles September more than payrolls, houseMiss. CPI printed exactly on consensus and moved September 6 points against payrolls' 15. The size of a repricing comes from the surprise, not the importance of the series

House record: 2 hits and 3 misses on five settled calls. The two wins are the Hormuz deal inside two weeks and no CLARITY floor vote before recess. The three losses are the oil-higher-two-weeks call, the Iran-Oman announcement, and the CPI. That is a losing record on a small sample, and the two misses this week were both calls I chased after moving them downward once too late. The pattern is the same as the memory call on the Stocks channel: when I keep revising a call in the same direction, the direction itself was the signal.

Seventy-one open calls carried into next week. The ones that matter: the September hold, which this week collapsed from 42.1 to 29 percent on a named Oxford Economics call and now has almost nobody against it. CLARITY's cloture vote on September 15, about five votes short of 60. The yen at 160 and the empty Exchange Stabilization Fund. And the Iran war, with the Hormuz deal at 60/40 inside two weeks now open again and the blockade-ending contract the one the market keeps marking down.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] Nvidia took the memory and optics trade and made it a Wall Street balance sheet
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The $500 billion financing platforms are the real news, the memory names are all sitting on their 50-day lines into earnings, and the 13F money is stacking the same picks.
item.content:encoded:
The $500 billion financing platforms are the real news, the memory names are all sitting on their 50-day lines into earnings, and the 13F money is stacking the same picks.

Friday the memory complex was the story. Over the weekend the financing architecture underneath it moved, and the 13F books are agreeing on where the money goes into next week. This is the week-ahead read on the trade that owns the tape.

Market context. The S&P closed at a record near 7,800, on pace for its best August in 41 years but on the lowest monthly volume in 22 years. $SPX 8,000 is about 2.8 percent away. The week's catalyst is Nvidia earnings on August 26, now eight sessions out, and the memory names are all clustered right on their 50-day moving averages into it. Equity options get pre-market trading from Monday at 7:15am ET, and Reddit joins the S&P 500 on August 18.

1. Nvidia's $500 billion financing platform is the second invention. The weekend's real story is not a chip, it is the money. Nvidia signed agreements with Per the AI financing video, Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to create platforms that can mobilize more than $500 billion of third-party capital for AI infrastructure. These are memoranda of understanding, not committed dollars, but six of the largest pools of capital in the world deciding AI compute is something they can finance is new. Nvidia has also cut its OpenAI data-center backing from $250 billion to under $120 billion, and eyes a $3 billion stake in SB Energy's Ohio campus.

This is the railroad moment the bears keep asking for. The first wave of AI capex ran on hyperscaler cash and venture debt. The next wave needs insurers, pensions, infrastructure funds and private credit, and that is what these platforms are. The risk is real: CoreWeave has a roughly $100 billion backlog and still loses money building it out, and GPU-backed debt is now being rated investment grade. But the financing invention is the thing that turns a bubble story into a buildout story. Watch the concentration, not the enthusiasm.

2. The memory names are stacked on their 50-day lines into a binary print. Micron, SanDisk, $SMH, $SOXX and $EWY are all sitting right on their 50-day moving averages, and Per the Market list, BofA's model puts Micron at $236 of fiscal-2031 EPS on 80 percent margins, against a consensus that peaks lower. SanDisk had a 40 percent move last week, a textbook breakout now testing that line. The setup into Nvidia earnings is the cleanest the AI trade has had in weeks: a four-figure case on the memory names, a fresh Washington tailwind pushing Apple off Chinese chips, and every one of them coiled at the same technical level.

The breadth rule does not let this take the whole edition, and it does not need to. The skeptical read is still live. Memory multiples expand before they compress, and a stock that has already run has farther to fall if the cycle breaks. But for the week ahead, the memory complex is the group with the most to confirm or deny on the twenty-sixth.

3. The 13F money is stacking the same names, and the biggest books are leading. Gavin Baker's Atreides fund put SpaceX as its largest position at $4.67 billion and added CoreWeave by 810,000 shares to 2.12 million, while trimming Micron. Druckenmiller's top ten is led by Natera at 17 percent and TSMC at 5.5 percent. Tepper added $1.19 billion of Amazon, $1.13 billion of Micron and $788 million of TSMC. The convergence is worth naming: when Baker, Druckenmiller and Tepper all land on AI infrastructure and TSMC, that is three independent desks on the same trade, and the house reads convergence as the strongest confidence marker the sources give.

The one name every desk seems to want is Uber, with Ackman up 14 percent, Tepper up 21 percent and Terry Smith buying 8 million shares. That is a consumer-financials bid sitting under a stock that has built a two-year base. It is the non-AI side of the same rotation, and it is the part of this ledger that does not depend on the buildout.

4. Tesla is the contrarian setup the 13F books are not crowding. Tesla reportedly demos a remotely operated flying Roadster this month with SpaceX thrusters and nobody inside, and it delivered 480,000 vehicles in Q2 against about 406,000 expected. Yet the stock sits near 12-month lows, about 30 percent below its recent high, and short sellers have made $9 billion on it this year. The bull case is the delivery beat plus a $10 trillion market-cap by the 2030s on a full-stack story. The bear case is that a broken consumer and a beaten stock do not care about a flying car demo. Either way the asymmetry is wider than the 13F money suggests, and it is the cleanest non-AI setup in the tape right now.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $MU. Back above its 50-day into Nvidia earnings, with BofA's $236 fiscal-2031 EPS model pointing at a four-figure price and Washington pushing Apple off Chinese memory. The resistance ladder is 1022, 1064, 1082, 1121 and 1155.
  • $NVDA. Earnings in eight sessions, a $302.83 Street target with 34 percent upside, and now the $500 billion financing platform story behind it. The options leader and the catalyst for the whole complex.
  • $CRWV. Backlog past $104 billion, more than $25 billion of new contracts in five weeks, and GPU-backed debt now rated investment grade. The purest expression of the financing thesis.
  • $UBER. Ackman, Tepper and Terry Smith all buying, a two-year base, and no dependence on the AI buildout. The non-AI side of the same rotation.
  • $TSLA. 480,000 deliveries against 406,000 expected, near 12-month lows, $9 billion of shorts against it. A broken-valuation setup with a live catalyst and a live bear case.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] Bitcoin went flat and that is the most bullish signal in the market
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: BTC shrugged off three straight negatives without budging, Clarity odds collapsed to 10 percent, and the Senate vote on September 15 is the binary that could flip the tape.
item.content:encoded:
BTC shrugged off three straight negatives without budging, Clarity odds collapsed to 10 percent, and the Senate vote on September 15 is the binary that could flip the tape.

Friday the question was whether the break under $63,000 was the start of the next leg. Over the weekend the tape answered by doing nothing at all, and in this market that is a signal. Bitcoin is not down on bad news anymore, and that is the read into the week.

Market context. Bitcoin is holding near $63,000 after six failed attempts above $65,000, with spot volume at its lowest since early 2019 and funding still positive. It sits just above the on-chain cost floor near $49,692. Ether is near six-and-a-half-year lows against the S&P. The proxy names are the bright spot: Nubank is up about 10 percent on its first billion-dollar quarter, and the tokenized-Treasury complex is drawing real flows. The week's binary is the Senate's Clarity vote on September 15, with the White House crypto meeting Wednesday.

1. Boring is bullish, and the market stopped caring. Per Milk Road, Bitcoin has gone through three of the worst headlines in its cycle without moving: the Situational-Awareness selloff, Saylor unloading his bags, and the Clarity Act getting punted again. Matt Hougan at Bitwise calls that the most bullish thing in the market right now. Bear markets die in apathy, and the market is apathetic.

The squeeze setup is still loaded, with a cluster of long-liquidations at $63,500 sitting against a thin book, and suppressed volatility is the fuel. The risk is the rollover Benjamin Cowen keeps flagging, that Bitcoin tends to roll over in the second half of August even while stocks make highs. Do not read a stabilization as a bottom. Read it as a market that has stopped selling the news.

2. Clarity is priced for failure, and that is the setup. The institutional odds on the bill collapsed. Per Scott Melker, Galaxy cut its estimate of the Clarity Act passing this year to 10 percent from 75 percent, Matt Hougan calls the bill a zombie that may never pass, and the Senate vote is teed up for September 15. Almost the entire market prices it to fail. That is exactly the kind of lopsided pricing a surprise clears. A pass would be a violent reflexive surprise, enough to push Bitcoin into the high 70s and flip it back into a technical bull market overnight.

The White House hosts crypto and prediction-market executives Wednesday, the event that could move that number. The house read stays the same as all week: Clarity's failure is priced, and the upside of a pass is not.

3. The miners turned into AI power plants, and Anthropic just paid to prove it. Anthropic signed a $9 billion deal with Riot, a former pure Bitcoin miner, and VanEck's Matthew Sigel argues an AI token is worth roughly ten times a Bitcoin token per unit of power. The miners are repricing from Bitcoin leverage to AI infrastructure, and that is why the Riot and CoreWeave-adjacent names have stopped trading like a Bitcoin proxy. The flip side is real: the AI pivot pulls hash rate off the Bitcoin network and turns miners into bigger Bitcoin sellers. Sigel calls it self-correcting once the economics shake out. The trade is to own the ones that already have the AI contracts, not the ones still hoping.

4. The infrastructure is building while the majors bleed. The stablecoin and tokenized-Treasury complex is the live trade. Tokenized US T-bills grew the most on Solana, up $378.2 million over 30 days, with Ethereum adding $272.2 million, and World Liberty is taking USD1 stablecoin issuance and reserve control from BitGo. Nubank printed its first billion-dollar quarter with 34 percent of gross profit from float, a stablecoin-style balance sheet up 10 percent pre-market. This is the plumbing that keeps growing while price goes nowhere, and it is the closest thing this market has to a structural bid.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. At about $63,000 below every major moving average, apathetic to three bad headlines, with the $63,500 short-liquidations cluster as the squeeze trigger. The September 15 Clarity vote is the binary.
  • $MSTR. Saylor is still selling into buybacks while the market stops reacting. The premium is the position and it keeps compressing.
  • $RIOT. Anthropic's $9 billion deal makes it the cleanest proof the miners repriced from Bitcoin to AI. It is no longer a Bitcoin proxy, it is an AI-revenue name.
  • $COIN. A named guest at Wednesday's White House meeting, the clearest regulatory tailwind it has had in months, with Clarity the swing.
  • $NU. First billion-dollar quarter, 34 percent of gross profit from float, up 10 percent. The stablecoin-adjacent fintech that is actually printing.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] The debasement trade finally picked a leg, and it is gold, not Bitcoin
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Gold is near $5,000 on the books while the dollar hits new lows and Bitcoin sits still, and the Fed minutes this week test whether the long end bends.
item.content:encoded:
Gold is near $5,000 on the books while the dollar hits new lows and Bitcoin sits still, and the Fed minutes this week test whether the long end bends.

The long end was Friday's story and it is still the driver, but the weekend moved the other half of the trade. Gold is running while Bitcoin is not, and that split is the freshest signal this tape has. This is a week-ahead read on the forces that own it.

Market context. The 30-year holds near 5.3 percent, its highest since 2007, against 175 basis points of cuts. The dollar is at new lows while gold nears the $5,000 forecast the books carry. Oil trades above $170 in Asia and Iran still holds Hormuz. The week hands over Fed minutes, the first PMIs, and CPI and jobs prints across Europe, Britain, Japan and Canada, with the White House crypto meeting on Wednesday.

1. Gold is running the debasement trade and Bitcoin is still on the bench. Kalshi traders forecast gold near $5,000 this year, and the flows underneath agree. China added 20 tons of gold in July, its largest monthly purchase since October 2023, and the Bank of Korea resumed buying after 13 years. The dollar is already at new lows and silver has moved. The one thing that has not moved is Bitcoin, and that divergence is the whole story. The debasement bid is real and it is not waiting for crypto to catch up. When the asset that used to be the hedge stays flat while the metals run, the buyers are rotating away from it.

2. The Fed minutes land this week, and the hike odds already collapsed. The week's rate catalyst is the minutes, and the pricing has moved before it. Per Visser Labs, September is down to 31 percent and the BOJ sits at 80 percent, from roughly even before payrolls. Warsh implied the PCE index could be jettisoned as the Fed's primary inflation metric as soon as January and speaks at Jackson Hole. The 30-year at 5.3 percent is the market's vote that nominal growth is running hotter than the cuts suggest. The minutes will not decide the regime, but they will tell us whether Warsh is the one moving it.

3. Oil holds Hormuz and the producers are printing cash. Oil above $170 in Asia is still the swing variable, and the drivers have not changed. Trump keeps threatening to declare the strait US territory while Iran holds the chokepoint, and Kalshi still puts only a 40 percent chance traffic returns to normal this year. The other side is big oil's record $70 billion of free cash flow in Q2, with the UAE glutting the market near 4.1 million barrels a day, and Cathie Wood calling the inflation pressure a deflation echo. The bull and the bear are both priced, and the difference between the Oman deal and the next attack is still a gap in either direction.

4. The leverage cracks keep widening just under the record. Jane Street lost more than $15 billion in July, its first losing month since 2016, and Nomura flags a $300 billion coiled spring of exotic exposure. A record Per the Kalshi list, 200 leveraged ETFs launched in 2025 against fewer than 50 in 2024, and retail bought $27 billion of Nvidia over the past year while selling $5 billion of Apple. None of this is a solvency story yet. It is the same warning as the long end: the leverage that carried the rally is the part that can turn first.

5. What to watch: the trade map and the debt engine. The US import map keeps reordering itself, with Per the People to follow list, China falling from the number one source at 20.2 percent to number four at 7.4 percent while Mexico takes the top spot and Taiwan climbs to third. Lutnick is pushing Apple away from Chinese memory chips, the policy tailwind behind the semiconductor trade. Underneath it all, tax revenue is up 65 percent to $5.3 trillion against spending up 96 percent to $7.3 trillion, and the 30-year at 5.3 percent is the funding cost of that gap.

Fed minutes, PMIs, and the jobs and CPI prints out of Europe, Britain, Japan and Canada decide the week. Gold near $5,000 against a dollar at new lows is the trade to watch. If the long end keeps selling into data that should have helped it, that is the regime change confirming itself, not a pullback.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] The White House handed Micron a tailwind, and the memory trade gets a four-figure case
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Washington is pushing Apple off Chinese memory chips, Micron closed back above its 50-day line, and BofA's model puts the stock at $4,000 on 80 percent margins.
item.content:encoded:
Washington is pushing Apple off Chinese memory chips, Micron closed back above its 50-day line, and BofA's model puts the stock at $4,000 on 80 percent margins.

Friday the memory complex was the story. Over the weekend Washington handed it a tailwind, and the neoclouds and the optics stack that feed it are pricing the phase shift into next year.

Market context. The S&P closed Friday at a record near 7,800, on pace for its best August in 41 years but on the lowest monthly volume in 22 years, so the move is thin. Reddit joins the S&P 500 on August 18 and was up about 13 percent on the news. Equity options get pre-market trading from Monday at 7:15am ET. The week's equity catalyst is Nvidia earnings on August 26, now eight sessions out, with that name still the options volume leader.

1. Micron got its catalyst, and the bull case now has a number on it. The White House is advising Apple to stop buying memory chips from China, a direct tailwind for a stock that had already turned. Micron closed Friday back above its 50-day line for the first time in about three weeks, with the resistance ladder at 1022, 1064, 1082, 1121 and 1155 and 991 the overnight gap target.

The weekend case for it is a target, not a hope. Per the Stocks list, BofA models 80 percent gross margins through 2030 and $236 of EPS in fiscal 2030, a 34 percent CAGR against a consensus that has earnings peaking next year and shrinking after. At 15 to 20 times that, the number lands between $3,500 and $4,700, versus a stock under $1,000 today.

The structural math underneath is the same one the house has tracked all week: memory is about 70 percent of hyperscaler capex, the projected 2027 spend is $761 billion, and demand is growing about 200 percent a year against 20 percent supply, with memory prices up 40 to 50 percent. The skeptical read is still live. The Teradyne-style comparison and the marketing-versus-real debate over the memory contracts did not go away, and a stock that has already run has farther to fall if the cycle breaks. But the setup into Nvidia earnings is about as clean as the AI trade gets right now.

2. The neoclouds printed the numbers and the rentals are pricing 2027. Nebius reported Q2 revenue of $582.3 million, up 454 percent, with AI cloud up 514 percent at a 49.7 percent margin, an adjusted EBITDA margin of 41 percent, and a committed backlog above $40 billion. It has contracted 5 gigawatts, more than a gigawatt a year from 2027, and roughly 70 percent prepayments cover half to 60 percent of capex. Daniel Koss guides the 2027 ARR past $20 billion and holds a $1 trillion long-term target against a price near $277. A Birmingham data-center case was allowed to keep building until a March 8 hearing, one less overhang.

Iren is the same trade with a darker-pool tell. It printed about $727 million of dark-pool volume the same day it delivered Horizon 1 to Microsoft, the biggest single-day dark print in a year, and it has 85 percent of year-end capacity contracted toward a $4.4 billion ARR target. The spot market backs the thesis: a three-year-old A100 generation is contracted through 2029 at full freight, and Nebius's first capacity auction cleared 15 percent above the prior record. CME plans to list compute futures in October, with Larry Fink calling compute a financialized resource, the market formalizing the scarcity the neoclouds are selling.

3. The optics stack is the quietest part of the AI trade and the one compounding fastest. The photonics names are printing the kind of numbers memory did two months ago. Applied Optoelectronics is the top pick, with its data-center revenue up from $32 million to $81.4 million year over year, a first 1.6T order above $200 million, and a $1 billion 2026 revenue target that would be up 107.6 percent. Lumentum did Q3 revenue of $808.4 million, up 90 percent, and guided Q4 to $960 million to $1.01 billion. Marvell's Q1 was a record $2.418 billion, up 28 percent, with Celestial AI capacity set to double by fiscal 2028. Coherent carries a $2 billion Nvidia equity stake on top of the optics cycle.

These four names have a common thread: they are the physical layer the hyperscalers cannot buy fast enough, and unlike the memory names they have not had their squeeze already. When Nvidia confirms the buildout on August 26, the optics complex is the group that has not yet repriced for it.

4. The fintech and consumer corners still work on their own numbers. Nu Holdings put up its first billion-dollar quarter, net income of $1.06 billion, up 67 percent, on revenue up 39 percent with return on equity at 33 percent, and the stock rose about 10 percent. The credit tell is the same one the house flagged in the Macro edition last week: 90-day nonperforming loans ticked up to 6.9 percent from 6.5 percent, the highest since 2024, on a portfolio up 37 percent. Nu is a real growth lender, but it is also the first place Latin consumer stress shows up.

Jack in the Box is the contrarian value setup. It trades at about 0.22 times sales against Papa John's at 0.5, Wendy's at 0.6, Starbucks at 3 and McDonald's at 7, after falling from $100 to about $10 and now consolidating. The bull case is that the discount already prices the decline and the franchise is stable enough to re-rate. The bear case is that a broken consumer hurts a value burger chain first. Either way the asymmetry is unusual for a name this beaten down.

5. The froth is real, and it is the counterweight to every bull case this week. Margin debt sits at a record near $1.5 trillion, up 49 percent year over year, about 4 percent of GDP against a 50-year norm near 1.5 percent, and the Shiller CAPE is near 41 against a long-run median of 16. About half of retail options volume is now same-day expiries. Roughly $3 trillion of AI data centers is financed with borrowed money and the industry needs close to $1.5 trillion more by 2028. South Korea is the cautionary example: the KOSPI doubled, retail poured in $70 billion net, and July was a 22 percent drawdown, the worst since the global financial crisis.

None of this makes the bull case wrong. It makes it fragile, and the fragility lives in the leverage, not in the earnings. Into a record close on thin volume with a leveraged book, the position to hold is the one that does not need the market to be right every day.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $MU. Back above the 50-day for the first time in weeks, with resistance at 1022, 1064, 1082, 1121 and 1155, and BofA's $236 fiscal-2030 EPS model points at a four-figure price. Apple-off-China-memory is a fresh tailwind into Nvidia earnings.
  • $NBIS. Q2 revenue up 454 percent, a 41 percent EBITDA margin, and a backlog above $40 billion, with Koss guiding 2027 ARR past $20 billion. The $277 price is the discount to that.
  • $IREN. The $727 million dark-pool day and 85 percent of year-end capacity contracted toward a $4.4 billion ARR target. The neocloud path to $200 runs through Microsoft and the 2027 buildout.
  • $NU. First quarter above a billion dollars of net income, ROE at 33 percent, stock up 10 percent. The 6.9 percent NPL tick is the tell that decides whether this re-rates or rolls over.
  • $JACK. 0.22 times sales against a market that pays 3 to 7 times for peers, after a 90 percent drawdown that is now consolidating. A broken-valuation setup with a live bear case.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] Bitcoin held $63,000 over the weekend, and the policy window is back open
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: BTC steadied under every major moving average while the White House meeting nears, Clarity odds sag, and the 13F money quietly came back to the ETFs.
item.content:encoded:
BTC steadied under every major moving average while the White House meeting nears, Clarity odds sag, and the 13F money quietly came back to the ETFs.

Friday the question was whether the break under $63,000 was the start of the next leg down. Over the weekend the tape steadied, and the divergence between a bear price and a building bid is the story into the week.

Market context. Bitcoin is trading around $63,000, still below every major moving average and roughly 50 percent off its high, but it has stopped sliding. The on-chain floor sits at $49,692, the level where the last washout bottomed. Ether is near six-and-a-half-year lows against the S&P. The proxy and fintech names are the bright spot: Nu Holdings is up about 10 percent on its first billion-dollar quarter, and the spot ETFs drew their first sustained buying in a while. The week's catalyst is Wednesday's White House crypto meeting.

1. Bitcoin is holding the line, and the squeeze setup is loading. The break below $63,000 did not extend. Bitcoin sits at about $63,032, just above the on-chain cost floor near $49,692, and the prediction market still prices a 45 percent chance Bitcoin falls below $50,000. That wide bear dispersion is exactly what a squeeze feeds on. There is a cluster of long liquidation risk at $63,500, where a roughly 2,000-coin short position sits against a thin book, and a break above it forces covering into a market with spot volume near seven-year lows.

The risk is the rollover Benjamin Cowen keeps flagging: in bear-market and midterm years, Bitcoin tends to roll over in the second half of August even while the S&P makes highs. That is the two-sided setup. The price has found a bid, but it has not made a higher low yet, and the path of least resistance is only up if the squeeze triggers. Do not read a stabilization as a bottom.

2. The policy window is the real catalyst this week, and it is two-sided. The White House is hosting crypto and prediction-market executives on Wednesday, with Coinbase, a16z, Ripple, Chainlink and Kalshi expected and Trump likely to appear. That is a genuine pro-crypto signal. The counterweight is Clarity, the stablecoin and market-structure bill. Per the People to follow list, BlackRock now puts its passage before the August recess below 50 percent, and Citi CEO Jane Fraser has publicly endorsed it while admitting improvements are still on the table. The plumbing keeps moving regardless: World Liberty Financial got preliminary approval from the OCC to operate a national trust bank for a US dollar stablecoin, the first window for a bank-chartered stablecoin issuer.

The read is the same as last week. The regulatory direction is set and the infrastructure is being banked, but the bill that would turn it into law is a coin flip this year. The meeting on Wednesday is the event that could move that number, and it is three days out.

3. Strategy is still unwinding, and Saylor is pricing the crash out loud. Saylor still holds about 847,000 Bitcoin, more than anyone except the Satoshi wallet, and he has now said the stock's debt stays over-collateralized even if Bitcoin fell to $5,000, a 92 percent drawdown from here. That is not a bull turning bear, it is the treasury model stress-testing itself. But the actions still speak louder than the rhetoric: Strategy has been selling coins to fund preferred-share buybacks, the same unwind the house flagged last week, and the buying bid that used to catch every dip is a seller at the margin.

The reason Saylor can say $5,000 and keep his structure is that the debt is over-collateralized at current prices. The risk is what happens to the stock's premium when the market hears the man who owns the most Bitcoin model it collapsing. It is a stress-test worth taking seriously even if the base case is nowhere near that low.

4. The money came back to the ETFs while the price bled, and that is the quiet tell. The 13F filings are the clearest sign the real bid never left. Per the Crypto list, iShares Bitcoin's list is 1,500 holders deep even after a 50 percent pullback, and Point72 and Tudor held 688,529 shares worth about $22.9 million at June 30, up from the prior quarter. JPMorgan raised its stake in the BlackRock Bitcoin ETF by 25 percent to 10.4 million shares and more than quadrupled its ether ETF position. That is institutional accumulation into weakness, the opposite of the retail flight the tape implies.

The custody scare is the one thing that could reverse it. The Trezor cold-wallet breach warning and a separate exchange-flow report showing Per the People to follow list, more than 30,000 Bitcoin moving to exchanges since the Coldcard event have traders on guard for a repeat of the FTX-style reverse flow. If a headline flips that, the 13F buyers are the natural floor, but they are not fast. Trust stays the load-bearing part of this market.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. At about $63,000 below every major moving average, with the on-chain floor at $49,692 and a 45 percent chance of sub-$50,000 on the books. The $63,500 short-liquidations cluster is the squeeze trigger.
  • $ETH. Near six-and-a-half-year lows against the S&P, with JPMorgan quadrupling its ether ETF stake into the weakness. The flow divergence from Bitcoin is intact.
  • $MSTR. Saylor holds 847,000 coins and now models a $5,000 Bitcoin, while the company still sells into buybacks. The premium is the position, and it is compressing.
  • $IBIT. The ETF list is 1,500 deep after a 50 percent drawdown, with Point72, Tudor, Harvard, Dartmouth and the Texas pension all in. The institutional bid is the floor under the price.
  • $COIN. The exchange is a named guest at Wednesday's White House meeting, the clearest regulatory tailwind it has had in months.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] The 30-year is at 5.3 percent and the bond market will not take the cuts
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Long rates are the highest since 2007 even after 175 basis points of Fed cuts, debt is crossing $40 trillion, and oil is the lever into a heavy data week.
item.content:encoded:
Long rates are the highest since 2007 even after 175 basis points of Fed cuts, debt is crossing $40 trillion, and oil is the lever into a heavy data week.

Friday's close left the S&P at a record, but the driver underneath was the long end of the bond market, and it is not taking the Fed's medicine. This is a week-ahead read on the forces that own the tape, and the long bond is the strongest of them.

Market context. The 30-year Treasury yields about 5.3 percent, the highest since 2007, and it has done that against 175 basis points of cuts since September. The 10-year closed Friday around 4.7 percent. Oil is the wildcard into Monday: US pump prices are the highest ever for this point in August, the strategic reserve is at 1983 lows, and the strait that carries the world's crude is the one unresolved driver. The week hands over Fed minutes, the first PMIs, and CPI and jobs prints across Europe, Britain, Japan and Canada.

1. The long end is calling the bluff on the whole rate regime. The 30-year at Per the Financial Markets list, 5.3 percent with only about 42 basis points of hikes priced through 2027 is the tell. The long end is bear-steepening through a Fed debate, and that shape of curve is how a market says nominal growth is running hotter than the consensus believes. The same move is global: France's 30-year printed 4.85 percent, its highest since the global financial crisis, and Japan's two-year sits at 1.66 percent, the highest in 31 years.

The key is what did not happen. Inflation retraced its entire spike and bonds never caught a bid, so the pressure on the long end is structural, not cyclical, Per Capital Flows Research, with the S&P, the 30-year and the dollar starting to lock into the same alignment. The whole post-2020 trade, the 60/40 and the thirty-year-refi playbook, was built on a regime of ever-falling rates. That regime ended, and the industry has not repriced the habit.

2. The debt engine is compounding while the Fed runs QE. The July deficit printed at a record $432 billion, the Treasury is set to borrow $1.367 trillion across 182 days, and national debt is about to cross 40 trillion dollars against roughly 19 trillion a decade ago. Interest payments now exceed national defense spending, behind only Social Security and Medicare, and they are the fastest line in the budget. Tax revenue is up 65 percent to $5.3 trillion over ten years while spending is up 96 percent to $7.3 trillion, so the gap is structural, not a one-off.

The uncomfortable part is the Fed's role. It has cut rates and is expanding its balance sheet again while inflation has run above target for 65 straight months at about 4 percent a year since 2019. Easing into an inflation you cannot shake is how a central bank ends up choosing between the bond market and the dollar. That is the choice Warsh and Bessent are being handed this autumn, and the market is pricing for one side of it.

3. Oil is the week's real lever, and the signals point both ways. The bulls and the bears are both here. The bullish resolution: Iran confirmed an agreement with Oman on a new Hormuz shipping-traffic plan, the classic way a chokepoint trade unwinds.
