The escalation side: Bessent says Washington is readying an economic isolation of Iran the world has never seen, the UAE accuses Iran of a third attack on its ADNOC facilities, and Trump keeps threatening to declare Hormuz US territory. Only two vessels crossed the strait Friday and neither carried crude.

The physical market is already paying for the risk. Oil traded above $170 a barrel in Asia, US gas is $4.07 a gallon, the highest ever for this point in August, and the strategic petroleum reserve is at its lowest since 1983 after a 52 percent drawdown in five years. Last week's claim that the reroute was priced was premature. This is the single largest swing variable into Monday, and the difference between the Oman plan and the next attack is a gap in either direction.

4. The first cracks in the leverage are showing, just under the record. Jane Street, one of the largest market makers in the world, lost roughly $15 billion in July, its first red trading month since 2016, on exposure to the Aschenbrenner book that collapsed a month ago. Net trading revenue is still up about $40 billion for the year, so this is not a solvency story. It is a warning about how concentrated the unwind can get when a single momentum book turns, and it is worth holding next to the record equity valuations that rely on that leverage staying calm.

What I am watching this week: Fed minutes, the first August PMIs, and the CPI and jobs prints out of Europe, Britain, Japan and Canada, plus the White House crypto meeting on Wednesday. The bond market is the driver and oil is the swing. If the long end keeps selling into prints that should have helped it, that is the signal the regime change is real, not a pullback.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] SanDisk's investor day put a floor under the memory trade, and Micron ran at $1,000
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: SanDisk guided to roughly 80 percent gross margins through 2030 on $94 billion of locked contracts, JPMorgan set a $2,250 target, and Micron cleared $965 on its way at the four-figure line.
item.content:encoded:
SanDisk guided to roughly 80 percent gross margins through 2030 on $94 billion of locked contracts, JPMorgan set a $2,250 target, and Micron cleared $965 on its way at the four-figure line.

Yesterday the question was whether Nebius could hold its run against Burry. Today the memory complex answered a bigger one, and the S&P closed at another record on top of it.

Market context. The S&P 500 closed at a record 7,798.99 after clearing 7,800 intraday, with the Nasdaq up 0.81 percent. Hedge funds bought $6.8 billion of US equities last week, the largest weekly buy in 18 years, while retail sold $4.1 billion and institutions sold $1.1 billion. The tape rotated into semis and neoclouds. Options volume leaders were Nvidia at 2.4 million contracts, Tesla at 2.0 million, and Micron at 1.0 million, with Nvidia earnings now eight trading days out on August 26.

The scoreboard. I said on July 30 that the July low holds into mid-August, and I trimmed the odds to 60/40 the week after. The S&P is now at an all-time high with hedge funds re-grossing at an 18-year pace, so that low held and then some. Hit.

1. SanDisk put a number on the memory supercycle and Micron ran at $1,000. SanDisk's investor day was not a story, it was a guide. The company is targeting roughly 80 percent non-GAAP gross margins through fiscal 2030 on about $94 billion of locked long-term contracts, with multi-year agreements already covering half of fiscal 2027 bit supply and two-thirds by 2028. JPMorgan resumed coverage at overweight with a $2,250 target and a view that the contracts hold margins even at floor pricing. The stock closed up about 14 percent Thursday and added roughly 6 percent premarket, and it is up about 50 percent since the fund that blew up on it liquidated.

Micron is doing the tape's work on the way to four figures. It hit $987 premarket, cleared the $965 target the house has been tracking, and needs a close above $991 to confirm the next leg toward $1,022. The structural numbers underneath are the ones that matter: about 70 percent of hyperscaler capex is now going to memory, the projected 2027 spend is $761 billion, demand is growing roughly 200 percent a year against 20 percent supply, and UBS models DRAM undersupplied until the second quarter of 2028. SK Hynix's chairman said the shortage worsens into 2027 and that even doubling capacity in five years is not enough.

The skeptical read is real and it came from the desks today, with some calling SanDisk's HBF marketing and dividing the addressable market by two to four. That is the debate the whole memory thesis turns on, and it is live, not settled.

2. The neoclouds got validation, and the rentals are pricing it. Iren delivered Horizon 1 to Microsoft, earning Nvidia's Exemplar Cloud status, and guided to about $3.4 billion of annualized AI Cloud revenue by the end of 2026 on the $9.7 billion Microsoft deal, with capacity moving from 480 megawatts to 1.2 gigawatts through 2027. CoreWeave's CEO said the company signed $25 billion-plus of new contracts in the five weeks since its quarter closed and that the depreciation debate is put to bed, pointing to Blackwell B200 rental rates that have climbed from roughly $2 per GPU hour a year ago to just under $4 now. Nebius held the Northland Street-high buy at a $410 target on $582 million of revenue up 454 percent.

The common thread is pricing power in the spot market. When a three-year-old GPU generation is contracted out to 2029 at full freight, the supply is not loose, and the neoclouds are being paid for it.

3. Nu Holdings put up its first billion-dollar quarter. Nu did $1.06 billion of net income in the quarter, up 67 percent and the first quarter above a billion, on revenue of $5.88 billion, up 39 percent, with return on equity at 33 percent and net interest margin at 22.9 percent. The stock rose about 10 percent. The number to watch is the credit one: 90-day nonperforming loans ticked up to 6.9 percent from 6.5, the highest since the third quarter of 2024, on a portfolio up 37 percent to $39.4 billion. That is the first sign of the consumer stress the Macro edition flagged, showing up in a Brazilian lender before it reaches US names.

4. ZIM is a cash machine that trades like a shipping line. The container carrier trades near $27.50 with roughly $25 a share of cash on the balance sheet, so the market is paying about two and a half dollars for the shipping franchise. Second-quarter cash generation is on track to add $8 to $10 a share by the third quarter, and the desks put assets plus cash near $100 a share against an $8 to $14 earnings range. That is a broken-valuation setup in a name the market is treating as cyclical at the bottom.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $SNDK. Investor day guided to roughly 80 percent gross margins through 2030 on $94 billion of contracts, JPMorgan set a $2,250 target, and the stock is up about 50 percent since the forced liquidation. The marketing-versus-real debate is live.
  • $MU. At $987 and through the $965 target, with $991 the confirmation line toward $1,022. Memory at 70 percent of hyperscaler capex and DRAM undersupplied to Q2 2028 is the structural case.
  • $NBIS. Northland's Street-high $410 target on $582 million of revenue up 454 percent and the ability to sell 2027 capacity today. Burry is still short from higher.
  • $NU. First quarter above $1 billion of net income, ROE at 33 percent, stock up 10 percent. The 6.9 percent NPL tick is the credit tell to watch into next quarter.
  • $ZIM. About $25 a share of cash against a $27.50 price, assets plus cash near $100. The market is pricing the shipping line as cyclical at the bottom while the cash stack grows.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] Bitcoin lost $63,000 and the treasury companies started selling
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Bitcoin closed at $62,829 below every major moving average with ETF outflows accelerating, and Strategy sold 6,948 coins to fund preferred-share buybacks.
item.content:encoded:
Bitcoin closed at $62,829 below every major moving average with ETF outflows accelerating, and Strategy sold 6,948 coins to fund preferred-share buybacks.

Yesterday the argument was which floor binds first. Today Bitcoin settled the argument by breaking through the one it was supposed to hold.

Market context. Bitcoin is at roughly $62,829, down about 1.3 percent on the week and 2.3 percent on the month, and below every major moving average. It sits just above the August low near $62,662, with the June low near $57,000 as the next real support. Bitcoin is down about 12 percent against the Nasdaq this month. ETF flows turned against it decisively: US Bitcoin ETFs shed about 2,015 coins on the day and 3,890 over the week, roughly $243 million, while Ethereum ETFs added 22,908 ether over the week, about $43 million. The band Bitcoin trades in is the tightest in more than a year.

The scoreboard. John Gillen said hold $64,000 on the retest and Bitcoin runs to $70,000 to $71,000, and lose it and the sweep goes to $58,000. Bitcoin closed the week at $62,829, below every major moving average and just above the August low. The level is lost and the lower path is live. Miss.

1. Bitcoin broke the range it was supposed to hold. The $63,000 area was the line, and Bitcoin spent the week underneath it. The Quality Trade numbers put it below every major moving average with the August low at $62,662 the only thing left before the June low near $57,000. The flows tell the same story as the price: US Bitcoin ETFs are bleeding while the ether funds accumulate, and the diverging flow is now five-plus sessions old.

The prediction market is not holding the bull case either. Kalshi prices a 45 percent chance Bitcoin finishes the year below $50,000. When the reference price and the prediction market and the ETF flow all point the same way, that is not noise. The house's own earlier read that $64,000 was the pivot is what just failed, and the honest scoreboard says so.

2. Strategy is selling Bitcoin to fund buybacks, and that is a regime change. Strategy sold 6,948 Bitcoin across four disclosures, with the latest 1,690 coins going for $108.6 million, all of it below the $75,385 average cost, to fund preferred-share buybacks. The Quality Trade flagged it as the treasury-company unwind the house has been tracking since the weekend deep-dive. The company that spent the cycle accumulating is now liquidating at a loss to service its structure.

That is the adoption-versus-price divergence turning bearish on the price side. Saylor's line that 30 percent a year is the risk-free rate and the stock buys at one times revenue has not stopped the sell, and Norway's sovereign fund buying more MSTR is not the retail bid that used to catch it. The treasury-company bid that propped the market is now a seller.

3. The superstruct week got quieter than the price. The Clarity Act still looks unlikely to become law this year, and the SEC canceled today's crypto-offering vote, leaving a neutral reading on Bitcoin and ether with the startup and tokenized exemptions unresolved. Kalshi is reportedly in talks with Sequoia and Wellington to raise $750 million at a $40 billion valuation, nearly double the $22 billion it fetched in May.

The plumbing is the part that is healthy. Tether passed its first full Big Four audit, with KPMG issuing a clean unqualified opinion on $180 billion of USDT and reserves that exceed liabilities by $6.8 billion. Gemini posted a $107.7 million quarterly loss, so the profitable-legacy story is not universal. The infrastructure is being built while the price bleeds, the same divergence the deep-dive has argued for two weeks.

4. The alt tape has real pockets of strength under a weak headline. Hyperliquid open interest sits at an all-time high near $11.73 billion, and Geoff Kendrick at Standard Chartered says its own $100 Chainlink 2030 target is too low even after UNI gave back 13.3 percent on the fee-switch unwind. Figure's lending business keeps compounding, with volume up 132 percent and net income up 192 percent in the quarter. The strength is in infrastructure names and lending businesses, not in the majors, and that points to real usage holding up while the speculative bid leaves.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. At $62,829 below every major moving average with $62,662 the last support before the June low near $57,000. ETF outflows are accelerating and Kalshi prices a 45 percent chance of sub-$50,000 this year.
  • $MSTR. Sold 6,948 Bitcoin below the $75,385 average cost to fund preferred buybacks. The treasury-company bid that helped the market is now a seller.
  • $ETH. Ether ETFs added 22,908 coins over the week against Bitcoin's $243 million outflow. The flow divergence is the cleanest signal in the market.
  • $UNI. Standard Chartered's $100 2030 target is, by its own analyst, too low, and the stock is down 13.3 percent on the fee-switch unwind. The buyback-and-burn structure is live.
  • $FIGR. Volume up 132 percent, net income up 192 percent, and a Q3 guide up 102 percent. The lending business is compounding while the majors bleed.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] The consumer cracked and the pricing would not budge
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: July retail sales fell 0.6 percent, sentiment sagged to 51, and the market still prices an 80 percent chance the Fed hikes next year.
item.content:encoded:
July retail sales fell 0.6 percent, sentiment sagged to 51, and the market still prices an 80 percent chance the Fed hikes next year.

Yesterday the driver was the rate-hike trade breaking. Today the data joined it, and nothing moved. That gap between a weakening consumer and stubbornly hawkish pricing is the story.

Market context. The S&P 500 closed at a record 7,798.99, up 0.65 percent and clearing 7,800 intraday for the second straight session, with the Nasdaq up 0.81 percent. The VIX has traded in lockstep with the index six of the last nine days and sits where a sub-13 print would be a caution flag. The US financial conditions index is near 1.29, the easiest reading since 1997, and corporate credit spreads are the tightest since 1998. Oil fell about 2 percent on Thursday, but that is the least important part of the tape.

1. The consumer cracked, and the market priced nothing. July retail sales fell 0.6 percent month over month against a 0.1 percent gain expected, the first negative print since March, and the control group fell 0.4 percent. The Per the People to follow list, University of Michigan sentiment index came in at 51 against 55 expected, and one-year inflation expectations reaccelerated to 4.3 percent from 4.2. The soft read landed on top of a cooler PPI, unchanged month over month and up 4.7 percent year over year, which dialed back September hike odds further.

None of it moved the pricing that matters. Kalshi still puts an 80 percent chance on a Fed rate hike next year. The thirty-year sits higher than it did before the prints. Weak data, cold inflation, and a bond market that will not take the bait is the needle Bessent and Warsh are trying to thread, and today it held in their favor. The consumer is the lag, not the lead, and this market keeps pricing the Fed's inflation worry over the consumer's.

2. The blockade is now indefinite, and the strait never returned to normal. The United States said it could maintain the naval blockade of Iran indefinitely. Kalshi puts only a 40 percent chance that Hormuz traffic returns to normal this year, down from the near-certainty that opened the window. A tanker was hit by a drone in the strait, and the first Kharg VLCC loaded 2 million barrels, the first such loading in two weeks. The Defense Department signed framework agreements with Boeing and Raytheon to raise SM-3 interceptor component production, a quiet signal that Washington is planning for a long standoff, not a quick one.

This is the same thread the house flagged when the July 27 Abqaiq strike was first reported. Oil is down on the day because the physical market has priced the reroute, but the chokepoint risk is structural and the odds have not improved.

3. The AI financing loop is the risk the record hides. Michael Burry's circular-financing map has about $46 billion of direct equity cycling against $879 billion of purchase commitments across Oracle, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, CoreWeave, Nvidia and AMD, and the Bank for International Settlements counts $1.65 trillion of hyperscaler off-balance-sheet obligations against $1.35 trillion reported. Jack Mallers called OpenAI's $250 billion Ohio build-out outrageous, arguing it is 135 percent of the company's retained earnings and that a 100-times-cheaper Chinese alternative would break the creditworthiness the whole stack leans on.

The bull case and the bear case agree on the mechanism, and that is why it is worth stating plainly. The record is being funded by off-balance-sheet commitments that no earnings stream yet services. The market is pricing the build, not the financing, and the financing is the part that can turn.

4. The dollar is cracking against Asia while the deficit sets records. The Chinese yuan is at its strongest level against the dollar since 2023, and $131 billion flowed into Japanese stocks with the Nikkei up 1.75 percent as the BOJ, Japan's central bank, moves closer to a hike as soon as September. The July deficit printed at a record $432 billion, the national debt sits at a record $39.9 trillion, and Fitch affirmed the United States at AA+ with a stable outlook. The dollar is doing the opposite of what the fiscal numbers imply, and the yen's drift back toward the intervention zone keeps the funding question alive.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] Nebius ran 34 percent, Burry doubled down, and the S&P broke 7,800
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Nebius posted 454 percent revenue growth on $582 million, raised its contract book to $46 billion, and the afternoon brought Burry with a fresh short at $247 plus a $94 billion memory thesis that nobody was carrying this morning.
item.content:encoded:
Nebius posted 454 percent revenue growth on $582 million, raised its contract book to $46 billion, and the afternoon brought Burry with a fresh short at $247 plus a $94 billion memory thesis that nobody was carrying this morning.

Yesterday I said the neocloud earnings were the real news and the depreciation argument had no purchase on a business that pre-sells capacity above cost. Today the market agreed and kept going.

Market context. Per the Market morning list, the S&P 500 broke above 7,800 for the first time ever in a session that opened green on the post-CPI momentum and kept running. The VIX touched 14.39, its lowest level of the year, on the lightest volume in thirteen sessions. The S&P has now printed 26 all-time highs this year. $NVDA closed at $224, its first close above 220 in a month. $META fell 3.3 percent and $MSFT 2.2, the rotation inside the rally that says semis are back and the software trade is taking a breather. Options volume leaders: NVDA 3.6 million contracts, SMCI 720,000, MU 1.3 million.

1. Nebius put up the numbers and Burry answered with a bigger short. Per the Crypto PM list and the Stocks PM list, Nebius did $582.3 million of revenue against $573 million expected, up 454 percent year over year. Adjusted EBITDA was $236 million against $173 million. AI Cloud revenue rose 514 percent. The company raised contracted capacity to 5 gigawatts, expects more than 1 gigawatt a year of deployment from 2027, and carried about $46 billion of multi-year AI cloud contracts including $27 billion with $META and $17 billion with $MSFT. Customer prepayments are expected to top $9 billion in 2026 alone, at 50 to 60 percent of capex.

Per the Stocks PM list, the pricing is the real weapon. Nebius signed its first deal at $40 to $50 million per megawatt, against a normal rate of about $20 to $25 million and a baseline of $9.8 million. Its first capacity auction cleared 15 percent above the highest price it had ever charged for Blackwell. It could sell its entire 2027 capacity today and is choosing not to. Per Shay Boloor, short-notice deals pay back in under two years with customers funding roughly half the capex upfront.

The stock ran from roughly $195 to $275 before fading slightly in the close, a move that puts Burry's $211.77 short from Tuesday underwater and his new $247 short from today barely flat. Per burrytracker, Burry added NBIS shorts at $247, MU short at $924, and ORCL short at $152 today, with a quote that Nebius is what the top of a boom looks like. Per the Jose Najarro stream, the question is how many of his 300,000 Substack followers are covering a 30 percent short float in a stock that is up ten times in eighteen months and answering on every quarter.

The after-hours earnings gave the longs a breather. NBIS faded about half a percent in sympathy with Cerebras, which fell 14 percent on operating expense of $500 million against $80 million expected at a $60 billion market cap. At that valuation on less than a billion of revenue, the credibility was inside the margin math.

2. SanDisk just put a match to the memory complex, and the size of the thesis is what matters. Per the Market PM list, SanDisk unveiled its HBF architecture, NAND repurposed as AI memory, and the numbers are not incremental. HBF matches high-bandwidth memory at 12.8 terabytes per second of bandwidth while using one-eighth the GPU resources at one-quarter the footprint. It achieves twice the GPU efficiency at one-eighth the capex, because one HBF GPU runs the same model that requires eight HBM GPUs.

Per Shay Boloor, SanDisk guided mid-to-high-teens revenue growth, roughly 80 percent non-GAAP gross margins, and about 50 percent adjusted free cash flow margins, with 100 percent of excess cash returned. Eight customers have signed contracts totalling roughly $94 billion in lifetime value. Key-value cache workloads are expected to drive 35 percent of AI data centre NAND workloads by 2030, and BiCS NAND delivers 54 percent more bits per wafer at 27 percent annual productivity improvement. Sell-side targets are running back to $3,000 from the current $1,404.

This is a thesis that would exist even if Nvidia stayed flat. The memory call the house has been fighting over for two weeks is now sitting on top of a named architecture with numbers, and the argument over whether multiples expand or compress just got a third term that neither side was pricing.

3. AMAT reported a beat and fell on it, and the month has a new earnings rhythm. Per the Reddit post and the Stocks AM list, Applied Materials beat earnings and raised guidance on its semiconductor systems, guided AGS revenue growth above 20 percent and advanced-packaging revenue growth above 70 percent for 2026, and fell 5 percent after hours because the expectations were higher than the beat. That is the same pattern Cerebras hit and the same one Coherent hit with a double beat that faded six percent: the bar for a clean after-hours reaction on earnings day inside a stock at an all-time high is not a beat, it is a blowout, and nothing short of a blowout that clears the valuation question gets a pass.

Per the Chip Stock Investor stream, DigitalOcean raised full-year guidance to 30 to 31 percent from 25 to 27, called for 50 percent growth by the end of fiscal 2027 on $400 million a quarter, and an analyst noted the cleanest balance sheet in the cloud infrastructure space with net cash and stock buybacks actively offsetting dilution. The stock faded after its own Q2 but the guidance keeps stacking.

Per the Financial Markets AM list, Coherent did $2.1 billion against $1.98 billion, guided Q1 to $2.3 billion against $2.1 billion, and has its revenue trajectory pointing above $3 billion a quarter by the end of fiscal 2027 on a backlog booked through calendar 2027. The after-hours faded anyway.

The Meta and Microsoft drops inside an index making all-time highs are the same signal in reverse. $META down 3.3 and $MSFT down 2.2 tells you this is a rotation within the rally, not a distribution event. The semis ran, the software gave back, Cisco beat on networking up 40 percent and faded in sympathy, and the after-hours trade painted its own picture.

4. Ackman rebuilt his portfolio and Peltz is coming for Wendy's. Per the Market AM list and Walter Bloomberg, Bill Ackman added six new holdings in his biggest portfolio revamp in years: $NFLX, $V, $MA, $ALC, $ICE and $SPGI. He bought $NFLX in 2022 at about $350 a share for $1.1 billion, sold at a roughly $400 million loss, and is now back in with the stock roughly half what he paid. His thesis is double-digit revenue compounding and about 20 percent annual earnings growth. Pershing Square USA is down 3.5 percent through July against the S&P up 13.

Nelson Peltz's Trian Fund Management is preparing a take-private of Wendy's at up to $8.80 a share with a consortium including BlueFive Capital and the Flynn Group. The stock has a 30 percent short float on 160 million shares and Heisenberg called the price today directly.

Per the Reddit post and Bloomberg, the California Public Utilities Commission was scheduled to vote today on Charter Communications' merger with Cox, the last major regulatory step before it becomes the largest broadband and cable provider in the United States at 38 million subscribers surpassing Comcast. The stock trades at $150 on a 3.9 times earnings multiple with $4.9 billion of net income and a 50 percent short float, and the SpaceX consumer mobile partnership talks reported by Bloomberg and Reuters in June sit on the other side of the close.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $NBIS. $582 million of revenue, 454 percent growth, $46 billion in contracts, and the ability to charge $50 million a megawatt on short notice against a baseline of $10 million. Burry is short at $247 and the stock touched $275 same day.
  • $SNDK. $94 billion of lifetime contracts on a memory architecture that matches HBM bandwidth at one-eighth the capex. The re-rate is priced at $1,404 and the sellers are calling $3,000.
  • $MU. At $890 with a 50-day moving average at 965 and the memory complex catching the SNDK halo. The buyback and dividend lift around December 6 is the first hard catalyst this name has had in months.
  • $DOCN. Guidance raised to 30 to 31 percent growth with 50 percent by end of fiscal 2027, a clean balance sheet, active buybacks, and a customer pipeline that is scaling faster than the capacity.
  • $CHTR. CPUC voted today on the Cox merger. At $150 on a 3.9 times multiple with a 50 percent short float and a SpaceX partnership rumor sitting on the other side of the close.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] The FIMA trigger has a number now, and the trade just broke Bitcoin's way
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Arthur Hayes says the $60 billion FIMA repo cap is the next Bitcoin liquidity trigger, while Macro's hammering of the rate-hike trade removed the single biggest headwind this asset has been fighting.
item.content:encoded:
Arthur Hayes says the $60 billion FIMA repo cap is the next Bitcoin liquidity trigger, while Macro's hammering of the rate-hike trade removed the single biggest headwind this asset has been fighting.

Yesterday four models were converging on two different floors and nobody was sure which one would bind first. Today the arguments about direction got quieter because the picture around them shifted.

Market context. Per the Crypto PM list, Bitcoin spot held roughly $64,000 with Market Outlook number 89 carrying a read of $65,310 against ETH at $1,926, the Nasdaq 100 at $29,838, gold at $4,355 and dollar-yen at 158.49. The key levels are two-sided. Support sits at $62,500 and the February low at $60,000, while the anchored VWAP is at $67,600 and the final boss remains $80,000. Bollinger band width is the narrowest it has been since October 2023.

Per Lookonchain, US Bitcoin ETFs shed 1,132 coins on the day, about $72 million, for a seven-day net of minus 202 coins. Ethereum ETFs added 3,947 ETH, about $7.5 million, for a seven-day net of plus 65,941 ETH and about $125 million. The flows have diverged for five straight sessions at the narrowest band in nearly three years, and that is a setup, not an accident.

1. Arthur Hayes just named the FIMA cap as Bitcoin's next trigger, and he gave it a number. Per Scott Melker and the Crypto PM list, Hayes says the $60 billion Fed FIMA repo facility cap is what unlocks the next Bitcoin leg and that a rate hike is not needed for the move, merely an expansion of the facility that lets foreign central banks borrow dollars against Treasuries rather than selling them. The mechanism is the same one Bessent proposed in July for the BOJ's intervention: Japan, the largest foreign holder of Treasuries at about $1.2 trillion, gets to borrow against them instead of selling, which removes the forced seller from the long end and adds dollar liquidity through the back door.

The call lands directly on the Macro edition today. The September hike odds collapsed from 42.1 to 29 percent, the December hike moved from 73.8 to 62.3, and the market is no longer pricing any hike in 2026 above 50 percent. The single biggest headwind Bitcoin has been fighting was a four-hike year. That trade just broke.

Per Cav, open interest relative to market cap is elevated across both perpetuals and Deribit options, and a break above the range will not be a slow stair-step rally. A short cascade is priced into the open interest structure, not just the tweet sentiment.

2. Figure reported and the lending business is growing faster than the price. Per the Crypto PM list, Figure did diluted earnings of 35 cents a share against roughly 25 cents expected. Capital Lending Markets volume hit $4.26 billion, up 132 percent year over year. The net take rate compressed to 3.6 percent from 4.0, adjusted EBITDA came in at $119.4 million at a 54.6 percent margin against 47.2 percent, net income rose to $87 million, up 192 percent, and the lender count reached 489. The company guided third-quarter volume to $4.8 to $5.2 billion and the Kiavi acquisition is pending at $717 million.

Per the house calls ledger, Figure was a catalyst call due today after a run of quarters. The beat clears the bar and the guide says the next quarter is bigger, which makes it a hit on the numbers and leaves the open question of whether the volume growth is priced into a stock that is up substantially on the year.

3. Standard Chartered put a $200 price target on Chainlink, and the reaction was a lot quieter than the number. Per Arbitrage Andy, Standard Chartered initiated coverage on $LINK with a $200 target for 2030, about a 2,400 percent return from the current price near $8, and the argument is that Chainlink becomes the critical data infrastructure for the entire tokenized real-world-asset economy. The report landed the same week that Link quietly crossed a series of integration milestones that the desk has been tracking.

The price is the problem more than the thesis. A coin at $8 with a $200 target is a 24-bagger and that is the kind of number that invites a fade even when the bank putting it up is a real one. VirtualBacon noted today that XRP still has ten times potential, that altcoins outside the top five carry the same return characteristics as 2021 and 2023, and that total altcoin market cap growth follows the Bitcoin market cap expansion whatever the multiple. A coin with a named institutional target at a five-handle price is the shape of the thing his framework is describing.

4. Robinhood Chain is pumping memecoins while the crypto segment that funds it is shrinking. Per 0xResearch and Degen Sensei, Robinhood Chain flipped Base in DEX volume in July, memecoins are 51 percent of spot volume against 5 percent for the real-world assets it was built for, and PumpFun revenue is surging as the chain's fee engine. The other side is the Robinhood corporate numbers. Monthly metrics released after the close showed crypto volumes down substantially, which was expected after a July that was tough across every trading metric, and the crypto segment revenue fell 38 percent year over year to $100 million in Q2.

Per Degen Sensei, Solana reclaimed DEX volume leadership from BNB Chain, on-chain has been strong, and the majors have been printing some of the lowest volatility days in history, which normally means a big move is coming. The sentiment bias is toward a dip before the rip, and the cash the desk has been telling you to keep ready is the same cash he is telling his readers to keep ready.

A fourth voice, Milk Road, noted Solana usage is exploding while price lags. That is the same tension driving the "adoption versus price" deep-dive the Sunday memo carried two weeks ago. The signal has not changed direction.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. At roughly $64,000 with support at $62,500 and $60,000, resistance at $67,600 and $80,000, in its narrowest Bollinger band since October 2023. ETF outflows of 1,132 coins on the day against the September hike trade collapsing in Macro.
  • $FIGR. 35 cents of diluted earnings against 25 expected, $4.26 billion of lending volume up 132 percent, and a guide of $4.8 to $5.2 billion for Q3. The Kiavi close at $717 million and the ARC mainnet on September 16 with BlackRock, Visa and DTCC as validators.
  • $LINK. Standard Chartered $200 target for 2030 on a thesis of critical data infrastructure for tokenized RWAs. At $8, the target is 24 times the price and a real bank is standing behind it.
  • $STRC. Brazil's largest Bitcoin treasury firm is planning an ETF with 95 percent allocation to Strategy, and the house has been tracking the treasury-company unwind-to-accumulation shift since last week.
  • $HOOD. Its chain leads L2 fee revenue and PumpFun is the engine while the corporate crypto segment shrank 38 percent to $100 million. The memo on this is that the chain is a memecoin chain wearing an RWA costume, and the corporate numbers confirm it.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] The rate-hike trade just broke, and the S&P ran straight through 7,800
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: September hike odds collapsed from 42.1 to 29 percent in one session on a hold call from Oxford Economics that said the Fed may not move for the rest of the year.
item.content:encoded:
September hike odds collapsed from 42.1 to 29 percent in one session on a hold call from Oxford Economics that said the Fed may not move for the rest of the year.

Yesterday the market still had a September hike at 42.1 percent chances after a CPI that landed on the estimate to the decimal. Today the floor fell out.

Market context. The S&P 500 broke above 7,800 for the first time ever, an intraday record, and the VIX touched 14.39, a new 2026 low. The session ran on energy: a Houthi attack on the Aramco refinery sent diesel cracks through $98 a barrel for an all-time high, gold futures held above $4,500 for the first time since June 5, and the yen inched back toward 160 per dollar. The 30-year auctioned at 5.21 percent on Tuesday and has not come in. Volume was the lowest in thirteen sessions for the S&P, which has now printed 26 all-time highs in 2026.

1. The hike odds broke, and the pivot reversed faster than it built. On Tuesday the market priced a September hike at 48.4 percent. On Wednesday it was 42.1 after the CPI. Today it is 29, and the hold stands at 70. Oxford Economics published a note saying the Fed is likely to hold for the rest of 2026, pointing to PCE inflation of 3.6 percent year over year in July against 3.7 in June and a labour market that is weakening but not breaking.

That is a fast trip. A month ago the September hike was at 69 percent. The jobs report took it to 48, the CPI nudged it to 42, and today a four-line forecast from a named shop took it to 29. The sequence is telling: a single payroll print, a single house call, and a single refinery attack have now dismantled more than 40 points of hike pricing in nine days. One more print, one more hawk to retreat, and the hold is a consensus.

The dissent is thin and it is not about the data. Warren Pies is still at a hike at 38 percent, arguing that the committee is under political pressure from a persistently missed inflation target, and he names Beth Hammack directly. Hammack herself said today that raising rates is painful but the Fed must not let growth and investment overheat. She did not say September and she did not say hold. The other hawk, Warsh, was quiet today.

What makes the pivot faster than the build is that the tail is pricing the same thing the front is. The December hike fell from 73.8 to 62.3. The October hike moved from 62.2 to 48.6. Any hike in 2026 is now at 47 percent, down from above 75 two weeks ago. When the back end of the year moves more than the front, the market is not just pricing a delay. It is pricing a reversal of the call. Goldman Sachs already declared the hold on Wednesday and nobody has stepped in front of them.

2. Iran is now asserting control over the strait and the oil market noticed. Iran said today that no vessel can transit the Strait of Hormuz without its permission. It reorganized its military to be more aggressive abroad, the State Department told embassies to draw up reduced-staff plans on fears of a return to war, and the US is sending a fresh carrier group led by the USS George Washington. The Reaper drone fleet is down about a quarter, with 45 MQ-9s lost at a replacement cost above $1.3 billion. The Pentagon is seeking $67 billion to replenish them.

The price is in diesel. Cracks broke above $98 a barrel, an all-time high, after the Houthis hit a Saudi Aramco refinery. A market that was oversupplied on paper at 106.3 million barrels a day of supply against 104.8 million of demand closed at a chokepoint it cannot control. Iran says it can keep the strait shut as long as necessary and that it is considering prolonging the war until Trump leaves office. Trump himself said the US has total control of the strait and thinks it will keep it.

Yesterday the Polymarket contract on the US announcing an end to the blockade by October 31 fell from 93 percent to 73. It has not moved back up today. The year-end contract sat at 81 cents.

3. Three firms reported after the bell and the after-hours trade is saying what the session trade already told you. Coherent beat, guided above the street, and fell six percent. Cerebras beat and fell fourteen, because operating expense came in at $500 million against $80 million expected and at a $60 billion market cap on less than a billion dollars of revenue, the valuation math matters the moment the numbers are not perfect. Cisco beat on networking products up 40 percent year over year and a Q1 guide more than a billion above the street, and still faded to red after hours.

The pattern is the same one the morning held: the S&P rallied 0.6 percent to a record and the headliners inside it, the $NVDA and the $NBIS and the semis, did the running, while the rest of the index held still. The equal-weight S&P is up fourteen of the last sixteen months. The cap-weight index is rallying because the megacaps are rallying, and the after-hours earnings are selectively punishing the ones whose numbers were not clean enough.

4. The bond market is doing its own thing and the yen is the link. The thirty-year auctioned at 5.21 percent on Tuesday, the highest in a quarter century, and the yield has barely moved from there. Japan's two-year hit 1.64 percent, the first time since 1995, while the yen pushed back toward 160 per dollar. At 160 the intervention question returns, because that is the level that triggered the first coordinated US-Japan intervention since 1998 last month alongside the Bessent FIMA repo proposal.

CreditSights published a note today saying the Fed could hold into 2027. If the long end is at 5.21 and the front end is holding, that is the steepener trade the rate-cut trade was built on. The yen at 160 and the thirty-year at 5.21 are two sides of a funding question, and the fuel on both sides is the deficit. The national debt hit a record $39.94 trillion today, this fiscal year's deficit is already larger than all of last year's, and $1.1 trillion a year in interest is the floor under the long end regardless of what the Fed does with the overnight rate.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] Both neoclouds beat, Burry got squeezed, and my memory reversal was wrong
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Nebius put up 454 percent revenue growth and CoreWeave broke a five-quarter losing streak on earnings day, while Goldman modelled DRAM prices up 250 to 300 percent next year.
item.content:encoded:
Nebius put up 454 percent revenue growth and CoreWeave broke a five-quarter losing streak on earnings day, while Goldman modelled DRAM prices up 250 to 300 percent next year.

Two days ago I reversed the memory call to compression on the argument that five-year contracts had capped the pricing lever. Today Goldman published a DRAM price forecast that makes that look like the wrong read of the wrong market.

Market context. Per the Kalshi morning list, Tuesday closed with the S&P down 0.3 percent, the Nasdaq 100 down 0.6 and the Russell 2000 up 0.3. Today opened green on the in-line CPI Macro has, then chopped on the lightest volume in thirteen sessions, with Fear and Greed at 62. The drawdowns underneath the index are the part to hold onto: per the Financial Markets list, from all-time highs $META is off 27 percent, $GOOGL 16.4, $AAPL 13 and $MSFT 10.8, with $NVDA down only 5.5.

The scoreboard.

  • Hit. My CoreWeave call said the print turns on whether the first quarter was the true bottom in adjusted operating margin. It was. Section one.
  • Miss. My Nebius call carried Rick Orford's bearish framing at 105.5 times sales with Burry short at $211.77. Nebius beat and ran more than 20 percent. Section one.
  • Miss. My Supermicro call carried Rick Orford's bearish case from July 28. Revenue came in at $11.1 billion against $11.55 billion expected, adjusted earnings at $1.70 against $0.96, and the stock rose 8 to 10 percent after hours because the guide was the story: next quarter $14.5 to $15.5 billion against $11.68 billion, and full-year 2027 $65 to $72 billion against a $52.5 billion consensus. The bear case was right on the facts and a backlog guide beat a balance sheet.
  • Reversing again, and this one needs an explanation rather than a number. The memory call goes back to 60/40 that multiples expand before they compress. Section two is why, and why I should not have moved it on Monday.
  • Confirmed, and my number was light. My July 22 call said Paramount owes a ticking fee above $600 million a quarter if the deal does not close by September 30. It is $7 million a day from October 1, about $637 million a quarter, with trial set for May 2, 2027 and roughly $1.2 billion accrued by then.

1. Both neoclouds beat, and the pricing disclosure is the real news. Per the Stocks morning list, CoreWeave did $2.6 billion of revenue against $2.56 billion expected, adjusted EBITDA of $1.5 billion against $1.43 billion at a 59 percent margin, with backlog at about $104 billion, up 46 percent, and full-year guidance raised to $12.4 to $13.2 billion. Per the People to follow morning list, earnings came in at minus $1.14 against minus $1.45 expected, a 21 percent beat, on a net loss that widened to $626 million.

Per the Market morning list, it ran from minus 3 percent to plus 14.39 percent within an hour, its first green earnings reaction in six tries after five straight of minus 11.4, minus 18.5, minus 16.3, minus 20.8 and minus 2.5.

Nebius was the bigger number. Per the People to follow list:

Nebius Q2Figure
Revenue$582.3 million against $572.75 million expected, up 454 percent
Adjusted EBITDA$236 million against $173 million expected
Contracted capacity guideraised to 5 gigawatts from over 4
Customer prepayments expected in 2026over $9 billion, at 50 to 60 percent of capex
AI cloud adjusted EBITDA margin24 percent, then 45, now 50 across three quarters

The disclosure that matters is what a megawatt costs. Per the Stocks list, mid-term deals run $20 to $25 million per megawatt with half to sixty percent of the capex paid upfront, short deals run $40 to $50 million, and the first capacity auction cleared 15 percent above the highest price it had ever charged for Blackwell. Management said it could sell all of 2027 today and is choosing not to.

That is the answer to the depreciation argument, and it does not require anyone to win a debate about useful life. Burry's short says these companies overstate profits by depreciating GPUs too slowly. Nebius is being paid more per megawatt each quarter and collecting most of the capex before the machines run. Per Edelbridge Alpha, its $775 million facility at SOFR plus 250 covers more than 100 percent of the capex it funds and is repeatable against more than $40 billion of contracted revenue. A business that pre-sells capacity above cost does not need the accounting to be generous.

The counterweight is what Nvidia's $500 billion actually is. Per TBPN, the mechanism is securitization: Nvidia supplies depreciation insurance up to 25 percent plus reference designs that make data centres fungible, so the debt can be tranched into investment-grade paper and sold to pension funds and insurers. The banks are swapping project-specific credit risk for sector-wide risk and collecting fees for the trip. Per Milk Road AI, the money is "not in 2026 or 2027, but over time," and across six sources today nobody produced a per-firm number or a first-dollar date. Treat it as a distribution channel that has been built, not as demand that has been committed.

2. I generalised a NAND concession to DRAM, and that was the error. On Monday I reversed this call because Chip Stock Investor, holding SanDisk through a drawdown, conceded that five-year hyperscaler agreements had ended the wild average selling prices. That concession was real and it was about NAND.

Per the Stocks morning list, the DRAM market is going the other way and the sell side is not being subtle about it. Goldman revised DRAM price forecasts to up 250 to 300 percent in 2026 and up 300 to 350 percent in 2027. Bernstein models average selling prices reaching $2.23 a gigabyte by the end of 2027, roughly five times the 2025 level. Micron posted an 81.2 percent operating margin.

Per the Stocks list, the mechanism is capacity rather than sentiment. A gigabyte of high-bandwidth memory takes three times the wafer capacity of standard DRAM, so every line converted to HBM removes conventional supply at the same time and you get a shortage in both at once. Operating margins across all three makers run 70 to 80 percent. The confirming detail is small and hard to argue with: Google raised the Pixel 11 by $100 to $899 and cited a severe memory crunch.

So the call goes back to 60/40 that multiples expand first, and I am flagging it as low conviction rather than pretending this is insight. I have moved this three times in seven days. A call that moves three times in a week is one I do not have an edge on, and the honest label is a view rather than a position. What I got wrong was treating one company's NAND contract structure as the whole memory complex.

3. Goldman bought an ETF issuer, and it is the second one this year. Per Eric Balchunas, Goldman Sachs is acquiring Neos ETFs for $2.3 billion. Neos is only a few years old and got big fast, at $32 billion, mostly in covered-call monthly income funds. Goldman bought Innovator, the buffered-ETF house, immediately before it, and Balchunas reads the pair as a bet on what he calls boomer candy.

Two acquisitions in a row in defined-outcome and income products is a house buying what sells when investors stop trusting the index. That is a read on flows rather than markets, from a firm that spent this morning declaring a September hold.

4. Texas just cut its own power forecast in half, the first hard brake on the buildout. Per the Polymarket morning list, Texas cut its 2027 power demand growth forecast to 6 percent from 14 after auditing data centre interconnection requests. Per the Stocks list, ERCOT has paused new power deals to Texas data centres outright.

Set that against what power is fetching. Galaxy leased 800 megawatts to CoreWeave at $1.2 billion a year, and its Helios II block of 830 megawatts is expected to clear above $1.4 billion.

The audit is the interesting half. If the queues were inflated by speculative requests, the demand figure everyone has been underwriting was inflated too, and the constraint moves from generation to permission. Names holding energised capacity get more valuable and names holding a pipeline get less. That is a sorting mechanism rather than a sector call.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $NBIS. Revenue up 454 percent, contracted capacity guided to 5 gigawatts, and megawatt pricing stepping from $12 million to $20 million to above $40 million on short deals. It closed Tuesday at $193 and traded around $225. Burry is short from $211.77 and now underwater.
  • $CRWV. A 59 percent adjusted EBITDA margin, $104 billion of backlog and a first green earnings reaction in six quarters, against a net loss widening to $626 million and over $10 billion of new unsecured debt. The margin question is answered and the funding question is not.
  • $MU. An 81.2 percent operating margin into Goldman modelling DRAM up 250 to 300 percent next year, with HBM conversion shorting conventional supply at the same time. The buyback and dividend restriction lifts around December 6, the first dated catalyst this name has had in months. 891 has to hold and 955 is the line above.
  • $FCX. Per Joseph Hogue and Ross Givens, new copper mines take 15 to 20 years and AI alone could lift demand by half. It trades at 20 times this year against a five-year average of 21 after a 58 percent run, with 30 percent profit growth modelled next year.
  • $GS. Two ETF acquisitions in a row, Innovator and now NEOS at up to $2.3 billion for $32 billion of mostly covered-call assets. The buyer of income and buffer products is telling you what it expects investors to want next.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] A fourth model puts the low at $56,000, below the leg I have been carrying
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Jesse Eckel dates the capitulation to October on a 200-day convergence and rules out $40,000 outright, because this drawdown is already far shallower than 2017 or 2021.
item.content:encoded:
Jesse Eckel dates the capitulation to October on a 200-day convergence and rules out $40,000 outright, because this drawdown is already far shallower than 2017 or 2021.

Yesterday three independent frameworks converged on $67,000 as the flip. Today a fourth arrived, ignored that level entirely, and put the bottom below the one I have been carrying.

Market context. Per the Financial Markets morning list, three separate on-chain transfers imply Bitcoin at $63,611, $63,693 and $63,814, so call it $63,700 and unchanged. Bollinger band width is the narrowest since October 2023.

The leverage map is the tradeable part. Per the Crypto morning list, four bears are short a combined 5,375 coins, about $343 million, with liquidations stacked at $64,101, $64,577, $66,007 and $66,030. Two longs hold 1,547 coins with liquidations down at $61,200 and $61,832. The nearest bear stop sits under one percent above spot and the nearest long stop is four percent below, so the squeeze risk is asymmetrically upward from here.

Flows went the other way. Per the same list, US spot ETFs took $865.3 million over five sessions for a 2.2 percent gain, behind the Nasdaq's 3.0, and have now flipped to $144.6 million of net redemptions.

1. Eckel's low is $56,000 and he dates it to October. Per Jesse Eckel, the test is a convergence rather than a level: price and the 200-day moving average meet around October 2026, exactly one year after this cycle's high. Bitcoin has been below that average since October 2025 and was rejected directly on the line the one time it tried to reclaim it.

His path is a drop from 63 to 64,000 down to about 56,000 in an October capitulation, then a turn. The derivation is decay in the post-chop drawdown across cycles: 51 percent in 2017, 20 percent in 2021, about 12 percent now.

Eckel's cycle arithmeticReading
Days into the bear when the chop began199 in 2017, 219 in 2021, 240 now
Cycle gain579x, then 129x, then 22x, now 8.16x
Chop zone depth below the high67 percent in 2017, 72 in 2021, 49 now

That last row is why he rules out $40,000 and $30,000 for this cycle outright. A drawdown already this shallow does not, on his own decay logic, produce a 2018-style flush.

This is same-direction confirmation of my 60/40 for $58,000 before $75,000, and it is also a warning about my timing. He agrees the low is lower and he puts it in October, not this week. Note also that his flip line is the 200-day, not the $67,000 that On-Chain Mind, VirtualBacon and Sykodelic all landed on yesterday. Four frameworks, two different lines, and nobody has reconciled them. Per the Crypto list, On-Chain Mind himself today switched to a different tool entirely and called Bitcoin "firmly in the Value Zone" at 60 percent of his DCA channel.

I am holding 60/40 and moving nothing. When four models disagree about the line and agree about the direction, the direction is the information.

2. Cramer sold everything on quantum, and the physics says he is early by a decade. Per Milk Road, Jim Cramer said on August 3 that he is selling every last one of his Bitcoin, because quantum computers crack it within about three years. He had interviewed IBM's Arvind Krishna days earlier, who put the window at three to four.

The research genuinely moved. A March paper from Google Quantum AI with the Ethereum Foundation and Stanford put breaking Bitcoin's cryptography at fewer than 500,000 physical qubits and about nine minutes per key, roughly twenty times less hardware than previously estimated. Caltech and a startup called Oratomic claimed 26,000 qubits over ten days on different hardware.

Then the number that settles it for now. The largest key publicly broken on real quantum hardware this year was 15 bits. Bitcoin uses 256. None of the existing machines are error-corrected at anything near that scale.

The exposure is real and old: wallet formats from 2009 and 2010 wrote public keys straight to the chain, and that plus every wallet that has ever sent is about a third of all Bitcoin ever mined, of which roughly 1.1 million coins are Satoshi's and can never be moved. The defence is already merged, with BIP-360 keeping keys off-chain since February 11 and live on testnet with more than fifty miners.

Cramer selling a 256-bit problem on a 15-bit result is a sentiment event, not a security event. The thing that actually moves this asset inside ninety days is the CLARITY cloture vote in mid-September that Macro laid out.

3. Robinhood Chain is a memecoin chain wearing a real-world-asset costume. Two sources published opposite readings of the same chain on the same day, which makes this easy to adjudicate.

Per 0xSammy, the bull case is that Stonkbrokers fees buy Nvidia and Apple shares onchain and distribute them into token-bound wallets, that a new project called Tickeryard went from a $200,000 mint to $4 to $5 million, and that Robinhood Chain dominates EVM chain fees. He discloses he holds many of the assets he names.

Per 0xResearch, Blockworks measured it. Memecoins are 51 percent of Robinhood Chain spot volume against 5 percent for real-world assets, its stated purpose. Known revenue annualises to $54.8 million, about 14 percent of Robinhood's crypto revenue, and Robinhood's Q2 crypto revenue fell 38 percent year over year to $100 million.

One more number closes it. The Stonkbrokers collection this desk logged on Sunday at $80 million fully diluted is quoted today at $54 million, under a piece titled "Explodes."

4. Two businesses onchain are actually earning money, and neither is a memecoin. Per 0xResearch, Circle posted second-quarter revenue and reserve income of $701 million, up 7 percent, adjusted EBITDA of $143 million, USDC supply of $73.3 billion, up 19 percent, and $14.8 trillion of onchain transfer volume, up 151 percent. The stock rose 16 percent on the week to about $71. Two dated catalysts follow: Arc mainnet on September 16 with BlackRock, Visa and DTCC as founding validators, and federal approval of Circle National Trust.

Aptos is the stranger case. It is the only general-purpose chain with positive token-holder net income, at plus $6.33 per $10,000 of fully diluted value against Ethereum at minus $0.95, Solana minus $1.89 and Sui minus $6.18. It got there by repricing gas ten times, halving staking to a flat 2.6 percent and capping supply. Revenue rose about sixteen times while transactions went from 4.5 million a day to over 12 million at ten times the fee. There is no listed proxy, so it is a token trade or nothing. Carry it for the mechanism: a chain raised prices and kept its users.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. At $63,700 in its narrowest band since October 2023, with bear liquidations at $64,101 and $64,577 barely above and long stops four percent below. Eckel's October target is $56,000 to $57,000, under my own $58,000 leg, and he rules out $40,000 for this cycle.
  • $XRP. The price dropped below $1 today per the Financial Markets list. Per Lark Davis, it is down 72 percent from its high on the most oversold monthly reading in its twelve-year history, while Aviva, a $351 billion manager, put a regulator-approved tokenized fund on the ledger and XRPL real-world assets reached $4.5 billion. The overhang is 32.4 billion tokens in timed release.
  • $CRCL. $701 million of quarterly revenue, $73.3 billion of USDC and $14.8 trillion of transfer volume, with Arc mainnet on September 16 carrying BlackRock, Visa and DTCC as validators. The catalyst has a date attached, and that is rare here.
  • $HOOD. Its chain leads L2 fee revenue at $3.6 million in July and is still 51 percent memecoin volume, while the crypto segment that funds the story fell 38 percent year over year to $100 million.
  • $MSTR. Phong Le says the company returns to buying during the year, after selling 1,638 coins at $63,957 last week. Treasury companies were net movers rather than buyers, with MetaPlanet shifting 1,473 coins and Hut 8 another 493.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] The print landed exactly on consensus and moved September by six points
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: I said CPI would settle September more than payrolls did, and it did not come close, so that call is a miss and this is what it actually moved.
item.content:encoded:
I said CPI would settle September more than payrolls did, and it did not come close, so that call is a miss and this is what it actually moved.

Yesterday I said the thing to watch was whether the month-over-month number started with a 2. Headline started with a 1, core started with a 2, everything printed on the estimate, and September barely moved.

Market context. The print was in line on every line that was published.

July CPIActualEstimatePrior
Headline, year over year3.4 percent3.43.5
Core, year over year2.5 percent2.52.6
Core, month over month0.2 percent0.2minus 0.0
Headline, month over month0.1 percent0.1

One correction to yesterday. I printed a monthly consensus of 0.32 percent from a single source. The number the desks were actually carrying was 0.1 percent on headline and 0.2 on core, and the print matched it. The 0.32 was wrong and I should have checked it against a second source before publishing it.

Per the People to follow list, core goods rose 0.2 percent, the biggest monthly increase since September 2025. That is the one line inside the report that does not read friendly. Gold went the other way from a benign print. Per the Kalshi list, gold futures surged back above $4,500, the first time since June 5, against spot near $4,408 overnight. Per the Financial Markets list, the yen is inching toward 160 per dollar and raising re-intervention concerns, and the session ran on the lightest volume of the past thirteen trading days.

The scoreboard.

  • Miss, and cleanly. On the 6th I called the August 12 CPI the print that settles September more than payrolls does. Payrolls moved September hike odds from 55 percent to roughly 40. CPI moved them from 48.4 to 42.1. Payrolls moved it more than twice as far. Section one is the accounting.
  • Miss, and I saw it coming too late. My call that a joint Iran-Oman announcement lands inside a week expires today with no announcement. I opened it at 70/30, cut to 55/45, then to 40/60 yesterday. The direction was right at the end and the original number was not. Section two.

1. Six points is what a perfectly in-line print buys you. Per the People to follow list, the post-CPI repricing was orderly and small.

Fed hike odds, after against beforeReading
September 1642.1 percent, from 48.4
October 2856.3 percent, from 62.2
December 973.8 percent, from 78.9
Any hike in 202655 percent, from over 75 earlier this month

Per the Polymarket list, Goldman Sachs went further and declared outright that the Fed holds in September. That is the first named house call for a hold in a week of this desk carrying one.

My 60/40 for a September hold is now roughly where the market is, with a hike at 42.1 against my implied 40. Holding it is no longer a contrarian position, and saying that is more useful than claiming vindication.

The dissent is specific and it is not dovish. Per the Stocks list, Warren Pies says a September hike at 38 percent is underpriced, that he would hold but that the committee is "increasingly feeling the political pressure of persistently missing its inflation target," and that today's data is not decisive enough to offset the political dynamics. He names Beth Hammack directly.

The reason my call missed is that I confused a scheduled event with a decisive one. A print that lands on the estimate to the decimal on four separate lines cannot move a distribution much, almost by construction. Payrolls surprised by 103,000 jobs and moved it fifteen points. CPI surprised by nothing and moved it six. The lesson I am taking is that the size of a repricing comes from the surprise, not from the importance of the series, and I priced importance.

Note what did not move. December still sits at 73.8 percent for a hike. The year is not settled and today did not settle it.

2. Hormuz resolved, and it resolved against everybody who wanted a deal. No joint Iran-Oman announcement landed. What landed instead was worse.

Per the Polymarket list, Iran says there are no talks to extend the ceasefire, adds that the ceasefire never officially took effect, and accuses Washington of violating it inside 48 hours. The State Department has ordered US embassies across the Middle East to draw up contingency plans for operating with reduced staff on fears of a return to war. Per the Kalshi list, Iran is reported to be considering prolonging the war until Trump leaves office. Trump's own line today was that the US has "total control" over the Strait of Hormuz and "I think we will keep it."

The cleanest read is in a price. Per the People to follow morning list, the odds of the US announcing an end to the Iranian blockade by October 31 fell from 93 percent to 73 in a single week on $12.2 million of volume, with the cliff starting on August 8. A separate contract on the blockade being lifted by year end decayed from above 95 cents to about 81. The market spent the week pricing the deal further away, not closer.

I opened this at 70/30 for an announcement inside a week and it finished at zero. The cut to 40/60 yesterday was right and late. The error that produced the original number was treating Iran's route agreement with Oman as a proxy for the strait reopening, which Iran itself spent this week explicitly denying.

3. Gold cleared $4,500 into a benign inflation print, and that is not what it is supposed to do. Per the Kalshi list and the Financial Markets list, futures are back above $4,500 for the first time since June 5 and spot ran about 1 percent overnight to $4,408.79. Somebody keeps buying it in size, with a third unusual multi-million-dollar call print inside a week.

Against that, per the People to follow list, Cathie Wood expects a deflationary boom and gold to fall. The betting markets are not with her and not fully with gold either: traders price only a 17 percent chance Bitcoin outperforms gold in 2026, down nine points.

Gold rallying on a cooling CPI while the long end still prices three quarters odds of a December hike is the debasement trade rather than the inflation trade. Those are different arguments and only one of them cares what the print said.

4. The yen is back at 160 and that is the number that ends the quiet. Per the Financial Markets list, the yen is inching toward 160 per dollar and raising re-intervention concerns. That is the level that produced the first coordinated US-Japan intervention since 1998 last month, the one that came with the Bessent proposal to expand the Fed's FIMA repo facility so Japan could borrow dollars against Treasuries rather than sell them. Per the Financial Markets morning list, Japan's two-year yield hit 1.64 percent, the first time since 1995, and Japan is the largest foreign holder of Treasuries at roughly $1.2 trillion. The US 30-year is at its highest since 2007.

The oil side gives the yen no help. Per the Financial Markets list, the IEA revised 2025 demand up to 104.8 million barrels a day against supply of 106.3 million, US crude stockpiles posted an unexpected build, Russian output ran nearly a million barrels a day below its OPEC quota in July, and US imports of Venezuelan crude hit a nine-year high. A market that is oversupplied on paper and closed at a chokepoint in practice is one headline away from either direction.

If the yen takes 160 while Hormuz stays shut, the intervention question comes back inside weeks rather than months. That is the thing on the calendar that nobody has a date for.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] The Micron bull case arrived and quietly changed the subject away from price
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Rick Orford's hidden moat turns out to be automotive and robotics lock-in, and he concedes analysts expect margins to normalize once supply catches demand.
item.content:encoded:
Rick Orford's hidden moat turns out to be automotive and robotics lock-in, and he concedes analysts expect margins to normalize once supply catches demand.

Yesterday I reversed the memory call to 55/45 that multiples compress before they expand, on the argument that five-year hyperscaler contracts capped the pricing lever. Today the counter-case showed up, and it never mentions pricing.

Market context. The tape did nothing while it waited. Per the Financial Markets list, the S&P touched a session low down almost 0.2 percent in the afternoon and both it and the Nasdaq proxy sat near the lows of the day, with CPI tomorrow the only thing anyone would name as a reason. Monday finished roughly unchanged near 7,753. The breadth underneath is better than the headline: the equal-weight S&P printed new all-time highs, and J.C. Parets has the average Nasdaq 100 stock as strong as it has ever been. Per the Market list, Heisenberg called the gold fund at $370 and it hit $404 today, and he is trimming half.

The scoreboard.

  • Held, and the counter-case did not touch it. My 55/45 that memory multiples compress first. Section one is why the bull argument moving to automotive strengthens it rather than weakening it.
  • Reported today, result not in hand. Supermicro, on Rick Orford's July 28 bearish case. Not one source across today's material carries a number from it, so it stays open rather than getting graded on a guess.
  • Reports tonight, not Wednesday. CoreWeave, against a June quarter consensus of $2.56 billion on EPS of minus $1.45. I had the date a day late.
  • Reports Wednesday. Nebius, and it walked into the print with a problem. Section three.

1. The Micron bull case changed the subject, and that is the strongest thing I learned today. Per Rick Orford, Micron's hidden moat is automotive and robotics end-market diversification, held together by long-term strategic customer agreements with automakers that give certainty on supply and pricing. The supporting numbers are real: cars with L2-plus autonomy need more than five times the memory of a typical vehicle and are over 20 percent of new sales this year, heading to 40 by 2030, and a humanoid robot needs about ten times an L2 car.

Notice what is absent. He never addresses contract against spot pricing, never mentions the five-year hyperscaler agreements, and never uses the phrase take-or-pay. He also concedes the other side outright, saying the market believes the company is near peak earnings and that analysts expect margins to normalize once supply catches up with demand. His answer is that the floor under each cycle keeps rising, and that is a decade-long argument rather than a next-quarter one.

A bull case that retreats from pricing to end markets is a bull case that has conceded the near term. I am holding 55/45.

The valuation is the honest tension. Micron trades at 9.2 times earnings against SK Hynix at 19, with 40 analysts at strong buy and targets implying 82 to 144 percent upside. Cheap is not the same as early.

The rest of the tape is split. Per the Stocks list, Kyle Reidhead's UBS model has DRAM margins rising to a 95 percent peak by late 2027 with commodity DRAM going $11 to $18 a gigabyte, and calls the cyclical thesis dead until 2029. In the same feed Milk Road's house view is a bust in 18 to 24 months, and intelfabs draws the line that matters: HBM margins hold near 75 percent while conventional DRAM walks a classic commoditization path. That split is where this call settles.

2. A pathologist made the clearest bear case of the day and it is not about AI. Per Chip Stock Investor, Dr. Bradley Gibson's mechanism is that Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement is frozen in nominal dollars while costs inflate. The CMS conversion factor was $31 in 1992 and $32.34 in 2025 against more than 120 percent of cumulative inflation.

The dated catalyst is small and specific. His practice got an email last month about a 4.3 percent across-the-board Medicaid cut in Kentucky because the state ran out of money, and close to a third of Kentucky's roughly 130 hospitals already lose money even after subsidy.

Where the exposure sitsThe number
Healthcare as a share of GDPabout 18 percent, roughly $4 trillion a year
Against total income tax receiptsabout $2 trillion
DaVita's dialysis windowthe 30-month private-to-Medicaid transition pays 3 to 4x Medicaid rates and is responsible for essentially 100 percent of operating profit
UnitedHealthemploys 90,000 doctors, just under 10 percent of US physicians, and swung from +$7 billion to a roughly $1 billion loss in 2025

His rule is to bucket by who actually pays: avoid reimbursement-dependent providers and insurers, prefer pharma and especially medical hardware and software that price in cash and sell internationally. He is bearish on AI drug discovery too, because AI speeds discovery while the trials hold the cost.

3. Rocket Lab and AST both reported, both moved, and both finished flat. Per the People to follow list, Rocket Lab did $234 million of revenue against $231 million expected, up 62 percent, with backlog at $2.36 billion, up 137 percent, and guided the third quarter to $250 to $265 million against a $239 million estimate. It missed on EPS at minus $0.08 and guided an adjusted EBITDA loss of $17 to $23 million against $11.8 million expected.

AST SpaceMobile was the messier one: revenue $32 million against $34 million, EPS of minus $0.77 against minus $0.29, more than a two-times miss, with 2026 revenue guidance nonetheless raised to $175 million.

The reaction is the lesson. Heisenberg had the expected move on both above 11 percent, and by half an hour after the bell his read was "Rocket Lab flat now, HIMS flat now. Both had huge implied moves. Option writers win again?" Per the Stocks list, Rocket Lab later sold off about 10 percent on Peter Beck calling the Neutron year-end window "narrowing," which is one word costing more than a $2.36 billion backlog earned.

Nebius goes into Wednesday carrying its own version of that risk. Per the same list, it has now admitted the roughly 300 megawatt Vineland project slips from year-end 2026 into 2027, after leadership spent weeks saying it was on track. The print is a credibility event before it is a numbers event.

4. Hitting your plan is now the thing destroying your equity value. Per Invest Like The Best, Benchmark's Eric Vishria has the cleanest frame anyone offered on software this week. The 2021 cohort of public software companies traded at 30 times revenue, has quadrupled in size, and now trades at six times. The multiple fell by a factor of six while the businesses got four times bigger.

His line to those chief executives is the part worth keeping: "you have a choice, get to AI or be worth three times revenue," and "every single day that you are hitting your plan, you are destroying equity value." The competitive frontier moved, so executing the old plan is now value-destructive rather than merely dull.

The mechanism he gives is databases, where the moat was always migration cost. Agents do not tire of translating one specification into another and the interfaces are well specified, so migration gets cheap and cost plus scaling becomes the arbiter. Behind that sits an overhang nobody is pricing: roughly 500 private software companies between $100 million and $500 million with no tender, no exit and a missed listing window.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $MU. Nine times earnings against SK Hynix at 19, with the bull case now resting on automotive and robotics rather than on price. Per the Market list, every pop above 900 has been sold for a week, and the stated rule is to avoid the upside until it closes above 900 and holds three days.
  • $HIMS. Revenue $753 million, up 38 percent against about $700 million expected, with full-year guidance raised to $3.1 to $3.3 billion, and it still round-tripped to flat because GAAP EPS was minus $0.37 against minus $0.05 and gross margin fell from 76 to 64. International went from 1.4 percent of sales to 17.4 in a year.
  • $RKLB. A record quarter, a $2.36 billion backlog up 137 percent, and a third-quarter guide well above the street, sold off on one word about the Neutron schedule. The EBITDA guide is the real soft spot.
  • $SAIL. Per Ticker Symbol: YOU, Palo Alto paid about 20 times ARR for CyberArk at announcement and 15 at close. SailPoint's $1.16 billion of ARR at those multiples implies roughly $20 billion, close to double its market cap, with non-human identities now 14 percent of managed identities and 40 percent of growth. No offer exists.
  • $INTC. Per the People to follow list, the offering was upsized to $20 billion at a $95 minimum on more than $100 billion of demand, roughly five times oversubscribed, and the stock reclaimed $100 after falling 4 percent on the announcement. Funded, dilutive and catalyst-free for about three weeks.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] Three independent models now put the flip at $67,000, and Saylor sold at $63,957
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Bitcoin is sitting exactly on a 200-week average at $63,800 that Strategy publishes on its own website as book value, and it sold 1,638 coins right on the line.
item.content:encoded:
Bitcoin is sitting exactly on a 200-week average at $63,800 that Strategy publishes on its own website as book value, and it sold 1,638 coins right on the line.

Yesterday the weekly close failed and the man who drew the level went short. Today two more desks arrived at the same number from completely different directions, and the largest holder in the world sold into it.

Market context. Per the Crypto list, Bitcoin traded near $63,700, down 1.68 percent, with aixbt attributing it to Brent above $90 keeping the Fed on guard. The flows are two-sided again.

The tapeFigure
Spot Bitcoin ETFs, one dayminus 2,209 BTC, about $141 million out
Spot Bitcoin ETFs, seven daysplus 8,545 BTC, about $546 million in
Ether ETFs, seven daysplus 110,579 ETH, about $208 million
Crypto miners, weekminus 15.0 percent, the worst index on the board

Per 0xResearch, layer twos gained 7.7 percent on the week while Bitcoin fell. Ether sits near $1,926.

1. Three desks, three methods, one number. Per On-Chain Mind, his adaptive trend model has been bearish for 87 days, since it flipped at $78,000 in mid-May, and it turns back at $67,000. The level is volatility-adaptive, so it compresses as daily ranges tighten.

Per VirtualBacon, the instruction is the same and he gets there from risk-reward rather than from a model. Do not buy here, because a relief rally targets 75,000 to 77,000 while the only true invalidation is a new cycle low below 57,800, so the trade is 16 percent up against 10 percent down. What he wants instead is a daily close above $67,000, then a long near 68 with a stop at 64.

That is now three frameworks landing on the same figure, because Sykodelic's short from $65,300 carries its invalidation at a strong daily close above $67,000 too. When a trend model, a risk-reward frame and a short's stop all converge on one number, the number stops being an opinion and becomes the level everyone is trading against.

The rest of his board is more balanced than the headline. Price sits exactly on the 200-week moving average at $63,800, which has compounded 30 percent a year for four straight years, and on a kernel baseline of $64,300, so nothing is stretched either way. A higher low has printed, the first necessary condition for a reversal rather than confirmation of one. His weekly velocity RSI reads just over 14 percent, inside the sub-15 band that has marked every generational bottom.

I am holding 60/40 that $58,000 comes before $75,000, and the honest position is that it is getting harder to defend. Per Lark Davis, the long-term to short-term holder realized cap ratio is 3.9 against the threshold of 4 that has marked every prior cycle bottom, and Bitcoin has now absorbed a Korean market down 45 percent, AI stocks halved, 360,000 Korean retail liquidated inside 27 days and a Coldcard exploit costing over $100 million, all without breaking $60,000. A bear case whose perfect catalysts arrive and produce nothing is a bear case on a clock.

2. Saylor published the floor on his own website and then sold on it. Per VirtualBacon, strategy.com now displays the Bitcoin 200-week moving average and the premium to it, labelled book value, currently about 0.5 percent above with the average at $63,500. Strategy then sold 1,638 Bitcoin at an average of $63,957, that same line to within half a percent.

The definitional problem is the interesting part. By Saylor's own stated meaning of book value, the last price at which the average coin changed hands, the right metric is realized price at $52,900 to $53,800, not $63,000. Publishing the 200-week instead gives a fair-value story now and a different one if price goes under it.

Per threadguy, the obligation underneath explains the urgency. Strategy owes about $1.7 billion a year in perpetuity to STRC holders against a USD reserve of roughly $4.65 billion, so a little over two years of coverage, with STRC at 95.
