That is the same gate I flagged yesterday at $99 to $100, seen from the liability side. Watch what the largest holder does rather than what its website says.

3. The miner trade quietly became a landlord trade. Per Milk Road, VanEck's Matthew Sigel gives the mechanism: an AI token is worth roughly ten times a Bitcoin token per unit of electricity, and GPUs are debt-financeable where Bitcoin ASICs never were. So a miner moves from pure equity funding with revenue that halves every four years to debt plus equity at a lower cost of capital.

The anchor deal, per 0xResearch, is Riot providing Anthropic 191 megawatts under a 20-year agreement expected to generate about $9.1 billion. The stock was up as much as 29 percent in extended hours and faded to about 7.

Sigel's valuation frame is three parts: the discounted value of signed leases with investment-grade counterparties, the terminal value of a 20-year asset, and the uncontracted pipeline. The selloff has taken most of these names to paying nothing for terminal value and little for pipeline, so signed contracts alone cover the price. The offsets are dated and real. New York is delaying new data centre construction by about a year, a Texas audit may push energization back a couple of months, and the sector is down 15 percent on the week while miners sell coins rather than buy machines.

4. There is a mania running and Bitcoin is not in it. Per 0xResearch, the trading app Fomo did a record $3.2 million of revenue last week, an eighth straight weekly gain and 70 percent above the record set a week earlier, and ranked tenth in the US App Store finance category. It has no token.

The listed proxy is Pump. It did $10.7 million of revenue last week, annualising near $556 million, and sends half of it programmatically to buy and burn, which implies about $278 million of annual buybacks against a $1.08 billion circulating market cap, a 26 percent buyback yield.

Per threadguy, who is long it, the framing is blunt: "the first bull run in the history of crypto where Bitcoin flat out does not participate." His evidence is a set of ratios that already bottomed against Bitcoin at different times, and Pump Fun bought back $847,000 of its own token yesterday, the largest single day since January.

Treat it as what it is. A 26 percent buyback yield funded by speculative volume is a real cash flow and a fragile one, because the revenue and the token price come from the same crowd.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. At $63,700, sitting exactly on a 200-week average of $63,800, with three independent frameworks putting the turn at $67,000 and the long-term holder ratio at 3.9 against a threshold of 4. Below, the analog model points to roughly $62,000 over three weeks.
  • $ETH. Near $1,926 against an April anchored VWAP at $1,973 that it is consolidating under. A rejection there and a weekly close back below $1,750 targets $1,500, while acceptance above $2,000 opens $2,400 to $2,500. Ether funds took $208 million over seven days while Bitcoin funds bled on the day.
  • $MSTR. Sold 1,638 coins at $63,957 while publishing a $63,500 book-value line, owes about $1.7 billion a year to STRC holders against a $4.65 billion reserve, and STRC sits at 95 against the $99 to $100 that reopens issuance.
  • $RIOT. A 20-year, 191 megawatt, roughly $9.1 billion Anthropic contract, up 29 percent in extended hours and faded to 7, inside a sector down 15 percent on the week. The signed lease is the floor and the pipeline is the free option.
  • $PUMP. A 26 percent buyback yield on $10.7 million of weekly revenue with half of it burned, and the largest single-day buyback since January. The cleanest expression of onchain speculation, and it will trade like it.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] Iran says the Oman deal and the strait are separate, and crude went through $90
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Tehran now wants the war ended and its funds unfrozen before the strait reopens, and I am cutting my own announcement call to 40/60 the day before it comes due.
item.content:encoded:
Tehran now wants the war ended and its funds unfrozen before the strait reopens, and I am cutting my own announcement call to 40/60 the day before it comes due.

Yesterday I cut the Hormuz call to 55/45 because Iran had started separating the Oman route from the strait itself. Today the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council said it in a sentence, and the oil market believed him.

Market context. Crude is doing the arguing. Per the Market list, oil surged 5 percent Monday as Hormuz deal hopes faded, with Brent settling at $87.72 and WTI reaching $82.13. Per the Financial Markets morning list, Brent was around $88 this morning, and per the Crypto list it then traded above $90. Gold went with it, reclaiming $4,400 for the first time since early June per the Kalshi list, where traders also price 75 percent that gold outperforms Bitcoin this year. Equities did nothing at all. Per Arbitrage Andy, the S&P finished Monday roughly unchanged near 7,753, and per the Financial Markets list today was another consolidation session with the index near its lows, waiting on tomorrow.

The scoreboard.

  • Due tomorrow, and I am cutting it below even. My call that a joint Iran-Oman announcement lands inside a week goes from 55/45 to 40/60 against. Section one is why, and this now resolves as a miss more often than not.
  • Due tomorrow. The August 12 CPI I called on the 6th as the print that settles September. Consensus is 0.32 percent month over month and 3.4 percent year over year against 3.5 prior. Section three is what it decides.

1. Iran separated the two agreements out loud, and that is the thing I got wrong twice. Per the Market list, Mohsen Rezaei said at 3:49pm that if an Iran-Oman transit agreement is reached, "this will be a separate matter from the closure of the strait." Three minutes earlier he set the price of reopening: "as long as the US does not change its behavior and accept Iran's conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened," with the war ended and Iranian funds unfrozen named specifically and other conditions passed through mediators.

My call names the announcement, not the reopening, so it is not dead. It is now a call on a document Iran has publicly stripped of consequence.

The route track is alive. Per the Polymarket list, Qatar says the Oman-Iran negotiations are at an advanced stage with positive feedback from both, and Pakistan's defence minister told Bloomberg the US and Iran are "close to some sort of arrangement."

Per CaspianReport, the sticking point is a toll. Iran wants its right to collect tolls on transit recognised and says the June agreement implied it. Washington disagrees, and that rejection triggered the worst fighting since the April ceasefire. Oman has reportedly secured Gulf Arab backing for a voluntary toll system, and the two capitals are still far apart on it. Iran absorbed the strikes without conceding, so the price of a deal went up rather than down. Trump's framing today was that Iran "agrees privately, refuses publicly."

I am cutting to 40/60 rather than closing it out, because Qatar and Pakistan both describe a document in its final stage and the date is tomorrow. Two of my last three moves here have been downward, for the same reason each time: I kept pricing the route as though it were the strait.

The physical market is where the disagreement shows. Per the morning Financial Markets list, Hormuz remains closed to LNG traffic, curtailing about 20 percent of global supply, while Trump says the strait "is open now" behind an "infallible" Navy blockade. Per Capital Flows, the MOVE index is at its lows against a resilient economy and a crude supply shock is what blows it out. Brent moved ten percent in two sessions while rate volatility sat still, and the strategic reserve is below 300 million barrels for the first time in over forty years.

2. The Fed argument is hike against hold, and almost nobody is pricing a cut. That matters because my 60/40 is a hold call, and a hold is the dovish end of the live range rather than its middle.

Where September is pricedReading
Bank of Americastill 75bp of hikes this year, first one in September
FedWatch before the payrolls miss, per Milk Road55 percent chance of a hike
FedWatch after it, per Milk Roadhold is base case at 60 percent, Kalshi 65
FedWatch before and after, per ClearValue Tax67 percent hike, then 51.7 against 48.3 no change
Atlanta Fed's Venable, today"inflation is too high"

Those readings do not agree and I will not pretend they do. One has a hold as the clear base case, another has it at a coin flip, and per VirtualBacon the September 16 meeting sits at 48 percent no hike against 51 percent hike, the most indecisive he has seen. What they agree on is direction: per the Stocks list, the payrolls miss took a hike off the table rather than putting a cut on it, and July's FOMC held 9 to 3 with three members wanting to raise.

Per the Market morning list, Bank of America is sticking with the hiking call despite payrolls falling 23,000 and prior months revised down by 103,000, because inflation remains its central concern. Per ClearValue Tax, who carries the FedWatch series, has his own money on no increase in September, bought when it was a bigger underdog than it is now. The bond market is with the hawks: per Capital Flows, the weakness is bear steepening, and a long end selling off faster than the front end says policy is not restrictive enough.

I am holding 60/40 for a hold, and I want to be precise about what it is not. It is not a call that the Fed eases. Almost nobody in today's material expects that. It is a call that a committee looking at negative payrolls does not hike into them, and two separate series have that at roughly a coin flip. VirtualBacon's cumulative number is the uncomfortable one: 80 to 85 percent odds of at least one hike by year end, which makes September a question of timing rather than direction.

3. Tomorrow's print comes with a threshold attached rather than just a forecast. Per Milk Road, consensus is 0.32 percent month over month against their own break level of 0.20, so consensus already sits above the line that flips their posture from risk-on to caution. An in-line print does it without running hot. Meanwhile July average hourly earnings grew 3.2 percent against a June CPI of 3.5, so real wages are negative while the labour market sheds jobs. The thing to watch is not the headline. It is whether the month-over-month number starts with a 2.

4. CLARITY finally has a date, and the odds that matter did not move at all. Per VirtualBacon, John Thune filed cloture on Sunday and the vote is set for 2:15pm Eastern on Tuesday September 15, once the Senate work period resumes on the 14th.

The arithmetic is why nobody is excited. Cloture needs 60, Republicans hold 53, Thune's committee counts two Democrats already on board, so the bill is about five votes short.

CLARITY, as pricedOdds
Kalshi, becomes law this year23 percent, up from 13 before the date was set
Polymarket27 percent
Galaxy Research30 percent
By October 202740 percent, against 41 before the announcement

That last line is the whole story. Scheduling a vote moved the this-year number ten points and moved the eighteen-month number down one. The market read a date as a timing detail rather than as new information about whether it passes, and given that cloture only decides whether to take the bill up, with thirty hours of debate, amendments and a likely second cloture sequence behind it, that looks right.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] The memory bull just conceded the pricing lever, so I am flipping my own call
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Chip Stock Investor is holding SanDisk through a 40 percent drawdown and says the wild average selling prices are finished, locked away by five-year hyperscaler contracts.
item.content:encoded:
Chip Stock Investor is holding SanDisk through a 40 percent drawdown and says the wild average selling prices are finished, locked away by five-year hyperscaler contracts.

Yesterday I held the memory call for a third day and said I was the minority view in my own edition. Today the man still holding the stock explained why I was wrong, and he did it while defending the position.

Market context. Friday closed at a record and the internals are the argument against it. Per the Financial Markets list, S&P 500 profit margins hit 16.9 percent in the second quarter, the highest ever, the index is up 14 percent on the year after being down 7 on March 30, and the dividend yield is 1.04 percent, the lowest in history. Goldman's Panic index fell from the 90th percentile to the zero percentile in a single week. Per the Market list, Heisenberg has this on pace for one of the best Augusts in 41 years, and the only two comparables, 1986 and 2020, both gained 7 percent and were followed by Septembers that fell 10 and 8.4. Per the Market morning list, Rocket Lab and AST SpaceMobile report after the close, with Supermicro and CoreWeave tomorrow and Nebius Wednesday.

The scoreboard.

  • Reversing after fifteen days. My 60/40 that memory multiples expand before they compress is dead. I am now 55/45 the other way. Section one is the reason and it is not a sentiment change.
  • Due tomorrow. Supermicro, on Rick Orford's July 28 bearish case. It ran 31 percent into the print anyway, so this resolves on the number rather than the setup.
  • Catalyst passed, trade still live. Grab reported today and no source carries the result. The January $3.50/$4.50 call spread runs to expiry, so it stays open on its own clock.

1. The memory bull conceded the pricing lever, and that is the whole call. Per Chip Stock Investor, who is holding $SNDK through a fall from over $2,000 in July to roughly $1,200 and says nothing has fundamentally changed for the worse: "we can no longer rely on the really wild average selling prices on their SSDs. That is now over now that SanDisk and the other memory companies have signed long-term agreements, usually five-year agreements, with the hyperscalers."

Read that against what I built the call on. My 60/40 rested on Bernstein modelling roughly 35 percent of all bits shipped from 2027 to 2029 as take-or-pay at a $0.26 per gigabyte floor against $0.29 spot. I called that a floor under the price. It is the same contract structure, and from inside the position it reads as a ceiling.

Both descriptions are correct, and that is the problem. Take-or-pay at a fixed band protects the downside and removes the upside, and multiple expansion needs the upside. Nobody pays more for earnings pre-sold at a floor price for five years.

The guide says it without the framing. FY26 revenue finished up over 370 percent, the September quarter is still guided to 300 to nearly 400 percent year over year and is flat sequentially, with adjusted EPS guided to a $45 midpoint against $39.25 just reported. The answer offered is $4.5 billion of buybacks in a quarter. Companies buy back stock when the operating lever is spent.

Per the Stocks list, Jan van Eck has argued for weeks that the memory names "weren't growing volume, they just upped prices." I treated that as a bear talking his book. Today a holder said it about his own stock.

What keeps me at 55/45 rather than 70/30 is that the spot tape has not turned. Per the Market list, Bank of America has SK Hynix DRAM prices up 25 percent quarter over quarter in the third quarter, Kioxia guiding revenue up 35, and NAND spot up 5 to 6 percent on the week. Spot is still ripping. It no longer reaches the contracted book.

2. Kratos lost the competition that mattered and kept the airframe anyway. Per Rick Orford, $KTOS did $371 million of first-quarter revenue, up 23 percent, on $605 million of bookings for a 1.6 book-to-bill and a backlog near $2 billion, with full-year guidance raised. All of it posted after the Air Force passed it over in the first collaborative combat aircraft production competition, the loss that knocked the stock down.

The XQ-58A Valkyrie is flying regardless. Northrop picked the airframe for its winning US Marine Corps solution, Airbus is integrating it with a European mission system, and GE Aerospace is working on propulsion. The OpenSpace ground segment adds a Space Systems Command agreement running to a $446.8 million ceiling, and Orford is careful that a ceiling is not recognised revenue.

His bear case is fair: the Valkyrie could stay a demonstrator that never gets its own production line. The thesis is that losing the prime slot while keeping the airframe is a better business than the market priced. No target here, so size it rather than trade it.

3. CoreWeave and Nebius report into a short who has already named his price. Per Jose Najarro, who owns $CRWV six figures, June quarter consensus is $2.5 to $2.6 billion for CoreWeave and about $575 million for Nebius.

Into the prints$CRWV$NBIS
Year to date+14 percent+108 percent
Active powerover 1 gigawatt310 megawatts
Backlog or ARR$100bn backlog, 2027 ARR above $30bn, 75 percent contracted2026 ARR $7bn to $9bn
2026 capex$31bn to $35bn$20bn to $25bn, already raised
The catchinterest expense $650m to $730mmargins pre-guided lower

Najarro's single question is the right one: was the first quarter the true bottom in CoreWeave's adjusted operating margin? Management says margins expand to low double digits by the fourth quarter. If they walk that back tomorrow, the stock up 14 percent against a peer up 108 gets cheaper for a reason.

Per Edelbridge Alpha, Michael Burry is short Nebius at $211.77 and Oracle at $144.63 with Nebius near $187, and his argument is not valuation. It is that these companies depreciate GPUs too slowly, overstating Oracle's earnings by 26 to 27 percent by 2028. Two of today's sources sit thirty cents apart on Oracle. Per Stocks with Josh, he called it at $132 for a $145 minimum, hit that, and now expects continuation above $145 on an oversold RSI turn. Burry is short from $144.63 on the accounting. Only one of those has a multi-year clock.

4. Biotech is beating the tape and almost nobody is writing about it. Per the Stocks list, $XBI is up 29.5 percent this year and 10 percent on the week, the best sector print in the feed and the least discussed.

The bid is structural and dated: 33 buyouts above $500 million already this year against $200 billion to $300 billion of patent-cliff revenue pharma must replace by 2030, with three to four more deals expected in August.

Two names carry catalysts. $VERA has EFGR data next month framed as a plus 30 or minus 50 percent event. $NKTR has come back from the 50s on over $1 million of premium paid for September 100 calls, a bet on a royalty deal or a takeout inside four to six weeks.

5. Galloway put a number on the AI question and a second source answered it against the bulls. Per Prof G Markets, hyperscaler capex needs about $2.5 trillion of incremental AI revenue to earn a reasonable return, against $150 billion of cumulative AI revenue today. That is a fifteen times gap, and $2.5 trillion exceeds all of big tech's current revenue combined. The concentration underneath is sharper: OpenAI was 70 percent of Microsoft's AI sales last year and lost $21 billion.

Gavin Baker has said publicly that OpenAI is almost certainly generating significant free cash flow. Per Jordamøn, that did not survive the day. OpenAI filed a confidential S-1 on May 22, on roughly $2 billion of monthly revenue while losing $1.22 for every dollar it earns. Annualised, that is a bigger loss than the leaked figure Galloway quoted. The original listing target was September at $852 billion to $1 trillion, and SEC rules put the public prospectus about fifteen days before the roadshow, so the full financials would have had to land in late August.

I am staying 60/40 with Steve Eisman against Burry on the broad AI trade. The 40 was always customer concentration. Today it got a number rather than a new argument.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $SNDK. Down about 40 percent from over $2,000 in July, still the best S&P component of the last two years, and now the clearest expression of a thesis its own bulls have narrowed. The next leg has to come from volume and buybacks rather than price.
  • $CRWV. Reports tomorrow at $2.5 to $2.6 billion consensus with a $100 billion backlog and 75 percent of a $30 billion 2027 target contracted, against $650 to $730 million of interest expense. The margin trough is the whole print.
  • $NBIS. Reports Wednesday near $187 with Burry short at $211.77 on depreciation rather than multiple. Margins were pre-guided lower, so the bear headline is scheduled and the surprise would be the capex and ARR guides going up.
  • $KTOS. A 1.6 book-to-bill, a $2 billion backlog and raised guidance, all delivered after losing the award that took the stock down. Northrop, Airbus and GE Aerospace are each building on the airframe it was passed over for.
  • $VERA. EFGR data next month framed as plus 30 or minus 50 percent, inside a sector up 29.5 percent on the year and 33 buyouts deep. Position it as the binary it is.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] The $66,000 close failed and the man who drew the line is short
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Two whales moved about 14,000 coins over three weeks into the best ETF inflow week since April, and the tape still could not hold the level.
item.content:encoded:
Two whales moved about 14,000 coins over three weeks into the best ETF inflow week since April, and the tape still could not hold the level.

Yesterday I wrote that Kalshi had flipped the distribution and that my downside call finally had the betting market on its side. The weekend supplied the confirmation and it was not the comfortable kind.

Market context. Per the Crypto list, Bitcoin sits at $64,000 to $65,000 after a weak weekly close. Demand and supply both showed up and supply won.

The weekend, both sidesFigure
Spot Bitcoin ETF inflows, week$853 million, best since April, with $IBIT at about $693 million
One whale, selling7,513 BTC, $486.9 million over three weeks, implying about $65,160 a coin
A second whale, possibly a miner, into Binance6,494 BTC, $420.5 million over three weeks, implying about $64,750
Most liquidated asset over 24 hours$TUT at over $44 million, more than Bitcoin or Ether

That is roughly 14,000 coins distributed into the best demand week in four months, and the close still failed. Per 0xResearch, miners were the week's worst index at minus 12.93 percent while gold ran 6.89 and Bitcoin managed 2.46.

The scoreboard.

  • Resolved, and it went to the branch I did not want. Yesterday's call, from Sykodelic, was that a weekly close above $66,000 sends this higher and a rejection puts $60,000 first. The close was weak, so the rejection branch fired exactly as written. Marked a hit for the framework rather than for the direction I would have preferred.
  • Still open and now better supported. My 60/40 that Bitcoin sees $58,000 before $75,000. Section two is why I am not raising it despite the weekend.

1. The man who drew the line took the trade. Per the Crypto list, Sykodelic posted overnight: "My short is filled. After waiting weeks for a clear trigger, we now have one. The $65,300 level was taken out and we got a weak weekly close."

His book is specific: trigger $65,300, already taken, target $60,500 to clear the equal lows, and invalidation at "a strong daily close above $67,000."

What matters for my own position is where he stops. My call needs $58,000. His needs $60,500. Not the same trade, and the gap is the distance between being right about direction and right about size.

Per Milk Road, the ceiling on the other end is a failed run at $72,000, capped by the delayed CLARITY Act vote, with Polymarket pricing the bill passing this year at about 27 percent.

2. A permabull's clock and a bear's reversal met in the same month. Per Benjamin Cowen, the range between the 200-week EMA and the bear-market resistance band breaks down more often than up near the end of midterm years, and "I would lean towards breakdown." His dated version: the cycle low is most likely October, possibly late September, could slip to December, and by late November it is in or close to in. Social interest reads 0.2 against roughly 0.5 four years ago, matching August 2018, his analogue year, and the MVRV Z-score has not gone below zero. Bitcoin normally bottoms only when it does. He says he has bought some anyway.

Coming the other way, per 0xResearch, Clemente cut his remaining Bitcoin in January and spent the year in commodities. He now argues deep value: price consolidating at the 2021 highs below the 200-week average, MVRV near prior bear-market lows, and long-term holders accumulating against $5 billion of ETF outflows. He is building spot again, still open to one final leg down this year, and hedging with cheap options.

That convergence is why I am holding 60/40 rather than raising it. A bear who left in January is buying, a bull is leaning breakdown, and both put the resolution in the autumn rather than this week. Clemente's structure is the honest expression of my own view: own the downside through options rather than spot, because the timing is the part nobody has.

3. Ether is losing the price argument and winning the flow argument. Per Lark Davis, the flip is in supply and flows and he says plainly that price has not caught up.

Ether, the flow caseFigure
ETH ETF net flows, Julypositive $365 million after two months of outflows
Staked supply41 million ETH, 34 percent of supply, an all-time high
Exit queue, if everyone leftalmost three years
BitMine's holding5.78 million ETH, nearly 4.9 million staked, over $250 million a year, bought weekly without regard to price
ETH against Bitcoinratio near 0.03 against a 2025 peak near 0.077, with a weekly MACD cross live for three weeks

The last line has history attached. The previous time that weekly signal fired, Ether outperformed Bitcoin by 132 percent over the following months.

I am holding the 60/40 one-more-leg-down on Ether with less conviction than a week ago. The price case is intact and the flow case is not what it was. What would move me is the staking ratio holding above 34 percent through a red Bitcoin month, because a supply lock that survives a drawdown is a different fact from one only tested in a bounce. Blockworks Research also puts low odds on EIP-8363 being adopted, so the mechanism that would cut the staking yield is fading rather than arriving.

4. Strategy said the words out loud and told you where its own gate is. Per the People to follow list, chief executive Phong Le on CNBC: "Bitcoin is going through a bear cycle right now." He is not a forced seller, and he made the point with the balance sheet: 842,000 Bitcoin, over 4 percent of all that will ever be mined, past BlackRock last quarter, and over $4 billion of cash.

Per the Crypto list, aixbt supplies the mechanical version and it is the most checkable trigger in today's material. That $4 billion covers more than two years of dividends and debt interest. That is what backs STRC at $95. The 12 percent rate supports par, issuance stays shut below $100, and if STRC holds $99 to $100 Strategy reopens $17.5 billion of capacity. A four to five percent move in one preferred security decides whether the largest holder returns as a buyer, and Bitcoin only gets the bid if the proceeds actually buy Bitcoin.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. At $64,000 to $65,000 after the $66,000 weekly close failed, with Sykodelic short from $65,300 into $60,500 and invalidation at a strong daily close above $67,000. Two whales moved about 14,000 coins over three weeks and $853 million of ETF demand could not absorb it.
  • $ETH. Near $1,900 with 34 percent of supply staked at an all-time high, a three-year exit queue, $365 million of July ETF inflows and a live weekly MACD cross against Bitcoin whose last signal preceded 132 percent of outperformance. The bear case here is now price alone.
  • $MSTR. Holds 842,000 coins and over $4 billion of cash, and its chief executive called this a bear cycle on television. Reopening $17.5 billion of issuance capacity gates on STRC holding $99 to $100 against $95 now.
  • $HOOD. Robinhood Chain total value locked is just under $500 million, roughly 10 percent of Base and Solana, while its stablecoin supply passed $600 million and doubled in a month. The market cap is more than twice Coinbase's and the chain is still filling.
  • $HYPE. Matt Hougan has it at 16 to 17 times earnings against a normal 30 for this kind of business, and that arithmetic is how he reaches $150 before Hyperliquid looks fully valued. A multiple argument rather than a catalyst, so it needs patience.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] Iran is close on Oman and says that still does not reopen the strait
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Tehran's price is now US withdrawal, war reparations and the blockade lifted, Polymarket has a deal by month end at 30 percent, and both crude benchmarks rose a dollar on the doubt.
item.content:encoded:
Tehran's price is now US withdrawal, war reparations and the blockade lifted, Polymarket has a deal by month end at 30 percent, and both crude benchmarks rose a dollar on the doubt.

Yesterday I said the Hormuz call was the one I was least comfortable with. Tehran spent the weekend proving the discomfort was right and the number was not.

Market context. Gold is the asset doing the arguing. Per the Financial Markets list, it is easing back from a seven-week high of $4,372 while the dollar recovers from its post-payrolls slump on renewed Hormuz risk. Per the Kalshi list, Kalshi's traders forecast $4,566 this year, about 4.4 percent above that high. Crude went the other way from the headlines, with Brent and WTI each up more than a dollar. Wednesday's CPI is the only event on the calendar that matters.

The scoreboard.

  • Due Wednesday, and I am cutting it. My 70/30 that a joint Iran-Oman announcement lands inside a week goes to 55/45. Section one is the reason.
  • Due Wednesday. The August 12 CPI print I called on the 6th as the thing that settles September more than payrolls did. That still looks right, and it is now carrying more weight than I wanted it to.

1. Iran got closer to Oman and further from reopening, and those are two different agreements. Per the Market list, Iran says it is "very close to an agreement with Oman" on a new maritime transit route, and in the same breath warns that an Oman deal would not mean the strait reopens.

That distinction is the whole trade, and I underweighted it. My call was written on the route agreement being real, and the route agreement is real. It just turns out to be the cheap half.

Tehran's stated price for the strait itself is now explicit and maximal.

| Iran's preconditions to reopen Hormuz | |---| | US forces withdrawn from the region | | The naval blockade lifted | | Sanctions removed and frozen assets released | | An end to proxy warfare | | War reparations | | An end to hostile rhetoric |

Against that list, per the Polymarket list, the market prices a US-Iran Hormuz agreement by the end of the month at 30 percent, and it moved to that from a higher projection. Per the Kalshi list, Iran rejected talks outright over the weekend.

The two governments are also describing different games. Trump told Axios the US is only "semi-negotiating" and that it is "low-keying it", with oil near $75 doing the work of cushioning the consumer while the blockade grinds. Araghchi says no talks are happening at all and cannot restart while Washington breaches the June interim agreement. Pezeshkian says now is the best time for a deal. Three positions, one government on each side, and only one of them is a negotiation.

I am cutting the announcement call to 55/45 rather than killing it, because the Oman route genuinely is close and that is what the call names. What I got wrong was treating the route as a proxy for the strait. It is not, and Iran said so itself.

2. The Fed question that nobody would put a number on today. Friday's payrolls settled nothing. Per Milk Road, July shed 23,000 jobs against an expected gain of 80,000, and unemployment still fell from 4.2 percent to 4.1 because 264,000 people left the labour force. Participation is 61.4 percent, the lowest since early 2021. A print that bad on the headline and that ambiguous underneath is why nobody moved.

What did move is the framing. The Fed risk in this feed is being discussed as a hike, not a cut, with the Street reading Asian currencies as buoyed by reduced rate-hike prospects. Funds sit at 3.50 to 3.75 percent and roughly one hike is still priced for 2026.

Milk Road's mechanism for that hike never arriving is the one specific thing on offer: Kevin Warsh has five task forces running on inflation, jobs, data and the balance sheet, and the expectation is that one returns hawkish and four return dovish, which hands him the cover to cut instead.

I am holding 60/40 for a September hold, unchanged from yesterday. Not one source in today's material published a September probability, and Jordi Visser, who had it at 45 percent, wrote three thousand words on Japan without restating it. When the desks that were arguing go quiet in the same week as the print, the print is the argument. Wednesday settles it.

3. The yen rescue got its plumbing explained, and the answer is the Fed's balance sheet. Per Jordi Visser, the intervention was the first coordinated US-Japan action on the yen since June 1998, and the fix for Japan's Treasury problem is not the currency leg at all. Bessent has publicly proposed the Fed expand the FIMA repo facility, with Treasury willing to raise the cap, so Japan can borrow dollars against its Treasury holdings rather than sell them.

Visser's read on that is the honest one. FIMA is not money printing, and it is "a verbal bazooka indicating they are scared." Watch what it produced: the largest monthly rise in the US 30-year yield since this administration took over, and the highest monthly yield close in more than twenty years.

One caution on the source. Visser describes this as a dollar-yen operation throughout and never mentions the euro leg, and he lists no conditions attached to the rescue. This desk has been carrying both. Treat his account as filling in the mechanism rather than as agreeing on the terms.

4. Gold is beating positive real rates, and the household is paying the bill. Lyn Alden's framing, carried in the same Milk Road letter, is that gold rallying against positive real rates is supposed to be impossible. Fiscal dominance is what makes it possible: with debt above 100 percent of GDP, raising rates blows out the federal deficit faster than it slows bank lending. The policy rate stopped being a brake and became a line item.

The cost of that shows up in one series. Per the Financial Markets list and the St. Louis Fed, the 30-year mortgage is 6.69 percent, the highest since July 2025, with the 15-year at 6.01.

The decade on a median homeThenNow
30-year mortgage rate3.4 percent6.7 percent
Median price$250,000$446,000
Monthly payment$887$2,302, up 160 percent

The same letter carries a warning that private credit default rates are at recent highs and that internal loan-health reviews point to worse. That is the other end of the same rate: gold is the hedge against the deficit, and the mortgage and the private loan book are where the deficit gets paid for. Wednesday's print decides which of the two the Fed is allowed to care about.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] SpaceX printed a beat, tripled its float, and rose fifteen percent anyway
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: A 34 percent short interest that never squeezed on the print, a funding gap near $350 billion, and roughly a thousand special purpose vehicles nobody has mapped.
item.content:encoded:
A 34 percent short interest that never squeezed on the print, a funding gap near $350 billion, and roughly a thousand special purpose vehicles nobody has mapped.

This channel covered SpaceX in every edition it has published since the split. That is not because the ticker is always doing something. It is because one company ran a complete cycle in five sessions: the most crowded short in the market, a beat nobody had modelled, the largest lockup expiry of the year, and a fifteen percent rally on the day the supply arrived.

The interesting part is that the consensus was wrong at every single stage, including mine.

The week in one arc

DayWhat happened
TuesdayReports into 34 percent short interest with 95 percent of borrowable stock already lent. Consensus EPS spanned a $1.26 loss to a $0.33 profit
WednesdayBeat at $7.8 billion against $6.8 billion expected. Guided to a $100 billion exit run rate. Capex came in 39 percent hot
Thursday911.5 million shares unlock, more than 140 percent of the public float. Lowest close in company history
FridayRises 10 to 15 percent, from about $108 to $132, back above Meta's market capitalisation

Four editions, four different reasons to be wrong.

1. The print said the business is real and the balance sheet is not finished

Per the All-In Podcast, revenue was $7.8 billion, up 92 percent year over year and 67 percent sequentially, against $18 billion for all of last year. EPS came in at $0.09 against an expected 26-cent loss, with a $500 million net loss against an expected $2 billion.

Then the line that mattered more.

Q2Figure
Capex$18.4 billion in the quarter, six times a year ago, roughly a $75 billion run rate
Capex against revenue$2.35 spent for every dollar earned
2027 capex guidancenone given
Connectivity$4.3 billion revenue, $2.6 billion adjusted EBITDA
Spaceminus $200 million, call it break even
AI$2.6 billion, more than tripled sequentially

Starlink is the part that already works: 12 million subscribers, doubled year over year, at $66 a month and growing 20 percent sequentially, approaching a 24 million run rate. David Friedberg's extrapolation is $40 billion of revenue and $30 billion of free cash flow inside a year, which at 30 times would make Starlink alone a trillion-dollar company within 18 months.

The guidance is where it stops being a satellite business. Per Limitless, Elon Musk put $100 billion of annual recurring revenue by year end "if we do nothing" and pulled the $1 trillion revenue year forward from 2031 to 2030. Morgan Stanley's 2030 estimate is $325 billion. Those two numbers are not in the same universe, and the gap between them is the entire investment debate.

2. The unlock was the setup, and everyone including me had the direction backwards

Going in, the mechanics looked one-sided. S3 had 95 percent of borrowable stock out on loan and short interest at 34 percent of float. I read that as a squeeze and went 55/45 that the stock would trade higher on Thursday. It closed at its lowest price in company history instead, having shed roughly $1.6 trillion of market value since the June high.

Then Friday happened. Per the Stocks list, it ran from about $108 to $132 on the day after 911.5 million shares came free, traded 1.7 million option contracts on unlock day itself (second only to Nvidia across the whole market), and finished back above Meta's capitalisation. LuxAlgo's summary was the correct one: new rule, SpaceX unlocks are bullish.

The lesson is not that I was directionally wrong. It is that I put a date on a mechanical call. Supply cliffs are knowable in size and unknowable in timing, and a 24-hour window on a structural event is a coin flip dressed as analysis.

The supply is not finished. Per the People to follow list, the float went from 5 percent to 20 percent on Thursday and reaches roughly 40 percent by December 9, with tranches near 7 percent on August 21 and again on September 10, then smaller blocks through the autumn. Musk himself becomes eligible around 46 percent in June 2027. Tom Lee's framing is the cleanest: the company raised $18 billion in its life, is worth north of $1.4 trillion, floated $75 billion at the IPO, and over $1 trillion of stock unlocks by year end.

3. The bull case

The compute economics are genuinely better than the comparables, and that is measurable rather than rhetorical. SpaceX generates $30 million to $50 million of annualised revenue per active megawatt. CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN sit at $9.4 million to $10.4 million. Digital Realty and Equinix sit at $3.5 million to $4.4 million. SemiAnalysis puts SpaceX at roughly nine times revenue for a gigawatt of GB300 against the neocloud five-year infrastructure average.

The payback compressed. The CFO says newly deployed compute pays back inside a single calendar year, against three to four years for a typical neocloud and fifteen to twenty for real estate. A few months ago the company itself was modelling four.

Capacity is contracted and scaling. 1.4 gigawatts today, about 2 by year end, 5 to 10 next year, with line of sight to 20. At $30 million to $50 million per megawatt per year, a 6 gigawatt incremental add is worth roughly $300 billion of annual revenue on Brad Gerstner's arithmetic. SemiAnalysis models a path to $305 billion of revenue by 2027 with $235 billion, or 77 percent, from AI compute.

The sponsorship is real. JPMorgan raised its target to $240, Morgan Stanley carries $300, Argus upgraded to Buy after the quarter, Cathie Wood holds 4,051,080 shares, and Alphabet's own equity book is 95.1 percent SpaceX.

4. The bear case, and it is arithmetic rather than sentiment

The funding gap is roughly $350 billion and nobody has explained who fills it. The arithmetic comes from SouthernValue on the Stocks list.

Building 10 gigawattsFigure
Implied capex at $50 to $60 billion per gigawattabout $500 billion
Cash on hand, including the $85 billion IPO raiseabout $100 billion
Cash from operations, first half 2026$3 billion
Anthropic and Google spot GPU dealsabout $26 billion of annual recurring revenue
Estimated exit-2026 forward operating cashabout $50 billion
Residual gapabout $350 billion

The conclusion that follows is uncomfortable and it is the same structure as the OpenAI campus: Nvidia customer financing has to come into play. The chip supplier underwrites the buyer, and SpaceX has just committed to Nvidia exclusively on Vera Rubin. Gavin Baker's version is worse. At 8 gigawatts and roughly $100 billion per gigawatt, capex is $800 billion from this company alone, and component costs have already doubled in four months.

Capex is running 39 percent above expectations with no 2027 guidance. A company spending $2.35 per dollar of revenue and declining to guide the following year is asking for trust on the single largest line in the model.

The supply calendar is public and unfinished. Roughly 20 percent more of the company becomes tradable between August 21 and December 9. The Meta 2012 analogue is the honest comparable: down about 50 percent at the 91-day lockup and still down 36 percent a year later.

And there is a layer underneath that nobody has mapped. Per Diet TBPN, bankers estimate at least 1,000 special purpose vehicles hold SpaceX stock. One has already failed publicly. Late Stage Management told an investor it had sold his exposure in 2024 at roughly $105 a share, before a five-for-one split, while his portal and his 2025 tax document still showed 2,500 shares. He put in $17,250, believes the stake was worth over $300,000 at the June IPO, has filed an SEC complaint, and thinks more than 100 others are affected. Three sales executives connected to the firm pleaded guilty in February and March inside a $528 million scheme that hid markups of 10 to 100 percent and diverted roughly $88 million.

That is not a valuation risk. It is a supply risk of unknown size sitting in vehicles with no disclosure obligation, arriving into a stock whose float is already tripling.

What to do with it

Own it as a compute business, not a launch business. Connectivity and AI produce all the money. Space is break even and it is the part everyone talks about.

Let the calendar work. The tranche dates are published. There is no informational edge in front-running a supply schedule everyone can read, and Friday demonstrated that positioning into these events is more dangerous than the events themselves. The next two are August 21 and September 10.

Size for a 4-beta outcome. This is a $1.4 trillion company that has moved 30 percent in a week in both directions this month.

The single number to watch is the 2027 capex guide, whenever it arrives. That converts the $350 billion gap from an analyst estimate into a disclosed obligation, and it is the moment the vendor-financing question gets answered in public.

Watchlist for the week ahead. $SPCX into the August 21 tranche. $NBIS reports Wednesday at 105 times sales into Michael Burry's fresh short, and it is the cleanest read on whether the market still pays for neocloud growth. $MU and $SNDK, where the contracted floor held all week and the tape ignored it. $RKLB reports next week after the $8 billion Iridium deal flipped it to net debt. And $GRAB Monday and $SMCI Tuesday, both of which come due on this channel's book.

The scoreboard, Stocks & ETFs

Eight calls settled, six hits and two misses. Read the raw count with care: three of the six hits are the same SpaceX unlock catalyst carried across three editions, and two more are the same AppLovin print counted twice. Eight settled entries represent about five distinct events.

ResolvedOutcome
The August 6 unlock frees up to 911.5 million shares, Prof G MarketsHit, on the date and at the size
SpaceX at its lowest price ever with a lockup on August 6, Vest ExchangeHit
SpaceX below its $135 listing with $1.2 trillion gone, Market listHit, and it widened to $1.6 trillion
SpaceX Q2 expects $6.8 billion of revenue, Kyle ReidheadHit. Actual was $7.8 billion
AppLovin's Q2 is the first real scorecard, Milk Road, two entriesHit. Revenue grew 53 percent and the stock lost a fifth
SpaceX trades higher on Thursday, house, 55/45Miss. It fell, then rose 15 percent on Friday. Right mechanism, wrong day
Micron is the consensus dip-buy, Joseph Hogue and MarketBeatMiss. Hyperscaler memory spend went from $72.8 billion to a modelled $761 billion and $MU still had its worst month since June 2005

House record on settled calls: zero for one. One house call has resolved on this channel and it lost. There is no hit rate to quote yet and I am not going to manufacture one out of relayed calls that other people made. The honest statement is that the book is young, the only decided house position was wrong, and it was wrong on timing rather than direction.

131 open calls carried into next week. The live ones on this subject: the $350 billion funding gap, the $135 billion 2027 revenue case, the unlock schedule to 40 percent by December 9, "the unlock was the bottom", and the SPV layer. Elsewhere: the memory call at 60/40, recorded under pressure after five sessions of the complex going nowhere while the S&P made a record. AppLovin higher in three months. Eisman over Burry at 60/40. Siemens Energy rerating before the US grid names. And Damodaran's write-off tell. That is the one I most want to be watching when it triggers, because there has still not been a single major AI capex write-off and the first one will not be gentle.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] Every measure of crypto usage rose this week and no price followed
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Crypto cards at $759 million a month, Hyperliquid burning $175 million of fees, and an $91.3 billion study that found zero institutional buyers of tokenised assets.
item.content:encoded:
Crypto cards at $759 million a month, Hyperliquid burning $175 million of fees, and an $91.3 billion study that found zero institutional buyers of tokenised assets.

The single most repeated finding on this channel since the split is not a price call. It is a gap. In four of five editions the same thing happened from a different angle: something measurable about crypto adoption went up and the tokens did not.

That divergence is now large enough, and specific enough, to be the week's subject rather than a recurring aside. This memo is about whether it closes, and what has to be true for it to.

The evidence, gathered in one place

What roseBy how much
Crypto payment card volume$759 million in July, 2.5x from $306 million a year earlier, from under $1 million in October 2023
Hyperliquid fees, Q2about $175 million, 80 percent from perpetuals, buying and burning the token
Solana tokenised equity volume$1 million in June 2025 to over $3 billion in June 2026
Robinhood Chain, seven-day DEX volumenearly $3 billion, with perpetuals up 130 percent
Tokenised RWA deposits$2.3 billion to $7.4 billion
Tokenised stock holders1.2 million, up 1,406.8 percent in a year
BlackRock tokenised products on Ethereumtwo funds, then twelve more announced days later
JP Morgan's Kinexysroughly $5 billion a day, with a collateral fund nearing $1 billion on public Ethereum

Against all of that: Bitcoin sits near $64,800, roughly 49 percent below its October high of $126,198. Ether is near $1,906, from almost $5,000 six months ago. Tokens broadly are at 2026 lows, about 40 percent off the May peak. Bitcoin volatility is at three-year lows and 23 percent of the top miners are running at a daily loss.

Two years of adoption compounding and the asset prices went backwards.

1. The bull case: this is a lag, and lags close

The revenue actually inflected, and that is datable. Per Milk Road, a Bitwise analyst puts the trough in network revenue between late 2025 and early 2026, with revenue rising since while prices kept falling. That is not a narrative claim, it is a series with a turn in it.

Some of it accrues directly. Hyperliquid's roughly $175 million of quarterly fees, 80 percent of them from perpetuals, buys and burns HYPE. Pons on Robinhood Chain routes about 80 percent of receipts into buybacks and burns and has already retired 24 percent of its supply. Where the mechanism exists, the cash flow reaches the token.

Ether has a genuinely new demand source for the first time in a year. Robinhood's chain has no token of its own, so transactions on it consume Ether, and a large portion of the supply has already been bridged there. That is roughly 30 million users generating base-layer demand by construction rather than by speculation.

The institutional pipe is being built by the people who matter. Per the Milk Road Show, BlackRock did not tokenise two funds and stop, it announced twelve more within days. JP Morgan is running $5 billion a day through Kinexys and has a collateral money market fund approaching $1 billion on public Ethereum. Ethereum holds 52.2 percent of tokenised real-world asset market capitalisation and 69.4 percent of euro stablecoin supply.

And the desk that gets paid to be right is buying. Per DeFi Dad's interview, Fundstrat's Sean Farrell puts us at "the seventh inning stretch, maybe even later in the game" and says plainly: "you could buy the majors right now... and sell them at a higher price, say a year from now."

2. The bear case: none of it has to accrue to a token, and mostly it does not

The card business is the cleanest example and it is damning. Per a16z crypto, $759 million a month, growing 2.5 times a year, nearly 9 million purchases at about $86 each. Settlement is 58 percent USDC and 26 percent USDT, with euro stablecoins collapsing from 88 percent of volume to 2. And it runs almost entirely over Visa. That is a payment rail compounding beautifully in digital dollars, and there is no token anywhere in the value chain. Stablecoin adoption is not crypto-asset adoption.

The tokenisation buyers are crypto itself. This is the number of the week. An Arrakis study carried by Blockworks of $91.3 billion of on-chain acquisitions across ten tokenised dollar-yield products found two thirds came from protocol and DAO treasuries and not one dollar traced to a traditional bank, pension fund or asset manager. Wallets above $1 million were 4 percent of buyers and 93 percent of the capital.

So the plumbing is being laid by BlackRock and JP Morgan, and the volume through it is crypto recycling its own treasury cash. Both halves of that sentence are true, and the second one is the one that decides prices.

Ethereum's own architecture leaks the value. Per 0xSammy and the Ethereum Institutional founders, Robinhood's layer two brought roughly 30 million users and sends the base chain "a couple of thousand dollars" in fees. Joe Lubin's stated position is growth over rent extraction. That is defensible for a network and terrible for an asset. Vitalik's Lean Ethereum roadmap then targets a tenfold fee reduction, a bear case for accrual before it is a bull case for adoption.

Coinbase's own AI lead conceded the point. Asked whether agentic payment demand accrues value to tokens, the answer was that block space is commoditised and agentic payments could run on a parallel chain. The host called it an extremely controversial answer. It is also probably the correct one.

And the forced sellers are still there. Farrell names them: miners selling to fund capex, holders on the four-year cycle, treasury companies unable to raise below one times net asset value and now selling, and redemptions from liquid funds. The real two-year yield is at a cycle high. That is the liquidity condition that has to change first.

3. The arbitration

Both cases are correct about different things, so the resolution is not "which one wins" but "which assets are on which side of the line."

The divergence closes for assets with a fee-to-token mechanism and does not close for the rest. Hyperliquid has one. Pons has one. Ether has a partial one that its own roadmap is about to weaken. Bitcoin has none and never claimed to. That is why usage data was never going to move it.

The honest weakness in the bull case is the resolution condition. Asked when the gap closes, the Bitwise answer was "when people start understanding what's going on on chain," with no date, no target and no flow number attached. A fundamentals case with no catalyst is a reason to own something, not a reason to expect it to move.

I am 60/40 that Bitcoin sees $58,000 before $75,000, unchanged. Two independent frameworks put the cycle low in the fourth quarter: Benjamin Cowen has us on day 1,354 against prior bottoms at 1,432 and 1,436, and day 304 against an average bear bottom on day 406, with October as base case. Trader Mayne puts the bottoming range at $40,000 to $60,000. Farrell's bear case is a four handle. My number sits between credible desks rather than outside them.

On Ether I am 60/40 with CryptoKaleo's one-more-leg-down against Arthur Hayes calling $5,000 by year end, for the accrual reason above rather than an adoption one.

What to do with it

Separate the two trades and stop calling them one sector. Owning Bitcoin is a liquidity and debasement position. Owning a fee-burning protocol is an equity-like cash-flow position. This week they diverged and they will keep diverging.

If you want the adoption theme, the honest expression is the equity, not the token. The card volume runs over Visa. The tokenisation plumbing runs through BlackRock and JP Morgan. The retail bid runs through Robinhood, whose event contracts now out-earn both its equities and its crypto lines.

Watchlist for the week ahead. $BTC into a fourth-quarter low that three independent clocks agree on. $ETH, where the institutional case and the accrual case point opposite ways and Glamsterdam lands in the third quarter. $HYPE as the cleanest fee-to-token mechanism in the market, with 433,025 coins just unlocked against the burn. $HOOD, where the chain is the funnel and the brokerage is the business. And $MSTR, which Farrell names as the sector's tail risk through its putable bond repurchases.

The scoreboard, Bitcoin & Crypto

This is the youngest book of the three and the record reflects that.

ResolvedOutcome
Robinhood Chain holds $400 million a day of DEX volume by August 10, aixbtHit, four days early. Seven-day volume ran near $3 billion, roughly $428 million a day
ERCOT's Batch Zero round stays frozen under the Texas audit, m0xtHit. The round came due August 7 and did not advance

Two settled calls, both hits, and both are other people's. Zero house calls have resolved on this channel. There is no hit rate to report and quoting 100 percent off two relayed calls would be advertising rather than scorekeeping, so the honest line is that this book has not been tested yet.

Fifty-five open calls carried into next week. The ones that carry the argument above: Bitcoin at $58,000 before $75,000 at 60/40. CLARITY's failure already priced at 65/35, which this week supported when the bill died and Bitcoin rose the same afternoon. Ether at 60/40 for one more leg down. The on-chain revenue divergence itself. The Arrakis finding that no institution has bought a tokenised asset. Crypto card adoption at $759 million a month. Galaxy landing a Helios tenant before the Texas audit clears. And Tilman Holloway's call that Coldcard drives ETF inflows three, six and nine months out. That one has the longest fuse and the cleanest test.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] The September hike was born on Tuesday and died on Friday
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Kashkari wanted it immediately, Warsh attached a condition, a negative payroll print destroyed the premise, and Bank of America still wants three hikes starting next month.
item.content:encoded:
Kashkari wanted it immediately, Warsh attached a condition, a negative payroll print destroyed the premise, and Bank of America still wants three hikes starting next month.

In five sessions this channel moved its own September call three times. That is either a system with no spine or a week in which the underlying facts genuinely reversed twice. It was the second one, and the reason is worth an entire memo, because the same sequence is about to repeat on Wednesday.

The chronology, because the order is the argument

DayWhat changed
TuesdayISM at 55.6, the best since May 2022, GDPNow raised to 6.2 percent
WednesdayKashkari says the Fed should begin raising now, backing 25 basis points
ThursdayThe Financial Times reports Warsh is prepared to raise in September, Cook says she is ready, Kalshi prices a hike this year at 65 percent
FridayPayrolls print minus 23,000 against plus 80,000, with May and June revised down 103,000
SaturdayBofA keeps 75 basis points starting September. Morgan Stanley says none this year

Three days of hawkish escalation, one data release, and a 75 basis point disagreement between two of the largest desks on the street. Nothing about the reaction function changed. What changed is that one side is weighting a survey and the other is weighting a payroll.

1. Warsh's condition has two legs, and the second one is a mirror

The Chair did not say he would hike. Per the Market list, he said he is prepared to raise rates in September if inflation prints run hot and markets price in higher borrowing costs.

Read the second clause again. The market pricing a hike is itself part of the trigger for one. That is a reaction function with a feedback loop inside it, and it means positioning is not merely predicting the decision, it is an input to it. When Kalshi went to 65 percent on Thursday, that number was not just a forecast. It was evidence toward Warsh's own condition.

Which is why Friday mattered more than it should have. Hike odds fell from 60 percent to 30 inside a morning. That did not only reprice the probability, it removed one of the two legs the Chair named.

The context underneath is the part nobody enjoys. The Wall Street Journal reported Trump held multiple undisclosed calls with Warsh, dated by Bloomberg to May. A Chair turning hawkish while taking private calls from a President who wants cheap money is the least comfortable possible sequence. It also argues the hawkishness is genuine, because political pressure runs the other way.

2. What the payroll print actually broke

Per the Polymarket list, the headline was minus 23,000 against an expected gain of 80,000. The revisions were worse: May and June cut by a combined 103,000.

A single negative month is noise. A negative month plus 103,000 taken off the two before it is a trend being discovered late, and it means the Fed spent three weeks arguing about tightening into a labour market that was already softer than the data on its desk.

The rest of the release complicates it rather than settling it.

July jobs reportReading
Unemployment4.1 percent, a one-year low
Average hourly earnings3.2 percent, slowing
Participation61.4 percent, down and near a five-year low
June JOLTS openingsdown 178,000 to 7.359 million against 7.454 expected

Unemployment falling to a one-year low in the same release that shows job losses is not a contradiction. It is what happens when people leave the labour force rather than lose jobs, and the St Louis Fed flagged prime-age participation as the line to read in this exact report before it landed.

So the hawkish case did not lose an argument. It lost its premise. You cannot run "the labour market is too tight" as a reason to hike when payrolls are negative and participation is falling.

3. Who is on each side, and the honest read of the gap

Per the August 7 Market list, Bank of America kept 75 basis points of hikes this year starting in September, explicitly after the print, on the stated reason that inflation remains the Fed's primary concern. Morgan Stanley's chief strategist says there will be no rate hikes this year.

That is the widest spread this channel has recorded between two large desks. Both cannot be roughly right.

Per the Polymarket list, Goldman supplied the frame that decides it: inflation now matters more than jobs for the Fed. If that is the reaction function, a cracking labour market is background rather than a reason to hold, and Wednesday's CPI is the whole question. The market has not fully picked a side either, with a 44 percent September hike still priced and more than one tightening built in before year end.

The dissent that deserves more weight than it gets is Invesco's, arguing the Fed is not behind the curve at all, with neutral at 3.5 to 4.0 percent against a current 3.50 to 3.75 range. If that is right, both the hikers and the cutters are solving a problem that does not exist.

4. The thing this week actually settled, which was not the Fed

While the rate argument went in circles, the funding story underneath it resolved. Joseph Wang, on the Financial Markets list: "Treasury has now spent all the ammo in their Exchange Stabilization Fund. They sold Euros to buy Yen because that's all they have in the ESF."

That confirmed something this channel had been calling a novel mechanism and reframed it as something worse. It was never a clever cross-currency strategy. Treasury sold euros because euros were what remained. Jordi Visser dates the action as the first coordinated US and Bank of Japan intervention since 1998, against 30-year yields at 20-year highs.

An empty stabilisation fund means the next yen defence needs either a Bank of Japan hike or Japan selling from its trillion dollars of Treasuries. Japan's own choice, as put plainly this week: raise rates and blow up the domestic debt market, or cut and kill the currency. There is no exit, only a decision about how it gets wrecked.

Set that beside Treasury guiding to $739 billion of privately held net marketable borrowing this quarter, $68 billion above the May estimate, with interest expense already running $827 billion through June against $749 billion a year earlier and 33 percent of the debt maturing inside twelve months. A September hike is not a 2027 problem for the fiscal path. It is a 2026 one.

What settles it, and what would change my mind

Wednesday, August 12, CPI. This is the print Warsh named. A hot core reading restores the first leg of his condition and Bank of America is right with a labour market cracking underneath. A soft one kills September and probably the year.

Tuesday, September 16, the FOMC. Between now and then the only other thing that matters is whether the payroll revisions continue, because two consecutive months of downward revisions stop being a data artifact and start being a recession signal.

I am at 65/35 for a September hold, above where this call started the week. I am less comfortable at 65 than the number suggests, for one reason: Bank of America is not a fringe desk, it looked at the same jobs report I did, and it did not blink. What would move me back toward a hike is a core CPI print above expectations combined with the market re-pricing the odds itself, because that combination satisfies both of Warsh's legs at once and he has told us in advance that it would.

What would move me further toward a hold is a third consecutive month of downward payroll revisions. That would make Friday a trend rather than an event, and no committee tightens into that.

The scoreboard, Macro & Policy

Ten calls settled on this channel's book. Read the raw number with care, because four of them are the same CLARITY event counted across four editions, so ten settled entries represent roughly six distinct events.

Resolved this week and lastOutcome
No CLARITY floor vote before the recess, house, 85/15Hit. Cloture never filed, Senate left, earliest procedural vote September 15
A Hormuz agreement inside two weeks, house, 60/40Hit. Iran and Oman agreed the route in two days, through Oman rather than the Qatari channel I named
Oil higher two weeks out, house, 65/35Miss. Called early and marked early. The route agreement removed the premium and I resolved it rather than letting the date lapse
Warsh and Bessent coordinating the buildout as a national project, Capital FlowsHit
The US intervening in the yen using euros, Prof G MarketsHit, and upgraded by Joseph Wang's confirmation that the fund is empty
Payrolls stronger but not a blowout, Kathy LienMiss by 103,000
Steil optimistic the Senate gets CLARITY across, relayedMiss
Kalshi and Polymarket odds moving up on CLARITY, relayedMiss. The direction reversed to an all-time low of 16 percent
Senate floor math rules out passage before recess, Brendan PedersenHit
CLARITY comes down to three or four Democrats, Josh RymanExpired. Never tested, no roll call happened

House record: 2 hits and 1 miss on three settled calls. That is a small enough sample that the percentage would be advertising rather than scorekeeping, so here is the number without the decoration: two right, one wrong, and the wrong one was an oil call I marked as a loss four days before its due date rather than waiting for the calendar to do it quietly.

Sixty-one open calls carried into next week. The ones that matter: the September hold at 65/35, revised twice in three days and now above where it started. CPI on Wednesday. A joint Iran-Oman announcement at 70/30, due Tuesday. Two Abqaiq calls due Friday. CLARITY not becoming law in 2026 at 85/15, raised from 80/20. The China AI dumping thesis. Japan's no-exit. And the Exchange Stabilization Fund being empty. That is the one I would least like to be wrong about, because it has no natural resolution date and the way you find out is a disorderly one.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] Washington owns twelve public companies and just told you which ones
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Thirty government equity stakes in a year, Redwire's defence revenue up 380 percent, and the memory complex sitting 115 percent above a mean it has never failed to revert through.
item.content:encoded:
Thirty government equity stakes in a year, Redwire's defence revenue up 380 percent, and the memory complex sitting 115 percent above a mean it has never failed to revert through.

This morning's memo said to let the SpaceX calendar work. The more interesting list this weekend is the one where the government is already on the register, because twelve of those names are public and most of them have run.

The week ahead. Friday closed at the S&P's 26th record high of 2026, up over 14 percent for the year after being down 7 percent on March 30. Macro has Wednesday's CPI tonight.

The counterweight is positioning, not fundamentals. Per the Financial Markets list, Heisenberg has this on pace for one of the best Augusts in 41 years, and the only two comparables both broke: September 1986 fell 10 percent peak to trough and September 2020 fell 8.4. Per the Financial Markets morning list, Barchart has Bank of America's Bull and Bear indicator at one of the strongest stock market sell signals this century. Benjamin Cowen expects a correction to begin by late September.

The scoreboard.

  • Due Monday. Grab reports. The July 10 call was the January $3.50/$4.50 call spread with options pricing almost no move into the print.
  • Due Tuesday, and it has already run. Supermicro. Per Joseph Hogue, $SMCI is up 31 percent last week and 19 percent on the month into a print carrying a $60 billion-plus backlog, gross margin guided as high as 17 percent against roughly half that on the Street, and FY revenue near $40 billion on 80 percent growth. The criminal probe and the underwater $27.50 raise I flagged on July 28 have been swamped by the numbers.
  • Under pressure for a second day. My 60/40 that memory multiples expand before they compress. Section three is the case against me.

1. The government took stakes in thirty companies this year and twelve of them trade. Per Joseph Hogue, this is now a policy programme rather than a series of one-offs, and the terms are public.

NameThe dealMove
$MP Materials$400m preferred converting to 15 percent+145 percent since the July leak
$INTC Intel$8.9bn for 10 percent, warrants for another 5+131 percent
$USAR USA Rare Earthup to $277m direct plus a $1.3bn loan+28 percent, was as high as $26
$GFS GlobalFoundriesup to $675m across two CHIPS loans, plus 1 percentran +90, now back at the pre-announcement price
$LAC Lithium Americas$184m debt deferral, 5 percent of the company and 5 percent of Thacker Pass+11 percent
$TMQ Trilogy Metals$36m for 10 percent plus warrants for 7.5+68 percent, $68m market cap

The rest of the twelve are $LHX, $QBTS, $INFQ, $QNTM, $RGTI and $ALMU. One caution on that tail: Infleqtion trades at 57 times an expected $41 million of revenue and is the only one of the twelve net down.

The forward hook is the part nobody is trading. Washington wants domestic refining capacity back and is looking at reopening a refinery closed in 2021 that was built for Venezuelan heavy sour crude. The names under that are $VLO, the largest pure-play refiner and up 123 percent on the year, and $MPC, larger on capacity but diluted by MPLX.

This is the cleanest non-AI thesis available right now, and its edge is that the buyer has already announced itself.

2. Redwire's defence segment grew 380 percent and the market is still pricing a space company. Per Rick Orford, $RDW put up roughly $97 million to $100 million of first-quarter revenue, up about 58 percent, and the split is the story.

Redwire, Q1 2026Figure
Space segment$52.7 million
Defense Tech$44.3 million against $9.3 million a year earlier
Orders booked$186.5 million on $97 million of revenue, book-to-bill 1.92
Backlogrecord, near $500 million
Gross margin26.6 percent, up from 14.7
FY2026 guidancemaintained at $450 million to $500 million

The contracts are named: over $20 million of Marine Corps orders, a $15 million Army follow-on that is the third in eight months, and a multi-year high-eight-figure Penguin award to a NATO country. It was also selected onto the MDA SHIELD vehicle tied to Golden Dome, though that is multi-award and guarantees no revenue.

The honest gaps. Net loss was $76.5 million, over $44 million of it non-recurring including a $42.5 million Edge Autonomy stock-comp charge. Adjusted EBITDA is minus $9.2 million, free cash flow is negative, and the share count is rising to fund the transformation. No price, no multiple and no target, so this is a thesis rather than an entry.

I am 60/40 that the defence segment passes the space segment in revenue before year end. A 1.92 book-to-bill does not reverse in two quarters.

3. The memory bull case is now arguing with the chart, and the chart has history on its side. The year-to-date table is the bull case in one column. Per Evan of StockMKTNewz, fifteen S&P names have more than doubled this year and the storage and memory complex owns the top of it: $SNDK up 410.7 percent, $DELL up 260.5, $MU up 207.5, $STX up 195.1 and $WDC up 152.1.

Then per the Stocks list, the mean-reversion case. Every time the semiconductor index or $SMH has traded more than 100 percent above its 200-week average, it has reverted through the mean rather than stalling above it. Three completed instances: the index at 272 percent above in 2000, 104 percent in 2021, and $SMH at 113 percent in 2021. $SMH peaked near 180 percent above in June and still sits near 115 percent after the pullback.

The rest of the tape agrees with the chart more than with me. Korean semis fell 40 percent in 40 days. Jan van Eck's read is that the memory names "weren't growing volume, they just upped prices." FinX called the top outright. Jordi Visser has already sold Micron and rotated into silver, Bitcoin and Eli Lilly. And per the Polymarket list, Apple has started testing CXMT memory chips. That is the demand side going shopping in China for the first time.

Against all of that sits the only argument that has held: Elon Musk's line that memory supply grows about 20 percent a year against demand growing about 200. Roundhill's chief executive still calls SanDisk a $2,200 stock.

I am holding 60/40 for a third day and I am now the minority view in my own edition. What would break it is a CXMT qualification at Apple, because that converts a pricing story into a share story.

4. Visser says the crash is over and pointedly did not raise his target. Per Jordi Visser, the July drawdown was a positioning event and "the bottom is in as far as I'm concerned on a probability basis."

The confirmation is broad rather than narrow. The S&P rose 3.6 percent on the week and the Nasdaq proxy 5, with new all-time highs on the equal-weight S&P, the Russell, the NYSE Composite, the DAX and the FTSE in the same week. Earnings growth is running near 50 percent on 15 percent revenue growth, with margins at 17 percent against 13 a year ago.

His single best datapoint is on Nvidia, via Gavin Baker: it trades at its lowest forward earnings multiple in ten years, while B200 rental went from the mid $2 per GPU hour seven months ago to just under $4. Rising rental rates against a falling multiple is the shape of a market that has stopped believing the revenue.

What he did not do is raise the target. Last week he called for many AI names at new all-time highs by year end. This week he repeated the bottom call and attached no new number to it. Treat that as a call carried forward rather than reaffirmed.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $SMCI. Reports Tuesday after a 31 percent week, with a $60 billion-plus backlog and gross margin guided near 17 percent against a Street at roughly half. The setup has already moved, so the risk here is the reaction rather than the number.
  • $NBIS. Reports this week. Goldman raised its 2030 revenue estimate to $35.5 billion from $22.1, a 61 percent lift, and models about $30 billion of EBITDA by 2030 on contracted power above 4 gigawatts. It rose 14 percent Friday into Michael Burry's short.
  • $SNDK. Up 410 percent this year and the cleanest expression of whichever side of section three is right. It beat on Friday and closed red, the first time the tape has ignored a good memory print.
  • $USAR. The one fully specified position on the board. Per Rick Orford, called at $13.30, near $20 now, stop raised to $18, target zone $19.75 to $21.75. He flags that his own daily signal has not crossed yet, so he is holding rather than adding.
  • $RDW. Defence revenue up 380 percent year over year with a 1.92 book-to-bill and a record $500 million backlog, still burning cash and still diluting. Own the trajectory or wait for free cash flow, but do not call it a space stock.
  • $VLO. The refining leg of the same government-capital thesis that has already repriced $MP and $INTC, up 123 percent over the past year and the largest pure-play in the group. Nobody is front-running this one yet.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] Kalshi flipped the distribution: $50,000 is now likelier than $100,000
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Spot ETFs took $865 million this week, the biggest in four months, while a whale moved 6,494 coins onto Binance and the derivatives book emptied of humans.
item.content:encoded:
Spot ETFs took $865 million this week, the biggest in four months, while a whale moved 6,494 coins onto Binance and the derivatives book emptied of humans.

This morning's memo argued that usage keeps compounding while tokens do not. The weekend added the uncomfortable half: the people who price this for a living have stopped waiting for the gap to close upward.

Market context. Bitcoin spent the weekend in the mid $60,000s and every read agrees. Per the Crypto list, On-Chain Mind has it 14.5 percent below a True Market Mean of $75,800, and that mean is falling about $1,000 a week. A Whale Alert transfer implies roughly $65,175. Polymarket's Sunday close band of 64,000 to 66,000 traded at 92 percent.

The flows are genuinely two-sided for the first time in weeks.

Weekend flowFigure
Spot Bitcoin ETF net inflows, week$865 million, the biggest in four months
A single whale, possibly a miner, into Binance6,494 BTC, about $420.5 million, over three weeks
Stablecoin supplyabout $307 billion, roughly 4 percent off the mid-May peak, shrinking three months running
Tokenised Treasuries$6.5 billion to nearly $16 billion in a year, up 56 percent in six months

Sykodelic has the level that matters: a weekly close above $66,000 and this goes higher, a rejection and $60,000 comes first.

1. The betting markets moved the distribution, not just the price. Per the August 8 Kalshi list, Kalshi now prices Bitcoin as more likely to reach $50,000 before $100,000. That is the first time this cycle the downside target has been the favourite.

Set it against the people still selling the upside. Bitwise's Matt Hougan calls $250,000 to $400,000 "a reasonable range" for the next bull market, which from here is a four to six times move. Novogratz has a $60,000 to $80,000 base case and says plainly he does not think rates get cut this year. BitcoinJesusETH expects any relief rally to fail near $72,000.

The distance between Hougan and Kalshi is not a disagreement about Bitcoin. It is a disagreement about when, and Kalshi is the one with money on a date.

My 60/40 that Bitcoin sees $58,000 before $75,000 is unchanged and now has the betting market on its side rather than against it. The thing that would move me is the $865 million ETF week repeating twice more, because two consecutive four-month-high inflow weeks is a different tape from one.

2. The derivatives book has no humans left in it. Per Trader Mayne, CryptoFace says that in eight years he does not recall seeing what the Bitcoin liquidation heat map shows now. He counts six identical structures, mirrored and repeated, and the conclusion is blunt: "there is no human money. There's not even a blip."

That is the mechanical explanation for volatility sitting at three-year lows. Liquidation clusters are what retail leverage looks like on a chart, and there are none. What is left is market makers trading against each other.
