He also gave the tripwire, and it is more useful than the observation. The turn comes when human liquidation clusters reappear on the heat map, not when a price level breaks. It is a positioning signal rather than a technical one, and it has not fired.

Lyn Alden supplies the flow version of the same thing. Bitcoin follows global money supply 83 percent of the time and this is the other 17 percent, because the enthusiasm that would have hit spot went into treasury-company premiums instead. Strategy trades at three times net asset value and MetaPlanet at eight.

3. The alt bull conceded the argument, and he was the one defending them. Per Milk Road, a venture investor brought on to rebut Anthony Pompliano's claim that everything except Bitcoin is dead instead agreed with most of it: most other altcoins "probably don't deserve to be around." He will defend exactly four names, Ethereum, Near, Venice and Hive.

Then the line that matters more than the concession, offered as a caveat on Solana: "value capture is a different dimension than value creation." That is the bear case on tokens stated by a bull, and he never closes it for any asset he owns.

Ethereum's own bull case arrived in the same shape. Per Milk Road, Austin Arnold's framing is that Ethereum is running the Uber playbook, subsidising adoption through layer twos and stablecoins with the fee switch ready to flip later. Read it carefully and it concedes the token collects nothing today and asks for patience instead of evidence.

The mechanics argue against the patience. Per the August 9 Crypto list, aixbt is blunt: "No ETH scarcity trade yet." EIP-8363 is an open draft, 2.44 million Ether is queued to enter staking against an empty exit queue, and the baseline change would cut the staking yield from about 2.6 percent to 1.2. His conclusion is to skip the Ether-against-Bitcoin long.

I am holding 60/40 with CryptoKaleo's one-more-leg-down on Ether. Three separate sources this weekend described the bull case as a mechanism that has not been switched on yet.

4. The fork resolved and the Coldcard damage finally got sized. Per the Crypto list, the BIP-110 challenge failed outright. About 99.85 percent of hashpower stayed with Bitcoin, the competing branch mined two blocks and is more than 80 behind, and miner signalling ran at 2.6 percent. Saylor's summary and aixbt's agree: block production is 85 to 2.

The Coldcard number is the correction worth printing. aixbt puts the confirmed damage at 1,719 Bitcoin, about 0.0082 percent of the network's capitalisation, and notes Bitcoin closed 0.22 percent higher between July 30 and August 8. At current prices that is roughly $112 million, consistent with the figures this channel has been carrying, but the share of the network is the part that reframes it. This was a vendor failure, not a protocol failure, and the market has now priced it as such.

Not everything about the episode is clean. Per the Financial Markets list, Tone Vays says Ocean Mining left the BIP-110 default in place through a 17-hour window from 4pm to 9am Eastern, and that a few hundred thousand dollars were probably wasted mining a dead chain tip by people who did not know it. He also says he predicted September 1 for Luke Dashjr's hard fork, so this is not over.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. Mid $60,000s with $66,000 the weekly line and $60,000 the alternative, against the biggest ETF inflow week in four months and a 6,494-coin whale deposit going the other way. Kalshi now favours $50,000 before $100,000, the first time the market has agreed with this desk's direction.
  • $ETH. Near $1,900 against almost $5,000 six months ago, with 2.44 million coins queued to stake, an empty exit queue and a staking yield heading from 2.6 percent toward 1.2. The Uber-playbook bull case is a fee switch nobody has flipped.
  • $SOL. The venue argument keeps getting better while the token does not. HYPE did $107 million in a day on Solana, more than on Coinbase or Binance, and tokenised equities there passed $600 million, about 21 percent of all onchain equity value. Birdeye's target is a new high above $300, possibly not until 2028.
  • $MSTR. Trades at three times net asset value while absorbing enthusiasm that used to reach spot. Saylor hinted at buying again this weekend and repeated that even at $5,000 Bitcoin the company stays over-collateralised.
  • $HOOD. Its chain's stablecoin supply passed $600 million and roughly doubled in a month, and prediction markets out-earned both its crypto and its equities lines last quarter. The coins are the funnel and the contracts are the business.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] Two independent desks put September near a coin flip, and I was at 35
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Benjamin Cowen has the hike at 43.9 percent and Jordi Visser at 45, the national debt crossed $40 trillion, and Iran hardened its terms for reopening the strait.
item.content:encoded:
Benjamin Cowen has the hike at 43.9 percent and Jordi Visser at 45, the national debt crossed $40 trillion, and Iran hardened its terms for reopening the strait.

This morning's memo said Wednesday's CPI settles September. It does. What changed over the weekend is that two people who model this for a living both put the hike near a coin flip, and my number was the most dovish on the board.

The week ahead. CPI lands Wednesday. Everything else is positioning into it.

September hike, as pricedReading
Benjamin Cowen43.9 percent
Jordi Visser45 percent
The Order Book, post-payrollsabout 40 percent, down from roughly 55
Kyle Reidhead35 percent, framed as "65 percent now agreeing with me"

Gold had the week the debasement trade wanted: up 7.2 percent, its third biggest week in 16 years, closing back above its 50-day for the first time since March after the third longest stretch below on record. Oil went the other way, near $75 and softening. The 30-year Treasury yield sits at a 19-year high.

1. I am trimming the hold call, and the reason is the distribution rather than the data. My 65/35 for a September hold implies a 35 percent hike. Per Benjamin Cowen that number is 43.9, and per Jordi Visser it is 45. The Order Book has the market at roughly 40 after the payroll print, down from 55 before it.

So three independent readings cluster between 40 and 45, and I was sitting outside them on the dovish side. I am moving to 60/40 for a hold. Not because the labour data changed over a weekend, but because being the most dovish voice on the board is a position that needs evidence I do not have.

Cowen supplies the mechanism I had underweighted. The two-year yield now sits above the 3.75 percent fed funds rate, and the Fed has historically chased the two-year rather than led it. His precedent is the late 1990s, where that chase ran for years before the cycle turned. A committee that is behind its own front end does not need a hot print to move. It needs an excuse.

2. Cowen's labour read is more careful than the headline and it argues against a recession. The July print was negative. His trigger is not that.

What Cowen actually watchesReading
Year-over-year total nonfarm payrollsnot negative. Every negative reading has been a recession. Came close in February and bounced
Initial claims189,000, roughly a 50-year low. His rule is that below 300,000 means no recession
Participation62.5 percent last November to 61.4 percent now
Unemploymentfell from 4.5 percent to 4.1, on participation rather than on hiring
His recession dashboard0.16, low

The growth rate is the honest worry. Total nonfarm grew 4 to 5 percent a year in 2022 and runs near 2 percent now, which he calls basically no net job creation. Visser's version is harder: aggregate weekly payrolls are at their weakest six-month rate of change since 2012 excluding the pandemic, average hourly earnings are down to 3.2 percent, and only healthcare has added jobs in 18 months.

Cowen's dated call is the one to carry, and it is about equities rather than the Fed. He expects a correction to begin by late September at the latest, keyed to midterm years 2014, 2018 and 2022, with the September 16 meeting as the pivot. That is falsifiable and it is six weeks out.

3. The debt crossed $40 trillion and the long end has stopped pretending. Per the August 8 Kalshi list, the number went through $40 trillion this week, roughly twice China's entire GDP, after adding $450 billion since July 1, over $15 billion a day. Kalshi prices $50 trillion by 2028 at 32 percent.

Per the Financial Markets list, Peter Mallouk put the consequence in one sentence: "You can't borrow trillions every year, tolerate persistently high inflation, and expect cheap financing forever." The 30-year at a 19-year high is that sentence with a price on it.

Two second-order items landed alongside it. Jan van Eck of VanEck says that by 2032 the government will not have enough to pay full Social Security benefits and scheduled payments drop 20 percent, "essentially a default in everything but name." And Japan's four largest life insurers now carry ¥15.13 trillion, about $96 billion, of unrealised domestic bond losses, up 7 percent in the quarter. That is the balance-sheet damage sitting behind the yen problem this channel has been tracking all week.

Anas Alhajji added the detail that reframes the intervention. Per the Nikkei read he cites, reopening Hormuz was one of five strings attached to the Bessent yen rescue, and joining in euros rather than dollars specifically reduced the pressure on Japan to liquidate Treasuries, which would have pushed the long end higher still.

4. Iran hardened its terms, and the reopening trade is now worse than it looked. Per the Kalshi list, Iran says the Strait of Hormuz "will not" return to its previous state. Per the Polymarket list, the price of reopening is now US forces withdrawn from the region, the naval blockade lifted, sanctions removed and frozen assets released.

Against that, Trump is reportedly willing to walk away from the conflict without a nuclear deal if the strait fully reopens. So both sides have moved toward a transaction and away from a settlement, and the transaction is expensive.

My 70/30 that a joint Iran-Oman announcement lands inside a week runs to Wednesday and it is now the call I am least comfortable with. A government listing four preconditions on Sunday is not a government signing on Wednesday. I am not revising it before the date because the route agreement itself is real and Oman is still the channel, but the honest read is that this resolves as a miss more often than 30 percent of the time from here.

The physical market has stopped caring either way. Anas Alhajji's second-quarter Asian demand data is negative across every country he tracks.

Q2 oil demand, year over yearChange
Chinaminus 12.0 percent
Pakistanminus 18.2 percent
Bangladeshminus 14.5 percent
Japanminus 6.2 percent
South Koreaminus 5.8 percent

Mike McGlone's conclusion follows from it: the North American liquids surplus is approaching 8 million barrels a day against near 3 million when WTI peaked near $130 in 2022, and "$40 crude is becoming normal." A closed strait was supposed to be the thing that broke that. It has not, and the demand side is why.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] The S&P set a record, gold beat it, and memory did not move at all
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Nebius reports Wednesday into Michael Burry's fresh short, Figure follows Thursday, and 745 on the tracking fund is the line that decides whether 800 is live.
item.content:encoded:
Nebius reports Wednesday into Michael Burry's fresh short, Figure follows Thursday, and 745 on the tracking fund is the line that decides whether 800 is live.

The index closed at a record on Friday and the memory complex did not move. That gap is the week in one sentence, and next week has three prints to close it.

The week ahead. Friday finished at a record high on the S&P. Per the Kalshi list, $2.8 trillion was added to the US market across the week, with the Nasdaq tracking fund up 5.3 percent. Gold still beat it, finishing almost 8 percent higher per the Stocks list, more than the two big index funds combined.

The calendar does the work from here.

Next weekWhat lands
Monday$GRAB earnings
Tuesday$SMCI
WednesdayCPI, plus $NBIS
Thursday$FIGR before the open
Also due$RKLB, $ASTS, $CRWV, $CSCO

Per Stocks with Josh, the level to hold is 745, and the path to 800 requires Wednesday's CPI to come in cool. His invalidation is unusually clean: "If at any time we cross back beneath this 745, then it means that this up move isn't likely going to happen and it means that this was the top." Set against a VIX near two-year lows and Kalshi at 67 percent for 8,000 this year, the asymmetry is not generous.

The scoreboard.

  • Due Monday. Grab reports. The July 10 call was the January $3.50/$4.50 call spread with options pricing almost no move into the print.
  • Due Tuesday. Supermicro, carrying a second criminal probe in Taiwan and a $7 billion raise whose 45 million shares at $27.50 are underwater.
  • Working. My 60/40 that the July low holds into mid-August runs to Friday, and the index closed the week at a record.
  • Under pressure, and I am saying so. My 60/40 that memory multiples expand before they compress. $MU, $SNDK, $WDC and $SKHY all went nowhere while the S&P made a new high. The thesis is contractual and the tape is not cooperating.

1. Nebius reports Wednesday into a short that just got bigger. Per Rick Orford, $NBIS has moved to a partner-funded model where partners fund, own and operate the physical build while Nebius supplies the design, the platform and the customers. The bricks are theirs, the brains are Nebius.

The guidance is the whole case: an annualised run rate of $7 billion to $9 billion by year end, from about $1.25 billion at the end of last year. Behind it sit a Meta agreement worth potentially $27 billion and 1.2 gigawatts of secured power and land in Pennsylvania. Nvidia holds a 9.3 percent stake after a $2 billion investment, and Goldman raised its own position from 7.2 to 10.5 percent this week.

The price is where it gets uncomfortable. 105.5 times sales, 7.7 times book, a 60-month beta of 4.1, and a 52-week range from about $50 to just under $300.

Michael Burry is short at $211.77 and spent this week adding to March semiconductor ETF puts and shorting more shares. This is the cleanest binary on the calendar: a 105 times sales name reporting into a famous short, with a beta of 4. I have no edge on the direction and I am not pretending to. What I would say is that a 4-beta name at that multiple is a position to size, not to be right about.

2. Mastercard grew 14 percent and the argument is entirely about the price. Per a breakdown on Reddit, revenue hit $9.28 billion, up 14 percent, with adjusted EPS of $5.04, up 21 percent, and operating margin expanding to 61.1 percent from 59.9. Expenses grew 11 percent against 14 percent revenue growth, and that gap is the EPS spread.

The mix is better than the headline. Value-added services grew 20 percent against 10 percent for the core payment network, and non-US switched volume grew 12 percent against 6 percent in the US. Cross-border volume rose 12 percent and was still running at 11 percent in July.

The poster's own conclusion is the honest one and it is not a buy: the difficulty with Mastercard is not the quality of the business, it is the valuation, and at a premium multiple even a great business produces mediocre returns if growth slows. I agree. It is still the cleanest non-AI compounder in the week's material, and the only one where the debate is price rather than durability.

3. Washington is writing cheques for minerals and lasers and almost nobody is trading it. Per the August 7 Market list, AeroVironment won a $400 million US Army contract for Locust laser defence systems, the Pentagon's first production-scale counter-drone laser award beyond prototype.

The critical minerals money landed the same week.

White House critical minerals awardsAmount
Westwater Resources, graphite$25 million
NioCorp, scandium$400 million
5E Advanced Materials, boron$8 million
HREE, magnet rare earths$4.8 million
Niron Magnetics and Standard Bauxite$150 million and $85 million

Trump announced more than $2 billion in critical mining projects plus $180 million for mining workforce education, on top of 160 mineral deals worth nearly $40 billion since January 2025.

The trade already moved once. Per Stocks with Josh, USA Rare Earth was called at $13.30 ten days ago on the magnets announcement and touched almost $20 on Friday, with the stop raised to $18 and a target zone of $19.75 to $21.75. He is holding rather than adding because the daily signal has not confirmed. Fifty percent in ten sessions earns that discipline.

4. Memory is sold out and the stocks went nowhere, and there is an arbitrage inside it. Per Milk Road AI, roughly 70 percent of hyperscaler capex is going to memory with a projected $761 billion next year, everything is sold out this year, and hyperscalers are signing three to five year contracts with price levels fixed. Elon Musk's version on the SpaceX call: memory demand is growing 200 percent a year and memory capacity is growing 20 percent.

Samsung is their pick as the laggard, with revenue up 130 percent, net profit up 52 percent, and it shipped HBM4 to Nvidia first, which retires the step-behind narrative. UBS sees it taking HBM share from SK Hynix next year.

Then the structural trade nobody will take. The NASDAQ wrapper for SK Hynix trades at a 22 percent premium, while SK Square, a holding company owning 20 percent of SK Hynix, trades at a 44 percent discount to its look-through value. Management KPIs are tied to closing that discount below 30 percent. Same asset, two listings, a 66 point spread and a paid incentive to compress it.

I am holding the memory call at 60/40 and acknowledging it has not worked for a week. Sold-out capacity with contracted pricing is a real floor. It is not a catalyst, and the tape has spent five sessions proving the difference.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $SPCX. Per the All-In Podcast, the first public quarter did $7.8 billion of revenue, up 92 percent, on $18.4 billion of capex in the quarter alone, roughly a $75 billion run rate. AI revenue more than tripled sequentially to $2.6 billion and Starlink's 12 million subscribers doubled year over year at $66 a month. Per the Stocks list it closed above $131, up 25 percent off the lockup, and is still 30 percent below the June listing at $1.4 trillion. The capex line is what you are underwriting.
  • $NBIS. Wednesday's print against Burry's $211.77 short, on 105.5 times sales and a 4.1 beta. Guidance says $7 to $9 billion of run-rate revenue by December from $1.25 billion. Size it like the option it is.
  • $MA. Fourteen percent revenue, 21 percent EPS, 61.1 percent margins expanding, value-added services growing double the core network. The whole question is the multiple, and nobody in the source will name it.
  • $AVAV. A $400 million Army award for the first production-scale counter-drone laser, inside a week when Washington also committed over $2 billion to critical minerals. The defence budget is the most legible non-AI spending in the market right now.
  • $PLTR. Per Chip Stock Investor, up 30 percent since the print at about $160, with US commercial revenue up 149 percent on customer count up only 35, so the growth is expansion inside accounts across 220 deals above $1 million. Their reverse discounted cash flow says $135 already implies 100 percent earnings growth for two years. Even the bulls are setting alerts below, not buying here.
  • $TLT. Macro has the driver tonight: Japan cornered, the stabilisation fund empty, the long end at an all-time low since 2002 on a 5.14 percent yield. Positioning is the whole appeal: seven puts for every call and a fifth of the float sold short, against a disclosed $82.20 cost basis targeting mean reversion to $88.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] Crypto cards hit $759 million a month while the tokens did nothing
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Fundstrat's Sean Farrell says buy the majors now and names a four-handle Bitcoin as his bear case, and CLARITY's earliest procedural vote is September 15.
item.content:encoded:
Fundstrat's Sean Farrell says buy the majors now and names a four-handle Bitcoin as his bear case, and CLARITY's earliest procedural vote is September 15.

Yesterday the bill died and Bitcoin went up. All week the same pattern held in miniature. Every measure of actual usage rose, and no price followed any of it.

Market context. Bitcoin sits near $64,800, derived from a 1,346 coin transfer out of Galaxy Digital worth $87.28 million on the Crypto list. Ether is near $1,906, from a whale who capitulated after three years, selling 7,323 coins for $13.96 million against a $2,723 average entry and more than $19 million of realised losses.

Tom Lee's framing of that is the week in one line: "6 months ago Ethereum was almost $5,000. Now it's $1,800. Has anything really changed? Not really."

The institutional bid is still there and still quiet. BlackRock's fund took $604 million over four days, and per Lark Davis Larry Fink's public read is that crypto had too much leverage, got washed out, and there is more stability at these levels. Underneath, Bitcoin volatility is at three-year lows and, per the Kalshi list, 23 percent of the top miners are running at a daily loss.

1. On-chain revenue inflected months ago and the prices never noticed. Per Milk Road, a Bitwise on-chain analyst puts the trough in network revenue at "between end of 2025 early 2026," with revenue picking up since while tokens kept falling.

The specifics are not small.

On-chainFigure
Hyperliquid fees, Q2 2026about $175 million, 80 percent from perpetuals, buying and burning HYPE
Solana tokenised equity volume$1 million in June 2025 to more than $3 billion in June 2026
Avalanchetransactions quadrupled on an RWA pivot, with FIFA running its own chain
Progmat, Japan's largest tokenisation platformbringing more than $2 billion of assets

The honest weakness is the resolution condition. Asked when the divergence closes, the answer is "when people start understanding what's going on on chain," with no date, no target and no flow number attached. A fundamentals case with no catalyst is a reason to own something, not a reason to expect it to move.

2. Crypto cards are the adoption number nobody quotes, and they are almost entirely Visa. Per a16z crypto, monthly crypto payment card volume reached $759 million in July, up roughly 2.5 times from $306 million a year earlier, and up from less than $1 million when tracking began in October 2023. Purchases hit nearly 9 million in July against 5.2 million a year ago, at an average of about $86 a transaction.

The composition shift is the real finding. Dollar stablecoins took the market: USDC now handles about 58 percent of card spending and USDT about 26, from roughly 48 and 7 a year ago. Euro-backed stablecoins went from 88 percent of volume in early 2024 to about 2 percent. Settlement moved with it, from Gnosis dominance to Optimism at 29 percent, Solana and Base at about 19 each, with Gnosis down to 2.

This is what adoption looks like when it stops being a narrative: a payment rail growing 2.5 times a year, denominated in digital dollars, running almost entirely over Visa. None of it accrues to a token. That is precisely why it has not shown up in a price.

3. Fundstrat says buy the majors and puts the bear case at a four handle. Per DeFi Dad's interview with Sean Farrell, Fundstrat's head of digital asset strategy is unambiguous about where we are: "we are in the throes of a bear market... if I had to put an inning on it, I would say that we are in the seventh inning stretch. Uh maybe maybe even later in the game."

His call is the only named allocation decision anyone made this week. "I feel pretty comfortable that you could buy the majors right now... I'm pretty sure you could buy the majors and sell them at a higher price, say a year from now." He is more patient on alts, because the ones he likes have already bounced 25 to 50 percent off the lows.

The bear case he asks clients to stomach is "a forehand on Bitcoin," meaning a $40,000s print. That sits below Mike Novogratz's $60,000 to $80,000 base case and well below the $72,000 level where BitcoinJesusETH expects a relief rally to fail.

His diagnosis of why is the useful part. Crypto is "an excess liquidity sponge" and there has been no excess liquidity, so marginal capital went to assets producing earnings. The forced sellers are named: miners selling to fund capex, holders on the four-year cycle, treasury companies unable to raise below one times net asset value and now selling, and redemptions from liquid funds. The real two-year yield is at a new cycle high.

I am holding 60/40 that Bitcoin sees $58,000 before $75,000. Farrell's four handle is more bearish than my call and Novogratz's floor is above it, so my number sits between two credible desks rather than outside them. What would change it is the liquidity condition Farrell names, and nothing next week supplies it.

4. Two handicappers disagree on CLARITY and both say it stopped mattering. The earliest procedural vote is now September 15. Per Jordi Visser, the odds fell from 40 percent to 17 and he calls it "officially being quote unquote done for this year." Farrell is the other side, "above a coin flip" that a compromise on the ethics provision lands, and says that absent that provision he would be at 100 percent.

They agree on the thing that matters. SEC and CFTC rules arrive regardless and are, in Farrell's words, "pretty aligned with what Clarity says."

That is the case for my 65/35 that the failure is already priced, and this week supported it. Bitcoin rose on the delay. What the two of them also expose is the real gating item, and it is not policy substance: the hold-up is Trump's own crypto earnings and the ethics language written to cover them.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. Near $64,800 with volatility at three-year lows and $604 million of BlackRock buying over four sessions. Farrell says buy the majors here for a one-year hold and warns you may see a four handle first. Both can be true, and position size is the only thing that reconciles them.
  • $ETH. Down from almost $5,000 six months ago to about $1,900, with a three-year holder capitulating into it. Farrell calls it "one of the most clean macro trades of the next cycle." Robinhood's chain has no token, so its transactions consume Ether. That is the first genuine new demand source in a year.
  • $HYPE. About $175 million of second-quarter fees with 80 percent from perpetuals, all of it buying and burning the token. HyperLabs unlocked another 433,025 coins worth $23.46 million this week, so supply is arriving alongside the burn.
  • $MSTR. Farrell names it as the sector's tail risk, specifically the putable bond repurchases that spiralled through the preferred and the broader complex. The company is deleveraging in public and the market is still deciding whether that was a choice.
  • $HOOD. Per the Financial Markets list, it formed a golden cross for the first time since January 2024, and the last one preceded a 440 percent run over thirteen months. Its chain is where the only live retail bid in crypto actually sits, even though the coins are now the loss leader against event contracts.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] Two banks read the same payroll print and landed 75 basis points apart
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Bank of America still wants three hikes starting in September, Morgan Stanley says none this year, and Wednesday's CPI decides which desk was reading the right number.
item.content:encoded:
Bank of America still wants three hikes starting in September, Morgan Stanley says none this year, and Wednesday's CPI decides which desk was reading the right number.

Yesterday a negative payroll print killed the September hike in a morning. It did not kill the argument. Bank of America read the same number and kept three hikes.

The week ahead. Wednesday's CPI is the only print that matters, because it is the one Warsh named as his trigger. Friday's labour data set the table.

July jobs reportReading
Nonfarm payrollsminus 23,000 against plus 80,000 expected
May and June revisionsdown a combined 103,000
Unemployment4.1 percent
Average hourly earnings3.2 percent, slowing
Labour force participation61.4 percent, down slightly

Rate-hike probabilities fell roughly 20 points on the day. Gold took the week, finishing almost 8 percent higher, its biggest weekly gain since January per the Financial Markets list and more than the Nasdaq and S&P tracking funds combined.

1. The desks are further apart after the print than they were before it. Per the August 7 Market list, Bank of America stuck with 75 basis points of hikes this year starting in September, explicitly after payrolls fell 23,000 with 103,000 of downward revisions. Its stated reason is that inflation remains the Fed's primary concern.

Against that, per the Polymarket list, Morgan Stanley's chief strategist declared there will be "no rate hikes" this year.

That is a 75 basis point gap on the same data, the widest this product has recorded between two large desks all year. Both cannot be roughly right.

Goldman supplied the frame that decides it: inflation now matters more than jobs for the Fed. If that is the reaction function, then a labour market cracking is not a reason to hold, it is background, and Wednesday's CPI is the entire question. The market has not fully picked a side either. Per Anthony Pompliano's guest Jordi Visser, there is still a 44 percent chance of a September hike priced, with more than one tightening built in before year end.

My lean stays where I moved it Friday. 65/35 for a September hold. The reason is not the labour data, it is that Warsh named a conditional and the condition has to be met by a print rather than by an argument. But I am less comfortable at 65 than I was, because Bank of America is not a fringe desk and it looked at the same jobs report I did and did not blink.

2. China is dumping AI the way it dumped steel, and one of the analogies is worse than the other. Per Prof G Markets, tokens consumed from Chinese large language models went from 8 percent share in January 2025 to somewhere above 50 percent now. The framing offered is deliberate: China is "trying to do to our market what they tried to do to our steel market 30 or 40 years ago and doing in kind of 20 weeks to Silicon Valley what Japan did to Detroit over 20 years."

Twenty weeks against twenty years is the part to sit with. Trade dumping normally gives the incumbent time to lobby for tariffs. This did not.

The pricing evidence underneath is specific. Anthropic's cost to deliver what it charges $6,000 an hour for is not a software cost structure. Per the same show, the two American labs have already split on the response, with Anthropic going premium and OpenAI going for volume at lower cost, "and the Chinese are of course waiting on the sidelines to throw the story into complete turmoil."

The capex spread is the trade this creates. Everyone is spending $150 billion to $200 billion while Apple spends $11 billion, and the verdict offered is that this becomes a case study in whether it is better to wait out the uncertainty and then decide what factory to build, rather than build the factory first. This is the driver. What it does to the semis chain and to the names carrying the capex belongs to Stocks.

3. Japan has to pick how it gets wrecked, and the long end is already voting. Per Stocks with Josh, Japan holds over $1 trillion of US Treasuries, and the trap is that the Bank of Japan cannot sell enough of them to defend the yen without breaking the US bond market that funds American deficits. The choice as put: raise rates and blow up the domestic debt market, or cut and kill the currency. "There's no exit. They just simply have to pick how Japan gets wrecked."

This is the same thread that produced Thursday's confirmation that Treasury emptied its Exchange Stabilization Fund defending the yen, selling euros because euros were what remained. Visser adds the detail that dates it: this was the first coordinated US and Bank of Japan intervention since 1998, against 30-year yields at 20-year highs. His read is blunt. "The yen intervention is a representation that we have no more tools left."

The long end has already priced some of it. The main long-duration Treasury fund is pushing all-time lows since it launched in July 2002, yielding 5.14 percent, with a put-to-call skew near 7 to 1 and a short float around 20 percent. Per a widely-read breakdown, its historic drawdown dates read as a list of macro accidents, and the author adds the current one by name: 2007, 2013, 2018, 2020, 2023, 2025, and "August 2026, Kevin Warsh."

Being at an all-time low is not the same as being cheap. It is what a market looks like when it believes the supply and the policy both get worse. The position belongs to Stocks.

4. The Hormuz deal is close enough that the market has stopped paying for it. Per the August 7 Market list, Trump said the deal to reopen the strait is "moving along good" and stocks bounced on it. That is the seventh time this week he has said he wants an agreement. Bessent floated a ceasefire announcement over the weekend, and per the Polymarket list a US official set the condition plainly: the blockade of Iranian ports lifts once a deal restoring unimpeded commercial shipping is announced.

My 70/30 on a joint Iran-Oman announcement runs to Tuesday and is still live. What has changed is that the payoff has shrunk, because the tape now moves a few points on each headline instead of repricing crude.

The physical picture argues the same way. Global commercial crude inventories sit more than 40 million barrels higher than a year ago, and Anas Alhajji's read is the useful correction: the oil crisis is in petroleum products, not in crude. That is consistent with US pump prices setting a record $4.06 a gallon on August 4 while inventories build.

Two things sit against a clean resolution. ADNOC has logged 15 vessel attacks as the risk mounts, and Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed a defence agreement in Mecca on Friday. All three border Iran, and none of them signs that document if they expect the strait to be quietly settled next week.

So the week has one question and one date. If Wednesday's CPI runs hot, Bank of America is right and the September hike comes back with the labour market already cracking underneath it. If it does not, the hike is dead until the December meeting and everything above resolves toward the doves.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] SpaceX ripped 15 percent the day after 911 million shares came free
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Rocket Lab bought Iridium for $8 billion and flipped itself to net debt, Damodaran put the hyperscaler capex spread at $200 billion against Apple's $11 billion, and a bad jobs number lifted everything.
item.content:encoded:
Rocket Lab bought Iridium for $8 billion and flipped itself to net debt, Damodaran put the hyperscaler capex spread at $200 billion against Apple's $11 billion, and a bad jobs number lifted everything.

Yesterday I marked the SpaceX squeeze call a miss. It was a day early. The float tripled, the stock went up fifteen percent, and the thing that did it was a jobs report.

Market context. Macro has the print tonight: payrolls at minus 23,000 against plus 80,000 expected, and a September hike repriced out of existence. The tape read it as the Fed being disarmed, and per the Kalshi list the S&P set a new all-time high at 7,740 shortly after the open. Pentosh1 put it plainly: the numbers were so bad they look bearish and are not, because now the Fed cannot hike.

Underneath, the warning lights are all on at once.

PositioningReading
VIXunder 15, lowest since January 13
S&P volatility dispersionhighest since the dot-com bubble
High-yield credit spreads16-month highs
Bank of Americainvestors are "too bullish"

Value is quietly winning the summer, with 90 percent of value managers beating their benchmark in June and 94 percent in July.

The scoreboard.

  • Miss, and wrong by one session. I went 55/45 on Tuesday that SpaceX trades higher on Thursday. It did not, then rose 10 to 15 percent on Friday. The mechanics were right and the date was wrong, and a dated call that needs an extra day is a losing call.
  • Working. My 60/40 that memory multiples expand before they compress. UBS models over $400 billion of Micron free cash flow through 2028, with $MU 30 percent off its high at under 6 times forward earnings.
  • Standing, and now cheap. The 60/40 that AppLovin is higher in three months, made the day it fell a fifth.
  • Due Wednesday. $NBIS reports into Burry's fresh short, with $RKLB, $ASTS, $SMCI and $CRWV behind it.

1. The unlock was the bottom, not the top. Per the People to follow list, $SPCX ran from roughly $110 to above $128 and finished the week back above Meta's market capitalisation, against a 34 percent short float. Per the Stocks list, TicTocTick had it "up 15%. Best performer... At $108. Now $132." LuxAlgo wrote the epitaph: "New rule: $SPCX unlocks are bullish."

The setup was the reason. Per the Market list, on unlock day the stock traded 1.7 million option contracts, second only to Nvidia, and closed strong rather than breaking. Everyone was positioned for a flood the buyers absorbed.

Now the part nobody priced. Per Diet TBPN, bankers estimate at least 1,000 special purpose vehicles hold SpaceX stock. One has gone badly wrong. Late Stage Management told an investor it sold his SpaceX exposure in 2024 at roughly $105 a share, before a five-for-one split, while his portal and his 2025 tax document still showed 2,500 shares. He put in $17,250, believes the stake was worth over $300,000 at the June IPO, has filed an SEC complaint, and thinks more than 100 others are in the same position. Three sales executives connected to the firm pleaded guilty in February and March inside a $528 million scheme that hid markups of 10 to 100 percent.

Tranches of about 7 percent follow on August 21 and September 10. The float is the story now, and the SPV layer underneath it is unmapped.

2. Damodaran's number is $200 billion against $11 billion, and he will not say which side is wrong. Per Prof G Markets, Aswath Damodaran framed the trade in one line: "Everyone is spending between 150 to 200 billion in capex, but Apple is at 11 billion." One of those strategies is wrong and he calls it a case study ten years out.

The cash flows already show the strain. Meta's free cash flow fell 91 percent. Amazon's and Alphabet's went negative.

Then the accounting. 85 percent of Amazon's net income was unrealised paper gains on its Anthropic and OpenAI stakes. For Alphabet, counting SpaceX and Anthropic, it was 87 percent. Multiples fell below 20 times earnings purely because earnings exploded on marks. His instruction: do not trust net income, climb the income statement, look at operating margins.

The circularity is sourced. Barclays puts 73 percent of Amazon's AI revenue on OpenAI and Anthropic, Wells Fargo 74 percent of Microsoft's, against his own rule that the architecture should be 10 to 20 percent of revenue rather than 80.

Two things to watch. Chinese models went from 8 percent of tokens consumed in January 2025 to above 50 percent now. That is margin compression arriving. And Damodaran names the tell nobody has seen: there has still been no major AI capex write-off. Michael Burry is not waiting. Per the Market list, he shorted $NBIS at $211.77 and $ORCL at $144.63: "The fish have gorged themselves on off-balance sheet liabilities. Backstops. Uncommenced leases. Purchase commitments. The fish have gotten very fat, very large, easy to shoot."

3. Rocket Lab paid $8 billion for Iridium and turned itself into a different company. Per Chip Stock Investor, $RKLB is acquiring $IRDM for $8 billion in stock and cash, taking on Iridium's $1.8 billion of debt and flipping itself from net cash to net debt.

The combination is the argument.

Trailing twelve monthsIridiumRocket LabCombined
Revenue$884 millionthe balance, roughly $700 millionabout $1.6 billion
Free cash flowplus $288 millionminus $316 millionminus $28 million
GAAP EBITDAplus $423 millionminus $173 millionplus $250 million

That is a launch company buying its way to positive EBITDA and near-breakeven cash, funded with leverage. Iridium brings 66 satellites in low earth orbit and L-band spectrum that ships direct-to-device this year on a software update alone.

The price is the problem. At roughly $50 billion of enterprise value on $250 million of EBITDA, the reverse discounted cash flow needs 35 percent annual EBITDA growth for ten years to reach about $5 billion by the mid 2030s. SpaceX did just over $4 billion of EBITDA in 2025. Their verdict is the right one: genius on strategy, expensive on price, wait for a better entry. The whole space complex ran today ($RKLB up 7.31 percent, $LUNR 5.96, $PL 5.52, $ASTS 3.49), so no discount is on offer yet.

4. Siemens Energy sells the AI trade without the AI multiple, and nobody noticed. The cleanest non-AI quarter of the week came from a European power-equipment maker, and the case for it is laid out on Reddit rather than by a broker. Revenue hit a record €11.4 billion, profit before special items more than tripled to over €1.6 billion at a 14.2 percent margin, and the backlog reached a record €162 billion with €7.2 billion of free cash flow booked year to date.

The line that matters: grid technologies grew nearly 29 percent. That is the data-centre power bottleneck showing up as revenue in a company nobody calls an AI stock. Siemens Gamesa turned a €75 million profit, its first since 2022.

The stock did not move on the print, blamed on a seasonally softer fourth quarter and weaker wind orders. Backlog projects carry higher margins than the crisis-era contracts rolling off, locking in expansion for two to three years, and a rebranding to Omterra is the stated unlock. I am 60/40 that this rerates before the US grid names do, because it is priced as European industrial rather than as picks and shovels.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $SPCX. Absorbed 140 percent of its float and rose 15 percent. The next tranches land August 21 and September 10, and the unmapped risk is the roughly 1,000 SPVs holding stock, one of them already carrying an SEC complaint and three guilty pleas.
  • $RKLB. An $8 billion deal that buys positive EBITDA and costs the balance sheet its net cash. Reports next week, and the reverse DCF needs 35 percent compound EBITDA growth for a decade to justify today's price.
  • $PLTR. Best day in company history, up about 30 percent on revenue +93 percent to $1.94 billion and US commercial +149 percent. Per Milk Road, revenue growth plus operating margin now sums to 155 and net dollar retention is 157 percent, on a multiple that fell from 300 times earnings to 125. Karp's $15 to $18 billion free cash flow guide two years out is the only number that matters, because everything above it is multiple.
  • $MU. Under 6 times forward earnings and 30 percent off its high, with UBS modelling over $400 billion of free cash flow through 2028 and 29 of 30 analysts at buy on a $1,560 average target. It cannot repurchase shares until December 9 under a CHIPS Act condition, so the buyback bid is a fourth-quarter event.
  • $FIGR. Per Milk Road, second on VanEck's Rule of 140 at 150.8 behind Palantir's 154.5, at roughly 30 times forward against Palantir's 85, having originated about $29 billion of home equity lending on its own chain. Reports August 13 with volume pre-announced, so margins and guidance are the open variables.
  • $GLD. Gold cleared $4,400 and rose 8.1 percent in 72 hours while the S&P made a record. Per Stocks with Josh, the levels are a pullback buy at 384 with resistance at 398 and 406. The last time it coiled this tightly was August 2025, ahead of a 60 percent move.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] CLARITY died and Bitcoin reclaimed $65,000 the same afternoon
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The Senate punted the vote to September, Kalshi's odds of it becoming law this year hit an all-time low of 16 percent, and BlackRock bought 9,269 coins over four straight days anyway.
item.content:encoded:
The Senate punted the vote to September, Kalshi's odds of it becoming law this year hit an all-time low of 16 percent, and BlackRock bought 9,269 coins over four straight days anyway.

Yesterday a hundred million dollars walked out of self-custody wallets and Bitcoin did not move. Today the bill this sector spent a year lobbying for died, and Bitcoin went up. Two days, one answer.

Market context. Per the Kalshi list, Bitcoin reclaimed $65,000 on the day the CLARITY vote slipped, roughly half its October high. Per the Crypto list, the bid behind it is institutional and it is not subtle: BlackRock logged four consecutive days of net inflows totalling 9,269 Bitcoin, about $604 million, with Morgan Stanley buying three days running and Bhutan selling $27 million into it.

The rest of the tape is flat to soft. Per Blockworks, ETF flows overall are still anemic, and the 60-day correlation between Bitcoin and Ether ETF flows has climbed to plus 0.67, so the two move as one allocation now rather than two decisions. Miners are distributing, MARA and Riot sending a combined 581 coins to NYDIG, and the proxies split on earnings rather than beta, Galaxy up 3.6 percent and Circle up 3.1 percent against an index down 1.1.

The scoreboard.

  • Working, and the delay is the proof. On Thursday I went 65/35 that CLARITY's failure was already priced. The Senate punted it, Kalshi's odds of passage this year hit 16 percent, an all-time low, and Bitcoin closed higher on the news.
  • Strengthened. My 60/40 that Bitcoin sees $58,000 before $75,000. Benjamin Cowen's cycle arithmetic now puts us three quarters through the bear with the low still ahead.
  • Due today, and it did not clear. ERCOT's Batch Zero study round stayed suspended under the Texas audit, so Galaxy's approved megawatts keep their scarcity value and its uncontracted pipeline keeps waiting.
  • Standing. The 60/40 that Galaxy lands a Helios tenant before the audit clears. Still no announcement.

1. The catalyst everyone was hedging died, and the hedge paid nothing. Macro has the vote math tonight: cloture never filed, Senate back September 14. What matters here is the price reaction, and there was not one. Traders had spent the week positioning for the opposite. Per Trader Mayne, CryptoFace was building a straddle into the vote on the view that a failure delivers "that one leg down." It did not arrive.

The reason is that the market had already marked the bill down to nothing. Michael Saylor's line, carried on the Kalshi list, is the framing that fits: "Bitcoin doesn't need CLARITY. America needs clarity." BitQua put the trader's version of it better: "The most bullish outcome for bitcoin is not necessarily a particular answer, it's getting an answer. Just, yes or no." A punt is the one outcome that resolves nothing, and Bitcoin rose anyway.

I am holding 65/35 and adding a leg: the unpriced risk sits in the alt market rather than in Bitcoin, because Coinbase has already said it keeps expanding offshore if the bill fails. Haseeb Qureshi, on the Crypto list, is the counterweight, noting Kalshi still prices better than 30 percent for next year and above 50 percent by 2028. Late is not dead.

2. Cowen has us on day 1,354 of a cycle that bottoms around day 1,435. Per Benjamin Cowen, the arithmetic is unusually clean.

Cycle positionReading
Days since the last low1,354, against bottoms at 1,432 and 1,436
Days since the peak304, against an average bear bottom on day 406
Moving averageslost the 50-week, lost the 100-week, now at the 200-week
His windowlate September to mid December, base case October

His verdict on whether the low is in: "Doubtful that it started yet, we could still go a little bit lower." He has been buying below 60,000 and says he got wrecked six months after doing the same in 2018 and 2022, and did not care six months after that.

Trader Mayne lands in the same place from a different angle, putting the bottoming range at 40,000 to 60,000 with a weekly market structure break as the trigger rather than a price. Two independent frameworks, no shared method, same fourth-quarter answer. This is the strongest support my 60/40 has had.

3. Ethereum won the institutions and the token collects nothing. Per the Milk Road Show with the three founders of Ethereum Institutional, the pipe is real. BlackRock tokenised two funds on Ethereum this week and announced twelve more products days later. JP Morgan's Kinexys runs roughly $5 billion a day, and its JLTXX collateral fund sits on public Ethereum approaching $1 billion. Ethereum holds 52.2 percent of tokenised real-world asset market capitalisation and 69.4 percent of euro stablecoin supply.

Now the part that decides whether any of it is investable. Robinhood's chain is an Ethereum layer two that brought roughly 30 million users, and the fees reaching Ethereum from it are "a couple of thousand dollars right now." Joe Lubin's stated position is growth over rent extraction. That is a defensible strategy for the network and a terrible one for the asset.

Vitalik's answer is the Lean Ethereum roadmap, per Lark Davis: recursive proofs so a validator runs on a phone, post-quantum cryptography by 2028 or 2029, and a state redesign targeting a tenfold fee reduction. Glamsterdam lands in the third quarter.

So the desks split. Per the Crypto list, Arthur Hayes wants $5,000 Ether by year end. CryptoKaleo sees "one last leg down." I am 60/40 with Kaleo into the fourth quarter, because a ten times fee cut is a bear case for accrual before it is a bull case for adoption.

4. Nobody has bought a tokenised asset except crypto itself. The most damning number of the week came out of an Arrakis study carried by Blockworks. Across $91.3 billion of on-chain acquisitions of ten tokenised dollar-yield products, two thirds came from protocol and DAO treasuries, and not one dollar traced to a traditional bank, pension fund or asset manager. Wallets above $1 million were 4 percent of buyers and 93 percent of the capital.

Set that against the institutional pipe above and the picture resolves. The plumbing is being built by BlackRock and JP Morgan. The volume through it is crypto recycling its own treasury cash.

Retail rotated rather than left. July gacha spend fell to $290.3 million from June's record $354.8 million while Pump.fun's daily average rose 21 percent.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. Reclaimed $65,000 on a dead legislative catalyst, with $604 million of BlackRock buying behind it over four sessions. Cowen and Mayne independently put the low in the fourth quarter, so treat strength as a bear-market rally until a weekly structure break says otherwise.
  • $ETH. The institutional adoption is genuine and the fee accrual is not. Glamsterdam in the third quarter cuts fees another order of magnitude. Hayes wants $5,000 and Kaleo wants one more flush, and the roadmap argues for Kaleo first.
  • $HOOD. Event contracts brought in $156 million against $129 million from equities and $100 million from crypto, up more than tenfold on 13.6 billion contracts, while crypto revenue fell 38 percent and app volume dropped 35 percent. The prediction market is the business now and the coins are the loss leader.
  • $GLXY. Up 3.6 percent on the quarter while the sector fell, still with no Helios tenant and ERCOT's Batch Zero round frozen. Every week the queue stays shut, its approved megawatts get scarcer and its uncontracted pipeline gets cheaper.
  • $MSTR. Built an all-time-high dollar reserve covering 2.3 years of dividends and interest, and Saylor is marketing STRC's 11.5 percent tax-deferred yield as the equivalent of an 18 percent bank account for a Miami taxpayer. The yield pitch is what replaces the coin-buying story.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] Payrolls lost 23,000 jobs and the September hike died in a morning
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: May and June were revised down a combined 103,000, Kalshi's hike odds fell from 60 percent to 30, and the S&P printed a record high on the news.
item.content:encoded:
May and June were revised down a combined 103,000, Kalshi's hike odds fell from 60 percent to 30, and the S&P printed a record high on the news.

Yesterday I reversed and said the Fed leans toward hiking in September. This morning's print took eighteen hours to make that look silly.

Market context. Per the Polymarket list, July nonfarm payrolls shed 23,000 jobs against expectations for an 80,000 gain, and May and June were revised down by a combined 103,000. The revisions are the worse half.

Where the rate path wentBeforeAfter
Kalshi, a hike this year60 percent30 percent, then 50 by the afternoon
Kalshi, Fed holds in Septembera 25bp hike was favourite67 percent, settling at 65
CME, a September hike54 percent on Thursdaythe print reversed it

Per the Kalshi list, unemployment hit a one-year low even as the payroll line went negative, and traders had been forecasting 4.2 percent. The S&P printed a new all-time high of 7,740 ninety minutes after the number. Gold futures went the other way and cleared $4,400, up 8.1 percent in 72 hours. CPI on August 12 is still the print Warsh named.

The scoreboard.

  • Wrong inside eighteen hours, and I am reverting. Yesterday I moved to 45/55 against a September hold on the strength of Warsh, Cook and Kashkari all turning hawkish in two days. A negative payroll print outranks three speeches. Back to 65/35 for a hold, above where I started.
  • Confirmed, and by the plumbing itself. I said Washington was defending the yen with euros. Joseph Wang, on the Financial Markets list: "Treasury has now spent all the ammo in their Exchange Stabilization Fund. They sold Euros to buy Yen because that's all they have in the ESF."
  • Resolved. Payrolls were the catalyst I flagged for today. Kathy Lien's "stronger payrolls, but probably not a blowout" missed by 103,000.
  • Due Wednesday. CPI, which now has to do all the work.

1. The revisions matter more than the headline, and the unemployment rate is lying. A single negative month is noise. A negative month plus 103,000 taken off the two before it is a trend being discovered late. That is the shape of a labour market that was already softer than the data said while the Fed was arguing about tightening into it.

The unemployment rate falling to a one-year low in the same release looks like a contradiction and is not. It is what happens when people leave the labour force rather than lose jobs. Per the Financial Markets list, the St Louis Fed flagged prime-age participation as the line to read in this exact report, noting more than half of the recent decline came from a January population correction and from ageing rather than from workers quitting.

June JOLTS pointed the same way before anyone was watching: openings down 178,000 to 7.359 million against 7.454 million expected, with the openings-to-unemployed ratio at 1.04.

So the hawkish case did not lose an argument. It lost its premise.

2. The Exchange Stabilization Fund is empty, and that closes the yen story. Joseph Wang's line above is the confirmation the euro-intervention story needed, and it reframes the whole thing. This was never a clever cross-currency strategy. Treasury sold euros because euros were what remained in the account.

An empty stabilisation fund means the next yen defence needs either the Bank of Japan raising rates or Japan selling reserves. Japan holds over a trillion dollars of Treasuries. Per the Crypto list, the ten-year sat at 4.73 percent with Fidelity's Jurrien Timmer calling anything above 4.5 percent the danger zone, and the warning attached is the one that matters: the Fed can cut and long yields can still rise.

Today's print pushes that day further out. It does not cancel it.

3. Bessent says he has Iran by the throat and the strait opens within days. Per the Polymarket list, the Treasury Secretary put a clock on it: "We have them by the throat, and they've got 150 to 180% food inflation, not able to pay the troops. I think shortly, maybe even today, tomorrow, we are going to see an agreement, a 30- to 60-day ceasefire, and the Strait will be open."

The enforcement numbers behind that leverage are real. Per the August 6 Polymarket list, CENTCOM has redirected 49 commercial vessels, disabled two and boarded two, and US imports of Saudi crude fell to zero in July, the first full month since 1985. Polymarket prices the blockade being lifted this month at 69 percent.

Tehran is not behaving like a government about to sign. An Iranian lawmaker has a preliminary bill barring US, Israeli and other hostile vessels from the strait with fines up to 20 percent of cargo value, and Trump's own read was "it's sort of open right now" with the caveat that "they can always shoot something."

Gold going up 8.1 percent in three days while a ceasefire is being announced tells you which one the money believes. I am 60/40 that a ceasefire is announced inside two weeks and under 50/50 that shipping volumes recover inside a month.

4. CLARITY is a September problem, and nobody filed the paperwork in time. Per the Financial Markets list, the Senate pushed the vote past summer recess. The mechanism was the one I named on Thursday: cloture was never filed. Eleanor Terrett had it live at the deadline, reporting worry on both sides that a failed cloture vote would bring the whole year-long effort down, and that if it was not filed that night it would not happen.

Elizabeth Warren supplied the durable objection, saying she supports crypto legislation but not this one, "written by the crypto industry to protect and advance the crypto industry." Thune ran out of floor time. Schumer wanted more talks.

Kalshi's odds it becomes law this year hit 16 percent, an all-time low. My 80/20 that it does not pass in 2026 is intact and I am raising it to 85/15, because the September calendar is already spoken for. The Senate comes back on the 14th with a government to fund and a Fed meeting two days later. Haseeb Qureshi is the useful counterweight, pointing out Kalshi still prices 30 percent plus for next year and above 50 percent by 2028. This bill is late, not dead, and the difference matters for anyone sizing a position on it.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] SpaceX's tradable float tripled today, and AppLovin grew 53 percent and lost a fifth
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Up to 911.5 million shares came free at once, more than 140 percent of the public float, while the S&P printed another record high on the largest option-call volume ever recorded.
item.content:encoded:
Up to 911.5 million shares came free at once, more than 140 percent of the public float, while the S&P printed another record high on the largest option-call volume ever recorded.

Yesterday AMD beat and fell ten percent. Today AppLovin grew revenue 53 percent at an 84 percent margin and fell twenty. Two sessions, one verdict: beating stopped being the bar.

Market context. The index does not know any of that. Per the Kalshi list, the S&P printed a new all-time high at 7,730 today, its twenty-fifth record of the year, and Kalshi puts 8,000 before year end at 70 percent. Tom Lee wants 7,900 to 8,000 this month, UBS 8,100 by December.

How it got there is the part to hold onto. Per the Financial Markets list, the Kobeissi Letter counted a record 4.0 million S&P call contracts on Tuesday, against a 700,000 daily average in 2020 and 2021. The put-to-call skew posted its largest two-day decline since 2017. Mr Derivatives supplied the necessary commentary: "Wowzers! What can possssssibly go wrong here?!"

Leadership underneath is thin. $GOOGL fell about 3.5 percent on the DeepMind reshuffle, and per Stocks with Josh the level that matters is $SPY 686, which has held all week. A loss of it opens 629.

The scoreboard.

  • Miss, cleanly. On Tuesday I went 55/45 that SpaceX trades higher today than it closed that night. It is down double digits into the unlock. I said I was trading the mechanics, and the mechanics are what beat me.
  • Resolved on the date. The August 6 lockup I have been flagging since July 16 arrived as advertised: 911.5 million shares, more than 140 percent of the public float.
  • Resolved, and the quarter was not the problem. AppLovin reported August 5 as the scorecard I said it would be. Revenue grew 53 percent and the stock lost a fifth.
  • Standing. My 60/40 that AMD trades above yesterday's after-hours level in a month. It sits at $472, with Jose Najarro raising his target to $750 on $25 of EPS at 30 times forward, and Burry short the complex.

1. SpaceX's float went from 5 percent to 20 percent in one morning. Per the Financial Markets list, over $100 billion of $SPCX shares unlocked today. Per the People to follow list, here is the rest of the queue.

$SPCX unlock scheduleShare of supply
August 6, from a 5 percent IPO floatabout 7 percent, taking tradable to 20 percent
August 21 through December 9about 29 percent more, reaching 40 percent
June 2027Musk eligible, about 46 percent

The print underneath was good and nobody cared. Per Ticker Symbol YOU, revenue was $7.81 billion, up 92 percent, against a $6.93 billion estimate, with EPS of $0.09 against an expected 26-cent loss. Then capex landed just under $18.5 billion, 39 percent above expectations, or $2.35 spent per dollar of revenue, with no 2027 guidance at all.

The stock closed at its lowest price in history yesterday, having shed roughly $1.6 trillion of market value since June's high, per Barchart on the Financial Markets list. Morgan Stanley still carries a $300 target.

The honest comparable is Meta in 2012, down about 50 percent at the 91-day lockup and still down 36 percent a year later. Own it as a compute business with a supply problem that runs four more months.

2. AppLovin grew 53 percent, printed an 84 percent margin, and lost a fifth of its value. Per Daniel Koss on the Stocks list, the quarter was $1.92 billion of revenue, up 53 percent, with $1.61 billion of adjusted EBITDA at an 84 percent margin, and the stock fell 19 percent before the bell.

What broke is smaller and more specific. Per VanquishTrader on the People to follow list, free cash flow conversion fell to 54 percent, buybacks were nearly halved, and management anchored long-term growth closer to 30 percent rather than the 50s. UBS blames a delayed ad-model upgrade and a slow nonendemic ramp, and kept a Buy.

The sell side did not.

$APP price targetFromTo
Piper Sandler, to Neutral$665$385
Scotiabank$775$515
Jefferies, RBC and BTIG$640 to $700$550 to $575

At 24 times forward earnings on a 0.5 PEG, this is a company repriced for decelerating rather than for missing, and the SEC overhang came off in the same quarter. I am 60/40 that $APP is higher in three months.

3. Memory got taken apart at 4am and bought back at the open. Per the Stocks list, $MU fell 29 percent in July, its worst month since June 2005, after a 189 percent year, and sits under $900 with Korea down another 5 percent overnight. Jefferies cut $SNDK from $3,000 to $1,750, a 42 percent haircut, with Citi to $2,100 and Mizuho to $1,900. RBC went the other way, up to $1,300.

Then the tape reversed it. Per ripster47 on the Financial Markets list, $SNDK, $WDC and $MU were all bought at the open.

The reason to fade the panic is contractual. Per Milk Road AI, Bernstein models roughly 35 percent of all memory bits shipped between 2027 and 2029 as locked into take-or-pay contracts (the buyer pays whether or not it takes delivery) at a floor of $0.26 per gigabyte against a $0.29 spot. Micron has taken $22 billion of customer prepayments for chips it has not made across 16 agreements, and its last quarter was $41.6 billion at an 81.2 percent operating margin.

Spot can crack. A take-or-pay floor on a third of three years of supply cannot crack the same way, and I am holding 60/40 that multiples expand before they compress. Dylan Patel, on the Hermes list, explains the premium better than any model: Micron trades above SK Hynix because "corporate governance exists."

4. Eli Lilly put up $23 billion and is losing the pill race it invented. Per Milk Road, $LLY reported $23 billion of revenue against $20.7 billion expected, up 48 percent year over year, with Mounjaro and the GLP-1 franchise at $9.9 billion in the quarter. Jefferies took its target to $1,440, Morgan Stanley to $1,419 and Leerink to $1,309.

The oral is where the fight is. Novo Nordisk sold roughly $495 million of its pill in the quarter against Lilly's $90 million, a five-to-one drubbing in the format that decides the next decade of this market. Lilly's answer is that prescriptions doubled in the last week of July.

That is one week of scripts against a quarter of sales, and I am taking it anyway at 60/40. Injectables were a manufacturing race and Lilly won it. Pills are a distribution race, and a company printing $23 billion a quarter can buy distribution.

5. Burry is short with entry prices, and Eisman will not follow him. Per the Financial Markets list, Michael Burry published his book with the levels attached: short $NVDA at $198, $MU at $1,051, $AMAT at $729, $TSLA at $416, $SOXX at $642 and $PLTR at $161, verdict "WE ARE NEAR A MAJOR TOP AND POSSIBLY A 1987-TYPE FALL." Per NoLimitGains on the Stocks list, the S&P is up more than 100 percent since he last told people to sell, in January 2023.

Steve Eisman's refusal is the more useful position. Per Prof G Markets, Eisman says "he doesn't have a data point that you and I don't have," and names his trigger precisely: "I need a price war in the LLM world." Until inference pricing collapses, the capex holds.

What sits against him is the customer base. Bloomberg puts 70 percent of Microsoft's AI revenue on OpenAI, Barclays 75 percent of Amazon's on OpenAI and Anthropic, UBS 30 percent of Google Cloud on the same pair. OpenAI lost $21 billion last year, Anthropic roughly $11 billion. Meta meanwhile grew revenue 28 percent against 55 percent expense growth and produced $785 million of free cash flow.

I am 60/40 with Eisman, and the 40 is that concentration number. A price war is not the only way this breaks. One of two customers slowing its orders does it.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $SPCX. Float tripled today and reaches 40 percent by December 9. The business beat by a billion and guided to $100 billion of run-rate revenue exiting 2026. Every buyer until Christmas fights a published supply schedule, so let the calendar work.
  • $APP. A 53 percent grower at 24 times forward with an 84 percent EBITDA margin, sold off because management stopped promising the 50s. Free cash flow conversion at 54 percent decides whether the deceleration is mix or model.
  • $LLY. $23 billion and 48 percent growth, and the next move is about a pill it sells at a fifth of Novo's rate. Three targets went up this week. September script data settles it.
  • $SNDK. Jefferies cut it 42 percent and RBC raised it inside the same 24 hours, and it bought back its premarket lows. Still the cleanest live read on whether NAND pricing is rolling over.
  • $CCJ. Bank of America raised its 2027 uranium forecast to $130 a pound, roughly 52 percent above spot, on utility contract coverage falling to 48 percent from 56. Target trimmed to $133, Buy kept. Oklo reaching first criticality at its Groves Test Reactor the same week is the demand side showing up.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] $100 million walked out of Coldcard wallets and Bitcoin moved less than one percent
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: A random-number bug from 2021 left older seeds guessable, more than 5,000 holders lost coins, and the only thing in crypto that reacted was Robinhood's memecoin chain.
item.content:encoded:
A random-number bug from 2021 left older seeds guessable, more than 5,000 holders lost coins, and the only thing in crypto that reacted was Robinhood's memecoin chain.

Yesterday Galaxy proved the miners had stopped being a Bitcoin trade. Today a hundred million dollars walked out of self-custody wallets and the price barely registered it. Nothing moves this asset anymore, and that is the read.

Market context. Per Milk Road, Bitcoin topped at $126,198 last October and sits roughly 49 percent below it this afternoon. Per VirtualBacon, it is up 3.6 percent over four days and still in a daily downtrend that began in May, with resistance at 66.7K and a break opening 76K. It sits on its 200-week average, the level that marked every prior cycle floor.

Benjamin Cowen's framing on NFA Live is the one to carry: Bitcoin sits at the same valuation against the S&P 500 as five to six years ago, while the S&P makes new highs. Per Blockworks, ETF net flows are anemic in both directions and Glassnode has options priced for no move. Miners were the worst asset on the board at minus 6.2 percent, with Cipher and Hut 8 both missing.

The scoreboard.

  • Hit, four days early. On July 11 I said Robinhood Chain had to hold $400 million a day of DEX volume by August 10 or the migration was churn. Seven-day volume is near $3 billion, roughly $428 million a day. It cleared.
  • Working. My 60/40 that Bitcoin sees $58,000 before $75,000. Three independent clocks now point at a low between October and December, and none point up first.
  • Called it, and it cost 13 percent. I said yesterday Galaxy's 830 approved megawatts needed a tenant within days. Novogratz had promised one by the end of summer and did not deliver.
  • Due tomorrow. ERCOT's next Batch Zero round, which the Texas audit suspended.

1. The Coldcard bug was born in 2021, and the coins left this week. Per Swan, a 2021 software integration made Coldcard seed generation fall through to a MicroPython pseudo-random number generator instead of the hardware entropy source it was meant to use. Coinkite puts affected MK2 and MK3 seeds at roughly 40 bits of effective search space, with MK4, MK5 and Q near 72 bits. The design target was 128.

Forty bits is not a lock somebody picked. It is a lock with a thousand keys.

Per the People to follow list, one researcher mapped 4,312 drained addresses with the exact block for each. Per Anthony Pompliano's guests, the total is more than 5,000 people and over $100 million, concentrated among the holders least likely to ever use a custodian. Bitcoin did not move more than about one percent on it.

The position is not a price call. Tilman Holloway expects ETF inflows to tick up three, six and nine months out as burned self-custody holders move to a custodian, against Coinbase and BitGo carrying roughly $5 million of insurance. The remedy circulating on Spaces is generating your own entropy with 100 dice rolls. That tells you how this ends.

The most damning line came from calle on the Crypto list: "not a single vulnerability was found by a US frontier model. Instead, we're spending $10k a day on open weights models like Kimi K3 and Qwen 3.8 to find vulnerabilities in Bitcoin infrastructure."

2. CLARITY's death is a buy-the-news event, and I am taking the unpopular side. Macro has the vote math tonight: 60 needed, 53 held, cloture filed on a different motion. Here it is a straight disagreement between desks. Per VirtualBacon, Bernstein says failure could trigger the final leg down in crypto valuations and JPMorgan calls it another headwind. Bitwise's Matt Hougan says the SEC and CFTC can supply the same path by rule rather than law. Altcoin Daily puts a failure at Bitcoin "maybe into the 50s, maybe into 48."

James Seyffart's point decides it. Traditional finance treats CLARITY as a catalyst for Bitcoin, not only for alts, so the disappointment is broad rather than confined to tokens that need a legal wrapper.

I am 65/35 that it is already priced. Polymarket went from 50 to 70 percent in January to 15 percent now, and an asset that ignored a $100 million theft is not holding a legislative premium. Hougan is the reason I lean that way. A rulemaking path does not need 60 votes.

3. Galaxy's missing tenant cost it 13 percent, and the frozen queue is why waiting is correct. Per Milk Road, $GLXY fell 13 percent to $19 on a $7.5 billion market cap, and none of it was the numbers. Helios phase one, 200 megawatts leased to CoreWeave for 15 years, is billing toward roughly $80 million a quarter.

Per m0xt on the Stocks list, the pipeline is 5.7 gigawatts with 4.3 contracted, contractable or Batch Zero eligible, and the Texas audit ordered August 3 suspended the next Batch Zero round, due tomorrow. Merlin's first phase is 74 megawatts, one under the 75 megawatt threshold that would have caught it. Caspian at 700 and Selene at 900 are grandfathered.

So the moat held and the announcement did not. I am 60/40 the tenant lands before the audit clears, because a landlord with grandfathered megawatts inside a frozen queue has the only product anyone can plug in.

4. The only live bid in crypto is on Robinhood's chain, and none of it is Bitcoin. Per 0xSammy, Robinhood Chain carries $411 million of DeFi value, $558 million of stablecoins, over $1 billion bridged and nearly $3 billion of seven-day DEX volume, with perpetual futures up 130 percent.

The economics are the interesting part. Apps on the chain took $1.6 million of gross fees in 24 hours and the chain kept $50 thousand. Fat apps, thin chain, no token to dilute. Pons alone runs 64 percent of launchpad volume on a $20 million market cap, and Uniswap has now deployed pools.trade on the same chain to take it.

The other half of the flow is real-world assets, compounding while everything crypto-native shrinks.

On-chainA year agoNow
RWA deposits$2.3 billion$7.4 billion
RWA perpetual notional, July$1.3 billion$150 billion
Tokenized spot volume, monthly$3.4 billion$14 billion

Crypto-native spot DEX volume fell about 70 percent over the same stretch. That is where the money went. Not out of the sector, sideways within it.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. Roughly 49 percent below October's $126,198 and resting on the 200-week average, with 66.7K the line that matters. Three bottom clocks (Cowen's capitulation event, the 13-month underwater cohort, Altcoin Daily's 200-week analogue) all land in the fourth quarter, none starting with a rally.
  • $GLXY. Down 13 percent for the absence of an announcement rather than a number, while its 830 approved megawatts got scarcer. Tomorrow's suspended Batch Zero round is the next marker.
  • $HOOD. Its chain does $3 billion a week in DEX volume and keeps almost none of the fees. That is deliberate: the chain is the funnel, the brokerage is the business.
  • $MSTR. Sold 1,638 coins for roughly $105 million, raised $1 billion off the common at about one times net asset value, and spent $1.3 billion retiring converts. Per Apyx's Parker White, the dividend reserve went from six months back to about 18 and nothing puts until September 2027. The deleveraging is working.
  • $COIN. The legislative catalyst is priced at 20 percent for the year and industry volumes fell double digits last quarter. Jack Mallers frames the split honestly: Coinbase cares more about its own chain and alts than about Bitcoin. That is the bull case now, because the chains have the volume.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] Warsh opened the door to a September hike, and Trump has been calling him
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The Chair says he will raise if inflation runs hot, Kalshi prices a hike this year at 65 percent, and Treasury needs $739 billion of fresh borrowing in the same quarter.
item.content:encoded:
The Chair says he will raise if inflation runs hot, Kalshi prices a hike this year at 65 percent, and Treasury needs $739 billion of fresh borrowing in the same quarter.

Yesterday the hawk was a regional president nobody has to obey. Today it is the Chair, and the man who appointed him has been on the phone since May.

Market context. Per the Market list, the Financial Times reports Kevin Warsh is prepared to raise rates in September if inflation prints run hot and markets price in higher borrowing costs. The data underneath him came in firm.

Today's printsReading
Initial jobless claims199,000 against 204,000 expected
Continuing claimsup 24,000 to 1,801,000
Q2 productivity, preliminaryup 1.4 percent against 0.6 expected
Kalshi, a hike at some point this year65 percent

The dollar has not caught up to any of it. MUFG has the dollar index near a seven-week low and still undervalued against eight of the nine other G10 currencies, and Brent came back under $80. Payrolls land tomorrow. CPI on August 12 is the print Warsh named.

The scoreboard.

  • Wrong, and I am reversing it rather than defending it. Yesterday I went 55/45 that September is a hold. The Chair, Governor Lisa Cook and Neel Kashkari all turned hawkish inside 48 hours. I am now 45/55 against a hold.
  • Right, and nearly settled. On Monday I went 85/15 that no CLARITY floor vote happens before the recess. Kalshi prices that at 3 percent.
  • Working, and not the way the tape reads it. My 70/30 on a joint Iran-Oman announcement runs to August 12, and both governments are preparing to designate the strait a transit corridor. Ryan Petersen of Flexport counts one or two transits a day against almost 100 at the peak, at 10 to 15 percent war-risk insurance. The paper is nearly signed and the water is empty.
  • Due tomorrow. Payrolls, which decides whether Warsh's condition is met.

1. Warsh's condition has two legs, and the second one is a mirror. Per the Market list, people close to Warsh say he has acknowledged "early communication mistakes that blurred his message on price stability and Fed reform."

He named two triggers. Hot inflation prints, and markets pricing in higher borrowing costs. The second is the market itself, so a market that prices a hike is helping satisfy the condition for one.

The rest of the committee arrived in the same week. Per the Kalshi list, Governor Lisa Cook said she is ready to raise if inflation stays high and Kashkari said it is "slowly" time to raise. Invesco is the lone dissent that matters, and it argues about whether policy is already restrictive rather than about direction.

Then the part that is not economics. Per the Financial Markets list, the Wall Street Journal reports Trump held multiple undisclosed calls with Warsh, and Bloomberg dates them to May. A Chair turning hawkish while taking private calls from a President who wants cheap money is the least comfortable sequence available, and it argues the hawkishness is real.

2. Treasury needs $739 billion this quarter and the interest line already passed defense. Per ClearValue Tax, the August 3 Treasury statement guides to $739 billion of privately held net marketable borrowing for July through September, meaning debt sold to real buyers rather than shuffled between government accounts. That is $68 billion above the May estimate on less cash flow than projected. October through December is guided at $628 billion, $1.36 trillion across the back half.

The stock and its costFigure
Total debt$39.7 trillion
Interest expense through June$827 billion, against $749 billion a year earlier
Average rate on the debt3.36 percent in FY2025, about 3.42 percent now
Maturing inside twelve months33 percent
